Uniform Title: *Matatrayaikyaprakāśikā* Author: Aiyaṇācārya Manuscript: IFP Transcript T0582
Description: IFP Transcript 582, copied from a manuscript (Tr. 275, 38-a-21) belonging to the Adyar Library, Madras.
*The Revelation of the Unity of the Three Views* by Aiyaṇācārya. This treatise proposes that the three views—namely, Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, and the non-dualist Vedānta of the Upaniṣads—are one.
Essentially, they teach the same non-dual reality.

Śrīḥ!
The Elucidation of the Unity of the Three Systems.
Composed by Ācārya Aiyaṇa.
May there be no obstacles.
I salute the beloved of Jānakī, the beloved of the cowherd women,
the bestower of pure intelligence, and the one who has expanded the multitude of the Vedas.
I bow to the Lord of Veṅkaṭa, the sun that dispels the darkness of ignorance, the piercer of the chest of the Daityas, and the bestower of all desired objects.
I bow to the friend of the sun, the sage of the auspicious ford, the companion of Hari;
the one initiated in the instruction of the wicked-minded, the side-glance of devotion; victory to the noble and preeminent Guru!
By whom the essence of the work was composed, and by whom the abundance of its stated reasoning was established.
I bow to that Vyāsa, the lord of sages, the moon to the night-lotuses of the learned, and the victorious Vijayīndra;
I perpetually prostrate before Rāghavendra, my guru, who is the moon to the ocean of the *Daśamatī* doctrine.
I also honor the noble Rāma, the bestower of desired boons, whose sublime form is invoked within his image.
I ever serve the lotus-feet of Rāma, who is a bee at the feet of Rāghava, the lord of the Raghus, and the abode of compassion;
I serve my preceptor, Vasudhendra,
who is endowed with auspicious qualities such as knowledge, dispassion, and devotion.

I bow to the teachers Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa and my noble elder brother; I, Aiṇa by name, son of Gopālācārya— the grandson of Śrī Rāmācārya— compose this work which illuminates the unity of the three systems of thought.
Having condensed and gathered together the various statements regarding the *liṅga* (essential nature) made by the venerable Mahānandatīrtha, Jayārya, Vyāsa,
and the Teachers (*deśika*), that which constitutes the primary object of knowledge (*prameya*) in the systems of Śrī Rāmānuja and Śaṅkarārya is here correctly set forth.
The *Matatrayaikyaprakāśikā*, which elucidates the essence of the Siddhānta of the Jewel who is the Guide to the Shore of Bliss.
And as for whatever else [is claimed], it is already established by the principles of "nothingness" (akiñcit); enough with further proofs.

May this work, which illuminates the unity of the three mantras, lead to the joy and debate of the wise who are free from envy, who understand the principles of logic, and who know the essential meaning of the doctrines.
May the wise, upon seeing my work, show me abundant compassion.

Is it not the case that the promise, "I shall compose the *Trimataikyaprakāśikā*," is untenable because it is contradictory? For, since numbers other than unity possess the property of implying a difference from their own substratum—which stands in a relation of co-referentiality with itself—and since this implies a distinct status, there would be a division of the ritual action (*karmabheda*) due to the number; such is the logic of the section on number (*saṃkhyādhikaraṇa*).

Because [the sacrifice] is already established, one offers three oblations; in such cases as "one immolates seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati," since the verbal form is in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word expressing the number seventeen, and because of the distinction between the substances and deities, separate sacrifices numbering seventeen are enjoined.

In the second [chapter], because it is not so [stated], and since in the present context there is no rule that the enumeration of doctrines must imply a difference in their respective substrates, this single [entity] may be described in many ways according to the difference of its objects:
"The Guru in speech, Arjuna in bowmanship, Bhīṣma in the wielding of arrows."

This [figure], though manifold in many ways due to the diversity of its objects, is subject to deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of the ornament *ullekha* (multiple description), as in: "Desire was viewed by women as their own body, by those seeking wealth as time, and by enemies as death. Furthermore, it occurs in cases such as "the non-duality of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman" or "the non-duality of the two qualified [entities]."
And because of deviation; for, according to the rule "the dual and singular endings are used for two and one," the dual ending denotes the number two.

For by seeing that [Self], the two selves have entered the cave; nor should the number be taken as [only] two, because of their distinctness and because of the excess. "The two drinking the reward in the world of good deeds, in whom the five groups of five and the light..."

[The Lord] is established [as one]. Because of contradictions in His own doctrine regarding such statements as "The Self and the Inner Self—Hari alone exists in two ways," and so forth; for although it is universally accepted that these three doctrines possess distinct objects of knowledge (*prameya*), and since the unity of a doctrine is contingent upon the unity of its object of knowledge, the manifestation of that unity [is as follows]:
It is thus asserted:
"The god Nārāyaṇa alone is independent, possessed of perfect qualities,
free from defects, all-pervading, the individual soul, and the self-sufficient cause of the worlds."
Therefore, the Lord is eternally distinct from the living beings, the insentient matter, and so forth;
and one who is certain that He is also distinct from His own attributes and the like attains liberation.
He alone, who is devoid of equals or superiors, explains the state of Nārāyaṇa.

"The Lord is independent and possesses perfect qualities. Although, according to the method of the commentary (*ṭīkā*), the two terms "Lord" (*deva*) and "possessor of perfect qualities" (*pūrṇasadguṇa*) are synonymous with the term "Nārāyaṇa," nevertheless, by that very same method: *nāra* refers to the liberated souls (*muktas*) and *nārā* to Lakṣmī; and *nāra* also refers to the faultless knowledge produced from the Vedas, [the Lord being] the substratum of these.

Since [agency] is not possible for one who is not independent, independence is understood by implication; thus, there is no fault in explaining it with the word "svatantra" (independent). The meaning is that he is independent with respect to the threefold nature of his activity, which begins from his very essence. He is one whose qualities—knowledge and the rest—are each complete and free from defects.

By this analysis, because the Lord acquires the qualities that serve as the numerous grounds for the application [of words], it follows that He is denotable by all Vedic terms; this is established even though it was already implied by the sense.

The Blessed One’s state of being faultless (*nirdoṣatva*) is a distinct characteristic (*lakṣaṇāntara*); thus, there is no inconsistency. By the word "by himself" (*svataḥ*), he excludes [the notion that] agency is dependent on material causes (*upādāna*), primordial matter (*prakṛti*), time (*kāla*), and so forth.
And by the phrase "having regard for his own will" (*svataḥ svecchām avekṣya*), he indicates that [his] agency is indeed intrinsic. Immediately after the word "of the worlds" (*jagatām*),...

The phrase "as appropriate" is to be understood as the ellipsis. "Hence" means: precisely because everything is an effect. By the word "always," it is indicated that difference is ultimately real (*pāramārthika*). In the term "own," the word *dharma* refers to qualities; the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to actions, parts, threads, and so on. The meaning is that [the Self] is absolutely distinct from these. The particle "but" (*tu*) serves to indicate a distinction. That...

And since [the Lord] is well-ascertained as being non-different from that which possesses distinctions, He—having been correctly made the object of hearing, reflection, meditation, and immediate intuition, and being gracious—bestows liberation upon qualified aspirants according to their fitness. By this, His status as the supreme among all, expressed by the single word [Brahman], is elucidated. That which...

For absolute reality is independent; it is the object of non-sublatable knowledge and exists as the threefold being—prior, posterior, and eternal. All else is dependent for its existence upon another. This applies to the Blessed One, while for others such as Brahmā and the rest, [their status] is due to being objects of non-sublatable knowledge.

The phrase "in terms of ultimate reality" (*pāramārthika-satyatve*) is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the sentence]. By the word "for" (*hi*), he indicates here that this is established by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). The meaning is that existence (*bhāva*) is of three kinds, characterized by prior non-existence, destruction, and eternal presence.
Furthermore, existence is considered to be of two kinds, according to whether it is sentient or insentient.
Due to the distinction between those fit for liberation, those who are fit [for it], and those who are eternally transmigratory,
the conscious being (cetana) is also to be known as threefold; and these are distinct from one another.
Those who possess a subtle body (aliṅga-śarīrin) always attain degrees of excellence;
having obtained the means such as knowledge and so forth, they reach the state of the bliss of their own essential nature (svarūpānanda).
Here, "fitness for liberation" (mukti-yogyatva) is intended to mean precisely the state of not being a locus for the absolute non-existence of liberation. By that [definition],...

There is no inconsistency in [the Lord’s] entering even the conscious being who is fit for liberation from Ramā; by the word "always" (sadā), it is indicated that there is a gradation both in saṃsāra and in liberation. By the word "but" (tu), a distinction is indicated: that for all others except Mahālakṣmī, there is a subtle body (liṅga-śarīra). By the word "knowledge" (jñāna), in its primary sense—

Hearing, reflection, meditative absorption, indirect knowledge, and devotion are included. By secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), grace is also included; and by the word "etcetera" (ādi), ignorance, false knowledge, and mixed knowledge are included.
The meaning is: without overstepping what was previously stated.
The eternal, the eternally-eternal, and the non-eternal—thus the non-eternal is considered to be threefold.
The insentient, the Śruti, and the eternal—the eternally-eternal is considered to be threefold.
That which is called the Purāṇa, the Unmanifest, and Time—the non-eternal is considered to be twofold.
That which is unmixed is mixed, and that which is mixed is unmixed; it is like the sky and not like the sky.
Intellect, mind, the ten senses, the elements, and the five objects—this entire collection is proclaimed as the "mixed egg" (saṃsṛṣṭāṇḍa).

All phenomena of an entity arise from the three qualities (guṇas) and are preceded by their genus; their form is twofold: that which persists as long as the entity exists, and that which is fragmented.
Here, even the unchanging is subject to change within the fragmented form.
And likewise between cause and effect, as well as between a quality and its possessor;
similarly between action and the agent of action, and likewise between a universal and its particular.

The connection [of the verse] is as follows: "The distinguished [category], as well as the two pure [categories], and likewise the part and the whole—thus, the non-conscious is considered to be of three kinds: eternal, both eternal and non-eternal, and non-eternal. By the word *hi* (for/indeed), he indicates the establishment of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) here;
by the word *śruti* (scripture) here, the fifty phonemes and the unevolved space (*avyākṛtākāśa*) are to be understood.
These [elements] are immutable and eternal; the ancient scriptures are eternal in their meaning, yet non-eternal in their sequence of letters, words, and sentences.

The unmanifest principle (*avyakta-tattva*) is eternal in its causal form, but non-eternal in its form as effects such as the Great One (*mahat*) and the rest. Time is eternal in its undivided form, but non-eternal in its forms of moments, instants, and so forth. Regarding the term "non-eternal": it refers to that which is not subject to transmigration.
The logical connection (*anvaya*) is that "the impermanent is of two kinds, namely, the unmixed (*asaṃsṛṣṭa*) and the mixed (*saṃsṛṣṭa*).

It should be understood that the states of being unmixed or mixed depend on whether they are useful or useless to the class of living beings beginning with Brahmā; this is indicated by the word "quality" (*guṇa*). Qualities, actions, and so forth are of two kinds.

[These are] those that exist as long as the substance exists (*yāvaddravyabhāvin*) and those that do not exist as long as the substance exists (*ayāvaddravyabhāvin*). Among these, the former are entirely non-different from the substratum (*dharmī*), while [the latter] are either entirely different or different [in some respect]. Between the material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect (*upādeya*), there is indeed both difference and non-difference. Even a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) exists as long as the thing exists (*yāvadvastubhāvin*).

It is twofold according to its future differentiation (*bhāvibheda*): in some cases it is absolutely different (*atyantabhinna*), and in other cases it is both different and non-different (*bhedābheda*).

It should be understood that there is absolute difference between the conscious part (*cetana*) and the whole (*aṃśin*), whereas there is difference-cum-non-difference between the unconscious part (*acetana*) and the whole.
Such is the summary of the doctrine of the venerable Ānandatīrtha.
May the learned scholars favor this work composed by the one named Aiyaṇa, which is devoid of identity with its own kind, difference from other kinds, and internal diversity.
That which is devoid of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), consisting of knowledge, bliss, and the eternal Self,
indifferent, without distinctions, and whose essence is the single flavor of consciousness—
that alone is Brahman, the supreme reality, to be known through the authority of the Vedas and other means.

In this context, the restrictive determination (*ekāvadhāraṇā*) found in the scriptural passage "one only, without a second" means that Brahman is devoid of internal, homogeneous, and heterogeneous distinctions; this is what is expressed by the first half [of the verse]. Furthermore, through the phrases "alone," "devoid of qualities," and so forth, its freedom from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is indicated, as well as its nature as truth, knowledge, and infinity.
Through such passages as "Consciousness, Bliss, Brahman," its nature as consisting of knowledge, bliss, and so forth is established.
It remains indifferent, like one who is neutral, unattached to those actions;
thus has the Elephant King been described as the non-dual Brahman-knower who attains the Supreme.

It should be understood that by such passages as, "He is indeed rasa; for having obtained rasa alone, this [individual] becomes blissful," qualities such as indifference (*udāsīnatva*), being without distinction (*nirviśeṣatva*), and being of a single flavor (*ekarasa*) are established. By the phrase "Brahman alone," [the following are indicated]:
"The divine, unique God Nārāyaṇa" and "In the beginning, there was indeed only Nārāyaṇa."

"Devoid of beginning, middle, and end, one, all-pervading, consciousness-bliss, formless, and wonderful; the supreme Lord, the Master, accompanied by Umā, three-eyed, blue-throated, and profoundly peaceful"—by such [passages].
Thus, the single Brahman, denoted by the synonymous terms *Śiva* and *Nārāyaṇa*, possesses the nature of the sole supreme reality (*paratattva*).
It is thus made known:
that obscuration which is ignorance is of a positive nature and consists of the *guṇas*.
It is considered to be of two kinds through the distinction between the collective (*samaṣṭi*) and the individual (*vyaṣṭi*), namely *tamas*.
Ignorance in its collective form is sung of as *māyā* by means of the measures [of cognition].
That [māyā], being of the nature of a superior limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), consists primarily of pure *sattva*.
Consciousness conditioned by that adjunct is omniscient and the cause of all.
Those proficient in the Vedas and scriptures generate [the concept of] Brahman as the Lord of all, possessing all qualities, the inner controller, the Sovereign, and endowed with attributes.
His lordship, agency, omniscience, and so forth,
should likewise be understood as false by those who perceive the Vedānta, because they are illusory (māyika);
for [the ignorant] are indeed obstructed by the unreal.
"Knowledge is veiled by ignorance; by that, living beings are deluded"—such are the Śruti and Smṛti texts.
These serve as the authority for ignorance being the concealer of Brahman.
[In that state,] there remains only the absolute, devoid of distinctions, which possesses both the nature of the substratum and the object.
For that which is already established as darkness cannot be the support nor the object of a subsequent [cognition].
Thus, the explanatory statement (*vivaraṇavākya*) is also an indicator for that very point. "Consisting of qualities" (*guṇātmaka*) means consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇātmaka*).
In this regard: "The unborn, one, red, white, and black, the power of the divine Self, hidden by its own qualities;
for this divine Māyā of Mine, composed of qualities, is difficult to overcome. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.5; Bhagavad Gītā 7.14)

The Śruti and Smṛti passages beginning with these words are the authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*). "Darkness" (*tamaḥ*) means ignorance (*ajñāna*). "By the measures" (*mānaiḥ*) means by such [scriptural] passages as "Indra through his powers of illusion" (*indro māyābhiḥ*). This is the reason for its being an "exalted limiting adjunct" (*utkṛṣṭopādhitva*).
He explains that very point [that it consists primarily of pure *sattva*] with the passage beginning "the consciousness conditioned by that" (*tadupādhika-caitanya*), and so forth.
That [Tamas] is primarily characterized by impure sattva; it is the individual form (vyaṣṭi-rūpa).
Consciousness conditioned by that [tamas] is proclaimed as the "jīva" (individual soul), endowed with qualities such as limited knowledge, lack of lordship, and being an enjoyer.
(p. 9) Some also maintain that the individual soul (*jīva*) is the consciousness of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇacaitanya*).
[The term] "predominantly impure *sattva*" means that its primary constituent is impure *sattva*.

The rest is easy to understand. [It is] like the specific transformation of the unborn Prakṛti presided over by Brahman; it is the locus of the mass of light produced through its connection with the consciousness of Brahman;
and it is the substratum for the two powers of eternal, immediate cognition and action.

This internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is always the locus of agency, enjoyership, and prior states; indeed, it should be known as such by those who know the scriptures. Agency, enjoyership, pleasure, pain, and so forth are its constant qualities.
Just as the redness of a hibiscus flower appears in a crystal,

so too, due to proximity, does the state of being presided over by Brahman appear within that which is called the individual soul (jīva), which is a specific transformation of ignorance (avidyā). This presiding by Brahman is the cause.

The term "brahmacaitanya" means that which is connected with the consciousness of Brahman; that is to say, it is colored by consciousness. For this very reason, it is eternally immediate (*nityāparokṣa*). The sense is that, by relying upon the power of consciousness (*vijñānaśakti*), it becomes the subject of worldly transactions such as "I am the agent," "I am the enjoyer," "I go," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "named Jīva": it refers to that which is denoted by the word *jīva*.

The meaning is: in consciousness (caitanya) as delimited by ignorance (avidyā) or delimited by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). The word "ca" has the sense of "eva" (only/indeed). It means that the attributes such as agency (kartṛtva) appear in the individual soul (jīva) solely due to the proximity of the internal organ; they do not truly belong to that [consciousness] itself.
And for those who have seen the superimposition of ignorance and the ego-sense, the inner self (pratyagātman) should always be known by the wise as the witness (sākṣin). Furthermore,
even this state of being a witness must be understood as false, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.

The meaning is that the inner self (pratyagātman), the witness (sākṣin), is to be known as the observer of the perpetual superimposition (adhyāsa) of ignorance (avidyā) and the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra). "Like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell" means, for example, just as there is the superimposition of silver and so forth upon a mother-of-pearl shell and the like.

The meaning is that just as false knowledge in the form of an object is superimposed upon Brahman, so too the superimposition of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and the like— which likewise takes the form of knowledge and its objects— is false.
This being the case, a certain distinction within our established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is now stated.

Brahman, conditioned by ignorance (avidyā) and omnipresent, is called the individual soul (jīva). Some say it is enveloped by that ignorance, while others declare it to be unenveloped. Consciousness (caitanya), when accompanied by the assistance of its mental modifications (vṛtti), is designated as the individual soul.
In both systems, that which is always the knower of its respective object is the consciousness of the internal organ known as the *jīva*. However,
in that view, it is the all-pervading Brahman-consciousness that is the actual knower of the object.
The heart and speech should be understood as being somehow united through correct investigation;
the nature of their functioning is to be known, and that is declared to be their activity.
Thus, this great play of knowledge should be understood by the learned.
There is yet another distinction regarding ignorance (*avidyā*), which I shall now describe:
there are two powers known as projection (*vikṣepa*) and concealment (*āvaraṇa*), which constitute a separate function.
These two powers are to be understood through analogies such as a mute person, a rope, and so forth; therefore, these two powers [are distinct].

The Brahman-consciousness reflected in ignorance (*avidyā*), which is all-pervading yet not covered by ignorance, is denoted by the term "jīva"; such is the Brahman-consciousness. There are two views regarding this: [one holds that] it is covered by ignorance and thus denoted as "jīva," while the first position maintains it is uncovered. Even though the consciousness of the jīva is all-pervading, due to its state of non-attachment (*asaṅgatva*)...

It is logical that [the internal organ], although not inherently illuminating objects, becomes the illuminator of various objects through the medium of being colored by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of those objects; just as, for example, the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth [are manifested].

Even though it is omnipresent, [consciousness] is colored only by that which possesses a dewlap and so forth; just as the light of a lamp, although pervading space along with forms, smells, tastes, and other qualities, does not illuminate those [objects], but illuminates only that which is in contact with formless things. Fire also is like this: though it is not a burner in its isolated state, it becomes a burner when mounted upon a mass of iron or similar objects. So too [is consciousness].

Even for objects such as a jar, which are not themselves conscious, it is logical that they are manifested by consciousness that is conditioned by a mental modification (*vṛtti*). In the second view as well, the all-pervading individual consciousness (*jīvacaitanya*), though veiled by ignorance (*avidyā*), removes the veil over the consciousness of Brahman— which is non-distinct from those respective objects— by means of a mental modification taking the form of those respective objects.

The meaning is that [the Self] is the illuminator of the object by its own nature, assisted by the mental modification (*vṛtti*), in some manner; this very point is what makes known the sense of "the illuminator. The word "always" (*sada*) is to be construed with what will be said later: "to be known through right inquiry. The phrase "in this very way" is the ellipsis (*śeṣa*). [The Self is] delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

In the view that the individual soul (*jīva*) is Brahman-consciousness, it is precisely the all-pervading Brahman-consciousness that illuminates objects; through the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)— which serves as the respective limitation (*avacchedaka*) for each individual soul— the consciousness of Brahman becomes differentiated by the mental modifications (*vṛtti*) assuming the forms of those respective objects,
and upon the manifestation of this distinction of Brahman-consciousness delimited by those respective objects, there occurs the illumination of those respective objects.

It is also appropriate that the experience of objects is designated as the "living self" (jīva) when it is somehow conjoined with the mental modification (vṛtti); this too has been explained. As for the nature of the mental modification: just as water from a reservoir flows out through a hole, enters a field via an irrigation channel, and assumes the very same shape as that field—such as being square or otherwise—so too [does the consciousness].
When there is contact between the sense organs and their objects and so forth, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which is composed of parts and consists of light,
goes out through the doors of the eyes and other senses, like the eye itself.

The meaning is that the nature of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) is to be understood from the *Vivaraṇa* and other texts, which state: "Having quickly manifested the object of transformation in the form of a long radiance, it becomes that very form; this is the modification.

Here, the word "for" (*hi*) has the sense of a reason (*hetu*). Therefore, the syntactical connection is: "Therefore, he speaks of that [modification]. The word "internal" (*antara*) denotes a specific distinction (*viśeṣa*).

The meaning is that this is [illustrated] by examples such as the king of clouds and so forth. For instance: even a small cloud covers the solar disc, which extends for many *yojanas*, by acting as an obscuration to the eyes of those who behold it;
likewise, although knowledge is limited, by its own power it [covers] the limited...

The power of concealment (*āvaraṇa-śakti*) is that by which the consciousness of Brahman, as the witness, covers [itself] by way of obstructing the intellect (*buddhi*). Just as the ignorance regarding a rope (*rajju-ajñāna*), through its own power,
brings forth a snake and so forth upon the rope that it has concealed, so too does ignorance, through its own power, [project objects] upon the Self that it has concealed.

It brings forth the manifold expansion (prapañca) of space and so forth. This is the meaning: one should know that such are these two powers of that ignorance (avidyā), namely the power of concealment and the power of projection.
And it has been described how ignorance is endowed with these two powers.
Consciousness conditioned by that [intellect] is the efficient cause by virtue of its own predominance,
and it is the material cause by virtue of the predominance of its own adjunct;
this is according to the principle of non-difference and through the analogy of the spider.

Just as a conscious spider is the efficient cause by virtue of its own predominance and the material cause by virtue of its body being predominant, so too consciousness conditioned by the ignorance denoted by the term "māyā" is the efficient cause by virtue of its own predominance and the material cause by virtue of the predominance of its own limiting adjunct.

Because this very point has been described in exactly that manner in the section [of the Brahmasūtras] beginning with "The difference from that [is established] on account of the words 'originating' and so forth" (p.
13): for that which is consciousness is indeed undifferentiated.

That which is to be expressed by the words at the end of the Vedas and known through the authority of the Śruti and other means is indeed the pure consciousness, the distinct Fourth (turīya), which is the indicated meaning (lakṣya). "Non-distinct" means characterized by omniscience and so forth, which are the effects of ignorance; this is the sense.

The explanation of "secluded" (*vivikta*) is "pure consciousness" (*śuddhacaitanya*). For this very reason, because it is devoid of the qualities that serve as the grounds for linguistic application (*pravṛttinimitta*), it is not denotable; rather, the meaning is that it is only to be indicated (*lakṣya*).
By the term "the fourth" (*turya*), [it is meant that] they consider non-duality to be auspicious and duality to be auspicious.
The word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates the well-known status of this [truth] in the Vedas; by the phrase "from which speech [turns back]," etc., it illuminates its establishment in the scriptures.

It is through the direct realization of this very [truth] that the word is understood as a means to liberation. That which arises from the Vedas and other sources is considered the subordinate element (*śeṣa*), while the Veda itself is regarded as the principal (*śeṣin*).

When the intellect (*matiyāna*) has become the residual substrate (*śeṣabhūta*) of hearing (*śravaṇa*), liberation (*mokṣa*) consists primarily in the destruction of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self (*brahmātmaikya-mati*). Furthermore,
the purport of all Vedāntas is that [this realization] pertains to the undivided Brahman.
Furthermore, there is another object of knowledge, a most great reality to be known;
yet, because this work is composed in brief, it has been presented by us without contradiction.
Thus ends this compendium of the essential meaning of the doctrine of Śaṅkarācārya.

The noble Āryan has indeed stated: "May the wise ones, who have well-ascertained the meaning through the wisdom of Vedānta, [be gracious]"; according to such authoritative evidence, the meaning is that immediate, non-conceptual knowledge of Brahman produced by verbal testimony is the means to liberation.
"By means of hearing and so forth" means by means of listening and so forth. Even there, "hearing" is the primary factor, as it constitutes the valid means of knowledge (*śabda-pramāṇa*).

Because it is primary and because there is no intervention regarding the comprehension of the object of knowledge (*prameya*). The meaning is that reflection (*manana*) and meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*), however, are its auxiliary parts. Regarding the phrase "of liberation," the syntactical connection is as follows: it should be understood that the cognition of unity and the experience of unity [are required].
Regarding the phrase "due to non-contradiction," the meaning is that there is no contradiction even at the outset with the object of knowledge according to our own established doctrine (*siddhānta*).
That which is the object of valid cognition is considered the "knowable" (prameya), and it is held to be twofold.

By way of the distinction between substance and non-substance, substance is also held to be twofold. By way of the distinction between the insentient and the sentient, the insentient is also held to be twofold.

Indeed, the non-inert (ajaḍa) is considered to be of two kinds according to the distinction between time (kāla) and nature (prakṛti). The internal (pratyak) is remembered as being twofold through the division of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara); and the external (parāk) is likewise considered to be twofold.
They classify *dharmajñāna* as "eternal existence" (*nityabhūti*).
Substance (*dravya*) is said to be of six kinds, beginning with time (*kāla*) and ending with eternal existence.
Their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are to be known, as well as their divisions (*vibhāga*) arising therefrom.

Immediately after the word "prameya" (the object of knowledge), the word "tat" (that) is understood by ellipsis. By the word "hi," he indicates that this [object] is well-established through the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). "Dharmajñāna" means knowledge that has become an attribute (dharmabhūtajñāna). Time, primordial nature (prakṛti), the individual soul (jīva), the Lord (īśvara), knowledge as an attribute, and the eternal realm (nityavibhūti)—this is the meaning of the sixfold substance (dravya).

Time is that which is characterized by states such as the moment (*kṣaṇa*), the instant (*lava*), the muhūrta, the day and night (*ahorātra*), and so forth. Primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is endowed with the qualities (*guṇa*) of *sattva* and the rest;

and it exists in twenty-four forms through its association with states such as the Great Principle (*mahat*), the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), the eleven organs, the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and the five gross elements, as well as through its association with the state of primordial nature itself.

And the state (avasthā) is a adventitious particularity of the attribute. While possessing atomicity, it consists of the nature of being a knower, the state of being a living soul (jīvatva), the consciousness distinct from the living soul, the state of being the Lord (īśvaratva), the manifestation of the knower and the known, the knowledge that exists as an attribute (dharmabhūtajñāna),
and that which is distinct from the substance of the three qualities (triguṇadravya) while being endowed with the quality of sattva.

Regarding "the eternal manifestation" (*nityavibhūti*): it has been stated—“It is of two kinds, consisting of the distinction between the substantial (*dravya*) and the non-substantial (*adravya*). Those who know it call it the *stabaka* (cluster/bunch).”

Substance (dravya) is divided into two kinds: the insentient (jaḍa) and the sentient (ajaḍa). The former consists of the unmanifest (avyakta) and time (kāla); the other is divided into the internal (pratyak) and the external (parāk). Among these, the first [the internal] is twofold due to the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa). Regarding the latter [the external], some say that the eternal manifestation (nityā bhūtiḥ) and cognition (mati) are non-sentient.
In that regard, substance (dravya) is tenfold; primordial nature (prakṛti) is endowed with the qualities beginning with sattva;
time (kāla) has the form of years and so forth; the individual soul (jīva) is atomic and possessed of cognition; the Lord (īśa) is another self (ātman);
and eternal being (bhūti) is declared to be likewise endowed with the three qualities and sattva.
It has been stated in summary that the definition of substance is cognition, which consists of the manifestation of both the knower and the knowable.
Now, I shall describe substance and its essential nature according to the path of the scriptures.
That which is devoid of conjunction is called non-substance (adravya), and it is said to be without material cause (anupādāna).
[The qualities are] sattva, rajas, tamas, sound, touch, form, and likewise taste.
Fragrance, conjunction, and power—these ten are traditionally held to be non-substantial (adravya).
Whatever state belongs to the cause, the effect is said to be endowed with that.
The conclusion is that the causal substance and the effect-substance are not different.

The meaning is that, because of the principle of non-difference from that [cause] and because it is established in exactly that way, they have declared its nature to be either the absence of conjunction or the absence of being a material cause (*anupādānatva*), even though it possesses substantiality (*dravyatva*). By the word "hi" (for/indeed), he indicates the establishment through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). It is a different state; it is endowed with another state.
The meaning is that it is qualified by that. The word *ca* has the sense of *eva* (only). It is connected with the word "does not exist" (*nāsti*) immediately following.

The section on non-difference (*ananyatva*) is clear in the Śrībhāṣya and will be explained further below. It is proclaimed that Brahman alone is both its material cause (*upādāna*) and its agent (*kartṛ*).
That which is the subtle state of both consciousness and matter, as well as their gross state, is likewise composed of both consciousness and matter;
because of the identity of these two with Brahman, it is called Viśiṣṭādvaita (Qualified Non-dualism).

The absolute difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman must indeed always be known; the scriptural texts concerning non-difference are to be understood as pertaining to the relationship between the body and the embodied. Furthermore, according to scripture, those who are liberated have attained the Supreme and thus possess equality with Brahman.
"Taking that as its material cause" (tadupādānaṃ) means it is the material cause of the aforementioned manifold world (prapañca).

The word "proclaimed" (prakīrtitam) implies "by those who know the Vedas. The prefix [pra-] is used to indicate the well-known authority of such Vedic passages as "from which... (*yato vā*). By the particle *eva* ("only"), he excludes any other possible material cause for such a thing. In this regard—

By the word *cit* (consciousness) is meant the class of living beings (*jīva-jāta*), and by the word *acit* (non-consciousness), matter and so forth. The subtlety (*sūkṣmatva*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), whose nature is inherently atomic, consists in the contraction of its attribute of knowledge (*dharmabhūtajñāna*). The subtlety of the non-conscious (*jaḍa*) consists in its having entered the state of being a cause. The equality (*tulyatva*) of the conscious (*cit*) consists in the expansion of its attribute of knowledge.

The meaning is as follows: the non-sentience and grossness [of the world] consist in its being established in the state of an effect; its being "endowed with that" (tadyuktatva) means being qualified by that [effect]. Thus, because of the identity between those two, it is called "qualified non-duality" (viśiṣṭādvaita). By the phrase "absolute difference between the individual soul and Brahman," he refutes the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference (bhedābheda);
and by the word "always" (sarvadā), he indicates that difference exists even in liberation (mukti). This is the sense conveyed by the particle "hi."

In this context, he illustrates the establishment through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). "Body" (*deha*) and "embodied one" (*dehin*): the meaning is that [the relationship] is based on the state of being the body and the possessor of the body, with the state (*bhāva*) as the primary factor. "From the scripture": the meaning is from the scripture stating, "The stainless one attains supreme equality."
The construction is: "the liberated ones have attained the supreme equality with Brahman. The word *tu* (but/however) serves to indicate a distinction.
And here, the word *ca* (and) has the sense of a conjunction (*samuccaya*) for other objects of knowledge, such as sound and so forth.
The means to liberation is the knowledge of Brahman, which is considered to be of two kinds:
namely, in the form of devotion (*bhakti*) and surrender (*prapatti*); its characteristics should likewise be understood.
Liberation is indeed proclaimed as consisting in the attainment of the bliss of Brahman.
There exists much more of this kind of knowable object (*prameya*) to be understood;
however, it is not written here for the sake of brevity in my work.
This concludes the *Śrīmadrāmānujācāryasiddhāntarasasaṃgraha*.
This was composed by Āiyaṇācārya; may the wise be pleased with it.
The demonstration that the Vedāntas lack intent regarding their superficially perceived meaning.

"Bhakti" means having the form of devotion, which is to say, the form of *prapatti* (surrender). Devotion (*bhakti*) is a remembrance (*smṛti*) that persists until death, consisting of unsurpassed love, whose form is identical to uninterrupted vision, like a continuous stream of oil.

The continuity [of practice] is as follows: *prapatti*, however, is a specific form of knowledge consisting of a prayer directed toward Īśvara in the form, "May you alone be my refuge. That [knowledge], when performed even once, is the means to liberation. Nor should it be argued that this would entail immediate liberation upon the destruction of *prārabdha* karma through *prapatti*, for [that is] not accepted.

Even though the destruction of *prārabdha* (commenced karma) is accepted, since that which has begun as *prārabdha* and is not destroyed by [the knowledge of] *Prapatti* exists, its absence is established. The word "only" (*eva*) is connected with the word "form" (*rūpa*). The meaning is that the liberation of the individual soul (*jīva*) consists in the attainment of the bliss of Brahman; this is what is sung in the scripture—this is the ellipsis. The word "iti" signifies completion.
Thus, since the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) for these three systems are each distinct, the manifestation of their unity is not logical; nevertheless,

because the Vedas alone are accepted by all cultured persons (*śiṣṭa*) as the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) due to their eternally faultless nature regarding the objects of knowledge cited by the respective proponents of those systems, the Vedas themselves are the authority.

They are to be taken as a refuge. Their authority does not extend to matters that are understood through mere superficial perception; for if it were so, there would be the undesirable consequence of contradicting established positions regarding the locus of the sky and so forth in the *Citrasūtra* and other texts. To explain: in whatever [text] there is an instruction on qualities...
Regarding the phrase "connected primarily," this was considered in the second [section]: In the *jyotiṣṭoma*, within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the stotra, it is heard:

"The *ājya* [verses] are fifteen. In that case, is clarified butter (*ghṛta*) joined with the number prescribed as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the stotra, or is the number alone prescribed with reference to the stotra by means of the word *ājya*?
In case of doubt, because the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) prevails, the word *ājya* refers to clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Consequently,

since prescribing both [the butter and the number] would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), and because clarified butter is the substance for mixing, even though the number fifteen does not inherently belong to it, the clarified butter qualified by the number fifteen is connected through the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) by means of the vessels.

Regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that this is an injunction (*vidhi*) as a subordinate element of the hymn (*stotra*), [it is argued that] because there is no compound in the phrase "fifteen *ājya* [verses]," there is no restrictive cognition of a qualified entity; consequently, since the connection with the injunction must be required for all [the verses] individually without mutual relation, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in enjoining meanings that are not directly connected.

By way of incidental discussion (*prasaṅga*), regarding the word *ājya* heard in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) "they praised with *ājyas*" (*ājyaiḥ stuvate*), which appears in the instrumental case, there is [the following]:

because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the hymn (*stotra*) which serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), and because of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) in the form of an etymological explanation— "as they rejoiced (*ajīmiyuḥ*), so is the *ājya*-ness of the *ājyas*"— in the originative injunction.

It was established [in the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā*] that since the word *ājya* (clarified butter) heard [in the text] is both a name and a praise, the hymn is referred to by the word *ājya*, and only the number is enjoined. Similarly, in the first chapter of the subsequent system (*Uttaratantre*), under the aphorism "The ether [is Brahman], because of its characteristic marks" (*ākāśas talliṅgāt*), it is considered that in the *Chāndogya* it is heard: "Of this world, what..."

"The destination is space," so said Vāca. Regarding the doubt as to whether the word "space" (ākāśa) in that passage refers to the elemental space (bhūtākāśa) or the Supreme Self (paramātman), it refers to the sky (gagana) because of the strength of its conventional usage (rūḍhi).

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it was established in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that Ākāśa is Viṣṇu, based on such indicative marks (*liṅga*) as being "higher than the high" (*parovarīyas*), being the *udgītha*, and being infinite.

In that regard, because the literal meaning as it appears is not accepted as authoritative in either case, and because even in passages such as "he found the jewel of speech" (*abhidhāmaṇim avindat*), the acceptance of the literal meaning as it appears is likewise not admitted; rather—
"Which wise man knows the application of the Vedic meters? He should supplement [the knowledge] with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
'The Veda fears the person of little learning, thinking: "He will harm me.
Because of such Śruti and Smṛti passages, the extreme profundity of the meaning of the Veda is declared; for this very reason, it has been stated in the Śābara-bhāṣya."

"For the treatise (śāstra) indeed [produces] cognition of that which is not in contact [with the senses] from the cognition of words. By this [definition], the utility of perception and the other [means of knowledge] has already been established by means of [the study of] grammar and so forth; having considered this, the definition of the treatise was formulated at the time of knowing the meaning of the treatise. Thus, in accordance with the connection stated by the author of the Vārttika, [one should accept] the instruction of the word.
Following the method stated in the Vārttika, "It is declared to be scripture alone," the scripture denoted by the term *codanā* is defined.

Here, the two words [in the compound] refer to a qualified word and its meaning; thus, from the knowledge of the meaning of the prescriptive word, there arises knowledge of the object to be enjoined (*vidheya*), which is not in immediate sensory contact.
In this context, the word *asannikṛṣṭa* (not proximate) has been explained by the author of the Vārttika:
"By the term 'not proximate,' two things are here intended to be excluded:
determination [of the object] through its actual form, and also [determination] through its opposite."
An object already cognized and an object cognized erroneously, even though they exist, are designated as "proximate" (*sannikṛṣṭa*).

The meaning [of the opponent's position] is that verbal testimony (*śabda*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding what is other than those two. However, if that were the case, the contradiction with the *Bhāṣya* and *Vārttika* concerning the section on *codanā* (the Vedic injunction) would be unavoidable. For this very reason—

Having understood what constitutes a valid object and what does not, one must distinguish between the sublation and non-sublation of general rules and exceptions; this cannot be done merely by observing their commonality.
The meaning of the scripture is understood in one way through a single chapter,
yet it is understood in another way when the complete work is taken as a whole with all its constituent parts integrated.
Indeed, in cases where the scriptures appear to contradict one another, [the truth is revealed only by such a comprehensive synthesis].
In that regard, their meaning is determined by following what is observed [in the text]:
"The opening and the conclusion, repetition, novelty, the fruit,
explanatory praise (arthavāda), and logical consistency— these are the marks for determining the intended meaning."

"Direct statement (śruti), indicative mark (liṅga), name (samākhyā), syntactical connection (vākya), and context (prakaraṇa)—each preceding one is more powerful than the following; thus is the determination of the scriptures.
Through such numerous scriptural statements, when the subject matter of the treatise has been thoroughly investigated according to its established principles, [the conclusion is reached].

Furthermore, because it has been stated that validity consists precisely in the object of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), therefore, in the present context, the intended meaning is revealed as being one and the same across all three systems,
through an investigation of Vedic sentences in their respective stated senses in due order.
In the beginning, the oneness of Nārāyaṇa is properly elucidated through reasonings that are consistent with the Vedas and Śāstras and are not contradicted by other doctrines; for it has been stated,
"Nārāyaṇa alone is the one God," thus establishing Nārāyaṇa’s status as the supreme of all, as expressed by the word "one."

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: it is clearly demonstrated that [the Advaita system] is not contradicted by the Rāmānuja doctrine, being consistent with other Vedic statements, consistent with other scriptures such as the Smṛtis and Purāṇas, and consistent with the principles of the various Śākhās and the Pūrva- and Uttara-mīmāṃsās.

(21) Now, even though there is no contradiction regarding Viṣṇu’s supremacy in the system of Rāmānuja, certain proponents of the Advaita school accept that Śiva alone possesses supremacy over all and is the cause of the origin and so forth of the universe, which establishes that status.
For it is thus: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone. "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone. "The gods, indeed, went to the heavenly world;
those gods asked Rudra: 'Who are you? He replied:
'I alone existed in the beginning, I exist now, and I shall exist in the future; there is nothing else whatsoever distinct from me.'"
"Neither existing nor non-existing, indeed Śiva alone is absolute; for Rudra is one, there is no second to Him;

Rudra is superior to the universe, the great seer"—according to these causal statements, by the maxim of the goat and the animal (*chāgapaśunyāya*), the word "existent" (*sat*), being employed as a common substratum for both the vast and the non-vast, refers to that which is denoted by the word "Brahman."

Just as the specific term *brahman*, when employed as common to both the conscious and the unconscious, is accepted as culminating in that specific entity denoted by words such as Rudra or Śiva— where the term *ātman*, likewise employed as common to both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*), also finds its final resolution.

The principle of the "goat and the sacrificial animal" (chāgapaśunyāya) is demonstrated in the eighth chapter on the characteristics of eligibility, specifically in the section [Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 8.1.16] beginning with "Or rather, the goat, because of the wording of the mantra. Regarding the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard in scripture: "One should immolate the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma. In this regard, a doubt arises: should any kind of animal be immolated, or specifically a goat?
Since no specific [animal] is heard mentioned in the injunction (*vidhi*), even though the wording of the mantra— "of the goat's omentum and fat"— mentions the specific form of the goat,
it is regarded as a partial restatement (*pākṣikānuvādaka*) out of a desire to avoid contradicting the primary injunction.

Since it is established by conceptualization that "any animal whatsoever is to be sacrificed," and because the generality of "animal-ness" understood from the injunction is fully present in each individual instance— including the goat— there is no contradiction with the primary injunction; furthermore, because it is recited as a constant rule within the context (*prakaraṇa*), its status as a contingent restatement (*pākṣikānuvāda*) is untenable.
And because of the impossibility of such a conceptualization, it has been established here that the animal to be sacrificed must be a goat, as obtained from the wording of the mantra;

for although [the texts state], "In the beginning, there was indeed only Nārāyaṇa, neither Brahmā nor Śaṅkara," and "Vāsudeva alone existed here in the beginning, neither Brahmā nor Śaṅkara," [it is further stated that] "From Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā is born."

Based on such scriptural passages as "From Nārāyaṇa, Rudra is born," and by applying the logic of the goat and the sacrificial animal (*chāgapaśunyāya*), since it is established that at the time of creation and so forth, it is specifically a particular form of Nārāyaṇa who is presented as *Sat* (Being) after first negating [the existence of] Brahmā, Rudra, and others, and because he is declared to be the progenitor of Brahmā and Rudra, the causal statements refer to Śiva and the like [only in a secondary sense].

Since the purport of words cannot be established without their being directed toward that [ultimate goal], it is determined that the purport of all sentences must reside therein; nevertheless, because the *kāraṇarudra*— the progenitor of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and others, who is distinct from the successive generations of Rudras— is established by the Śrutis, Smṛtis, and other authorities, it is that very one [who is the object].

It is logical that the purport (*tātparya*) of the Śruti and other authorities lies in [establishing] the state of being the supreme among all; for instance, it is stated in the *Uttaratāpanīya*: "The sevenfold and fourfold syllable *A* is Brahmā at the navel;
the sevenfold and fourfold syllable *U* is Viṣṇu in the heart; the sevenfold and fourfold syllable *M*..."
Rudra, consisting of seven aspects, four aspects, thirty-four aspects, and four aspects, [is located] between the eyebrows.

After the injunctions for the worship of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra— who are denoted by the three morae beginning with *a*, located at the heart, the space between the eyebrows, and so forth— the [text describes] the Supreme Fourth (*turya*), which is endowed with all sovereignty, to be worshipped at the "End of the Twelve" (*dvādaśānta*) as denoted by the syllable *oṃ*.
Reality is thus understood. Likewise, in the *Atharvaśikhā*, it is said: "The first [syllable] is red-yellow, belonging to the deity Brahmā;
the second is lightning-like and black, belonging to the deity Viṣṇu; the third is white, auspicious and inauspicious, belonging to the deity Rudra;
and that which is at the end, the fourth half-mora, consists of all phonemes and belongs to the deity Puruṣa."

That which is expressed by the three measures (*mātrā*)—namely, that which transcends Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—is understood as the fourth principle (*tattva*), called Puruṣa, which is expressed by the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*). Thus, it is said in the *Brahmasindhu Upaniṣad*:
"Herein, three gods are proclaimed, three worlds, the three Vedas, and the three fires."
The syllable *aṃ* consists of three measures (*mātrā*) and a half-measure; it belongs to the head.
The *Ṛgveda*, the *Gārhapatya* fire, the earth, and the deity Brahmā are the body of the letter *A*; thus it has been explained by the exponents of Brahman.
The Yajurveda, the intermediate space (antarikṣa), and likewise the Dakṣiṇāgni fire,
as well as the Lord Viṣṇu, the deity— these are proclaimed as the syllable *ukāra*. Furthermore, the Sāmaveda, heaven (dyu), and likewise the Āhavanīya fire [are proclaimed as the syllable *makāra*].
The Supreme Lord, the God, is proclaimed as the letter *M*.
Likewise, one should know the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*) situated above the *praṇava*;
it is subtle like the fiber of a lotus stalk and possesses a radiance equal to the sun at its peak.

"Bestowing boons upon all beings, she stands as the explanation of everything"—by such [verses], [it is shown that she is superior] to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, who are denoted by the three measures (mātrās) beginning with *ā*, and so forth.
A fourth distinct principle, denoted by the half-mora (*ardhamātrā*), is recognized; likewise, in the *Maitrāyaṇīyopaniṣad*:
"Now, that which is indeed its *rājasa* portion is this Brahmā who is the student (*brahmacārin*);
and that which is indeed its *sāttvika* portion is this Viṣṇu who is the student; and that which is indeed its..."

By the passage beginning with "That which is the tamasic portion of that [Being] is he who is Rudra," the fact that Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are partial manifestations (aṃśas) is stated; then, by means of the genitive case in the word "asya" (of him), another ontological principle (tattvāntara) that constitutes the whole (aṃśin)—the Fourth (turīya)—is revealed. Thus, there exists a Fourth reality distinct from Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra.

Although it ultimately culminates in being the very form of Śiva— being that which is denoted by the syllable *oṃ* and worshipped at the *dvādaśānta* in the *Uttaratāpanīya*, that which is denoted by the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*) and has Puruṣa as its deity in the *Atharvaśikhā*, and that which is denoted by the half-measure and bestows boons upon all beings in the *Brahmabindu Upaniṣad*— it remains so.

In the *Maitrāyaṇīyopaniṣad*, it is established that the fourth principle (*turīya-tattva*), which is denoted by the genitive case and constitutes the whole of which the three forms (*mūrti*) are parts, is indeed a distinct reality and not merely the form of Śiva; for there is an absence of any such indicative mark (*liṅga*) or scriptural statement (*śruti*).
Nevertheless, it must be stated that that which is denoted by the syllable *Oṃ*—which consists of the three forms as its parts—is indeed the very nature of Śiva.

And because there are indicative marks (*liṅga*) of Viṣṇu’s superiority. Nor is the reason unestablished (*asiddha*), since it is easy to prove Viṣṇu’s superiority by means of His being the denotable object of the syllable *oṃ* and so forth. Nor is the reason inconclusive (*aprayojaka*), because there is a subverting argument (*bādhaka-tarka*) against the contrary position: that if [the object were not Viṣṇu], the fourth state (*turīya*) would neither be the denotable object of the syllable *oṃ* nor possess the nature of being a portion of the three forms (*mūrtitraya*). [This applies] to the syllable *oṃ*.

Furthermore, because the excess of three measures in the possessor of parts (*aṃśin*) and the excess of parts [in the constituent] are established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is thus proven that the Fourth (*turīya*) is superior to Viṣṇu and is the cause of the birth and so forth of the entire world, being the most excellent of all. (Sakala, p.

Once it is established that [Śiva] is the cause of the birth and so forth of the universe, it follows that the purport of all scriptural passages concerning the cause of everything is that the Fourth Śiva alone is the supreme of all and the cause of the birth and so forth of the entire universe;
furthermore, in the Kaivalyopaniṣad: "Having meditated upon the pure lotus of the heart, in its center [one sees] the luminous, sorrowless [Self]."

I bow to the inconceivable, unmanifest, infinite-formed, auspicious, tranquil, immortal, yet appearing as mortal, the source of Brahman; that which is without beginning, middle, or end, the one, all-pervading, consisting of consciousness and bliss, formless, and wondrous;
the supreme lord and master accompanied by Umā, the three-eyed, blue-throated, and profoundly peaceful.
Having meditated upon the Sage who is the source of all beings, the witness of all, beyond darkness—
[who is] "along with Brahmā, along with Śiva, along with Indra, the imperishable, the supreme self-sovereign"— by such various scriptural indications (*śruti-liṅga*) and others,

it is established that the Fourth (*turya*), Śiva alone, who possesses the manifestations (*vibhūti*) of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and so forth, is the one propounded [in the Upaniṣads]. Likewise, in the *Atharvaśiras*:

"In that which is Rudra, he is indeed the Blessed Lord; and he who is Brahmā—to him be salutation after salutation! He who is Rudra, he is indeed the Blessed Lord; and he who is Viṣṇu—to him indeed be salutation after salutation! Thus, it is Paramaśiva alone, denoted by the word "Rudra" and possessing the manifestations (vibhūti) of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and so forth, who is designated as the Fourth (turīya). Likewise:

In the *Atharvaśikhā*: "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra—they are all produced from Him; so too are all the senses and the elements. But He is not caused by anything; He is the one to be meditated upon. Endowed with all sovereignty, the Lord of all, Śambhu, dwelling in the midst of space—Śiva alone is to be meditated upon, for He is the maker of auspiciousness."

Having stated here that Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and others belong to the category of effects (*kāryakoṭi*), [the text] speaks of Īśāna alone—the Fourth (*turya*)—as the cause by means of his unique names such as Śambhu, Śiva, and so forth.

The state of being the object of meditation is stated [as follows]. Likewise, in the *Uttaratāpanīya*: "One should contemplate this very Self, which has three bodies, as the Supreme Brahman which has three bodies—on account of its grossness and its enjoyment of the gross, on account of its subtlety and its enjoyment of the subtle," and so forth, up to "and on account of its enjoyment of bliss. This is that Self.

The first quarter is Vaiśvānara, the Universal, who has the waking state as his sphere, whose cognition is gross, who has seven limbs and nineteen mouths, who experiences subtle objects, and who is fourfold in nature.
The second quarter is Taijasa, the Radiant, who has the dream state as his sphere, whose cognition is subtle, and who has seven limbs... [and so on].
The second quarter is Taijasa Hiraṇyagarbha, who has nineteen gates, is a subtle enjoyer, and possesses a fourfold nature.
There, when one is asleep, one desires no desire whatsoever and sees no dream whatsoever.
That is deep sleep; in deep sleep, being in the state of deep sleep, one becomes unified as a mass of consciousness.

Thus, the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), the enjoyer of bliss, whose mouth is the mind, has four aspects; the wise one (*prājña*) is the Lord (*īśvara*), the third foot. Now follows this instruction: he is neither of gross cognition, nor of subtle cognition, nor of cognition in both ways, nor of cognition, nor of non-cognition.

They consider the Fourth (turīya) to be a mass of consciousness, unseen, beyond conventional usage, ungraspable, without characteristics, unthinkable, tranquil, and non-dual; it is the Self, that which is to be known. Thus, Śiva alone is the Fourth, distinct from Viṣṇu, Hiraṇyagarbha, and others who are designated by the terms Viśva and Vaiśvānara.
It is thus determined. Likewise, in a passage from the Taittirīya Upaniṣad, it is said:
"He moves within all beings, in the cave of the heart, among those of universal form.
You are the sacrifice; you are Viṣṇu; you are the *vaṣaṭ* call; you are Viṣṇu; you are Brahman; you are Prajāpati."
Thus, you— who possess the manifestations (vibhūti) of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the rest, and who are denoted by the word "thou" (tvam)— are declared to be none other than Śiva, the Fourth (turīya).
Although here only the word "thou" is heard and not the word "Śiva," [it is nevertheless established that] "the supreme Brahman is the eternal and the true."
Through the opening statement, "The Person, dark and tawny, with upward-directed semen and three eyes," and through the concluding statement,
"The Lord of all sciences," as well as by means of direct scriptural testimony (*śruti*), indicative marks (*liṅga*), and other criteria, it is determined that the referent of the term *tvam*—
which possesses the manifestations of the three forms and so forth— is indeed none other than Supreme Śiva. Likewise:
In the Kūrma Purāṇa, which serves as a supplement to this [work], it is stated after praising Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra:
"The God who is higher than them is the Trimūrti, the supreme body;
Maheśvarī, the three-eyed one, is eternally the bestower of peace. Thus it is said in the Uttara-bhāga.
Of all powers whatsoever, those consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu,
and Śiva are remembered as the primary powers of the Supreme Self;
beyond these three stands the eternal Lord, the Supreme Self.
The Great Lord Maheśvara, the wielder of the trident and the soul of all powers, is praised [thus]:
some call him Agni, others Nārāyaṇa;
some call him Indra, and others have sung of him as the vital breaths (prāṇas) or as Brahmā.
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Agni, Varuṇa, and all the gods along with their attendants—
these are proclaimed to be merely manifestations of the one Rudra alone.
Likewise, in the Śiva Purāṇa:

Brahmā is the initiator of creation, Viṣṇu is the sustainer through his power of delusion, and Rudra is likewise the agent of dissolution; he is the eternal controller of those two. Therefore, these three are declared to be the triad of causes of the world.
"Śiva is the cause of the three causes and the supreme cause.
Likewise, in the Skanda Purāṇa: "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are the manifestations of the Supreme Reality."
"For those three, the Lord is the cause of all, being their preponderance. Thus it is stated in the Parāśara Purāṇa:
"Of the Supreme Being himself, who is the witness of all things..."
"She is the supreme form, embodied, pure, independent, and the destroyer of sins;
her common form is that of Ambā, adorned with the crescent moon as her crest-ornament.
Beginning thus—
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśāna meditate upon Him incessantly"—
by this much, the state of the Fourth (Turīya) as Paraśiva has been declared. Likewise, in the Mahābhārata, the birth of the three forms within the body of Paraśiva is described.
This very Lord is Īśvara, renowned as the source of all principles;
he is the knower of the ordinances of all principles, the Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa. From his right limb, he created Brahmā, the originator of the worlds.
Likewise, from his left side, the Lord [Brahmā] created Viṣṇu for the sake of protecting the worlds;
and when the end of the Yuga arrived, he then created the Lord Rudra.
Thus, the nature of the Fourth as Śiva is established. For this very reason, it was also stated by Appayya Dīkṣita:
"Thus, my body is Brahman, the fourth state (turiya), the cause of the universe;
it is established that the Blessed One, the moon-crested Lord, has Umā as his companion.
Furthermore, in the *Harivaṃśa*, during the journey to Kailāsa, [it says]: "O Govinda, whatever names you have in the world..."
"And they are great; these very names are mine—there is no need for deliberation on this matter. Thus, by the words of Śiva addressed to Viṣṇu:
"Śiva, Maheśvara, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Pitāmaha [are one]."
The omniscient physician of cyclic existence, who destroys the sins of Śiva.

And by the statement of Āditya, "This group of eight names is meritorious," which makes known that Śiva is denotable by all names such as Viṣṇu and others, [it follows that] even terms such as Nārāyaṇa and Vāsudeva found in the causal statements [refer to him].

If it is argued that since the *turiya* (the fourth state) is supreme as Śiva, and because the purport of all the Vedas can reside in its being the most excellent of all and the cause of the entire universe, therefore the purport [of the Vedas] regarding Nārāyaṇa’s being the most excellent and the cause of the entire universe contradicts a portion of the Advaita doctrine, and thus the manifestation of their identity is impossible—then [we reply]: [This is not so. For the purport of the Vedas is established in accordance with the intention of the author of the *Śruti-prāmāṇya-siddhi*, which is consistent with the *Brahma-sūtra*. Furthermore, the fact that the *turiya* is the supreme Śiva and the cause of the entire universe is not established by the *Śruti-prāmāṇya-siddhi*; rather, it is established solely by the Purāṇas. Consequently, the Purāṇas themselves do not possess the status of being the primary means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for establishing the ultimate truth. Therefore, the claim that the purport of the Vedas lies in the supremacy and causality of Nārāyaṇa does not contradict the Advaita doctrine, and the manifestation of their identity is indeed possible. Thus, the objection is refuted.
To this it is replied:
According to the principle of the "all-branch" method (*sarvaśākhā-dinaya*), there must be one single, supreme reality;
that alone is what is designated as Nārāyaṇa—such is the definitive conclusion of the Vedānta.
That fourth reality, which is of the nature of Śiva and designated as Nārāyaṇa,
is thoroughly established by means of the Vedas and other authorities, as well as by logical principles (*nyāya*).

This means it is established through the principle of the uniformity of approach (*gatisāmānya*) for the sake of the uniform understanding of all branches [of the Veda] and the uniform understanding of all Vedānta texts.

Immediately after the phrase "supreme among all," the ellipsis is to be supplied as "the object of the purport of all the Vedas. It is thus thoroughly established— by means of scriptural citations (*śruti*), indicative marks (*liṅga*), and other logical principles such as the method of initial context (*upakrama*)— that the aforementioned supreme reality, the fourth state (*turīya*) which is the nature of Śiva, is indeed identical with Nārāyaṇa.

The meaning is as follows: for instance, in such passages as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1) and "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone" (*Aitareya Upaniṣad* 1.1.1), words such as "Being" (*sat*), "Brahman," and so forth are used in conjunction with terms like "one" (*eka*). For example: "Verily, in the beginning, Nārāyaṇa alone existed";
"Hiraṇyagarbha came into being in the beginning"; and "The gods, indeed, led [the sacrifice] to the heavenly world. Those gods...
They asked Rudra, "Who are you? He replied, "I alone existed in the beginning," and so forth—this being a consciousness unique to no other.

By the principle of the "cognition of all branches" (*sarva-śākhā-pratyaya-nyāya*), all portions of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*)— which are associated with words such as Nārāyaṇa, Hiraṇyagarbha, and Rudra that denote specific types of volition (*cetanā-viśeṣa*), and which, by being connected with the meanings required by those [words], have attained syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with them [the Upanishads]— [are to be understood as referring to the Supreme Self].

By the principle that all Vedānta texts have the same purport (*sarvavedāntapratyaya-nyāya*) and by the principle of the uniformity of the goal (*gatisāmānya-nyāya*), it is established beyond dispute that they have a single object; and this cannot be sustained unless there is a primary unity of purport regarding both the general terms such as "Being" (*sat*) and "Brahman" found in those respective passages, and the specific terms such as "Nārāyaṇa," "Hiraṇyagarbha," and "Rudra."
It must be accepted that there is only one single reality which is the intended object (*tātparya-viṣaya*) of the power of all words;
otherwise, the various causal statements cited— such as those concerning *sat*, *brahman*, *ātman*, and *Nārāyaṇa* read within their respective sentences— [would be inconsistent].

Furthermore, because this would result in the loss of the status of being the single subject of all the Śrutis—due to the consequence that there would be multiple independent causes denoted by their respective terms, and due to the consequence that Nārāyaṇa and others would each independently be the cause of the world—it [refers] to that which is established by the Śruti and the Sūtra: "From whence [comes] the birth etc.
of this [world]" and "From whence indeed these beings are born."

Furthermore, because it would result in the Brahman-characteristic falling into an extreme state, and because it would entail a contradiction with such scriptural passages as "one only, without a second," which establish the oneness of the reality that is the cause of the universe; therefore, the single supreme reality known as Nārāyaṇa, whose nature is the fourth [state] and Śiva, is the intended purport of all Vedānta.

Furthermore, the principle that all Vedic branches convey the same teaching (*sarva-śākhā-pratyaya-nyāya*) is established in the *Pūrva-mīmāṃsā* [Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 2.4.8–10]: "There would be a difference in ritual acts between different branches because of differences in name, form, and specific qualities, because of repetition, because of censure, because of incapacity, because of statements of completion, because of expiatory rites, and because of the observation of purpose. This was demonstrated in the second section of the second book (*dvitīyādhyāya-dvitīyapāda*). In that regard:
The Agnihotra and other rites as recited in various Vedic branches (śākhās), such as the Kāṭhaka, Kāpālika, Kāṇva, Mādhyandina, Taittirīya, and so forth.

When the doubt arises whether ritual action (*karman*) differs according to each branch (*śākhā*) or whether it is one and the same across all branches—given that there are differences in names such as "the *Agnihotra* of the Kāṭhakas" and "the *Agnihotra* of the Kāpālikas," and that in one branch one is told to "offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni," while in another [it is stated similarly]— [The answer follows: ...[omitted]... [The conclusion is: It is one and the same. Why? Because the form (*rūpa*) is identical. Just as the form of the *Agnihotra* remains the same in all branches, so too the form of the sacrifice to Indra and Agni is the same; therefore, the action is one. Furthermore, because the injunctions (*codanā*) are identical, the action is one. Moreover, because the name is the same, the action is one. For example, the name "*Agnihotra*" is common to all branches. And since the name is applied based on the presence of the root *hu* (to sacrifice) and the word *agni*, and since these two are present in every instance, the name is the same. Therefore, the action is one. Furthermore, because the results are identical, the action is one. For example, the result of the *Agnihotra* is the attainment of heaven, and this is the same in all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*) are identical, the action is one. For example, the preparatory rite for the *Agnihotra* is the same in all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the recitation (*japa*) is identical, the action is one. For example, the recitation of the *Sāvitri* verse is the same in all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the deities (*devatā*) are identical, the action is one. For example, the deity of the *Agnihotra* is Agni, and this is the same in all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the mantras are identical, the action is one. For example, the mantra for the *Agnihotra* is the same in all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are identical, the action is one. For example, the fee for the *Agnihotra* is the same in all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the time (*kāla*) is identical, the action is one. For example, the time for the *Agnihotra* is the same in all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the purpose (*prayojana*) is identical, the action is one. For example, the purpose of the *Agnihotra* is the same in all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is identical, the action is one. For example, the procedure for the *Agnihotra* is the same in all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the *Arthavādas* (explanatory passages) are identical, the action is one. For example, the *Arthavādas* regarding the *Agnihotra* are the same in all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the *Anuvākas* (recitations) are identical, the action is one. For example, the *Anuvākas* for the *Agnihotra* are the same in all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the *Ādeśas* (injunctions) are identical, the action is one. For example, the injunction regarding the *Agnihotra* is the same in all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the *Upadeśas* (instructions) are identical, the action is one. For example, the instruction regarding the *Agnihotra* is the same in all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the *Nigadas* (declarations) are identical, the action is one. For example, the *Nigada* regarding the *Agnihotra* is the same in all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the *Nivits* (interpolated formulas) are identical, the action is one. For example, the *Nivits* for the *Agnihotra* are the same in all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the *Praiṣas* (calls to the priests) are identical, the action is one. For example, the *Praisa* for the *Agnihotra* is the same in all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the *Prayogas* (performances) are identical, the action is one. For example, the performance of the *Agnihotra* is the same in all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the *Yajus* (formulas) are identical, the action is one. For example, the *Yajus* for the *Agnihotra* is the same in all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the *Brahmaṇas* (explanatory texts) are identical, the action is one. For example, the *Brahmaṇa* regarding the *Agnihotra* is the same in all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the *Mantras* are identical, the action is one. For example, the *Mantra* for the *Agnihotra* is the same in all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the *Stomas* (hymns/chants) are identical, the action is one. For example, the *Stoma* for the *Agnihotra* is the same in all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the *Dharmas* (duties/rites) are identical, the action is one. For example, the *Dharma* of the *Agnihotra* is the same in all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the *Viniyogas* (applications) are identical, the action is one. For example, the application of the *Agnihotra* is the same in all branches. Therefore, the action is one.
