Also, because the *Uddeshas* (indications) are identical, the action is one. For example, the indication regarding the *Agnihotra* is the same in all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the *Upasaṃhāras* (conclusions) are identical, the action is one. For example, the conclusion of the *Agnihotra* is the same in all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the *Upakramas* (introductions) are identical, the action is one. For example, the introduction to the *Agnihotra* is the same in all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the *Abhyāsas* (repetitions) are identical, the action is one. For example, the repetition of the *Agnihotra* is the same in all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the *Avasthās* (states/stages) are identical, the action is one. For example, the stages of the *Agnihotra* are the same in all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the *Samākhyās* (names/designations) are identical, the action is one. For example, the designation "*Agnihotra*" is the same in all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the *Sādharmya* (similarity) is identical, the action is one. For example, the similarity of the *Agnihotra* is the same in all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the *Vaishamya* (dissimilarity) is absent, the action is one. For example, there is no dissimilarity in the *Agnihotra* across all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the *Sādhāraṇya* (commonality) is established, the action is one. For example, the commonality of the *Agnihotra* is established in all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the *Asādhāraṇya* (uniqueness) is absent, the action is one. For example, there is no uniqueness in the *Agnihotra* across all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the *Pratyaya* (cognition/recognition) is identical, the action is one. For example, the recognition of the *Agnihotra* is the same in all branches. Therefore, the action is one. Also, because the *Pratyabhijñāna* (recognition) is identical, the action is one. For example, the recognition

Regarding the phrase "consisting of twelve potsherds," due to the difference in form, the statement concerning the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) is studied by some, while it is not studied by others; thus, there is a distinction based on the difference in the dharma consisting of the giving of the horse-killer (*aśvaghāsa*). Consequently, there is a specific distinction because a rite prescribed in one recensional branch (*śākhā*) is not prescribed elsewhere.

Furthermore, due to the practice of the characteristic of hearing [scriptural texts], because one hears censures regarding both the "risen" (*udita*) and "unrisen" (*anudita*) forms of ritual action, because it is impossible to combine all the auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) prescribed in every branch of the Veda, and because of the difference in statements of completion— where some say the rite is finished in one place and others in another— and because separate expiations (*prāyaścitta*) are prescribed for the "risen" and "unrisen" oblations.

The Upahavya is an Agniṣṭoma sacrifice characterized by the Rathantara Sāman; however, in one Śākhā it is heard that "the Upahavya sacrifice has the Bṛhat Sāman," while in another [Śākhā] it is heard otherwise. This is because of the statement regarding different purposes for the forms of the Rathantara and Bṛhat Sāmans, and because of the difference in context (prakaraṇāntara) due to the form of the other Śākhā.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is argued that the ritual action differs for each branch (*śākhā*), otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of contradicting the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that establishes such difference.

However, this being reached, [the established conclusion is as follows]: although the injunction of the ritual action is understood through the previously mentioned reasons such as repetition (*punarukti*), the distinction between those actions remains unproven; thus, within a single branch...
Since it is established that what is prescribed in one recension is a provision for another person [in another],

and because there is no lack of logical consistency (*anyathānupapatti*) [regarding this], there is no difference in the ritual acts (*karmabheda*) among them in the present case; therefore, [the act belongs] to one and the same person within one and the same recension.
Just as the injunction of the *agnihotra* and other rites for another person is purposeful, so too here,
the *agnihotra* and other rites taught in various recensions (*śākhās*) constitute one and the same rite for another person.

Furthermore, it has been established as a settled conclusion (*siddhānta*) that because [the rite] is prescribed again, there is no difference in the action (*karmabheda*), but rather it is one and the same; and this principle of "recognition across all Vedāntas" (*sarvavedāntapratyaya*) has been thus described in the third chapter, first section of the *Uttaratantre* (the Brahma-sūtras) in the aphorism: "There is recognition across all Vedāntas because of the non-difference of the injunction and so forth."
When the doubt arises as to whether the hearing of all true scriptures and so forth is not to be performed or indeed is to be performed—

because there is no evidence for Brahman being known through the methods taught in every branch (*śākhā*), and because one hears different meanings for it in each branch, such as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" in one branch— the [following is established].

Since it is understood that a particular meaning is to be known by the students of that specific recension (śākhā) alone according to the method stated in that recension, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) arises that one need not practice the hearing of all the authentic scriptures for the sake of that [single] meaning. In response to this, [the author states: "The description of differences in meaning for each recension is like the statement of differences in meaning within a single recension."

Because it possesses scope [as a valid inquiry] through its nature as a refutation of objections, a distinction [of meaning], a restatement, and so forth, there is no lack of differentiation in its meaning.
And by the Śruti: "The Supreme Lord is indeed to be sought after by means of all the Vedas; He cannot be realized by those who know only a small portion of the Vedas.
Therefore, one desiring liberation, having studied all the Vedas and reflected upon them, should desire to know Him. Thus says the scripture.
And according to the Smṛti: "Having understood the Vedas along with the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, Yuktikās, and Pañcarātras, Viṣṇu is to be known, and not otherwise"— thus,
in accordance with the manner declared in all the Vedas.

33) Furthermore, since it is understood that Brahman alone is the object to be known, it has been established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that for that purpose, one must practice the hearing of all the authentic scriptures and so forth. For this very reason, the principle of the uniformity of the way of approach (*gatisāmānyanyāya*) also applies.

In the *Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa* of the first pāda of the first adhyāya, within the *guṇasūtra* "on account of the uniformity of approach" (*gatisāmānyāt*), it is demonstrated that Brahman is primarily the subject matter of the purport of all the scriptures. Regarding the doubt as to whether this is appropriate for Brahman or not, [the sūtra cites] such scriptural passages as "from which words turn back" and "without sound, without touch," concerning Brahman.

Because it is understood that [the Brahmasūtra] has something to be expressed, and because there is no evidence for Brahman alone being the subject matter when well-known Vedic branches are available;

and because even something else might be presented as the cause in those well-known branches which are not studied nowadays—it is argued in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that it is not appropriate for Brahman to be "the source of all scriptures" for that purpose. To this, [the Sūtra replies]: "Higher than the high... (*parātparaṃ*).

Since Brahman is understood to be the object of vision from such scriptural passages as "He sees the Person dwelling in the city" and "One should see the Self in the very Self," and since Brahman— whose nature is known solely through the Word (śabda), as established by texts such as "The Vedas indeed make Him known" and "The Person known through the Upanishads"— is not accessible through perception (pratyakṣa) or inference (anumāna), [it must be known through scripture alone].
Because it is inexpressible due to its connection [with other attributes], and because no other mode of operation is possible for it, it cannot be inexpressible in the absence of such a possibility;

furthermore, since there is no lack of well-known scriptural texts that indicate its inexpressibility—such as "It is inexpressible" (avācyam tat) and so forth—these scriptures have scope as they intend to convey that it is entirely beyond the reach of speech. Thus, all the Vedas and the aforementioned arguments are authoritative regarding Brahman.

They reveal that supreme knowledge as indeed one alone; there is no contradiction. For this reason, it is said in all the Vedas and likewise in the Itihāsas: "The goal which all the Vedas proclaim" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.15), and "He into whom all names enter" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.11.21).
Page 34.

All the Vedas, all sounds, are but a single utterance; therefore they call him "the Hundred-versed One," though he is truly this very one. By all the Vedas I alone am to be known, the primordial cause of all effects, the supreme object of speech before words themselves.
In the Vedas, the Rāmāyaṇa, the Purāṇas, and likewise in the Mahābhārata,
Viṣṇu is sung of everywhere— in the beginning, in the end, and in the middle.
As many syllables of the Veda as are recited by the twice-born, [so many merits are gained].
"There are as many names of Hari as there are; no deliberation is required here.

Through such Śruti and Smṛti passages, it is made known that the one Supreme Brahman, known as Śrī Nārāyaṇa alone, is the object of knowledge for all the Vedas by way of primary signification (*mukhya-vṛttyā*). Thus, the status of Brahman as the source of the scriptures (*śāstrayonitva*) is established in its primary sense.
It has been established as a settled conclusion (*siddhānta*) that this is indeed logical. Thus, by means of the principles of the aforementioned topical discussions (*adhikaraṇa*),

once it is proven that all the Vedas have a single object and that there is a unity of meaning which is the intended purport of the power of all Vedic words, then— by the very logic of the "goat and the sacrificial animal" (*chāgapaśu*)— the Fourth State (*turīya*) is non-different from Śiva.

It is logical that the purport of all the Vedas is that the specific supreme reality known as Nārāyaṇa alone is the most excellent of all and the cause of the birth and so forth of the entire universe. Now, [one might object]: "This is not firmly rooted, because there is no evidence for the non-difference between the Fourth (Turīya) Śiva and Nārāyaṇa. To this, [it is replied]: "In that regard..."

The means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) must be either perception (pratyakṣa), inference (anumāna), or scripture (āgama). It cannot be the first [perception]. Even there, it would have to be either the perception of Brahmā and others, or the perception of people like us. It cannot be the former. For regarding the perception of Brahmā and others, [the question arises: "Are these two distinct, being the substrata of contradictory attributes such as Śiva and Nārāyaṇa?"
The latter [alternative] is not tenable (p.
35), because our perception—which does not have the mere nature of that [object] as its object—cannot possibly have its difference as its object. It is not...

The second [point] is that there is no evidence to establish non-difference between the two; moreover, by the principle of "different words" (*śabdāntara*) and others, the very difference between Śiva and Nārāyaṇa is understood. For instance, in the second chapter, second section, under the heading "Different Words" (*śabdāntarādhikaraṇa*), regarding the passage "he sacrifices," "he gives," and "he offers oblations," the meanings of the verbal roots—namely sacrifice, giving, and offering—are distinct.

In that very same section concerning qualities (*guṇādhikaraṇa*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) was reached by arguing that since verbal roots differ due to their distinctness, even verbal suffixes (*ākhyātapada*) become different words from one another; thus, because the meaning of many roots is not expressed simultaneously as a single unit, [the action] is not enjoined. Having established this, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) was reached: because there is a difference in suffixes for each individual root, it is precisely distinct *bhāvanās* qualified by the respective meanings of those various roots that are enjoined. Thus it was concluded in that very same section on qualities.

In the first festival of the Cāturmāsya, called the Vaiśvadeva, one pours curdled milk into heated milk; that is the *āmikṣā* dedicated to the Viśvedevas. Regarding the formula "to the Vājins, the whey (*vājina*)": since a sacrifice involving the *āmikṣā* is inferred from the relationship between the substance and the deity, the Viśvedevas, who partake of the *āmikṣā* as the substance in that sacrifice, [receive] the *vāja*, which is the *āmikṣā*.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is argued that by the etymological derivation "those for whom food (*anna*) consists of *vāja* (grain/food)," the dative-termined word *vājibhyaḥ* refers back to those very [deities] already mentioned, and the quality (*guṇa*) of having *vāja* as their food is enjoined for them; thus, it is not a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*). This is because, once the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice has arisen, it is already occupied by the quality established through its etymological derivation, and there is no room for the additional quality of having *vāja* as food.

Because of the impossibility of [the action] being established [as the same], and for that very reason because the word *vāja* refers to a different deity, it has been concluded as a final doctrine (*siddhānta*) that this is a different ritual (*karmāntara*) due to the distinction of the deity alone. For this same reason, it was considered in that very context, in the section on "difference of context" (*prakaraṇāntarādhikaraṇa*), regarding the *Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana*.

It is heard [in scripture]: "Having performed the *upasads*, one offers the *agnihotra* for a month. In that case, because the word *agnihotra* brings to mind the obligatory *agnihotra*, it is simply the quality of the month-long duration that is enjoined therein; it is not a separate ritual action.

Having established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is stated: "having performed the *upasad*s. Since the *upasad* sacrifice is absent in the obligatory *agnihotra*, the injunction "he offers the *agnihotra*" would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) if it were to apply to both [the obligatory and the optional] after having performed the *upasad*s—because the qualities consisting of different place, time, and occasion would have to be combined.

And because it does not refer back to the previous ritual action, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that another distinct ritual action named *agnihotra*, qualified by two additional attributes, is being enjoined according to the context (*prakaraṇa*). And thus, by that same principle, [the same applies] to names such as Nārāyaṇa,
Vāsudeva, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and Nṛsiṃha.
Furthermore, because names such as Śiva, Śambhu, Rudra, and Maheśvara are distinct from one another,

there are differences in qualities such as being the Lord of Śrī Lakṣmī, bearing the conch, discus, and other emblems, resembling the rising sun, residing in the Ocean of Milk, and so forth, as well as having Umā as a companion, possessing three eyes, and having a blue throat.

Furthermore, because qualities such as being the wielder of the trident (*śūlapāṇitva*) and residing on Kailāsa are absolutely distinct, and because Śiva and Nārāyaṇa are taught in entirely different branches (*śākhā*), as well as due to their being treated in separate contexts (*prakaraṇāntara*), it is logical that there is indeed a difference between them. For this very reason, the third [alternative] is not tenable; therefore, regarding the scriptures known as other branches (*śākhāntara-āgama*):

If it is argued that the manifestation of the identity of their views is utterly untenable— because the distinction between those two [traditions] is easily established through differences in terminology, qualities, context, and so forth, and because there is thus no identity between them—
we reply to this as follows: first, regarding the direct perception of Brahmā and the others...

Because its validity is possible on the grounds that it has as its object the identity [of Śiva] with the nature of the non-existent fourth state (turiya), which is distinct from Nārāyaṇa; for the direct perception of great beings [is such], as in the case of [scriptural passages like] "one only, without a second," and so forth.

Because it is impossible for [perception] to have as its object two things that are both contrary to scripture and yet supreme, the perception "these two are distinct," even though it has as its object the difference between Viṣṇu and Kāryarudra,
lacks the quality of having as its object the difference from Śiva; this is because Śiva and Nārāyaṇa are one.

Furthermore, because the attributes of those [entities] reside in one place, there is no contradiction in the form of non-coexistence (*sahānavasthā*). Moreover, inference (*anumāna*) is also a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in this regard; for instance: Nārāyaṇa is non-different from the fourth *Śiva*, because he is denotable by the syllable *Oṃ* (in its entirety), because he is denotable by the *mātrās* [of the *Oṃ*], because he is the fourth state (*turīya*), and because he is the progenitor of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the others.

The state of being denotable by the term "Bhagavat," which possesses the manifestations beginning with Brahmā, consists of oneness and so forth; this is because it possesses those unique attributes (asādhāraṇa-dharma) [of the Lord]. For whatever possesses the unique attributes of something is non-different from it—just as Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others, or Indra, Arjuna, and others—such is the possible application of the syllogism. Nor should it be said that the reason (hetu) is unestablished (asiddha), for those who indeed...
Salutations again and again to that Śrī Rāmacandra, the Blessed One, who is Oṃkāra;
salutations again and again to that Śrī Rāmacandra, the Blessed One, who is the fourth measure of meaning, namely Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ;
salutations again and again to that Śrī Rāmacandra, the Blessed One, who is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśvara. Thus.

In the Rāmopaniṣad: "Salutations again and again to that which is indeed Śrī Nṛsiṃha, the divine Lord, and who is Brahmā; salutations again and again to that which is indeed Śrī Nṛsiṃha, the divine Lord, and who is Viṣṇu;
salutations again and again to that which is indeed Nṛsiṃha, the divine Lord, and who is Maheśvara. Thus it is said.

In the *Nṛsiṃha-pūrvatāpanīya*: "By means of the king of mantras consisting of the nine syllables of Nārasiṃha, one should know the Fourth (Turiya). For this [mantra] illuminates the Self. Thus it is said in the *Uttaratāpanīya*: "Indeed, there was once only Nārāyaṇa...
"There was neither Brahmā nor Śaṅkara;

there were no Agniṣṭomas, nor heaven and earth," and so forth, in the Mahopaniṣad. Then: "Indeed, the Puruṣa Nārāyaṇa desired, 'May I create offspring. From Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā is born; from Nārāyaṇa, Rudra [is born]."
Thus it is said: "Now Rudra is Nārāyaṇa; Brahmā is Nārāyaṇa; Śiva is Nārāyaṇa. Furthermore:
"The eternal, stainless, untainted, changeless, ineffable, pure, divine One is Nārāyaṇa alone—there is no second whatsoever. He who knows this becomes Viṣṇu indeed. And so it is said.
"Brahmā, Śiva, Indra, the immortal, the supreme, the self-ruling," according to the Nārāyaṇopaniṣad;

"In the beginning, there was nothing whatsoever here; these creatures are born rootless and without support; the divine, singular God is Nārāyaṇa," according to the Subālopaniṣad—and by other such repeated and forthcoming scriptural and traditional (smṛti) authorities.
Since the previously mentioned unique attributes are determined to reside in Nārāyaṇa, there is no lack of establishment of the reason's own nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*); therefore,
for the sake of establishing that Nṛsiṃha and Rāmacandra— who are incarnations of Nārāyaṇa— are denotable by the letter *e*, they must be denotable by the *mātrā*.

Since these attributes are established by the logic of *kaimutika-nyāya* (the principle of "how much more so") in Nārāyaṇa— who is a non-differentiated portion of Him— by such names as "the possessor of portions of the glory beginning with Brahmā" and "the one denoted by the term Bhagavat," it is Śrī Nārāyaṇa alone who is directly [the locus] of them in the *Mahopaniṣad* and other scriptures.

Furthermore, because of the traditional teaching (āmnāna) regarding the dharmas, one should not argue that there is a distinction here between Śiva and Nārāyaṇa based on the presence or absence of being the progenitor of Viṣṇu;
for it is said: "Subsequently, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara were born from Māyā."
Śrī, Bhū, and Durgā— these three were the forms of Ramā.
Then, through union with Viṣṇu, at the end of a Parārdha, she became golden.
"O Goddess Salileṇḍa, wherein all this is placed"—

thus, because of other statements such as those in the *Varāha Purāṇa* stating that it was "created by Vāsudeva within Māyā," there is the possibility of birth in the form of manifestation even for the incarnation of the Blessed Lord known as Viṣṇu; therefore, [this applies] everywhere.

Since Viṣṇu’s manifestation is established as his primary birth, and since there is no contradiction in the absence of a mention of him alongside Brahmā, Rudra, and others in the context of that primary birth, and because the application of the term "birth" to Viṣṇu is justified by the analogy of the "umbrella-bearer," as seen in passages such as "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra— they are all brought forth."
Furthermore, because the *Rāmatāpanīya* and *Nṛsiṃhatāpanīya* Upaniṣads explicitly state that He possesses the three forms as His manifestations (*vibhūti*),

and because the cited scriptural passages declare His status as the Fourth (*turīya*) precisely by virtue of being the progenitor of Brahmā, Rudra, and the rest— thereby making known the procreative nature of both [Brahmā and Śiva]— any distinction between the two would contradict the fact that there is only one Supreme Lord (*sarveśvara*).

Just as in the cases of Rāma, Nṛsiṃha, and others, it is logical that even Turīya Śiva—who exists in the form of an incarnation of Nārāyaṇa—is non-different from Nārāyaṇa; therefore, inference is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the non-difference of Nārāyaṇa from Turīya Śiva. As for what was stated regarding their difference based on "different words" (*śabdāntara*) and so forth, that is not the case with different words and the rest.

Because it indicates nothing but disparity; for instance, in the *Śabdāntara* section, since the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is already occupied by the respective meanings of each root due to the difference between roots and suffixes, it is impossible for that [force] to be delimited by the meaning of another root; therefore, there is a distinction in the efficient force as well, and from that distinction, [there follows the distinction] among sacrifice, giving, and oblation.
The distinction has been established here because of the disparity in that logic due to the absence of [terms such as] *dhātu* and *pada*.

Furthermore, although there is a distinction among sacrifice (*yāga*), giving (*dāna*), and oblation (*homa*) because they are characterized by their own respective unique sets of constituent parts (*aṅgakalāpa*),
in the present case, [the term applies] to both.
40) Furthermore, because it has been stated that a distinction between the two is impossible due to the unity of the collection of uncommon attributes;
moreover, according to the principle of the section concerning different recensions (*śākhāntarādhikaraṇa*), [the rites are distinct] due to differences in name, form, and ritual duty.

Since the absence of difference has been stated [previously], it is also appropriate here that despite the difference in name and so forth between Śiva and Nārāyaṇa, there is indeed no difference in their essential reality; for the disparity in that logic is extremely clear, and because the two qualities can be included through the identity of both, [this applies] here.

Since the aforementioned and yet-to-be-stated means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) exist in their non-difference, it is possible for the principle of "distinct words" (*śabdāntara*) and so forth to have as its object the absence of a sublater (*bādhaka*). By this, the disparity between the principles of the *guṇādhikaraṇa* and the *prakaraṇāntarādhikaraṇa* is also established; therein, scripture (*āgama*) is also a means of valid cognition for non-difference.

For it is possible for the non-difference between Turīya Śiva and Nārāyaṇa— which is obtained through the "otherwise-unaccountability" (anyathānupapatti) of cited Vedic passages— to possess the status of being Vedic; this is because even the *apūrva* (unseen potency), which is obtained through the otherwise-unaccountability of the causal relationship between the sacrifice and heaven in the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," is accepted as being Vedic.

Furthermore, in the *Maitreyopaniṣad*, after introducing the meaning of the word "para" (the Supreme) by stating that "His foremost bodies are declared to be Brahmā, Rudra, and Viṣṇu; [if one were to say] they proceed to inequality,

that would be by means of something other than Him," and having subsequently described their status as His foremost bodies with the words "He alone, being one, has become threefold," it is stated even further on:
In this statement, their non-difference from the fourth reality—which is the referent of the word "supreme" (*para*)—is described as being exclusive (*sāvadhāraṇa*).

Here, one must state that according to the aforementioned authorities, the non-difference of the Fourth from Viṣṇu is primary (*mukhya*), whereas the non-difference from Brahmā and Rudra is secondary (*gauṇa*); for otherwise, in the absence of even mere non-difference, the authority of the scriptural word would be undermined. Furthermore, from this...
Thus it is clearly stated in the Śrīrāmopaniṣad (p. 41):
"Salutations again and again to him who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra, who is the Blessed One, and who is Maheśvara. He who indeed...

Salutations again and again to that Śrī Rāmacandra, who is the Blessed One and Mahādeva, the source of the earth and the intermediate space; to him, salutations again and again. To that Śrī Rāmacandra, who is the Blessed One—Oṃ, salutations to the Blessed Vāsudeva—who is Mahāviṣṇu, the source of the earth and the intermediate space; to him, salutations again and again. To that Śrī Rāmacandra, who is the Blessed One...

And because of the scriptural hearing of the non-difference between the fourth Śiva—who is the incarnation of Nārāyaṇa and is denoted by the terms Maheśvara and Mahādeva—and the primordial form of Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, and others, as expressed in such passages as: "Obeisance, obeisance to You, whose essence consists of the single flavor of existence, consciousness, and bliss, and who are the worlds Bhūḥ and Bhuvaḥ. For this very reason...
In the Purāṇas, which serve as supplements to this [Veda], it is revealed that the Fourth (Turīya) is indeed Nārāyaṇa; for instance:

"Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas are the qualities of Prakṛti; joined with these, the one Supreme Person here assumes the names Hari, Viriñci, and Hara for the sake of the world's maintenance and other functions. Among those, the auspicious goals of men are indeed attained through His seven forms."
Thus it is said in the *Bhāgavata*: "In the same way,
the one Lord Janārdana alone, assuming the names of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, undergoes the states of creation, maintenance, and dissolution."

Thus, in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*, having introduced the practice of austerity in this manner: "I shall take refuge in Him by whom the Lord of the Universe [created] offspring equal to Himself; may He grant me such progeny," he reflected.

Having thus stated his desire for a fruit, and then, while Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra were present there for the granting of the boon, after the performance of services such as praise and prostration, Atri addressed them with this question: "O Blessed Ones, who here is the one Lord who is manifold and the primary source?"
How is it that you have come here to procreate within the mind, you who are far removed from the minds of embodied beings? (p. 42)
"Speak! Be gracious! O Great One, there is wonder in me here.
"Just as you have formed this resolve, it must be exactly so and not otherwise;
for we are yours, O Brahmin, in accordance with your resolve and that which you meditate upon."
Thus, following the introduction of their reply, it is stated likewise in the words of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata:
"Brahmā, Dakṣa, and the others, as well as Time and all living beings—
these are the manifestations (vibhūtayaḥ) of Hari, the causes of the creation of the world."

Viṣṇu, Manu and the others, time, and likewise all living beings— these are the manifestations of Viṣṇu, who is the instrumental cause of maintenance. Rudra, Kālāntaka and the rest, and indeed all creatures [are his manifestations].
"These manifestations of Janārdana exist for the sake of the fourfold dissolution," according to the statement in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*.
I bow to the one seated in Vṛndāvana, the abode of bliss for Indirā,
the younger brother of Indra (Upendra), the embodiment of intense compassion, the supreme Lord of ultimate bliss.
I worship that primordial God, whose portions are the world-protectors known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, who is pure consciousness, stainless, and supreme.
Thus, in the *Bṛhannāradīya*:
"Those fools with minds fixed on fallacious reasoning who perceive me or Brahmā as other than Viṣṇu are then cooked in the hells."
And those fools and evil-minded ones who perceive me as distinct from Hari,
or as equal to Brahmā— for them, the sin is equal to that of killing a fetus.
And thus: "In this way, both you and I are indeed one within the Self of the Universe; we are the single cause of this world, though we appear established as distinct. (p. 43)
Whatever was given by you has been given entirely by me;
O Śaṅkara, you ought to perceive yourself as non-different from me.

In all the aforementioned scriptural passages— including the *Rāmatāpanīya*, *Nṛsiṃhatāpanīya*, *Mahopaniṣad*, *Nārāyaṇopaniṣad*, *Subālopaniṣad*, and others, as well as other Purāṇic statements such as "Persons whose selves are deluded by ignorance have a perception of difference"— the Fourth [State] is indeed present.
The reality of an object is determined to be of the very nature of Nārāyaṇa;

therefore, when in both human and non-human scriptures Śiva and Nārāyaṇa are described as being the Fourth State (turīya) and the Supreme (para), these descriptions indicate nothing other than the non-difference between the two.

There is no inconsistency whatsoever. In this regard, regarding the cited Bhāgavata statement and other such declarations such as "they see something other than Viṣṇu," the statements concerning non-difference everywhere refer to the non-difference of the fourth Śiva from the inner ruler (antaryāmin) of Kārya-Rudra and Brahmā; thus, there is no inconsistency, as established by the aforementioned and forthcoming authorities.

Since the non-difference of Turīya-Śiva from Nārāyaṇa is beyond dispute, and since there is no disagreement regarding Turīya-Śiva— who is an incarnation of Nārāyaṇa— also being the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of both,
it follows from the statements cited in the Bhāṣya that the Lord, in all His incarnations, is sometimes an incarnation of Śiva.

Because there is no dispute [to the contrary], and because in works such as the *Madhvavijaya* it is stated that the *liṅgas* of Ananteśvara, Rāmeśvara, and others are forms of Nārāyaṇa; furthermore, this will be established later by means of the logic of scriptural authority (*śruti*), indicative marks (*liṅga*), and other proofs within both the earlier and later Tantras, regarding the fourth state of Nārāyaṇa.
Because it is possible to establish his non-difference from Śiva; for instance, in the Kaivalya Upaniṣad (p.
44), immediately after the passage "He is Brahmā, he is Śiva, he is Indra, the supreme self-ruler," it continues: "He alone is Viṣṇu, he is Prāṇa, he..."

In the passage, "Kāla is his fire; the moon is his," it is stated that he is indeed Viṣṇu. By this scriptural statement of exclusive grammatical coreferentiality (*sāvadhāraṇa-sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the non-difference of the referent of the term Viṣṇu from the Fourth Śiva (*turīya-śiva*) is determined. Nor should it be argued that this non-difference is merely secondary (*amukhya*), as is the case with Brahmā, Rudra, and others.

In every passage that establishes the three forms, since Viṣṇu— who is recited as equal to Brahmā and the others— is heard in a restrictive grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the abode of immortality (amṛtasthāna), there must necessarily be an intention toward their primary non-difference;
otherwise, [the text would be inconsistent].

Because a restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) intended to exclude connection with anything else is untenable; for this very reason, in the *Pūrvatantra*, in the fifth chapter (*pāda*) of the section on "Subsidiaries" (*śeṣalakṣaṇa*), in the topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) beginning with "And because of the scriptural statement, there should be consumption [of the cup] for each ritual act," regarding those cups such as the Aindravāyava which are prescribed by the injunction "In the Jyotiṣṭoma,
one takes the Aindravāyava [cup]," etc.,...

Regarding the consumption of Soma—which is prescribed as a ritual disposal (*pratipatti*) by the rule "having gone back to the assembly hall, they consume the Soma"—there arises a doubt: is there a double consumption of the Aindravāyava cup, or is it not repeated? Since the Soma juice to be refined is a single entity, the refinement characterized by consumption must likewise occur only once.

Regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that [the consumption] is to be performed [once], the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the consumption of the *aindravāyava* cup must be performed twice; for it has been concluded that "he pronounces the *vaṣaṭ* call twice for this [cup]," and thus by the scriptural statement of the number two, the *aindravāyava* consumption is to be carried out twice.

In that very same *Śeṣalakṣaṇa*, in the sixth chapter (*pāda*), under the section titled "In a sacrifice consisting of a single *ṛc*, [the rules] are like those for Vedic study" (*ekarcasthānayajñeṣu syur svādhyāyavat*), it is stated that in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice, the *Rathantara* and other [sāmans]...

Regarding the doubt as to whether the *stotrīya* Sāmans should be sung to a single verse (*ṛc*) at the time of the ritual sacrifice, or rather to a triplet of verses (*tṛca*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that they should be sung to a single verse at the time of the sacrifice, just as they were sung to a single verse during the period of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*). However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that "one Sāman is performed upon a triplet of verses for the purpose of a *stotra*," because of the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) regarding the *tṛca*.
It has been established that those [verses] are to be sung to a *tṛca* (a triad of verses) at the time of the sacrifice.

Furthermore, since it is possible to determine that the Fourth Śiva (Turīya-Śiva) is an incarnation of Nārāyaṇa by means of the multitude of scriptural statements cited above that indicate non-difference, one might argue that Brahmā must also be an incarnation of Him, as non-difference from Him is also heard in scripture. This, however, should not be said; for the difference between those two [Brahmā and Śiva] is established by many authoritative means of knowledge.
Because that non-difference must be understood solely through the "umbrella-bearer" logic (*chatrinyāya*), for where there is no non-difference whatsoever,
there is no scope for the umbrella-bearer logic; since in the *Nārāyaṇopaniṣad*, Rudra is spoken of as an effect in the passage "From Nārāyaṇa,
Rudra was born," and then [later] in the statement "The three-eyed, trident-handed Person was born."

This is because the words *śūlapāṇi* (the trident-bearer) and *puruṣa* (the person) must necessarily refer to Śiva, the fourth incarnation of Nārāyaṇa. Furthermore, in the commentary on the *Guṇasūtra* in the Vaiśvānara section—specifically under the sūtras "If it be said that [Vaiśvānara] is not [Brahman] because of the word and so forth, and because of his abiding within; we say no, because of the teaching of seeing him as such, because of impossibility, and because they also read him as a Person"—it is established.
Then, one should worship the golden Self, subtler than the subtle, higher than the high, the all-pervading Hari;

[worship Him] as the universal name, the universal action, the universal gender, the universal quality, the universal desire, the universal duty, and the universal form. One worships this very Self, the universal Hari, with reverence. For him, in all worlds—

Because of the instruction to perceive Him alone through various names, marks, and so forth— expressed in the *Mahopaniṣad* and other scriptures cited in the Commentary as "He has freedom of movement among all beings and all Vedas," and by the statement "He is of all forms" which establishes that Nārāyaṇa is the source of all incarnations— it follows that Śiva, too, is an incarnation of Nārāyaṇa.

59) Since there is no deviation from established tenets (*apasiddhānta*) because [the subject] has been established as valid, and since it is untenable for the word "all-forms" (*sarvarūpa*) to mean non-difference with everything, one must state that it refers exclusively to all incarnations (*avatāra*).
Furthermore, because it is necessarily the case that the entire form [of the Lord] as expressed in conjunction with words such as "all" (sarva) must refer to all incarnations;
and since there is no contradiction in Nārāyaṇa, who is the source of all incarnations, appearing in the form of Śiva at some point in time,
[this applies to] the Ananteśvara, Rāmeśvara, Liṅga, and so forth.
Furthermore, because we accept that the glorious Nārāyaṇa is the presiding deity [of the Liṅga],

and because the *Tantrasāra* states, "The two spheres (the eyes) belong to Viṣṇu, while the third is proclaimed as his," it must be asserted that the Lord’s abiding in the Liṅga consists precisely in his having the form of a Liṅga composed of light (*tejomaya*).
"He is of the nature of Brahman in Brahman, and of the nature of Śiva established in Śiva," according to the Smṛti cited in the Bhāṣya.
And in the *Tīrthaprabandha*, in the *Rāmanāthastuti* composed by the ascetic Varadarāja:
"The enemy of Time (Śiva), who is expert in granting desired boons, whose body is illuminated by the glorious mass of matted hair..."

I bow to Rāmeśvara, established by Rāma, whose form was assumed for the sake of Rāma. Likewise: "At the end of the kalpa, Rāma, who is skilled in shattering ten million sins upon the earth, indeed worshipped Hara—the moon, the destroyer of gods, brahmins, and asuras—who had assumed a stone linga. Furthermore: "He worshipped the stone linga..."

This is because, through the words beginning with "Hari," it must be stated that Śiva— the Lord who is worshipped by Rāma— is indeed an incarnation of Nārāyaṇa who is non-different from himself; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the preeminent work of determination composed by the Great Sage (Vyāsa) would produce false knowledge.

Furthermore, in the *Bhāgavatapurāṇa*, the *Rāmāyaṇa*, and other texts, the worship of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the Blessed Lord Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others is indeed taught through such passages as, "That supreme light which is non-different and non-dual," and so forth.

In the *Madhvavijaya* as well, it is stated: "He resorted to the serpent-couch [of Viṣṇu] for a period of twelve years, and likewise sought refuge in Nārāyaṇa, the head of the community (kulapati)"; and by such passages as "He offered salutations to Viṣṇu, Śrī Rāmanātha," and so forth, the fact that the two liṅgas of Ananteśvara and Rāmeśvara have Nārāyaṇa as their presiding deity is declared.

It is appropriate to state that these two [Viṣṇu and Śiva] are respectively an incarnation of Nārāyaṇa and the locus (adhiṣṭhāna) of Śiva. Therefore, all these collections of scriptural, traditional, and logical statements harmonize by showing that the reality which is the form of the Fourth Śiva is essentially Nārāyaṇa and not something distinct from Him;
thus, everything is faultless. And so, this is the conclusion: [the definition of Brahman as] "from whose birth... and so forth.

The single Brahman, called Īśvara, which is described in the Sūtras as being variegated by *māyā*, at one time in the cosmic age, assuming the form of Nārāyaṇa, creates Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the others, thereby becoming the cause of the entire universe. At another time in the cosmic age, that same Brahman, having assumed the form of Śiva, creates Brahmā and the others.

He becomes the cause of the entire world. "That Nārāyaṇa is the supreme one to be meditated upon by those seeking liberation from this bond of karma"; such statements as "Nārāyaṇa is the great object of knowledge" are devoted to the worship of Nārāyaṇa alone for the sake of liberation. He is the cause; He is to be meditated upon, endowed with all sovereign powers.

"Having meditated upon Śambhu, the Lord of All, who dwells in the midst of space, the Supreme Lord and Master, three-eyed, blue-throated, and profoundly peaceful— the sage goes to that source of all beings, the witness of everything, beyond darkness. Such passages as these are devoted to the worship of Śiva alone for the sake of liberation.

By those residing in the fourth stage of life (turīyāśrama), Nārāyaṇa alone is generally to be worshipped; for this very reason, Śaṅkara’s Bhāṣya cites the *parāmarśa* [of Jaimini]: "Jaimini [thinks there is no injunction] because there is no scriptural injunction, and they prescribe [only] the state of being a recluse. (p. 61)

Thus, in this section, it has been determined that for those who take refuge in the Fourth State (*turyāśramin*), there arises direct, non-conceptual knowledge of the attributeless Brahman by means of the knowledge of the qualified Brahman. Furthermore, because [this work] was composed with great care at the very beginning of the *Viṣṇusahasranāmabhāṣya*,

those scriptural passages concerning the birth of Viṣṇu— which might suggest equality with Brahmā and others— are to be understood as referring to his incarnations (*avatāra*), such as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.

Since Viṣṇu is conditioned by *māyā* in which pure *sattva* predominates, he lacks identity with Brahmā and others; therefore, such passages must be interpreted only in a secondary sense, according to the "umbrella-bearer" analogy (*chatrinyāya*). Furthermore, statements that appear to censure Viṣṇu and Śiva one another must be interpreted according to the principle of "irony" (*nahi nindā nyāya*).

Passages such as "In the beginning, Hiraṇyagarbha arose," "Agni was the first among the deities," "These two are indeed kings of the deities," and "All these beings arise from space alone"— all such causal statements are to be interpreted as referring exclusively to either one of these two. For it is only these two that possess the status of being the cause.

Because there is an abundance of practitioners [who follow this path], the path in the established doctrine of Śaṅkarācārya is that Brahman is indeed one alone, consisting of the Fourth State (Turiya), Śiva, and Nārāyaṇa.
However, in the system of Rāmānujācārya, their non-difference must be explained in two ways. Regarding that, in the statement "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*):

Regarding the reality of the two terms, *jīva* and *brahman*, just as in Viśiṣṭādvaita, one must accept the non-difference between the fourth [state] Śiva and Nārāyaṇa in the form of qualified non-duality (*viśiṣṭādvaita*). Nor should it be argued that, unlike statements such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), no statement expressing the non-difference of these two is seen here; for [the scripture states]: "Brahmā is born from Nārāyaṇa."
The cause of the universe, designated as Nārāyaṇa and characterized by subtle consciousness and matter, is that which is taught by such scriptural statements as "From Nārāyaṇa, Rudra is born.

In the phrase "is to be meditated upon" (*dhyeya*), the term "cause" (*kāraṇa*) refers back [to Śiva]; thus, since it is possible to enjoin the non-difference of Brahman whose body is Śiva by means of the statement "Śambhu, endowed with all sovereignty, the Lord of all, in the midst of the ether," even in the *Kaivalyopaniṣad*, starting with "the lotus of the heart" (*hṛtpuṇḍarīka*)...
There is no contradiction, because the passage concludes with "the wonderful, formless consciousness-bliss" (cidānandamarūpamadbhutam) by way of restating the supreme reality known as Nārāyaṇa,

and then proceeds with "accompanied by Umā" (umāsahāyam) and so forth, intending to convey the meaning that one meditates upon Him as having Śiva as His body and thus goes to the Blessed Lord. In this manner, all scriptural passages concerning the worship of Śiva [are likewise consistent].

The statements such as "Śiva alone was indeed" are to be interpreted as being intent upon qualified non-duality (*viśiṣṭādvaita*). This is done so that the scriptural passages establishing Śiva's causality—such as "Nārāyaṇa alone existed"—are not contradicted by those unconditioned causal statements; rather, they refer to Nārāyaṇa whose body is Śiva.
These [scriptural passages] are to be interpreted solely as having the causality [of Brahman] as their primary purport for the sake of the meditation on Viśiṣṭādvaita;

for it is precisely this meaning that is logical, as it serves as the means to attain the supreme human goal (puruṣārtha). Alternatively, the supreme reality called Nārāyaṇa is non-different from the fourth state (turīya) Śiva; thus, He is denoted by such terms as "Śiva" occurring in the causal statements.

The meaning must be accepted as follows: the fourth state (*turīya*) is indeed of the nature of Nārāyaṇa, and it is not therefore empty [of him]. This is so in order to avoid contradicting the unambiguous primary scriptural statement: "In the beginning, there was indeed only Nārāyaṇa; neither Brahmā nor Śaṅkara existed. Furthermore, [it is for the sake of] this very Puruṣa, [who thinks], "Come now, let me enter all these... [and so forth].

Since it is necessary that Nārāyaṇa— who is the very self of the fourth state (*turīya*)— must be the referent of all names such as Śiva found in the causal statements, by virtue of scriptural passages beginning with "they enter into the names," the statement regarding the identity of Śiva and Nārāyaṇa is logically established; therefore, there is only one reality, which is the form of Nārāyaṇa.
"The fourth is the supreme reality"—
this is the path of the venerable authors of the Bhāṣya.

In our illustrious Ācārya’s established doctrine (*siddhānta*), however, non-difference (*abheda*) is to be defined in this manner: just as in the case of the Soma-sacrifice and others enjoined by sentences such as "One should sacrifice with Soma," there is the prescription of the connection with a fruit and so forth through sentences such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," so too here [in the context of the Lord], [it is stated] that "Verily, Nārāyaṇa alone existed; neither Brahmā nor... and so on.

The Brahman consisting of Nārāyaṇa—characterized by being devoid of a second entity such as Brahmā and Rudra as prescribed by statements beginning with "Śaṃkaraḥ," and by existing at the time of the beginning of creation—is indeed that which is qualified [by these attributes]. It is said:
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra are produced from Him; He alone is the Cause, the one to be meditated upon, possessing all sovereignty."

"Endowed with all lordship, Śambhu, situated in the midst of space, the one Śiva who brings about auspiciousness—abandoning everything else, He alone is to be meditated upon. In this passage from the *Atharvaśikhā*, the phrase "the cause is to be meditated upon" (*kāraṇaṃ tu dhyeyam*) refers to Him as the Cause; having first restated Him by the single term "Cause," [He is then described] because He is endowed with all lordship.

Meditation upon [the Lord] as being non-different from Śiva— the fourth state (turīya) who is an incarnation of Nārāyaṇa mentioned in the causal texts, who is designated by the word "Śambhu" because he makes all things auspicious through his nature as the Lord of All, and who resides in the midst of the ether— is enjoined for the sake of the fruit. It is not [merely] the fourth Śiva [that is meant], because the words "Lord of All" (sarveśvara) and "Auspicious One" (śiva) are established in their conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) with reference to that [Nārāyaṇa].
Because it is untenable to speak of two distinct grounds for the application [of the term], and because the title of the *Nārāyaṇopaniṣad*—namely, "From Nārāyaṇa Brahmā is born;
from Nārāyaṇa Rudra is born"—establishes that the cause denoted by the word "cause" (in the phrase "the cause of Brahmā, Rudra, etc. must necessarily be Nārāyaṇa. Thus...
In the passage from the *Kaivalyopaniṣad* beginning with "the lotus of the heart" and ending with "beyond darkness," [it is said]:
"The lotus of the heart... [and so on], up to "wonderful, formless consciousness-bliss.

By this much [of the text], having referred (anūdya) to Nārāyaṇa— the fourth [state] and the cause of the universe— with the words "Umāsahāyam" and so forth up to "tamasaḥ parastāt," the worship of Śiva as the fourth [state], who is the form of an incarnation of the Lord mentioned in the causal statements, is enjoined for the sake of its fruit. For this very reason, in the scripture cited in the Commentary, the Lord's nature as the source of all incarnations and so forth [is established].

In the statement of the *Atharvaśiras*, "He who is indeed Rudra, he is the Blessed One, and he is Brahmā," identity with Nārāyaṇa—denoted by the word "Blessed One"—is enjoined by referring to the referents of the words "Rudra" and so forth occurring in the causal passages. For such is the syntactical structure there: "He who is indeed Rudra" refers to the fourth [state] which is an incarnation of Nārāyaṇa.

"He who is Śiva and Brahmā the four-faced one is the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa"—thus it should be understood in subsequent passages as well, for otherwise there would be an inconsistency in the meaning of the sentence. Likewise, in the subsequent *Uttaratāpanīya* passage: "They consider the non-dual Śiva to be the fourth; that is the Self, that is to be known," [it is stated] regarding this "fourth."

With reference to Śiva, the state of being Nārāyaṇa—designated by the word "Self"—is enjoined as that which is to be known for the sake of liberation. In this same manner, all other passages devoted to the excellence of Śiva must be interpreted so as not to contradict this; they are intended to enjoin the meditation upon Nārāyaṇa as Śiva for the sake of the fruit [of liberation]. As for those passages devoid of the term "meditation" (upāsana), [they are to be understood as injunctions of knowledge].
By supplying the word "meditation" (*upāsanā*) [to the relevant passages], and for those [passages] where no fruit is heard, a fruit pertaining to this world or the next must be postulated;

for, by such statements as "through meditation on the Lord as Śiva, one attains the power to move at will in all worlds," a great fruit is declared. Thus, for those who possess a desire for enjoyments in this world or the next, [the appropriate fruit is to be understood].
Because it is possible for the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa to assume a playful form as Śiva for the purpose of being worshipped by royal persons.
Even all those statements concerning the Fourth Śiva (Turīya-Śiva) that are heard in scripture are indeed devoted to meditation (*upāsanā*);

therefore, the supreme reality known as Nārāyaṇa alone is of the nature of the Fourth Śiva. Alternatively, all the names of the Śaiva statements that lack the term "meditation" enter into Him, and so forth.
Because the cited scriptures demonstrate that the passages concerning the worship of Śiva have Nārāyaṇa as their ultimate referent,

and because they are intended for the worship of Nārāyaṇa— who is the inner controller (antaryāmin) of Śiva— as possessing the attributes of Śiva, all Śaiva passages indeed have Nārāyaṇa as their sole purpose.
"Established in Brahmā, he is of the nature of Brahmā; established in Śivā, he is of the nature of Śiva"—by virtue of the authority of such scriptural statements.
"And those who are devotees of other deities, who worship them endowed with faith..."
Even they, O Kaunteya, sacrifice to me alone, though not according to the prescribed rules;
for I am indeed the enjoyer and the Lord of all sacrifices. Yet, because they do not recognize me in my true essence, they fall away.
This is because of the authority of the statement in the Gītā,
and also because of the natural force of Śiva’s words to Mārkaṇḍeya in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "O child, I am the bestower of enjoyment, while Janārdana is the bestower of liberation."

Or rather, as it is stated in the *Sanatkumāra-saṃhitā* of the *Skanda-purāṇa* regarding the specific enumeration of fruits: "O intoxicated elephants! O horses with the speed of the wind! A woman with a face like the full moon—this is the fruit of the rite of Śiva-worship."

Because there is an abundance of people in this world—both rajasic and tamasic—who desire worldly enjoyments, the worship of Śiva is taught in many places in the Śrutis, Smṛtis, and other scriptures for their sake.

For there is no contradiction in hearing [the texts] concerning the worship of that [deity] and so forth; because, like the statement "one seeking to harm should sacrifice with the Śyena," the sentences of the Śruti and Smṛti are intended merely to describe the existence of the deity's own nature, as in:
"Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning; Agni was the first of the gods; these..."
Just as statements regarding causes composed of specific terms— such as "the elements arise from space alone" and so forth— are rightly understood as referring to Viṣṇu,
it is likewise appropriate that Śaiva statements also refer to Nārāyaṇa; for indeed, it is exactly thus.

If it is asked: "In the event that there is no contradiction among the statements of the Śaivas, what is the specific reason for the lack of contradiction [if one assumes] that Śiva is subordinate to Viṣṇu?"—the answer is: No. This is because there is an abundance of statements intended to exalt Śiva and endowed with Śiva-specific *śruti*, *liṅga*, and so forth; and because the terms "Śiva" and "Nārāyaṇa" do not refer merely to those individual manifestations (*vyakti*).

Furthermore, because the occurrence of Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava discourses would otherwise be untenable; because there is no contradiction in Śiva being non-different from Viṣṇu due to the cited evidentiary proofs and the absence of any subverting arguments; and because it is easy to interpret Śaiva statements as having Viṣṇu as their ultimate referent—for these reasons, [the status] of Śiva...

Whether one accepts the position that Nārāyaṇa is an avatāra or the position that Śiva and Nārāyaṇa— who are distinct from all individual souls and the like— are identical as the fourth state (turīya), the path of those who follow the venerable Ānandatīrtha is that there is only one supreme reality called Nārāyaṇa.

Thus, since these three views are for the most part not contradictory, it is appropriate to reveal the unity of the three systems (*trimataikyaprakāśa*). Thus [ends the work] by the venerable Mahānandatīrtha Bhagavatpādācārya, who is the abode of the compassion of Śrīmaccharaṇa, and the venerable Vasudhendratīrtha, the wandering ascetic teacher (*paramahaṃsaparivrājakācārya*) who is independent in all philosophical systems (*sarvatantrasvatantra*).

The first chapter in the *Trimataikyaprakāśikā*, composed by one named Aiyaṇa— the son of Gopālācārya, who was the son of Rāmācārya, and whose lineage is distinguished by the most excellent teachings of the Siddhānta— written for those devoted to the venerable Vāṇa.
It is finished.
(p. 67) || The Second Chapter of the *Matatrayaikyaprakāśikā* ||
But is this not improper, since the dualists maintain that Brahman— established by Śruti and Smṛti— is devoid of internal, external, and other types of difference? For instance,

in such statements as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi), which enjoin non-difference with Brahman by referring back to the individual soul (jīva), the term "thou" (tvam-pada) denotes [the soul] as a conscious entity.

Regarding the class of living beings (*sajātīya-jīvajāta*), even there, by means of *jahadajahallakṣaṇā* (indication that both excludes and includes), setting aside the qualified form and restating pure consciousness (*caitanyamātra*), the word "That" (*tatpada*)— by that same *lakṣaṇā* and through the abandonment of the qualified form—
prescribes the state of being pure consciousness for that which is presented [as the referent]. This applies to the consciousness of the individual soul (*jīvacaitanya*).

In the case of enjoining that [the individual self] has Brahman-consciousness as its nature, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the two words results precisely in non-difference. This is likewise the case in instances where there is an injunction of non-difference from the individual self (*jīva*) by way of restating Brahman, such as in "Know Me also as the Knower of the Field" (*kṣetrajñaṃ cāpi māṃ viddhi*). In such passages, oneness must be understood solely through the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) known as "relinquishing the parts" (*bhāgatyāga*). Now, then...

If it is asked how the supreme reality known as Nārāyaṇa can be distinct from the individual soul (jīva) without contradicting the doctrine of non-duality (advaita), we reply: the scriptural statements regarding the non-duality of the individual soul and Brahman have as their primary object the essential identity [of their natures].

That very [unity] is primarily understood through the distinction [of the means of knowledge] by means of scriptural authority and reasoning; just as sentences such as "the sound of a river" possess non-contradictory meaning,
so too the non-contradiction of the sentence concerning the identity of the individual soul and Brahman is to be understood.
That very sentence, such as "Thou art That" (*tat tvam asi*), which has as its object the non-difference of the indicated consciousness (*lakṣita-caitanya*),

takes as its object the non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman— the two literal meanings (*vācyārtha*)— by means of the arguments to be stated hereafter. This is just as the sentence "A hamlet on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*) is not contradictory due to the distinction between its literal and indicated meanings.

The meaning is that, in the same way, the statement of non-duality (*advaita*) is not contradictory; this is what is being said: the primary non-duality consists in the negation of difference relative to a co-essential living being (*jīva*) by virtue of [the Self's] being sentient (*cetana*), whereas non-duality [in other senses] is secondary.
If it is asked how this is so, we reply: because the counter-correlate is not delimited by the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*).

For the pure consciousness (*śuddhacaitanya*), which is the referent (*lakṣya*) of words such as "individual soul" (*jīva*) and which serves as the counter-correlate for non-difference from Brahman, is not delimited by the delimitor of denotability for words such as "individual soul"—namely, the nature of being a conscious entity conditioned by ignorance (*avidyā*).

Because it is not newly delimited [by the sentence]. In that regard, in such cases as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the word "That" (*tat*) is consciousness qualified by omniscience and so forth; and the delimitor of the denotative capacity of the word "thou" (*tvam*) is facing-consciousness, wherein "facing-ness" (*abhimukhatva*) is...

[The definition of verbal knowledge is: the state of possessing a cognition of a sentence which has as its qualificandum something other than the speaker, and which is the object of the speaker’s desire [to communicate] a mode that is connected with the verbal cognition under discussion. Thus, it must be stated that when the statement "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) is uttered, there arises in the hearer precisely the verbal cognition "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*).

And thus, you— the pure consciousness that is the referent (*lakṣya*) of the word *tvam*, which is not delimited by the delimitor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the word *tvam*— are made to understand oneness, in the form of the negation of difference, with that pure consciousness which is the referent of the word *tat*, [itself] not delimited by the delimitor of the denotability of the word *tat*.

Since the number "one" cannot apply to Brahman, which is devoid of attributes (*nirdharmika*), in passages such as "Know Me also as the Knower of the Field" (*kṣetrajñaṃ cāpi māṃ viddhi*), it is precisely non-difference— consisting in the negation of difference relative to the pure consciousness denoted by the word "Knower of the Field"— that is understood with respect to the pure consciousness denoted by the term "I" (*asmatpada*). Thus, [the identity of] the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, and so forth, is established.

In non-dualistic statements (*advaitavākya*) whose primary intent is to establish the non-difference between the Supreme Brahman— the referent of terms such as "Brahman" and "Jīva"— and the pure Brahman which is the literal meaning of those terms, the very distinction between the Jīva and Brahman, who are the primary meanings of the words "Jīva" and "Brahman," is actually reinforced; this is just as the literal meaning of the word "Ganges" (the river) remains distinct from the bank, even though the bank indicated by the word "Ganges" serves as the locus for a hamlet.
Since there is no contradiction in the fact that the flood denoted by the word "Gaṅgā" is not the locus of the cowherd settlement (*ghoṣa*), the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:
let the individual soul (*jīva*) be distinct from Brahman.

It is fitting [to say so], because that which is indicated by the word *jīva* (the individual soul) is non-different from Brahman. This follows from the rule: "That which is indicated by a term and is non-different from something else, is non-different from the denoted meaning of that term. For example, in such cases as "Devadatta is a lion," there is a non-difference between Devadatta and the primary referent "lion" based on their similarity. Nor is there a flaw in the reason...

It must be stated that there is an absence of the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*). For it has been stated in the *Sudhā* that in cases such as "the upper region possesses rain because of the river's flood in the lower region," the fact that the probans and the probandum reside in different loci (*vyadhikaraṇatva*) is not a defect, provided that pervasion (*vyāpti*) exists.

Alternatively, the reason (*hetu*) is "being denotable by a word other than one that denotes Brahman. In this case, the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is secured, and the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is easily grasped: namely, "whatever is denotable by a word other than that which denotes X is distinct from what is denoted by that word [X]. Thus, it follows that [the individual soul] must be distinct from Brahman.
Because of the pervasion (vyāpti) that "whatever is non-different from the indicated meaning (lakṣya) of a word is different from the denoted meaning (vācya) of that word"—
as in the cases favored by the Bhāṭṭas, such as "one should sacrifice with Soma" and "a blue pot," where the sacrifice and the pot,
though non-different from the indicated meanings of the words *soma* and *nīla*, are [respectively] different from the denoted meanings of the words *soma* and *nīla*.

Because of the perception of difference; and likewise, just as in the expression "a hamlet on the Ganges," there is no contradiction between the fact that the bank (the indicated object) and the literal meaning of the word "Ganges" both serve as the locus for the hamlet,
so too [there is no contradiction] between the literal meanings of words such as "Soma" and their respective indicated objects, in relation to the Soma-sacrifice and so forth.
And just as there is no contradiction between difference and non-difference, so too regarding the non-dual statements such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*),

there is the non-difference of the individual soul (*jīva*)— denoted by the word *tvam* and so forth— from Brahman— denoted by the word *tat* and so forth; and [there is] the non-difference of the pure consciousness indicated (*lakṣya*) by the word *tvam* and so forth, from the pure consciousness indicated by the word *tat* and so forth.

"Non-difference" [is asserted] because the non-contradiction between primary difference and secondary non-difference is accepted by all; and this is not the case in your own view, since the word *tvam*, which denotes the individual soul (*jīva*), [refers only to that soul and not to its inner controller].

Even if there were some manner of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the word *tat* within the Brahman-consciousness, how could that word—which denotes [Brahman] as qualified by attributes such as omniscience—indicate pure consciousness?

For it must be stated that [pure consciousness] is the very nature of that [Brahman], whereby there would be no contradiction between the two; [otherwise, this would apply only] to the Blessed Lord and His attributes.
For us non-dualists, at the stage of contemplating that even the pure Brahman becomes the object of qualified linguistic usage through the power of its limiting adjuncts (*viśeṣa*),
the state of being denotable by that [qualified] term is established solely through the contemplation of non-difference.

Because in the state of contemplating absolute purity (*kevala-śuddhatā*), there is no contradiction between the two—since it is possible for either the primary or the secondary sense of being the indicated object (*lakṣya*) of that word [“Being”] to apply; for this very reason, it is stated in the *Gauḍabrahmānandī*’s *Jaḍatvabhaṅgoddhāra*: “The words ‘Being’ (*sat*) and so forth have their direct denotative power (*śakti*) precisely in unconditioned consciousness (*anavacchinna-caitanya*).”

However, the conventional usage of the term "indicative" (*lākṣaṇika*) is secondary (*gauṇa*), based on the commonality of being a generator of cognition not delimited by the delimitor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*).

Now, it might be argued that one must state that both indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and the secondary (*gauṇī*) [function] are non-primary (*amukhya*) even when they are known [to exist]. If that were the case—

Because it would result in a contradiction with the third and subsequent sections [of the *Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra*]. In that regard, in the third chapter (*pāda*), under the sūtra "In the case of those who enter after, because of the commonality" (*anuprasarpiṣu sāmānyāt*), it was considered that in the *Rājasūya*, which is a modification (*vikāra*) of the *Soma* sacrifice known as the *Daśapeya*, it is heard [in the scripture]:
"Ten by ten, they should enter each cup; one hundred Brāhmaṇas [should drink] the *Soma*."

Regarding the phrase "they eat": since ten cups (*camasa*) are obtained from the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice, and since the drinking of the *rājanya-camasa* (the cup belonging to the *rājanya*) would also apply [to the priests], a doubt arises as to whether the ten *rājanya*s should drink from the *rājanya-camasa*, or whether only the Brāhmaṇas should drink it. In this doubt, [the rule] "ten by ten" [is applied] in the sentence "they should approach."

Because the injunction is directed toward each individual cup (*praticamasa*) by prescribing the number ten, the number ten prescribed by that specific statement supersedes the number one obtained through extended application (*atideśika*).

Since the cessation [of the term] occurs by virtue of its being a collective class (samājajāti), there is no cessation of the class "kṣatriya" (rājanyatva). Furthermore, because the word *brāhmaṇa* can refer to the kṣatriyas through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) in the sense of a group consisting of both Brāhmaṇas and non-Brāhmaṇas—according to the maxim of the "men with umbrellas"—it is not contradictory for the ten kṣatriyas alone to perform the consumption of the *rājanya-camasa*. Thus, the consumption of the *rājanya-camasa* belongs exclusively to the ten kṣatriyas.

Having established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the siddhāntin argues]: since the primary sense of the Vedic text is possible in the statement "a hundred Brāhmaṇas consume the Soma," it is improper to resort to a secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Thus, regarding the ten cups (*camasa*) obtained from the archetype (*prakṛti*), for the men moving along [the path], there is a repetition of "ten" for each cup.

Since ten is explicitly prescribed by rule, the number one hundred—which is obtained by implication—is restated; then, by treating the present tense (*laṭ*) as an option for the subjunctive (*liṅ*), the injunction of Brahminhood is established through the statement, "those hundred persons who might drink [the Soma] shall be Brāhmaṇas. Thus, even the drinking from the hundred cups belongs exclusively to Brāhmaṇas.

This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). For this very reason, it was deliberated upon in the first section of the ninth chapter [of the *Mīmāṃsā-sūtra*] that the repetition (*abhyāsa*) of the *sāmidhenī* verses should be considered a property (*dharma*) arising from their position (*sthāna*).
Regarding the injunction heard in the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), namely: "He recites the first verse three times;
he recites the last three times; thus they become fifteen," what is the purpose of this triple repetition?

When there arises a doubt as to whether "the state of being the first" refers to the nature of the *ṛc* or the nature of the position, the word "first" (*prathamā*)— due to its feminine gender indication— is accepted as referring to the *ṛc* by way of secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Thus, the threefold repetition possesses that property [of being the first] of the *ṛc*, specifically that of the first [verse] in the archetype (*prakṛti*), such as "Pravovājā" or "Jīyā."

Having established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that because [the quality] is absent in certain modifications (*vikāra*), there is no modification (*ūha*) of the triad [of mantras] therein, [the siddhāntin replies]:

since it is possible for the word "first" (*prathama*) to refer to primacy through its primary denotative function (*mukhyavṛtti*), it is improper to resort to a secondary indicative function (*jaghanyalakṣaṇā*) in the *ṛc* verse; furthermore, words expressing qualities take their gender and number from their substratum.
Since the feminine gender designation is a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*), the quality of being in the first position belongs to the triple repetition. (p. 72)

In the case of modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), it has been established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the threefold repetition occurs in the *ṛc* verse specifically characterized by priority, according to the rule "in both. In that very context, in the section concerning the rule "the end with the *patnīsaṃyāja*s applies to all [days] because there is no distinction," the primacy of the primary sense over the secondary sense is described;
for it is heard in the *Dvādaśāha*: "The days conclude with the *patnīsaṃyāja*s. They do not...

"He throws the *barhis* after [the offering], for at that time the sacrifice is not yet concluded"—this being the case, a doubt arises whether the conclusion with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings applies to all days, or only to those excluding the last.

Since there is no specific distinction in the injunction, it might be argued that the conclusion with the *patnīsaṃyāja*s applies to all days and thus there is no throwing of the *barhis*. However, this is not so, because of the statement regarding the non-conclusion of the sacrifice.

Regarding the principle of "remoteness over a long period of time," since the rule that the sacrifice ends with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings is obtained by the force of the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) even in the modifications (*vikāra*) of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), such as the two-night sacrifice (*dvirātra*) and others, there is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that there is no modification (*ūha*) of the formula. This is because the twelve sacrifices are to be performed together;
thus, having performed each preceding day ending with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, one completes the remainder of each preceding day.

When it is stated that "the subsequent [rite] is to be commenced," all sacrifices become performed together because the required injunction is obtained; this is for the sake of the primary sense of the statement regarding the non-consummation (*asaṃsthā*). Having performed the days ending with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, excluding the final day, on the second or third day at the end, one should perform the original *barhis*-spreading and other rites according to the context.
It has been established that everything must be accepted;

therefore, since the denoted meaning (vācyārtha) and the indicated meaning (lakṣyārtha) are respectively primary and secondary, we must accept that there is no contradiction between such difference and non-difference. And this must necessarily be so.

Otherwise, even such statements as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1) and "All this is indeed Brahman" would have to be understood as teaching the duality of the world with respect to Brahman; for in those cases as well, [the same logic would apply].

Because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), as in the case of "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) and similar statements, all words such as "all" and so forth, by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), have as their referent the consciousness of Brahman which is the substratum; thus, it is easily stated that the Brahman indicated [by these words] is non-different from the referents of words such as "Brahman."

Nor should it be argued that there is a disparity such that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in statements like "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) occurs in the sense of non-difference, whereas in statements like "All this, indeed, is Brahman" (*sarvaṃ khalvidaṃ brahma*), it occurs through sublation (*bādhā*). For even if the underlying logic were the same, there would be no reason for such a disparity. Furthermore, in the phrase "in the case of sublation," is the locative case used in the sense of locus (*adhikaraṇa-saptamī*) or in the sense of object (*viṣaya-saptamī*)?

Is it a locative absolute (*sati-saptamī*) or not? It cannot be the former; for in such passages as "All this, indeed, is Brahman," the sublation (*bādha*) consists in the knowledge that this entire world, distinct from Brahman, does not exist. This is because [the passage expresses] grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), which is the application of words with different grounds for their application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*) to a single referent.

Because the property of sound (śabdadharmasya) is absent in cognition. Not the second [alternative], because grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the form of a function has as its object the referents of words, and thus lacks the property of having the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañcamithyātva*) as its object. Nor does it mean "is sublated" by deriving it from the verbal root *bādh* with the suffix *karmaṇi*.

It should not be argued that the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with respect to that [object], as in "this is silver" and so forth, is justified because the word *bādha* refers to an object qualified by the form of falsity; for even in those cases, as in "That thou art," all such words refer,
through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), to the foundational consciousness (*adhiṣṭhāna-caitanya*) in terms of non-difference.

Since grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible—and since it is therefore possible for all statements concerning non-duality to have a single meaning—it is improper to assume a discrepancy [between them]; otherwise, there would be a contradiction between the sentient and the insentient.

If the word *sarva* and others, which denote a measure (*mātra*), were to signify non-difference through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of a single part [of their referent], there would be a lack of uniformity (*vairūpya*) because of the contradiction regarding grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Furthermore, even sentences such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) would,
by virtue of the term *tvam* denoting a qualified object that is illusory, result in nothing but sublation (*bādhā*).

The term "co-referential" (*samānādhikaraṇa*) is appropriate in all cases precisely because of the lack of dissimilarity [between the two referents]; for the individual soul (*jīva*), as qualified by ignorance (*avidyā*), is superimposed upon Brahman, and the analogy of nacre-silver and the like is accepted everywhere.
Furthermore, even in the case of the analogy, the word "silver" can denote the underlying substrate, the nacre, through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), whereby identity is possible. And thus:
