In the alternative view where the locative case is used in the sense of the object (*viṣaya-saptamī*) based on its etymological derivation from the root *kṛ* (to act), there is no loss for us; for we accept that in all instances such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), there is a non-difference consisting of a quality in the form of similarity. Nor is the third [alternative] tenable, because grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) residing in words exists at all times.

This is because there is no sublation of the nature of knowledge and its object immediately following [the cognition]. Thus, in sentences such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), according to the Advaita view, the two words convey the non-difference of pure consciousness through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*);
however, in the Rāmānuja view, it is the Brahman qualified by the body known as the individual soul (*jīva*) that is denoted by the word "thou."

The doctrine of *viśiṣṭādvaita* (qualified non-duality) teaches non-difference from Brahman as qualified by the subtle *cit* and *acit*, which is what is signified by the word "That" (*tatpadabodhya*). In our view, however, it teaches the non-duality of the Supreme Brahman, which is what is signified by the word "That," with the inner controller of the individual soul (*jīvāntaryāmī*), who is what is signified by the word "Thou" (*tvaṃpadabodhya*). Thus, there is generally no contradiction between these three views.

Thus: "All this, indeed, is Brahman"—"In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," and so forth. In the first position, the meaning of the word *sarva* (all) is that which conveys the difference between the pure Brahman indicated by the word *sarvam* and the supreme Brahman indicated by the word *brahma*.
In the second position, there is the indication of falsity; in [the view of] Viśiṣṭādvaita, there is the indication of qualified non-duality;
and in our own system, there is the indication of the falsity of the independence residing in that [Brahman], which is indicated by words such as "all" (sarva).

The three [statements]—the indication of the non-difference of the inner controller (antaryāmin) from Brahman, and the indication of the falsity of the independence residing in the individual soul (jīva)—are thus not contradictory.

Now, even if there is no contradiction regarding the non-difference of pure consciousness from both figurative (gauṇī) and secondary (lakṣaṇā) indications, [one might object]: *(Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the logical structure of the argument as presented.)*

If it is argued that there is indeed a contradiction with other systems regarding the identity of pure consciousness through the *jahadajahallakṣaṇā* (apparent exclusion-inclusion) mode of indication—because both [the opponent and the proponent] do not accept that mode—it is not so; for since *jahadajahallakṣaṇā* is not distinct from *jahallakṣaṇā*, there is no contradiction. To explain: Brahman is qualified by omniscience and other attributes.

Furthermore, as for the individual soul (*jīva*) qualified by attributes such as limited knowledge (*alpajñatva*), is it different or non-different from the pure consciousness that constitutes the substantive (*viśeṣyamātra*)? It cannot be the first case, because the cognition of the substantive alone is achievable solely through *jahallakṣaṇā* (exclusive indication). Moreover, since the qualified entity is one with Brahman, *jahadajahallakṣaṇā* (indication involving both exclusion and inclusion), which consists in the abandonment of one part, is untenable there. Furthermore—

Indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is like [the status of] being something to be established (*sādhyatva*). For in the Veda, there is no obstacle to the fact that even the cognition of that which is not delimited by the delimitor of the primary power (*śakti*) is achievable solely through indication (*jahallakṣaṇā*). Moreover, since the cognition of an object other than the one denoted by the primary power is obtainable through a function other than primary power, such a cognition can indeed occur through either *jahat* or *ajahat* indication.

Not the latter [alternative]. For if there were non-difference between the substantive—the pure Brahman—and the two referents of the words *tat* and *tvam*—namely, the qualified individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*)—then, since no distinction would exist therein, the words *tat* and *tvam* would have to denote only the pure consciousness that is their substantive; and thus, there would be non-difference between those two.
76) Because there would be no contradiction [between the two], it would follow that the *jahadajahallakṣaṇā* (the "partially abandoning" type of indication) is rendered impossible.
Furthermore, since the substantive (*viśeṣya*) possesses ultimate reality, [there could be] no ignorance regarding the specific individual souls and the Lord (*jīveśayoḥ*).

Because identity is impossible between two things characterized by *māyā* due to their falsity; furthermore, because the non-difference of the qualified (*viśiṣṭa*) and the pure (*śuddha*) would entail a contradiction with many logical principles. To illustrate: in the fourth chapter, third section, under the topic (*adhikaraṇa*) "In that [matter], all [are for one purpose] because of the distinction," it was considered that the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are for all [purposes] and the *Jyotiṣṭoma* is for all [purposes].

Thus it is heard [in the scripture]. In this regard, there arises a doubt: do all desires come to fruition in a single performance of the rite, or through different performances? Since the very same action that serves as the occasion for one desire likewise serves as the occasion for other actions, and because the occasion is common to all, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) view is that the attainment of all desires occurs from a single performance alone. Regarding these desires...

Since it is impossible to enjoin ritual action (*karman*) with reference to desire while it is already obtained through passion, and since action must be enjoined solely with reference to desire, there is a repetition of the performance of actions for each fruit according to the principle that "accessories repeat with each primary. In this regard, [the text says] "for all desires."

It has been established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that, although there is a cognition of a qualified entity in the form of a collection due to being indicated by a single word, because that [collection] resides in the subject (*uddeśya*), it is not intended to be significant—just like the "largeness" and "oneness" [in the case of *bṛhan ekaḥ*]. Thus, the attainment of all desired objects occurs only through distinct ritual applications (*prayoga-bheda*). In that regard, if that which is qualified by the form of a collection were merely the essential nature of the individual constituent parts, [the following would apply]:

For if [the sacrifice] were performed only once, there would be the undesirable consequence that all desired objects would be obtained simultaneously, thereby leading to the destruction of the basis for those [subsequent] rites.

For this very reason, it was deliberated upon in the tenth book, first pāda, in the section beginning with the sūtra: "And other things connected to the principal [rite] should cease from being undertaken, because they are subordinate members (*aṅga*). This refers to the sacrificial acts belonging to the *rājasūya*, such as the *anumati* and others, which are of the nature of *iṣṭi* offerings.
Other rituals are also heard of in the scriptures, such as the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), the Soma sacrifice, the ladle-oblation (*darvihoma*), and so forth. [For example:
"He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Anumati; he should sacrifice a pregnant ewe to Aditi."

In such passages as these, all of them are heard as being means for achieving a single result, namely: "One desiring self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) should sacrifice with the Rājasūya. Regarding this, there arises a doubt as to whether the *Ārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice should be performed in the *Anumati* and other rites which are modifications (*vikṛti*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa; [the view] previously held was that it should not be performed.

Since the performance of the auxiliary rites (*aṅga*) is accomplished by the very commencement directed toward both the auxiliaries and the principal rite (*pradhāna*), a separate commencement is impossible; this is the case, for example, in the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice, which is an auxiliary of the Soma sacrifice that is itself a modification (*vikṛti*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
Even though the *ārambhaṇīyeṣṭi* (commencement sacrifice) is omitted due to the loss of its gateway in the form of the characteristic of "commencement," here in the *rājasūya*,

since the *anumati* and other sacrifices are primary and can be commenced separately, the *ārambhaṇīyeṣṭi* must be performed because its gateway remains unlost. Having thus established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [it is argued that] in the archetype (*prakṛti*), it is only the commencement of the sacrifice as a whole...

Because it is understood to be the door [to the result]. In this case, however, within the Rājasūya—which consists of a collection of *iṣṭi*s, animal sacrifices, *soma* sacrifices, ladle-offerings (*darvīhoma*), and so forth—there is only one distributed commencement (*vyāsaktārambha*) and not separate, individual commencements. Thus, the commencement pertaining solely to the *iṣṭi*s, which was established in the archetype (*prakṛti*) as the means (*dvāra*), [is what applies here].

It has been established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that there is an omission (*lopa*) of the *ārambhaṇīyeṣṭi* sacrifice because it [the *rājasūya*] is already included within the *anumati* and other constituent sacrifices.

And thus, since the specific nature of the whole (*samudāyarūpa*)—which is qualified by its parts—is reduced here to the mere nature of the individual parts (*ekadeśarūpa*), the *rājasūya* as a whole is non-different from the *anumati* and other sacrifices; consequently, the door (*dvāra*) consisting of the *ārambha* (commencement) is absent.

If it were held that the *ārambhaṇīyeṣṭi* must be performed [in every sacrifice], there would be the undesirable consequence of nullifying that very section [of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtras]. For this very reason, in the third book, in the section beginning with "But in the case of the Aindrāgna, because of the absence of an indicative mark, it should be so," it was considered exactly in that way. In the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is a Soma offering for Indra and Agni [expressed as] "I take the Aindrāgna"; when its remnant is to be consumed, what [is the rule]?
When there is a doubt as to whether the consumption [of the Soma] is accompanied by mantras or without mantras, [it is concluded that] the Soma drunk by Indra and Agni was also drunk by Indra.

Thus, having established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the mantra "of what is drunk by Indra" (*indrapītasya*) may indeed be employed even for the consumption of the remnant of the *aindrāgna* [offering]— on the basis of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of its capacity to manifest Indra— one must conclude, according to the logic of the section on deities (*devatādhikaraṇa*) stated in the ninth book, that because the body [of the deity] cannot drink, [the mantra is not applicable].

By the word "yellow" (*pīta*), the meaning would be "of the Soma given to Indra" within the context of the characteristic of giving (*dāna*). However, in this case, the sacrificer did not give [the Soma] intending it for Indra. Thus, since the act of giving has a mixed scope and the mantra has a scope limited to one part, there is an absence of capacity to manifest both.
It has been established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the consumption of the remnants of the *aindrāgna* offering is performed without mantras;

for here too, it is stated that the whole is distinct from its parts. For this very reason, it was deliberated upon in the third book, seventh pāda, in the section titled "The recitation belongs to the Maitrāvaruṇa because of the direct instruction" (*traivānuvacanaṃ maitrāvaruṇasyopadeśāt*).

Regarding the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma, it is heard in the scripture: "The Maitrāvaruṇa priest both issues the command and recites. Since at the end of the mantra in the form of a recitation—"O Hotṛ, kindle the fire"—one hears the command, "O Hotṛ, sacrifice," there exists recitation joined with a command; likewise, there also exists the mere utterance of a command for Agni.

Regarding the injunctions such as "Recite for her who is kindling" (*samindhamānāyānubrūhi*), as well as the purely recitative passages such as *pra vo vājā abhidyavaḥ*, the question arises: does the meaning of Maitrāvaruṇa’s statement apply everywhere— both to purely injunctive sentences and to purely recitative ones— or is it restricted only to recitations that are joined with an injunction?
79) By the two words *preṣyati* ("he commands") and *anuvāha* ("he recites after"),

it is established that in all cases, the Maitrāvaruṇa is the agent of both the command (*praiṣa*) and the subsequent recitation (*anuvacana*), as well as of the combined act of commanding and reciting.

Regarding the meaning of the statement of the Maitrāvaruṇa: according to the *pūrvapakṣa*, since there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) because each individual [element] would be an object of reference (*uddeśya*) and the sentence would have to be completed for every such object, the single ritual act (*padārtha*) consisting of the recitation following the *praiṣa* (direction) is the sole object of reference. Therefore, the agency of the Maitrāvaruṇa belongs solely to the recitation joined with the *praiṣa*. Thus, [it is said] "the Maitrāvaruṇa..."

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that it is the meaning of the sentence; for if the recitation joined with the injunction were merely a single constituent part, it would result in the fallacy of *vākya-bheda* (splitting of the sentence) due to its becoming both the injunction and the recitation, which would lead to the collapse of that specific section of the treatise. Thus, in order to avoid contradicting many logical principles, [the action] is understood as a qualified whole consisting of the aggregate.

It must be stated that [the referent] is indeed distinct from the mere substantive alone. Therefore, it should be said that *jahadajahallakṣaṇā* is merely a secondary usage (*gauṇa*) within the scope of *jahallakṣaṇā*. There is no suspicion of contradiction whatsoever in accepting both difference and non-difference between the primary meaning and the indicated meaning; nor is it the case that *jahadajahallakṣaṇā* is not well-known in such instances as "This is that Devadatta."

This must be stated: the conventional usage of the term *jahadajahallakṣaṇā* (the "renouncing-non-renouncing" indication) in cases such as "This is that Devadatta" is merely superficially attractive. To explain: is this the form of cognition, the word, or the linguistic usage—as in "This is a jar"—in the case of "This is that Devadatta"? It cannot be the first, because in a cognition produced by the senses...

Because the [required] characteristic is impossible. Nor should it be argued: "Since the sense organs possess the inherent nature of generating cognitions whose objects are things connected with the present place and time, how can they have as their object things connected with past places and times?
For this applies only to external sense organs such as the eye and so forth.

The mental modification in the form of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), which has as its object a specific entity characterized by both the past and the present—expressed as "this is that"—is produced by the cooperation of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) generated by prior experience. (p. 80)
Because there is no subverting evidence against [the view that] it produces a distinction.

Now, in your own system, since there is a difference between an entity qualified by past time and so forth and one qualified by present time and so forth— wherein [the latter] is produced solely from the substratum itself— how can recognition have non-difference as its object?

If it is argued that [the cognition] is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), we say no; for validity is established regarding the identity of the particular by way of accepting both difference and non-difference between the adventitious attribute and the qualified substratum. Nor should it be asked how a cognition whose object is two qualified entities—such as "This is that"—can have the substratum alone as its object.

It can be asserted that a single cognition takes as its object both the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) and the qualified base (*viśeṣya*) through their distinction. Alternatively, difference and non-difference are accepted between the preceding and succeeding entities; thus, even if recognition such as "this is that" were erroneous, [the validity of] recognition such as "he is this" remains.

Validity is established because there exists non-difference between the earlier and later times, which is the object of recognition; even though [the cognition] has as its object the relation to two times and so forth,
in the case of a determinative recognition (*sāvadhāraṇa-pratyabhijñā*), the determination consists in the form of the relation to time and so forth.
Even though qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) and so forth serve to exclude other [possibilities] regarding the connection (*yoga*), they do not exclude the identity of the substratum (*dharmin*);

therefore, that [cognition] also possesses validity, because it takes as its object the fact that "he who was qualified by that place and that time at that moment is indeed now qualified by this place and that same time. And it has been stated in the *Sudhā* in the section on Time (*samayapāda*):
In the context of refuting the theory that [objects] are aggregates of atoms, it is said: "But when there is no difference between those occurring at prior and subsequent times...

Recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is accepted as having [both] the [past and present] objects as its domain. In that case, although recognition that includes a restrictive determination (*sāvadhāraṇa*) may be an error, the cognition "this is that" is not an error;
for when the object is the relation between the two times and so forth, then even the cognition with a restrictive determination is not an error.
Not the latter, because it cannot withstand critical analysis; for instance, is this [statement] a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) or does it convey a new meaning (*apūrvārtha*)?

Not the first, because it would lack authority due to being purposeless, and because a sentence that does not produce verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) does not depend upon a function (*vṛtti*). Otherwise, [the problem would apply to] that which occurs subsequent to knowledge...

The latter [alternative] is also not tenable, because even in the case of the restating sentence "This is that jar," there would result the undesirable consequence of verbal cognition through *lakṣaṇā* (indication) regarding a [jar] qualified by a past time and place;

furthermore, since a sentence such as "This is that Devadatta" is of the nature of a restatement of the form of a prior cognition, it is impossible for it to convey a previously unknown object. This is the case with the phrase "this is that."

Because the validity of verbal testimony (*śabda*) is impossible therein due to the object being directly perceived (*pratyakṣadṛṣṭārthatva*), for this very reason it is stated in the *Śābarabhāṣya*— in the passage "for scripture (*śāstra*) is indeed the cognition of an object not in contact [with the senses] arising from the cognition of words"— that there is an absence of validity for verbal testimony regarding an object that is in contact; and the same is stated in its corresponding *Vārttika*.

Because it has already been explained: therefore, since the sentence "This is that Devadatta"— which demonstrates the form of recognition— is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) and does not produce a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), there is no occasion for a third type of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for its sake.
And yet, even though it is a different function (*vṛtti*), because the qualified [entity] is something additional, there is no contradiction with the reasoning we have stated.

But even so, since the two words *tat* and *tvam* denote their respective qualified meanings through their primary powers (*śakti*), they must likewise possess power (*śakti*) with respect to the substratum alone—

just as words such as *daṇḍin* (staff-bearer) have power with respect to Devadatta alone, or words such as *dravya* (substance) have power with respect to a jar and so forth. As for the conventional usage of the term "indication" (*lakṣaṇā*) in cases such as *tat tvam asi*, [it is merely figurative].

The view of the Neo-Vedantins is that [the term] is secondary (*gauṇa*) because it generally produces a cognition whose qualifier is not the delimitor of the capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). Thus, they argue that the reason "because of being non-different from the denoted object of the word *brahman*" is unestablished (*asiddhi*). If this is objected, we say no; for it is difficult to establish a cognition of both [the primary and secondary meanings] through the power of denotation (*śakti*). To explain: in the cognition of a qualified object and its specific substratum...

Furthermore, if a word denoting a qualified object were to have [independent] denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to both [the qualifier and the qualified], it would follow that it too possesses multiple meanings (*nānārthatva*), just like the word *saindhava* and others. Nor is this an acceptable consequence, because there is an absence of grammar and other means for grasping its denotative power;
moreover, in the case of words such as *daṇḍin* ("staff-bearer"), since they are not used to denote a person alone, the application of denotative power is impossible. Thus...

In the view that the universal and the particular are distinct, one should observe that words such as "substance" (dravya) lack denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to objects like a jar. Furthermore, what is the meaning of the claim that words such as "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) bring about the cognition of a person alone through their denotative power? Does it mean a cognition having "staff-bearer-ness" as the qualifier (*prakāra*) and the person as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), or a cognition having "personhood" (*puruṣatva*) as the qualifier and the person as the qualificand?

Or [is it] a cognition whose qualificandum is [the person]? Not the first, because that consists of a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭabodha*), whereas a cognition that manifests "person-ness" (*puruṣatva*) alone is what constitutes a cognition of the person; furthermore, when the word "person" (*puruṣa*) is employed, such a cognition cannot arise through the primary power (*śakti*) of words like "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*). Nor the second, because of that...

Because [the understanding] is achieved through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) by virtue of its being a cognition whose mode (*prakāra*) is something other than the delimitor of the capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*).

Likewise, is the cognition of a jar and so forth, which arises from words such as "substance" (*dravya*) through primary denotation (*śakti*), one that has "substanceness" (*dravyatva*) etc. as its mode and the jar etc.
as its qualificand (*viśeṣya*), or is it one that has "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) etc. as its mode? [The latter. The jar etc. [is understood].
Or [is it] that which has the qualificand as its object? Not the first, because since that [word] denotes a substance, it lacks the capacity to denote a jar;
for a cognition having "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) as its qualifier is precisely what constitutes the cognition of a jar, and [the word in question] lacks the mention of "jar-ness."

Because it is impossible for that cognition to be a cognition of a jar [if it were not so]. Nor is the latter [alternative] tenable, because it has already been stated that such a definition cannot be established. Furthermore, even "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) cannot be the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the word "substance" (*dravya*), because otherwise it would follow that the words "substance" and "jar" are synonyms. Nor [can it be argued that] in cases such as "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍī puruṣaḥ*) or "the jar is a substance" (*ghaṭo dravyam*), [the property] belongs to the qualified object (*viśiṣṭaviśeṣya*).

It must be explained how there can be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the two words— the general term and the particular term— as well as the cognition of non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*).
For even in that case, both non-difference and coreferentiality are possible only through the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of one of the two words.

Regarding the statement that "words with distinct grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) apply to a single object," it is necessary that the word *pravṛtti* here means that one word possesses a primary denotative power (*śakti*) toward a single object, while another word possesses a secondary indicative function (*lakṣaṇā*) toward that same object; otherwise, if both words possessed primary denotative power toward the same object, [the distinction between them would be lost].

For this would entail the consequence that words such as *daṇḍin* (staff-bearer) would have their denotative power (*śakti*) residing in the person alone; nor is this an acceptable position, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish such a power, and because it would result in the synonymy of words like *dravya* (substance) and *ghaṭa* (pot), since *daṇḍitva* (the state of being a staff-bearer) and *puruṣatva* (the state of being a person) would likewise be non-different, just as *ghaṭatva* and *kalaśatva* are. Furthermore, the reality of the matter is as follows:

If the word *tat* were to have its primary denotative power (*śakti*) residing in the qualified [referent] and the word *tvam* likewise in its own qualified referent, then— since there would be no sublation to the identity between these two qualified entities—
it would be untenable to postulate that their denotative power resides in pure consciousness alone.
Therefore, having admitted the difference between the qualified and the pure substratum, [the author argues that] for the word denoting the qualified, [the power must reside in the substratum].

Therefore, the connection with non-difference through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) alone is unavoidable. For this very reason, in the third [adhyāya], fourth [pāda], it is stated in the section beginning "The occasional [rite] is in the archetype, because of the specific connection with its modification" (JS 3.6.2):
in the fifth pāda.
It is considered as follows: In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in scripture, "Seventeen [sāmidhenīs] for a Vaiśya.

Regarding this, does the seventeenfold nature (sāptadaśya), which is enjoined as a contingent rule (naimittika), enter into the archetype (prakṛti) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa as an auxiliary (aṅga) as an alternative to the fifteenfold nature (pāñcadaśya)? Or...

When there arises a doubt as to whether [the injunction] enters [the context] precisely as a sublater of the *pañcadaśya* (fifteen-fold nature), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that since there is no distinction between the two in terms of being understood through the context (*prakaraṇa*), there must be an option (*vikalpa*). In response to this, [it is argued that] the *pañcadaśya* enjoined by the sentence "One should recite fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses" [is connected] to the *sāmidhenīs* by virtue of the context.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: since the permanent (*nitya*) rule of seventeen [recitations], which is understood to be an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), still finds scope even in the performance by Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, whereas the occasional (*naimittika*) rule of seventeen—which applies only to the performance by Vaiśyas—finds no scope [among the former]; therefore, that [occasional rule] is inserted precisely as a means of establishing the permanent rule where it has been reached. In that regard:

The "possibility of an alternative application" (*sāvakāśatva*) for the permanent fifteen-fold recitation (*pāñcadaśya*) means its being directed toward another purpose through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). In that case, based on the context, one must assume a scriptural statement to the effect: "In the performance of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, one should recite fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses. By that statement, [the fifteen-fold recitation] is understood as a constituent part of the performance for which all persons are qualified (*sarvādhikārika*), in its primary sense.

Because, when there is a conflict between the permanent *pāñcadaśya* (fifteen-foldness) and the occasional *sāptadaśya* (seventeen-foldness), the specific cognition characterized by the performance being undertaken by Brahmin and Kṣatriya agents can only be achieved through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*). For this very reason, the low-voiced recitation (*upāṃśutva*) connected with the injunction would apply; and since that [low-voiced recitation] is absent in that [specific] case.
It is described in exactly the same way in the ninth section (nāvamikādhikaraṇa). Regarding the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture:

"Whatever [rites] are prior to the Agniṣomīya [sacrifice], with those they proceed in a low voice. In that context, the quality of being in a low voice pertains to the ritual acts occurring in the preceding portion.

85) Once it has been established that [the injunction] pertains to the mere nature of the action (*mātradharmatva*), then by means of the word *yat kiñcit*— which denotes multiple individual instances and is employed here in conjunction with the view of the ancient authorities— all ritual elements, such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and others, [are included].

Since it is possible to present each [mantra] in its respective reflected form, the extreme silence (*atyupāṃśutva*) of those [mantras] would otherwise follow; however, because there is no room for other injunctions of ritual properties such as "one should recite for the *dīkṣaṇīyā* with as much voice as one desires," the term "whatever" (*yatkiñcit*), which finds its scope elsewhere, is established as referring to that which is distinct from the *dīkṣaṇīyā*.

From "whatever it may be" (*yatkiñcit*), which is delimited by the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) consisting in the generic nature of being an object residing in the prior portion— from that generic object residing in the prior portion, which is delimited by the delimitor of denotability consisting in the generic nature of being an object residing in the prior portion.

It has been established that "having scope" (*sāvakāśatvam*) consists in the state of being directed toward another object— namely, that which is delimited by the delimitor of the indicated object (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*), which is the nature of being a ritual act (*padārthatva*) other than the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* occurring in the prior portion, on account of the commonality of the term "ritual act" (*padārtha*). And so it is stated in the aforementioned case:
The cognition of non-differentiation through the secondary signification (lakṣaṇā) of either one of the two words is unavoidable. Alternatively, the qualified (viśiṣṭa) is of two kinds:

that which exists as long as the substance exists (yāvadvastubhāvin), and that which does not exist as long as the substance exists (ayāvadvastubhāvin). Among these, the former is absolutely non-different from the substantive (viśeṣya), while the latter is both different and non-different. In the case of the former, by the power of both words in two co-referential (samānādhikaraṇa) terms...

Alternatively, the cognition of non-differential relation (*abhedānvaya*) may be established through the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) of one of the two words; in that case, all the functions of differentiation (*bhedakārya*), such as non-synonymy and so forth, are accounted for by the power of the specific property (*viśeṣa*). We shall explain the determination of this specific property later on. In the second case, however, since those effects are established through both difference and non-difference, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.
"This too must be accepted by both of you," as will be demonstrated later. Therefore, in both systems, [the status of] the word denoting the qualified [object]—(p.

Since [the word] produces the cognition of the qualified object through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), there is no deviation anywhere from the rule that the primary meanings must be distinct when the indicated meaning is not different; for this very reason, with all this in mind, it was established in the *Guha* section (*Brahmasūtra* 1.2.11) that the distinction between the individual soul and Brahman alone is the primary meaning.

In the Śārīrakabhāṣya, for instance, having cited the Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad passage, "The two who drink the reward of ṛta," a doubt arises as to whether these two who drink the fruit of action denoted by the word *ṛta* are the intellect (*buddhi*) and the individual soul (*jīva*), or the individual soul and the Lord (*īśvara*). [The opponent argues] that because the intellect and the individual soul are limited in size, their entry into the cave of the heart is possible.

Since the distinction between the two is established by their being insentient and sentient, like shade and sunlight, it might follow that these two are the intellect (*buddhi*) and the individual soul (*jīva*).

However, because the dual number in the word "drinking" (*pibantau*) serves as the delimiter for the sentience of both, it must be stated that they are the individual soul and the Lord (*jīveśvarau*). This is so even though the Lord is omnipresent.

Since it is possible for [the two] to reside in the limited region called the heart of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), even though both are sentient, their distinction is established by the presence of limiting adjuncts in one and the absence of limiting adjuncts in the other; thus, the conclusion is reached that "the two who drink" are the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*). And so, when it is said that "the two who drink" are the individual soul and the Lord...

Since it has already been stated that "the two are distinct," the dual number (*dvivacana*) denotes the count of duality (*dvitva-saṃkhyā*), and since that [count] cannot exist without difference, the intention of the Commentator (*bhāṣyakṛt*) is that the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is indeed primary. For this very reason, in the third section (*adhikaraṇa*) of the third quarter of the third chapter, under the aphorism *iyadāmananāt*—"because of the mention of this much"—[it is said]: "Truth (*ṛtam*)."

Regarding the doubt as to whether there is a difference in the knowledge (*vidyā*) or an identity of the knowledge in the two mantras from the *Kaṭhavallī* and the *Atharvaṇa*, namely "two birds" (*dvā suparṇā*) and "drinking the truth" (*ṛtaṃ pibantau*), [the answer is given] in this [passage]: "drinking the truth" (*ṛtaṃ pibantau*).

By means of mantras in the dual number, such as "Two birds" (*dvā suparṇā*), the state of being two enjoyers is indicated; yet in that very mantra, it is understood that one of them eats the sweet fruit (*svādvatti pippalam*) while the other does not eat (*anaśnan anyaḥ*). Thus, since there is a difference in the nature of the objects of knowledge (*vedyasvarūpa-bheda*), it follows that there is a difference between the two forms of knowledge (*vidyā-bheda*). This being the position reached:

In the third section of the first and second quarters [of the Brahma-sūtras], having established that the word "the two who drink" (*pibantau*), which ends in a dual suffix, refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), a doubt arises: even though the individual soul is the enjoyer of the fruits of its actions, since it is impossible for the Lord to enjoy the fruits of karma, how can both be the enjoyers of the fruits of action? Having raised this doubt regarding the individual soul...

The status of being the primary enjoyer belongs to the non-enjoyer, the Lord; the designation of the word "enjoyer" [for the Lord] occurs by way of the analogy of those under a royal umbrella (*chatrinyāya*). Thus, in reality, the two meanings are the enjoyer and the non-enjoyer. Consequently, the meaning of the statement "two birds" (*dvā suparṇā*) is also precisely these two. Since there is no difference in the object to be known (*vedya*), the number two applies to both cases.

Furthermore, based on recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), it is established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that both are indeed ignorance (*avidyā*). By the statement that the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) are primarily the enjoyer and the non-enjoyer, it follows that their status as substrata of contradictory attributes is innate;

thus, difference (*bheda*) is primary. Having reached the position that this is innate, the scriptural passage "Two birds" (*dvā suparṇā*) is interpreted as being intent upon [establishing] difference.

This is established for both the proponent and the opponent. According to the intention of the author of the *Bhāṣya*, the two sections [of the *Brahma-sūtra*] demonstrate that the two verses—"The two drinking the Truth" (*ṛtaṃ pibantau*) and "Two birds" (*dvā suparṇā*)—are distinct forms of knowledge (*vidyā*), and thus have as their purport the natural distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman; otherwise, if the sentence "Two birds" did not have distinction as its purport...

Otherwise, the established doctrine— that the statement "two birds" (*dvā suparṇā*) and so forth merely restates difference for the purpose of negating it by means of non-dualistic statements— would be undermined. Therefore, [this would contradict] the statement regarding both difference and non-difference.

It must necessarily be accepted that even the authors of the *Śarīrakabhāṣya* intend to establish both difference and non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, depending on whether one intends to express the primary or secondary meaning; for in their commentary,
they employ both difference and non-difference in a combined manner, and because the purpose of the Mīmāṃsā is to bring about an understanding of the meaning of the investigated subject matter.
Because, as the source [of all], it is impossible for statements concerning difference to have as their purport merely conventional difference;

therefore, this is the consensus of these three views: that the purport of all Vedāntas is primarily Śrīmannārāyaṇa alone, who is absolutely distinct from both homogeneous and heterogeneous categories—namely, from individual souls (*jīva*) and insentient matter (*jaḍa*).

Siddham. Thus ends the illumination of the unity [of Brahman] through the negation of internal differences. Now, this is incorrect, because of such scriptural and traditional texts as: "There is no diversity whatsoever here," "All this is indeed Brahman," "Vāsudeva is all," and "That Great-Souled One is very difficult to attain," which establish that the Supreme Brahman known as the illustrious Nārāyaṇa is distinct from heterogeneous entities such as ether and the rest.

From the cognition of that which is devoid of difference, the negation of difference therein is indeed twofold: in the form of non-difference, and in the form of an absence of a locus for a counter-correlative. Of these, the first is the non-difference of the individual soul and Brahman in such passages as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*); the second, however, concerns the world (*prapañca*) and Brahman. In that regard, [the negation] of the world...
Because it does not exist through falsity (*mithyātva*), the difference that is its counter-correlative is also false; thus,

since a primary non-difference is impossible, the meaning of the statement "Brahman is devoid of heterogeneous difference" is simply that the world (*prapañca*) is void (*śūnya*), being nothing other than the existence (*sattā*) residing in Brahman.
And just as in the case of "this is silver," the "this-ness" (idantā) residing in the mother-of-pearl is perceived in the silver,
and there is no "this-ness" in the silver apart from that; so too [is it here].

The negation of the difference between the superimposed [silver] and its locus, such as mother-of-pearl, consists precisely in the fact that the superimposed lacks any existence over and above the existence of the locus, which is characterized by its relation to space and time.

This is the intended meaning [of the passage]. For this very reason, in cases such as "the jar exists" (*saghaṭa*), it is easily stated that it is the existence of Brahman, the substrate, alone that is perceived in the jar. In passages such as "All this is indeed Brahman" (*sarvaṃ khalvidaṃ brahma*) and "Vāsudeva is everything" (*vāsudevaḥ sarvam*), grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) occurs precisely through sublation (*bādhā*), and it serves to reveal the falsity of the world.

Since scriptural passages such as "one only, without a second" exist for the purpose of establishing that Brahman is devoid of difference from anything of a different class, how can it be said that the purport of all the Vedas is that Brahman is insentient? To this it is replied:
even the words of a master accompanied by servants and attendants, as well as the speech of one who is destitute and possesses little wealth, [are authoritative].
Indeed, through the distinction between secondary and primary meanings, they attain non-contradiction.

In the same way, all statements regarding truth and falsehood should be understood as non-contradictory, out of respect for the great authority [of the scriptures]. As it has been said: "Regarding a man who possesses servants capable of performing their duties..."

The term "non-servant" (*abhṛtya*) is used figuratively because of the common absence of the function of a servant; just as, for example, the term "destitute" (*nisva*) is used figuratively for one who possesses little wealth. In a village devoid of any other principal persons, the conventional usage that "this is the only man here" is secondary (*amukhya*). In the same way—
The universe is real; Maghavan is the sovereign lord. Even the waters do not violate your decree.

I have proclaimed the great and true deeds of the Great One, the Lord of Truth. That which he has willed is indeed truth; I bow here to that beautiful form, worthy of praise, and to him who bestows the spoils of victory, according to his purposes.

The truthful Viṣṇu established all the qualities for eternal years; there is a distinction between the Truth (Satya) and the Lord of the individual soul (Jīveśa), but there is no mutual distinction between the Truth and the individual souls.
This world is real;
the internal differentiation within Viṣṇu is unreal, and nothing else is unreal.
This flow of the world is real, endowed with fivefold distinctions.

These and other such statements— including "One only, without a second," "There is no diversity whatsoever here," and "But where everything has become his very Self, by what and whom should he see?"— which are intent on establishing the negation of difference from dissimilar things, are to be understood as non-contradictory through the distinction between their primary and secondary meanings.

For what Mīmāṃsaka would say that when two scriptures contradict each other, one should be authoritative and the other non-authoritative? This means [it is not so] because of the statement of the learned (abhiyukta) and because of the lack of contradiction with the proofs to be stated later. And thus, [the nature of] existence...

The statements establishing the reality of the world have their primary sense [only] if they do not contradict the statements establishing its falsity—that is, its non-existence, which is synonymous with falsity consisting in being the counter-correlate of negation. [Objection: But how can the statements regarding the reality of the world be of secondary sense, while the statements regarding its falsity...
If it is asked, "Why should the opposite—that [the world] has primary reality—not be the case? we say no.
This is because the very fact that it cannot be otherwise (anyathānupapatti), due to its non-contradiction with the proofs to be stated hereafter, serves as the proof in this matter.
To explain: the negation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is what is established by non-dualistic statements such as "One alone," and so forth.

Non-existence in the form of being a counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*), or unreality (*asattva*), or phenomenal appearance (*pratibhāsikatva*), or empirical reality (*vyāvahārikatva*)— the first [option] is not [correct], because it would result in a contradiction with one's own established tenets (*apasiddhānta*). For this very reason, it is not [the case].

The second [point]: because empirical existence (*vyāvahārikasattva*) exists, for this very reason, linguistic usage such as "this is a jar" is possible. Indeed, there is no such thing as non-existence apart from the relation to space and time;
for there is no such cognition as "this is a rabbit's horn. And thus, [non-existence] does not exist in Brahman.

Even in the absence of a difference having a real counter-correlate (*sat-pratiyogika-bheda*), there is no contradiction whatsoever due to the existence of a difference having a merely transactional (*vyāvahārika*) counter-correlate. Nor should it be argued that even the transactional is non-existent because it is false;
for the transactional is established by perception, such as "this is a jar," and by scripture, such as "the universe is real."
Because there is no sublation of the difference in Brahman that is the counter-correlate [of the world] through the non-perception of its existence;

because figurative falsity does not contradict primary reality; and because "existence" itself is the meaning of the word "reality. For this very reason, in such expressions as "one should not resort to an untrue person," the word *asat* refers to ungrammatical words.
The application [of the term] is as follows:
the word "sat" (real) is employed in the sense of existence and in the sense of goodness;
yet whatever is offered, given, performed as austerity, or done without faith—[is all called "asat"].
It is called "non-existent," O Pārtha, for it does not exist either after death or here in this world.

Furthermore, from the statement in the *Gītā*— "the word 'sat' denotes that which is good"— and from the statement in the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*, moreover, because the world lacks independence (*asvātantrya*), it is designated as "non-existent" (*asat*); for independence is defined as existence (*sattva*), and that [independence] belongs to Kṛṣṇa alone.
And others say:
"O Bhārata, the non-existence of all other things is established by their lack of independence."

Thus it is stated in the *Bhārata*. Furthermore, because the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is subject to transformation and destruction, it is unreal; therefore, it is designated as not being the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
For that which does not assume another name even after the lapse of time—indeed, that alone is real.
O King, how can that thing be a real entity if it is not produced through transformation and the like?

"The wise accept that the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is non-perishing (*anāśin*)," according to the statement in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*. In some instances, it is designated as "false" (*mithyā*) because of its uselessness (*vṛthātva*), as seen in such passages as "this resolve is false. In other cases, it is so designated because of its being defective (*sadoṣatva*).

The designation "mithyā-śabda" [is used] because, in the commentary on the rule *mithyopapadāt kriñaḥ abhyāse*, the example *padaṃ mithyā kārayati* is cited and explained as "he repeatedly utters a word that is incorrect, unroyal, or defective. Furthermore, in the *Nyāsa* and the *Padamañjarī*, it is stated that by this [example], one expresses the meaning of the word *mithyā*.

In some cases, there is a designation of non-reality (*atātvikatva*) due to being subject to modification; as stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "That which remains established even when that [state] has ceased is declared to be real. In other cases, there is a designation of non-existence because it does not exist in relation to the individual soul (*jīva*).

"Only that which does not exist appears to the individual soul"—according to this statement from the Skanda Purāṇa. The description of [the world] as being similar to a dream and so forth is due solely to its impermanence and changeability;
that is, by way of its nature consisting of impermanence, changeability, dependence, and so on.
The world, being similar to a dream and such, is not sublated by awakening.
Thus, from the statement in another Purāṇa;
and from the Śruti: "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the wielder of Māyā as Maheśvara. [She is] the one consisting of the three guṇas.
"Prakṛti is Māyā; because the universe is born from that, it is of such a nature. The wise have called it 'Māyā' throughout beginningless and endless times"—so says the Smṛti.

Because it is of the nature of Prakṛti, the expression "consisting of Māyā" (māyāmaya) in certain instances is appropriate; for this very reason, its establishment [occurs] through generic similarity (jātisārūpya).

"Based on praise, status, the collection of characteristics, and the locus of qualities"—thus, in the *Tatsiddhipaṭala*, having established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the statement "The sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*)—namely, whether the word "sacrificer" is a name for the grass-bundle, or whether it is an injunction of a quality in the form of the sacrificer with respect to the functions of the grass-bundle such as holding it and so forth— [The siddhānta follows: ... [the word is a name]. Why? Because of the impossibility of the injunction of a quality. For the quality of being the sacrificer cannot exist in the grass-bundle. Furthermore, because of the contradiction with the primary sense; for the primary sense of the word "sacrificer" is the person who performs the sacrifice, and that cannot apply to the grass-bundle. Moreover, because of the lack of connection; for there is no syntactical connection between the sacrificer and the functions of the grass-bundle, such as holding it. And because of the presence of a reason; for the text provides a reason: "Because he is the support of the sacrifice. This reason would be appropriate if the word were a name, as one names something by its cause of origin. But if it were an injunction of a quality, what would be the reason? There is no reason for the sacrificer's quality of supporting the sacrifice to reside in the grass-bundle. Therefore, the word "sacrificer" is a name for the grass-bundle. As for the praise, it is expressed by the words "He is the support of the sacrifice"; this is a praise of the sacrificer by means of the grass-bundle. Thus, it is established that the word is a name. (JS 1.4.1–16)
Because the meanings [of "sacrifice" and "offering"] would be entirely distinct—like the words "cow" and "buffalo"—it would be impossible for it to be a name;

furthermore, since the offering would itself be the function of the sacrificial grass (*prastara*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasanga*) of the sacrificer's own offering into the fire being lost as a remainder of the ritual action.
Thus, the positions that it is either a name or a prescription of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) are untenable, given its nature as a means of accomplishing the sacrifice.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *prastara* (grass-bundle) is praised by the word "sacrificer" through a figurative application (*gauṇī vṛtti*) based on its connection with the qualities of the sacrificer; thus, it possesses the status of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). For this very reason, in the two sections concerning "genus" (*jāti*) and "similarity" (*sārūpya*), regarding such cases as "The Brāhmaṇa is indeed Agni" and "The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is Āditya," the question of whether the words "Agni" and "Āditya" function as names (*nāmadheya*) or as injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*) [is addressed].
Having thus established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*),

[the author concludes that] by means of the word "fire" (*agni*) through its metaphorical application (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*) based on the quality of being born from the mouth of Brahman residing in fire, and by the word "sun" (*āditya*) based on the quality of possessing brilliance residing in the sun, the Brāhmaṇa [is denoted].
It has been established as a *siddhānta* that the statement "the sacrificial post smeared with ghee is praised" is an *arthavāda*. For this very reason,

in the section concerning "Praise," regarding the passage "Other animals than cows and horses are indeed non-animals (*apaśavaḥ*)," the term "non-animals" refers to goats and other animals denoted by the word "others" in relation to cows and horses.

Having established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the quality consisting in the prohibition of the function of cattle is being enjoined, [the author] argues that if the word *apaśu* were an injunction prohibiting the function of cattle, it would result in the redundancy of the injunctions for goats and other cattle.
It has been established as a settled conclusion (*siddhānta*) that [certain passages] are *arthavāda* (explanatory or commendatory statements) because they consist of praises of cows and horses.

Thus, by the principles of the aforementioned topical discussions (*adhikaraṇa*), since the application of a word for one thing to another is non-primary, the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-satyatva*) is merely figurative; therefore, the reality of the phenomenal world is only metaphorical.

It has been made clear that the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-satyatva*)— consisting in its connection with space and time— is non-figurative and primary (*mukhya*) alone. For this very reason, the negation of a difference relative to a phenomenal world that is figuratively non-existent is inseparable from [the affirmation of] a difference relative to a phenomenal world that is non-figuratively existent.
Because it is real, the distinction between Brahman and the heterogeneous phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is indeed primary; thus, there is no logical inconsistency.
But is this not improper? [For the scriptures state: "One only, without a second"; "There is no diversity whatsoever here";
"But where everything has become his very Self, then what second thing is there? and "Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name."
"All this is what this Self is; there is nothing whatsoever beyond it. If the phenomenal world (prapañca) exists, it ceases—of this there is no doubt.
Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite. Indra [creates] by means of māyās; whatever is other than that is afflicted. And so forth.
The non-existence of the nature of falsity, as established by scripture, is not figurative but primary.
For it is said: "Brahman is devoid of a second entity; there is nothing diverse in Brahman.
In that state which is liberation, when everything has become the Self alone, that Brahman does not exist as a second.
The phenomenal world consists of transformations;
it is merely a support for speech, for the object does not exist at all. All this is this Self.
The non-existence of anything other than Brahman means that there is no reality whatsoever other than Brahman, whether higher or lower; thus,

by the word "infinite" (ananta), the statement that Brahman is in reality unlimited in nature expresses the illusory nature of the world-phenomenon (prapañca) and the falsity of the universe, as it is composed of māyā.

If it is argued that, by this very method of reasoning through capacity (*śakti*), only the falsity (*mithyātva*) consisting in the non-existence of anything other than Brahman is what is being perceived—

and since this is established by numerous scriptural passages (*bahuśruti*), it must necessarily be primary (*mukhya*) rather than figurative (*aupacārika*)— we say no; for in the cited scriptures, [the term "false"] refers to *mithyā*...

Since there is an absence of a primary falsity due to the non-existence of a presently existing locus (*vidyamāna-pada*), one must explain that the statement is figurative (*aupacārika*)— just as in the case of "one should not take refuge in a non-existent person"— and that its purport is simply the existence [of the object]. Furthermore, just as in the cases "the universe is real" (*viśvaṃ satyam*) and "that which he has willed is real" (*yacciketa satyam*), [we say] "the pot exists" (*san ghaṭaḥ*) or "this is a pot" (*ayaṃ ghaṭaḥ*).

Since, through such means of valid cognition as "the bird is here, the bird is not here," etc., all objects other than Brahman are perceived directly as objects of knowledge precisely in their capacity as entities whose reality consists in their relation to space and time,
it follows that their falsity— consisting in non-existence, which is the opposite of that reality— is merely secondary.

Because it must be so stated; moreover, because in the passage, "In whom the heaven and earth and the intermediate space are woven, along with the mind and all vital breaths," such scriptural statements establishing the reality of the world within Brahman are restricted to specific objects and lack any other scope, it is more logical that they intend only a non-primary (gauṇa) falsity.
Nor should it be argued that the existence of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) in Brahman— which is established by scripture— is negated in that very context by scripture itself,
and thus its falsity (*mithyātva*) is indeed primary; for this is not so, as evidenced by such scriptural passages as "There is no diversity whatsoever here" (*neha nānāsti kiñcana*).
Otherwise, there would result the negation of the reality of Brahman itself— which is established by such scriptural passages as "It is indeed established in the greatness of Brahman"—

as well as the reality of Brahman established by such passages as "In the beginning, this was non-existent" and "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent," which [contradicts] the passage "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone. It is not so.

For, by the statement "one should not harm any living beings," there would follow the prohibition of even that injury to animals such as the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, which is established by the injunction "one should immolate the animal for Agni and Soma.

In that case, just as there is a distinction between the primary and secondary senses, or between those [injunctions] that have scope and those that are without scope, so too is it in the case of the phenomenal world (prapañca).
For it must be stated that there is no contradiction between these two precisely because of their primary and secondary status.
Nor can the scriptural statement regarding the reality of the world—which merely reiterates the existence already apprehended by perception—be considered weak;
for it is the scriptural statement of the world's falsity, which is stronger, that establishes its primary sense, as that falsity is not established by any other means of knowledge.

It must be said that the opposite is indeed logical. For in the Advaita view, in the statement "the pot is existent" (*san ghaṭaḥ*), the meaning of "existent" is Brahman as distinguished [from all else]; thus, the existence of the pot and so forth is not established [independently]. Furthermore, in the two scriptural passages—"That which is real among the unreal" and "He who by his knowledge distributed the objects according to their true nature throughout eternal years"—[it is the Lord who is the subject].

Because it is precisely the status of being the creator of the real world—something not established by any other means of knowledge—that is the object of the injunction. [In the case of] "Earth," although the difference from others is established in respect to certain parts such as jars and the like, which are already established by perception (p.

Furthermore, just as [existence] is not established in that which is qualified by earthness (*pṛthivītva*), so too, even if existence is established by perception in a single part such as a jar or a cloth, it is not established in that which is qualified by "the universe" (*viśvatva*); thus, the possibility remains that the sentence is not a mere restatement (*anuvādaka*).
Moreover, with reference to the Soma sacrifice called *daśapeya*, which is included within the *vājapeya*, it is heard [in scripture]: "Each one..."

Just as in the sentence, "The ten should creep toward the cup; a hundred Brāhmaṇas consume the Soma," so too, when the six-day period of the Gavamayana sacrifice— which is a modification of the six-day period of the twelve-day sacrifice—
is performed according to the original order, there is the sequence of the [sāmans] known as Rathantara, Bṛhat, Vairūpa, Vairāja, Śākvara, and Raivata.
When the six *sāmans* prescribed as the means for accomplishing the *pṛṣṭha-stotra* are obtained across the six days,

then— just as in the case of the sentence "The *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha* should be performed with the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* *sāmans*, which prescribes the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* *sāmans* everywhere— one should offer the *prājāpatya* oblation of cooked rice (*caru*)."

Since, in the case of the statement "one desiring long life [should give] a hundred *kṛṣṇala* [weights of gold]," the sentence "he gives everything to the Brahmin" is not a mere restatement (*anuvāda*),
so too the sentence "the universe is real," and so forth, can possibly be non-reiterative; and because, in that context,
the priesthood (*ārtvijya*) belongs exclusively to Brahmins, as established by the logic of the final section of the *Śāstra*.

Just as, although ten Brāhmaṇas are already established for each of the *brāhmaṇacamasas*, they are not [automatically] obtained in relation to the other intended object consisting of the *rājanyacamasas*; so too, although the quality of having the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* Sāmans is obtained from the injunction for the first two days, the *rathantara* is to be performed first in a different specific portion, namely the third day and so forth.

Immediately thereafter, just as in the case of [the word] *bṛhat*, although the portion referring to Brahman has the sense of something already established (*prāptārthaka*), there is nonetheless a lack of establishment regarding its connection with Brahman in the other portions; likewise, in the phrase "the universe is real" (*viśvaṃ satyam*), [the same applies].
Although the truth of the universe is established regarding objects such as jars and cloths that are within the scope of perception,

it is impossible for it to apply to other parts— such as supersensuous, past, or future entities— that are not accessible to perception. Furthermore, in the Aśvamedha sacrifice, the mantra "twenty-six are its ribs," which is obtained through the archetypal model (*prakṛti*), [is modified].

Having set aside the statement [of the general rule], since the specific statement— "The thirty-four horses of the divine kinsman, the horse Vājin, come together"— is recited directly and thus obtained, one might again say "thirty-four"; therefore,
for the purpose of a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*), one should rather say "twenty-six," just as there is the obtaining of the dual number in the archetypal (*prākṛta*) case.

In this context as well, since the statement "the universe is real" (viśvaṃ satyam) can be meaningful as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) for the reality of the world— which was established by perception in the form "the pot exists"— and which was subsequently sublated by such scriptural texts as "one only,
without a second," for the purpose of negating the falsity of the world; it is for this very reason that [this point] is addressed in the fourth quarter of my [work].

In the section concerning the specific statement "of the horse there are thirty-four," it was deliberated that in the Aśvamedha sacrifice, regarding the horse, the ram, and the deer dedicated to Prajāpati, thirty-four verses for the horse are recited: "Thirty-four are the limbs of the swift horse, the friend of the gods; the cries of the neighing horse come together. Thus, thirty-four verses are prescribed for the horse.
In that very context, they record this statement: "One should not say 'thirty-four'; one should say 'twenty-six'.

Regarding this, there arises a doubt: does the specific mantra, though prohibited, still apply as an alternative option, or is there a fixed application of the original (prakṛta) mantra alone? In this doubt, concerning the specific statement obtained through the [specific] recitation—

Since it is sublated by an explicit statement (*pratyakṣavacana*), the word *madhyagu* from the original text (*prākṛta*) must necessarily be recited just like the word *irā*; this being the position reached, [it is argued] that because of the explicit statement regarding the word *irā*...
Since that [word "ṣaḍviṃśati"] is prescribed in place of the word *girā*, it necessarily supersedes the word *girā*;
and although the prohibition of the word *girā* could be understood as established by implication (*arthataḥ*), in the present case one should simply say "twenty-six" (*ṣaḍviṃśatir ity eva brūyāt*).
Because this [injunction], its power being impaired by the particle *eva*, lacks the capacity to enjoin the original (archetypal) recitation, it is a specific (exceptional) rule.
Since the prohibition of the statement is not established by implication (*arthataḥ*), that statement must be enjoined by the very words "he should say thirty-four" (*catustriṃśad iti*).
Furthermore, a prohibition presupposes a prior possibility of occurrence (*prāpti*), and such a possibility cannot exist without a scriptural basis.
Therefore, it must be inferred that there exists a specific Vedic statement (*vaiśeṣika-vacana*) which serves as the source of that possibility, namely: "He should say 'thirty-four'."

Because there is no difference in the authoritative status of both the scriptures of injunction and prohibition, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that they constitute an option (*vikalpa*).

Likewise, in the present case as well, since there is no difference in the authoritative status of both the statements regarding the reality and the falsity of the world, there is an option; and if both were intended primarily to convey the reality and the falsity of the world respectively, it would result in a contradiction of the nature of the thing itself (*vastu-vairūpya*).

Based on such statements as "One should not rely upon an untrue person," it is logical that these [scriptures] primarily and secondarily intend to establish the reality of the world and the falsity [of duality].
For this very reason, there is the state of being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitā*) to negations pertaining to all times and all places.
That which is called "existence" is [defined] with respect to its respective counter-positive;
for when perceiving it at its own time, direct perception— by precluding a negation that pertains to the three times— indeed grasps its absolute non-sublatability.

Thus, because it has been stated according to this logic— that since [the Veda] is not connected with space and time, its meaning is not non-existent, and it is devoid of action and so forth— it is impossible for it to possess the primary form of falsity (mithyātva). This is the view of those who maintain the authority of the Vedas.

Since even all those who hold other philosophical systems (sarvasamayibhiḥ) must accept the non-primary form of falsity— characterized by being as good as non-existent and so forth— as described above,
there is no contradiction between the various views; thus, all Vedāntas primarily [refer] to that which is distinct from the individual soul, insentient matter, and the like.

Thus it is established that the primary purport [of the scriptures] is Śrī Nārāyaṇa, who is devoid of any internal differentiation. This concludes the illumination of the unity [of all things] through the negation of heterogeneous entities.
If it is argued that this is untenable— because although there is no contradiction in qualities such as knowledge and bliss being non-different from Brahman,

one must nevertheless accept their difference from Brahman because qualities such as having true desires, having true volitions, omniscience, being the Lord of all, and possessing all-powerful activity are false— then it is replied:
Just as there is distinction among knowledge and the other qualities, so too is their non-distinction accepted;
for this very reason, there is no contradiction among the attributes such as having true desires.

Just as there is scriptural evidence for the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of knowledge, bliss, and so forth— as in "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and bliss"— so too is there such scriptural hearing of coreferentiality in "He whose desires are true, whose resolve is true," and "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving."

The non-difference between desire, volition, and so forth must be accepted; therefore, the meaning is that there is no contradiction between our two positions here. This is because we hear grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in such passages as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite," "Brahman is consciousness and bliss," "He whose desires are true, whose volitions are true," and "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving," and so on, according to the *Citrājyādhikaraṇa*.
By means of logic and through the scriptural statement of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānyādhikaraṇya*), the connection of knowledge, bliss, will,
volition, and so forth with the non-difference of Brahman is established; this constitutes the [specific] section on that topic within the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa*.

Thus it has been established. To explain: regarding the passage "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā; there are fifteen Ājya-stotras," when the doubt arises as to whether the word *citrā* is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) or a name of a ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*), [the prima facie view is that] because the word *citrā* by conventional usage (*ruḍhi*) denotes an object qualified by variegatedness (*citratva*) and femininity (*strītva*), a quality in the form of variegatedness and femininity is enjoined in the archetype (*prakṛti*).
Or rather, that which is qualified by those attributes is what is enjoined; for if two separate attributes were enjoined, it would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

Furthermore, because of the complexity (*gaurava*) involved in enjoining a qualified entity, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the various substances mentioned in the originative injunction: "Curd, honey, clarified butter, water, grains, and rice—mixed together with these, [it is] the offering to Prajāpati. Thus, the qualified entity is what is enjoined.

The identity of the sacrifice with the meaning of the word *citrā* has been established; likewise, in the case of "there are fifteen *ājyas*," the identity of the *stotra* with the meaning of the word *ājya* is established because of their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Thus it is said: "His power is indeed heard to be manifold."

It must be stated that the difference between attributes such as power (*śakti*) and so forth is indeed heard in scripture; however, this is accepted as being non-primary (*amukhya*). Furthermore, there is no proof for non-difference [of the self] based on the scriptural hearing of the reality (*satyatva*) of desire (*kāma*) and other qualities. Nor can it be argued that because the objects are false, the desire and other qualities conditioned by them are also false; for the same logic would apply to cognition itself, which is beginningless (*anādi*).

Since there is an absence of the knowledge of a mental modification (*vṛtti-jñāna*) regarding Brahman, even though the object serves as a differentiator by its mere presence, it does not possess an internal form; thus, the knowledge is independent of objects and is not qualified by them.

This is because the *Anuvyākhyāna* states that since the falsity of objects and so forth is described as being non-primary (*amukhya*), it does not contradict their ultimate reality (*pāramārthika-satyatva*).
Nor should it be argued that there is a difference between us two based on whether Brahman is with parts (*sakhaṇḍa*) or without parts (*akhaṇḍa*).

For it is precisely through possession of attributes (*saviśeṣatva*) and absence of attributes (*nirviśeṣatva*) that the states of being determinate (*sakhaṇḍatva*) and indeterminate (*akhaṇḍatva*) are established. Nor should it be argued that difference (*bheda*) arises from those two alone;
for possession of attributes consists precisely in having infinite distinct attributes, while the absence of attributes consists in being devoid of infinite distinct attributes.

This is because the absence of distinctions is logically established. Nor should it be argued that non-synonymous and absolute terms are accepted as having a primary (mukhya) application toward Brahman for the sake of attaining those specific qualities which serve as their respective grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), whereas I, on the other hand, accept that they possess only secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the qualityless Brahman; for what difference does this make with respect to Brahman?

Since there is no contradiction between us regarding the negation of internal difference (*svagatabheda*), it is certainly not a rule that words lack denotative power (*vācakatva*) in cases where the basis for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is non-different. If that were the case, then words such as "knowable" (*prameya*) or "denotable" (*abhidheya*) would [be unable to function] except by means of a non-different property such as knowability (*prameyatva*), denotability (*abhidheyatva*), or the very nature of being [the object itself].

There would be no denotation of categories such as the "knowable" (*prameya*) and so forth. If that were the case, what fault would there be in the words "truth" (*satya*), "knowledge" (*jñāna*), and so on also denoting Brahman solely by way of their non-different attributes? For if the status of being the primary referent of words like "truth" belongs to Brahman, it is not a fault, just as the bank indicated by the word "Ganges" is not itself the Ganges.

Since it would follow that even Brahman—the object indicated by words such as "Truth" (satya)—would be unreal, and because Brahman must therefore be described as being only the secondary (amukhya) indicated meaning of words like "Truth," "Knowledge" (jñāna), and so forth.

Brahman is the indicated object (*lakṣya*). Furthermore, it is contradictory to say that its nature consists of truth, knowledge, and so forth; moreover, if Brahman were the indicated object by the word "indicated object" itself, it would follow all the more that it lacks the status of being an indicated object. Furthermore, because words would have to alternate between primary and secondary (indicative) meanings, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result. [Therefore,] that which is indicated by the word "without attributes" (*nirviśeṣa*) is not [the case].

It cannot be said that [the term] "without distinction" (nirviśeṣam) is redundant because Brahman would otherwise incur the status of having distinctions, nor because all other words would become redundant through secondary figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) when applied to Brahman; nor can it be argued that the other words are meaningful for the purpose of conveying the exclusion of falsehood and so forth, because such exclusion is useless for the cognition of pure consciousness devoid of any qualifying attributes (niṣprakāraka). Nor...
It cannot be argued that the exclusion [of other attributes] is purposeful because it serves as a means for the cognition of the essential nature;

for even if it were a means, since the cognition of the essential nature could be established by a single word alone through the medium of cognizing a single exclusion, the redundancy of the other words would remain unavoidable. This is because, in the case of the cognition of the mere undifferentiated essential nature, [no such utility exists].

There is a purpose for the cognitions of various exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*). Furthermore, it is difficult to avoid the conclusion that the exclusions of falsehood and so forth serve merely as gateways (*dvāra*) to the cognition of the true nature of Brahman. To explain: do these exclusions serve as gateways by being the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) of Brahman—like proximity (*sannikarṣa*) and other such factors—or by virtue of being intermediate operations (*avāntaravyāpāra*)? It cannot be the first.

Because it is untenable for those [attributes] to constitute the definition of Brahman. Is the definition a form of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), identical with the essential nature (*svarūpa*), or distinct from it? Not the first, because it is untenable for a form of exclusion—which is devoid of any unique attribute that constitutes its own nature—to serve as the essential definition (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*) of the essential nature, which is of the form of indivisible consciousness. Nor...
Nor can it be said that negative attributes (niṣedharūpā-dharmāḥ) are accepted as non-different from consciousness;

for by the same logic, the possibility of positive attributes (bhāvarūpa-dharmāḥ) being distinct from consciousness arises. Nor is the latter [position] tenable, because [consciousness] would then consist of unique attributes distinct from its own essential nature (svarūpa).
Since the realization of the nature of Brahman is established by the very knowledge of its defining characteristics such as truthfulness (*satyatva*),

it is a far-fetched interpretation (*vaktragati*) to assume that the knowledge of a defining characteristic in the form of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti-rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) generates the realization of Brahman. Thus, it is not [the case].

The second [point] is that, since the cognition of exclusion (vyāvṛtti) is produced by that [Veda], it cannot be an intermediate operation because it lacks the quality of being a producer of what is produced by that [Veda].
