Nor should it be argued that it is logical for the cognition of exclusion to produce a cognition of Brahman— which is itself produced by the Veda— while being produced by the Veda.

If the cognition were of the nature of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), it would be untenable for it to be produced by words such as "Being" (*sat*). For these words would have either a primary denotative power (*śakti*) or a secondary indicative power (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to exclusion. It cannot be the first, because there is no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to establish that [denotative power]. Nor can it be the latter, because indicative power is untenable in the absence of a relationship with the primary meaning.

Because there is no connection between "unreality" (asatyatva) and that which is qualified by "possibility," "being an entity" (bhūtatva), "truth" (satyatva), and so forth, there is all the more an absence of connection even with the exclusion of those [qualities]. Furthermore, it is improper to postulate a connection with something else when such a connection has never been observed anywhere. This applies to the words "truth" (satya) and the rest.

Since the cognition of the essential nature (svarūpa) is established simply by the cognition of the exclusion [of others] (vyāvṛtti) to be indicated, and because it is illogical for the essential nature itself to be the object of indication (lakṣaṇā), and furthermore,

since the door consisting of the cognition of exclusion is not required when the words "Being" (satya) and so forth convey the mere essential nature through indication; for [the cognition of the essential nature does not arise] from a word [directly] as its own referent...

Some objection must be addressed: [it might be argued] that in verbal cognition, just like the recollection of word-meanings, there is no need for the cognition of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), because it is unreal; furthermore, the claim that the referent (*lakṣya*) of words such as "real" (*satya*) is "excluded from the unreal" (*asatyavyāvṛtta*) contradicts all the established principles of the Tantrikas.

Therefore, since either the being denoted by words such as "truth" (*satya*) and "knowledge" (*jñāna*), or the exclusion of the untrue (*asatyavyāvṛtti*), must be metaphorical, if the exclusion of the untrue were metaphorical, it would follow that Brahman is unreal; [hence] the word "truth," etc., [p.

The non-primary status of being indicated by words must be accepted by all the crest-jewels of the Vedic tradition. For this very reason, such scriptural passages as "from which words turn back" and "without sound, without touch," as well as statements regarding its being unknowable and inexpressible, and the force of expressions such as "it is indescribable because of its wondrous nature," must be understood only in a figurative sense. And for this same reason:
Since the words such as "truth" (satya) denote only the essential nature [of Brahman], and since Brahman consists of knowledge and bliss, it is free from internal differentiation;

thus, this view that Brahman is devoid of internal distinctions is not in conflict with the three systems [of Śaṅkara, Rāmānuja, and Madhva]. In the *Tanmat aikyaprakāśa*, the non-difference of qualities, actions, parts, and incarnations is clearly elucidated according to the system of Rāmānuja.
"Everything is irreproachable" (*sarvam-anavadyam*) means the manifestation of unity through the negation of internal differentiation. By this [is meant the following scriptural passages]:

"His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold; His knowledge, strength, and action are innate," "That which shines is the immortal form of bliss," and "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," and so forth.
The non-conditioned nature of Brahman—which, according to scripture, consists of inherent qualities such as knowledge and bliss;

the neutrality of the Lord who bestows fruits in accordance with karma; the featureless nature resulting from the absence of distinct qualities like [limited] bliss, as expressed by the passage "here there is no diversity whatsoever"; and [the fact that He is the essence], as expressed by the passage "He is indeed the essence."

Thus, it is demonstrated that all this—the state of having consciousness as the sole essence—is not in conflict with the three philosophical systems (*mata*). This concludes the discussion on the consequence of unity arising from Brahman’s lack of adjuncts (*anopādhikatva*).
Now, [the opponent objects]: even so, there exists primordial ignorance (*ajñāna*) consisting of the three *guṇas* in a positive form (*bhāvarūpa*), which veils Brahman; and that...

It is twofold, distinguished by the collective (*samaṣṭi*) and the individual (*vyaṣṭi*). Brahman, as qualified by *māyā*—which is called ignorance (*ajñāna*) in its collective form—is the Lord (*īśvara*). And he [the Lord] is the cause of the world, and so forth.

Is it that the Brahman characterized by the previously mentioned qualities— whose omniscience and so forth are all false— is the *jīva* when qualified by individual (*vyaṣṭi*) ignorance; or is the *jīva* characterized by limited knowledge, non-sovereignty, the state of being an enjoyer, and other such attributes, being the Brahman delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)?

"Two views," and so forth. The object of knowledge (*prameya*) stated up to the end of the passage—namely, that "consciousness conditioned by those [attributes] is the efficient cause by virtue of its own primacy"—is indeed contradictory to your own position. This is because, as before, it is impossible to establish any lack of contradiction for that [position]. Thus, in this respect, the contradiction between the two views is difficult to avoid.

If this is argued, it is not so; for among the primary and secondary objects of knowledge (*prameya*) therein, it is possible to state [the identity] without contradiction by treating some as non-primary. To explain: in my own view, that which is denoted by terms such as *ajā* (the unborn), *prakṛti* (primordial nature), and *avyakta* (the unmanifest) is indeed the *pradhāna* (the primary cause), [and it is also] *māyā*, *avidyā*, *jñāna*, and so forth.
By means of words, it is figuratively described through the Śruti and Smṛti:
"O mighty-armed one, the qualities born of Prakṛti— sattva, rajas, and tamas— bind the imperishable embodied soul within the body."
"That which consists of the three qualities, unmanifest, eternal, and composed of both being and non-being—
what they call Pradhāna and Prakṛti, undifferentiated yet possessing differentiation"—
according to this statement from the Bhāgavata.
O son of Vinatā, from the massed darkness (tamas), the massed passion (rajas) is to be known as twice as great; indeed it is so, and not otherwise. From the massed passion (rajas), O son of Vinatā...
"Likewise, the aggregate of beings is declared to be twofold;
these are born from the primal nature (mūlaprakṛti), but the primal nature itself is not considered to be born [from anything].
By this statement from the *Garuḍapurāṇa*, that which is designated by the term "primal nature" (*prakṛti*) and so forth—

107) Because it must be stated that the *pradhāna* simply does not exist, and because it is impossible for it to be eternal since it would be the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of the destruction of ignorance; and because [the scripture] states, "Know *māyā* to be *prakṛti*," with reference to the meaning of the term *māyā*.

Furthermore, because its purpose is precisely the cessation of the knowledge regarding that ignorance which conceals [the Self], and because the term "ignorance" (avidyā) is used figuratively for the insentient primordial nature (prakṛti) due to the common property of being an obscuring factor,
it is also logical that the concealment of Brahman consists in its acting as an obstacle to the knowledge of Brahman. For this very reason, there are two unborn [entities].
When the two innate defects reside individually among men,

one is the "self-attribute-obscuring" (svaguṇācchādikā) and the other is the "supreme-obscuring" (paramācchādikā). Having abandoned the self-attribute-obscuring, one should resort to the supreme-obscuring.

Furthermore, because the *Bhāgavata-tātparya* states: "The Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) grants the path to liberation by breaking [it]," this establishes that *prakṛti* possesses the quality of being an obscuring agent (*āvarakatva*). Since it also consists of the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*), its nature as an obscuring agent is easily explained. Therefore, *pradhāna* alone is ignorance (*ajñāna*) and so forth.

By the term "padam," we also accept—as it is figuratively used in the Śruti, Smṛti, and other texts due to the aforementioned reasons—that positive ignorance (bhāvarūpājñāna) which veils the individual soul (jīva) and rests upon it:
"Knowledge is veiled by ignorance; by that, living beings are deluded."

Because of this statement from the *Gītā*, the meaning of that passage is intended to convey that the knowledge which constitutes the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) is veiled by ignorance (*ajñāna*) in its positive form; for it is stated in the *Tattvaprakāśikā* that "by others whose eyes are obstructed by the film of nescience (*avidyāpaṭala*)," and in the *Tattvodyota* that "the darkness resides in the person alone," referring to the mind as one's own essential nature (*svarūpamanas*).
Because it is stated that [the Self] is the substratum of ignorance and is concealed by it, that very ignorance is what brings about the transmigratory existence of the individual soul (jīva);
this bondage is caused by beginningless nescience (avidyā), desire (kāma), action (karman), and so forth.
Since bondage consists of negligence, liberation is likewise appropriate:
"The phenomenal world is the relationship between body and self for this embodied being;
nevertheless, it appears through [the soul's] identification with the body and so forth."

This is also because it is stated in the *Śrīmad-bhāṣya*: "Nor should it be argued that because bondage called *saṃsāra* is an effect of ignorance (*avidyā*), it follows that it must be illusory (*mithyā*). For even though that which has ignorance as its material cause (*upādāna*) is illusory, that which is caused by it (*nimittaka*) is not necessarily illusory.
Therefore, this bondage is caused by ignorance, desire, karma, and so forth."

The statement that ignorance (*avidyā*) is beginningless is due to its similarity to desire, action, and so forth. If it is asked how ignorance can be the cause of bondage, the answer is no; for it is accepted as the cause of bondage by way of producing false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*).
To explain: beginningless ignorance indeed obstructs the true knowledge (*tattvajñāna*) which removes the bondage of the individual soul (*jīva*).
It produces obstructive false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*). That, in turn, generates the group of six beginning with desire (*kāma*).
These produce active karmas (*pravṛttikarma*). And the karmas cause the individual soul (*jīva*) to attain a body appropriate to itself.
Thus, for the bound soul, its beginninglessness and reality by way of a continuous stream (*pravāha*) are logical. Such is the case for the wandering soul.

When, by virtue of one's own fitness, the opportunity for the means that bring about the cessation of bondage has arrived and a true guru is found, one should accomplish hearing and the other [limbs of knowledge] through the performance of virtuous actions as instructed by him;
thereby, having dispelled ignorance, doubt, and error, one attains the vision of Brahman.
Liberation, which consists in the experience of one's own bliss, occurs through the cessation of all undesirable states such as desire;
thus, even in the phrase "because it has negligence as its essence," the meaning is "because it has activity as its causal basis."

Because we observe the metaphorical treatment of cause and effect as non-different in such passages as "The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth," those who understand the purport of the Vedānta likewise accept that this phenomenal world, consisting of knowledge and the objects of knowledge, has ignorance as its cause.

By accepting that the bound state (*baddha*) is only figuratively false while maintaining its ultimate reality, those who uphold the authority of the Vedas (*vedaprāmāṇyavādin*) would remain consistent; otherwise, if the bound state were primarily false, it would entail the consequence of the Vedas being non-authoritative. For non-authority does not arise from anything other than the falsity of the object.
Because an instigator [of such a claim] is difficult to find, therefore, even by all those who uphold the authority of the Vedas, the primary reality of that which is bound must be admitted.
As for the delusion of ownership regarding the body, senses, objects, and so forth— which belong to the individual soul (jīva) but are not its own— [this is merely an illusion].
Our position is that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which has ignorance as its material cause (*upādāna*) and consists of the relationship between self and owner, is false (*mithyā*).
This is because it has been stated exactly so in the *Sudhā* and in the *Māṇḍūkya-bhāṣya*, where it says, "The proponents of reality (*tattva-vādinaḥ*) say," and so forth.

Therefore, even for the Rāmānujīyas, who are non-dualists [in this context], there is no inconsistency whatsoever in interpreting the scriptural passages concerning the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-mithyātva*) as having this very sense. As for the claim that the ignorance denoted by the word *tamas* is twofold—distinguished as collective (*samaṣṭi*) and individual (*vyaṣṭi*)—and so forth, which contradicts your own doctrine, that is not the case; for it is precisely the *pradhāna* denoted by the word *tamas* [that is meant].

Because it is twofold, distinguished as the collective (*samaṣṭi*) and the individual (*vyaṣṭi*), therein, consciousness conditioned by the *mahat-tattva* in which *sattva* predominates is indeed called Caturmukha (the Four-faced One),
because of its status as the agent of creation.

110) However, that [Lord] is described as distinguished by qualities such as omniscience which are appropriate for Him. Since He, known as the Four-faced One (Caturmukha), is a portion (*aṃśin*) of the fourth manifestation of the Blessed Lord, all attributes such as universal sovereignty (*sarveśvaratva*) reside in Him.
They are treated [as such] metaphorically; yet all those [attributes], being non-metaphorical and limitless, are false in the Four-Faced One (Brahmā).

By the phrase "consciousness conditioned by the adjunct of ignorance in the form of the individual [self] whose primary nature is impure *sattva*," it is meant that the consciousness of the living being (*jīva-caitanya*) has a body primarily characterized by the quality of *rajas* with an abundance of *tamas*, and the quality of *sattva*.

Because the living body, composed of the five elements, is of such a nature; and because if consciousness conditioned by primary ignorance were the individual soul (*jīva*), it would follow that the soul is false. Thus, the reality of the soul [is established], as well as the Vedic statements that teach its attributes such as limited knowledge and non-omnipotence.

Validity is thus established. The individual soul (*jīva*) also becomes the locus of knowledge, desire, effort, agency, enjoyership, pleasure, pain, and so forth, solely through its own nature (*svarūpa*) and the internal and external organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*); however, these [qualities] do not appear as belonging to the soul itself. For if they did, it would follow that the means for attaining knowledge and the like would be erroneous.

Because it would follow that ultimate liberation is non-existent, since the knowledge of reality alone is the means to liberation; for this very reason, consciousness conditioned by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is only figuratively called the "Lord" (*pati*) in relation to the individual soul (*jīva*), but not in the primary sense. This is because the internal organ, even though it is real, has as its material cause a specific portion of insentient primordial nature (*prakṛti*) denoted by the word *ajā*.
Due to the connection with the individual soul (jīva) residing in Brahman, it is logical that [the soul] possesses all greatness, such as being composed of light and so forth.

It should be understood that everything other than this is to be understood figuratively; for instance, the superimposition (adhyāsa) of ignorance (avidyā) and the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), and so on, is primary in the case of the "silver in mother-of-pearl" analogy. When that analogy is stated, the superimposition of ignorance and the ego-sense is primary.

Even the falsity of the witness is secondary; it consists of the unmanifested space (avyākṛtākāśa) as its locus, and has the nature of pleasure, pain, desire, knowledge, and consciousness, which have the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) as their material cause.
The witness (*sākṣin*) is said to be precisely the knowledge of one's own nature (*svarūpajñāna*) regarding objects such as time and so forth. And this is generally not contradictory.

This being the case, the portion from "and thus established is the final conclusion" (*siddhānta*) up to "therefore, the two powers" (*śaktidvayaṃ tataḥ*) should be understood according to their respective application.
It is examined according to the capacity [of the argument]:

Is the primary or secondary reflection of the all-pervading Brahman-consciousness—which is unobscured by ignorance—within ignorance [the cause]? Not the first, because it is unestablished; for what is called "being reflected" is as follows:

Reflection is the state of being reflected and the act of reflecting. It occurs when there is a clear substance as the material cause (*upādāna*) and the proximity of the original object (*bimba*) serves as the efficient cause (*nimitta*). Thus, it is the state of being an entity similar to the original object, produced from a clear substance with the proximity of the original object as its cause.

The state of being a reflection. For such a state of being a reflection is not primary in the case of consciousness (caitanya) as limited by the adjunct of ignorance (avidyopādhika). This is because ignorance, like darkness which is opposed to light, is an opaque substance; as such, it is opposed to knowledge, and therefore the reflection of consciousness upon it is impossible. Otherwise, even the light of the sun would [reflect] upon the darkness that opposes it.

Because it would entail the consequence of [the reflection] being a mere counter-reflection (*pratiphalanā*). Nor should it be argued that by the term "ignorance" (*avidyā*), the insentient primordial nature (*jaḍaprakṛti*) is understood in a secondary sense;
for even in that state, the reflection of the Brahman-consciousness is impossible.
Indeed, it is not logical that the Brahman-consciousness, which is of the nature of valid cognition (*pramā*), should reflect when pervading the non-lucid *pradhāna*.
And by the term "ignorance" (*avidyā*), the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)— which is the material cause of *prakṛti*—

is understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as a transparent substance whose nature is luminosity due to the proximity of the Lord as the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*) and due to its predominance in the portion of light. Within that [internal organ], there exists the form of the Inner Controller known as the "original image" (*bimba*).

It must be stated that it is that very [consciousness] which, named "jīva," reflects back; for we too accept that the jīva is of the nature of consciousness reflected in the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) at all times. (p. 112)

Since the state of being a *jīva* belongs precisely to that which is reflected within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) in its own essential form (*svarūpa*), the relationship between the *jīva* and Brahman as original object (*bimba*) and reflection (*pratibimba*), as well as their distinction, is established as eternally real. Furthermore, the reflection—the *jīva*—possesses similarity to the original object not merely through qualities such as consciousness (*cetanatva*), but by virtue of being a reflection itself; yet this does not imply total identity.

Because the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) in its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is eternal, and because the Lord who serves as the original image (*bimba*) is also eternal, it follows that the non-destruction of the living being (*jīva*) is likewise logical, since the proximity of the original image itself is never lost. Nor should it be argued that the living being would also be subject to destruction because it is reflected in an external limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) that is non-eternal.
Because it is accepted that the reflection of the individual soul (jīva) occurs only within the limiting adjunct (upādhi) consisting of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) in its own form—
it should not be argued that the conventional designation of the external internal organ as an adjunct is untenable;
for this mind is indeed a mixture of consciousness and unconsciousness as long as transmigratory existence (saṃsṛti) persists.

Thus, by this fundamental statement, it is established that during the state of saṃsāra, because only the external internal organ (bāhyāntaḥkaraṇa) conjoined with the internal organ of one's own essential nature (svarūpa-antaḥkaraṇa) performs all functions such as cognition and activity, its status as a secondary limiting adjunct (upādhi) is logically consistent; like a hibiscus flower [coloring a crystal], it serves as the locus for pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and so forth.

Alternatively, since it is possible for that [ignorance] to be the primary limiting adjunct (*mukhyopādhi*) by virtue of its non-existence in all phenomena, the reflection of the individual soul (*jīva*) in ignorance is not primarily tenable. Therefore, the individual soul is the reflection in the limiting adjuncts consisting of the essential nature and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); thus, the state of being reflected in ignorance [is not the primary definition].

Only the non-primary [view] should be accepted; for this very reason, the second [position] is not tenable, since it has already been stated that this would result in an undesired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).
Furthermore, regarding what was said on page 113—that the view is that the all-pervading Brahman-consciousness reflected in ignorance is the *jīva*—and so forth, in that case as well:

It can be rightly stated that the *jīva* is consciousness (*caitanya*)—which is similar to the all-pervading Brahman-consciousness—reflected in ignorance (*avidyā*), having as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) characterized by the state of ignorance. That [consciousness] is veiled by ignorance;
for darkness (*tamaḥ*) is indeed the supreme Person veiled by positive ignorance (*bhāvarūpājñāna*). As it is said: "by those whose eyes are covered by the film of ignorance."

Except for what is stated in the root commentary (*mūlaṭīkā*), everything else should be understood according to the primary [view]. Furthermore, as stated regarding the first position: although the consciousness of the individual soul (*jīvacaitanya*) is unobstructed and all-pervading, it does not by itself illuminate objects due to its insubstantiality (*asaṅgatva*); nevertheless, through the assistance of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) assuming the form of the object, it becomes colored by that respective object.
"It illuminates each respective object"— this is true. By asserting that the non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is not primary,
and by accepting the primacy of their difference, [the text refers to] the reflection of Brahman, which resembles the all-pervading, unconditioned Brahman.

The consciousness of the living being (*jīvacaitanya*), which is self-existent, atomic in form, supremely subtle, and composed of consciousness and bliss (*cidānanda*), does not manifest external objects by itself; however, through the medium of "coloration" (*uparāga*) characterized by conjunction with the modifications of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*),
it comes out through the doors of the senses such as the eyes and, by coming into contact with objects such as a jar, manifests those objects.

Nor can it be said that the external and internal organs themselves [are the agent], nor that the internal organ conjoined with its own essential nature (svarūpa), nor that the modification (vṛtti) transformed by the internal organ is conjoined with consciousness. For the inert internal organ, being merely conjoined with its own essential nature, lacks the capacity to produce an effect. Therefore, [the agency must belong to something else].

This is because the illumination of external objects must be explained solely by way of the activity of that [mental modification] as its effect. Nor should it be argued that this is impossible because consciousness cannot go outside; for there is no contradiction in the light non-different from consciousness occupying only the location of the door through which the mental modification passes, just as [consciousness] pervades the body.
Nor should it be argued that, if this were the case, there would be no distinction between indirect (*parokṣa*) and direct (*aparokṣa*) cognitions;

for cognition is indeed indirect by virtue of the specific nature of the manifestation residing in the mental modification (*vṛtti*), which consists of both potentiality (*śakti*) and actualization (*vyakti*).

Because indirectness (*parokṣatva*) is logically established—given the statement in the *Anubhāṣya*: "Just as indirectness and non-indirectness are two specific qualities belonging to cognition"—and given the statement:
"The individual soul (*jīva*) perceives all these states of affection at all times. Therefore, [it is] *cinmanas*...

The meaning is "mixed with the external mind. That the modification (*vṛtti*) takes on the form of the object has been correctly established in the *Nyāyāmṛta* and the *Tattvodyota* as being the primary [view]. Thus, even in the second view—that the individual soul (*jīva*) is consciousness delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—the external and internal [objects] are conjoined with the essential nature and the internal organ.

Since it is logically consistent that the knowledge consisting of the functioning of the instruments (karaṇavṛtti-jñāna) alone is the illuminator of objects, the luminosity of consciousness (caitanya) toward objects must be understood as being extremely secondary; thus, even by those who accept the non-difference of the individual soul and Brahman (jīvabrahmābheda) and the reality of the phenomenal world (prapañcasatyatva).
The statement that "ignorance possesses the powers of concealment (*āvaraṇa*) and projection (*vikṣepa*)" is also to be understood as being secondary (*amukhya*) from the very beginning;
therefore, the entire intermediate process is secondary and is not absolutely contradictory to our [view].
This is the summary. Thus ends the illumination of the unity of the intermediate and subordinate processes.

But even if this is so, and even if there is no contradiction whatsoever regarding the aforementioned collection of objects of knowledge, the Brahman’s status as the non-different efficient and material cause— which we accept— is contrary to your own view; for instance, it is Brahman, characterized by the limiting adjunct of *māyā*, that is the cause of the world as propounded in the Sūtra "From which the birth, etc., [of this world proceed]," and that [Brahman]...

If it is argued that there are two causes— namely, the efficient cause (*nimitta*) by virtue of its own predominance, and the material cause (*upādāna*) by virtue of the predominance of [its own] substrate— and that this is just as a conscious spider is the efficient cause with respect to its own effect, the thread, by virtue of its own predominance, and the material cause by virtue of the predominance of its own body; so too [is Brahman].
To this it is replied:
The cause is like its modification, yet it is also characterized by being free from modification.

When it is declared by the crowns of the Vedas— that is, those who perceive the truth through their minds— that Brahman alone is one, though described through the distinction between primary and secondary meanings,
a certain investigation should be undertaken without contradicting the three philosophical systems.

Brahman alone is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), being changeless like a potter; and it is also the agent—the two "ca" particles serve to conjoin these roles mutually. This statement that "Brahman is the material cause" is not to be taken in its primary sense;
rather, "Brahman as the material cause" refers to either Māyā related to Brahman or to the insentient primordial nature (*jaḍa-prakṛti*).

Because [the self] accepts being the material cause (*upādāna*) of that which possesses modification; because, as in the case of "a hamlet on the Ganges," it is non-primary (metaphorical), like saying "the hamlet is on the bank"; and because here too, all three types of relationship exist—the relationship between the limiting adjunct and the limited, the relationship between the governed and the governor, and the relationship of body and embodied—[therefore] in its own material cause...

The meaning is that the Vedāntas establish that Brahman’s agency consists in its possessing the desire to act and the volition for immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*), as well as its being changeless (*nirvikāra*); this is the primary sense [of its agency]. Furthermore, in passages such as "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā," the term *māyā* [is used].

The meaning is that those who understand [the term] to denote *prakṛti*, who perceive the essential meaning of the doctrine, and who are free from envy, should not entertain any doubt regarding the non-contradiction of the three views. Now, another view is as follows: like two threads on a rope, Brahman qualified by *māyā* is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world; the meaning is that *māyā* resides in Brahman as the material cause. As for the scriptural texts concerning its being changeless (*nirvikāra*), [they refer to something else].
Or, Māyā is that which has Brahman as its sole support;
116) Brahman, through the influence of Māyā, is the material cause of the world, while Brahman undergoes modification [only figuratively], for scripture declares it to be changeless.

Alternatively, Brahman is the material cause of the world because it is the substratum of *māyā*, which is colored by that [Brahman]; just as cloth has threads as its material cause, so Brahman has *māyā* as its medium for being the material cause of the world. Furthermore, the Śruti is intent on negating modifications that are not mediated [by *māyā*], or else [it refers to] an unreal internal form.
The production of an effect (*kāraṇaprapatti*) is an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*); transformation (*pariṇāma*) is the assumption of another real form.
Mere assumption of another form constitutes the material cause (*upādāna*), and this is compatible with Brahman’s being an illusory manifestation.

As for the scriptural texts concerning its changelessness (*nirvikāra-śruti*), they intend to convey the absence of any real modification (*tāttvika-vikāra*). It is not [the case that Brahman is subject to change].
Alternatively, it is like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, which has both as its material cause because it is a transformation of ignorance and because the mother-of-pearl is its substrate;

or else, it is that which is the object of the cognition of having undergone a change of form, or the object of the cognition of non-difference from another form, because it is an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of Brahman and a transformation of ignorance.

Alternatively, we accept that being the material cause consists in being the object of the cognition of non-difference from the effect; and this is indeed contrary to your own view. Likewise, the agency of Brahman is either merely its status as a locus—as in the case of mother-of-pearl and the like—or it is a technical designation, or it is the state of being perceived through superimposition by one who is deluded.

Whether it be the quality of deluding others like a magician, or the possession of effort directed toward material causes like a potter—these four positions are all contrary to your own doctrine. Therefore, if you claim that Brahman’s status as both material cause and agent is established as being primary, we reply: in all these stated views, [there is a contradiction].
The status of Brahman as the material cause (*upādānatva*) is primary, whereas its status as the agent (*kartṛtva*) is accepted by all as primary;
for instance, in the first position—that Brahman qualified by *māyā* is the material cause of the world—[it is *māyā* that serves as the material cause].

The meaning is *prakṛti* (primordial matter). Since it has been stated in accordance with the scriptural text, "One should know Māyā as *prakṛti*," just as potters and others possess the means such as lumps of clay for effects like jars, so too Brahman possesses the means such as *prakṛti*, which serves as the material cause (*upādāna*) for effects such as the Great Principle (*mahat*). This state of being endowed with that [material cause] is its qualification; this is its status as the material cause.

The primary [meaning]—which, like a lump of clay and so forth, rests solely upon primordial matter (prakṛti) and the like—is that Brahman, as qualified by its attributes, is the material cause based on the authority of Śruti and Smṛti; this secondary [usage] must be understood according to the maxim of the umbrella-bearer.
Furthermore, there is no difficulty in avoiding contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning the changelessness (nirvikāra) of Brahman.

In the second view as well, if the term "māyā-śakti" is explained as meaning "the power called māyā," there is no difference from the first view; and if it is explained as meaning "the power which is māyā," there is likewise no difference from the first view because of the non-difference between the power and its possessor. In the third view too, that which is designated by the word "māyā" is simply the *pradhāna* of Brahman.

And "being the substratum" (tadāśrayatva) is intended here precisely as being the inner controller (antaryāmin), having that as one's body (taccharīraka), possessing its existence and activity, and being its regulator.
The illustration beginning with "by means of the thread," etc., refers merely to the state of being a substratum for existence. And thus, this [present case] is also the same.

Even in the fourth view, which is included within the previous positions and does not contradict the three views, the absolute status of Brahman as the material cause (*upādānatva*) is untenable. This is because, according to the method of explaining the unity of the negation of heterogeneous things and their manifestation, it is impossible for Brahman to be the material cause of an illusory transformation (*vivarta*) consisting in the assumption of an unreal form; for Brahman is changeless (*nirvikāra*).
Because transformation (*pariṇāma*), which consists in the assumption of another real form, resides in *prakṛti*, it cannot belong to Brahman.

Furthermore, as for what was said—that the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of the shell because it is a transformation of ignorance (*ajñāna*)—(p. 118) [this is incorrect].
Regarding the phrase "derived from both": as for the word "just as," that is not the case, because it is impossible for the mother-of-pearl to be the material cause (*upādāna*) of the silver.

For instance, being the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of a superimposition cannot be the technical definition of "material cause," since the term "material cause" is never used in reference to a substratum; even if it were used in some way, such usage would be non-primary (*amukhya*).
If it is argued that because there is no purpose [in asserting such a thing], and even if that were the case, it would not contradict our own view, and furthermore,

that the designation of "having the mother-of-pearl as its material cause" is figurative because it actually has as its material cause the ignorance that veils the consciousness delimited by the mother-of-pearl—
this too is not correct, because it is impossible for color (rūpa) to have as its material cause the ignorance that veils the consciousness delimited by the mother-of-pearl.

To explain: is the production of silver, which has ignorance as its material cause (*upādāna*), in a mother-of-pearl shell accepted on the strength of experience, or because it cannot be explained otherwise? It is not the first, because there is no such experience as "the silver in the mother-of-pearl shell has been produced," unlike experiences such as "a pot has been produced" or "a cloth has been produced. Nor is it the second.

Is it cognition or something else that accounts for the production of silver and so forth? Not the first, because cognition whose objects are past, future, and so on does not account for the production of those objects; therefore, the cognition of silver and so forth likewise cannot account for their production.

Nor should it be argued that non-perceptual cognition, like that of jars and the like, serves as the cause for the production of [the object]. For when one perceives directly the absence qualified by its counter-correlate (pratiyogin) in the form "there is no jar on the ground," even this perceptual cognition cannot be said to cause the production of the object. Furthermore, at that time, there is no perceptual cognition [of the jar] as being located in the space before one.
It must be stated that the status of being an object (*viṣayatva*) is that which makes the production of the object possible—
since [objects] exist in the space in front even without being produced at the time of the rising of the sun and so forth.

Because it is observed to have an object that is not immediately present (*aparokṣa*), that [nescience] also cannot be the cause of its production. Nor is the latter [alternative] correct, because such [an immediate object] is not perceived. Furthermore, [the error] has as its material cause a cognition that veils the consciousness delimited by the mother-of-pearl (*śukti*) which serves as the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

Because the statement "silver has arisen" is untenable, one must ask: is that silver produced by such ignorance (ajñāna) co-existent with its causal capacity (*śakti*), or does it exist only for the duration of its cognition? It cannot be the first, because it would follow that the silver in the mother-of-pearl lacks the status of being *prātibhāsika* (illusory); for being constituted solely by cognition is precisely what constitutes *prātibhāsikatva*. Furthermore...
Furthermore, [the first alternative is untenable] because it would entail an infinite regress of objects produced by the ignorance that veils the consciousness delimited by the mother-of-pearl.
Nor is the latter [alternative possible], because even if all the causal conditions were assembled beforehand, there would be no cause for its production at the very moment of perception;
therefore, in accordance with experience, all parties must accept that the silver is absolutely non-existent (*atyantāsadeva*).

It must be accepted that [the silver] is perceived as immediate precisely by the sense organ in contact with the mother-of-pearl, which has had its power imparted by the force of a defect; thus, even in the fourth view, the status of Brahman as the material cause (*upādānatva*) is indeed primary.
Furthermore, regarding the two views mentioned—namely, that being the object of a cognition of non-difference from another form constitutes material causality—even there:

Being the object of a valid cognition (*pramā*) whose mode is non-difference from another form is the definition of being the material cause through transformation (*pariṇāmopādānatva*); being the object of a valid cognition whose mode is non-difference from the effect is the definition of being the material cause through illusory manifestation (*vivartopādānatva*). Furthermore, that [material cause] is indeed real.

According to the method stated by Prakāśa on page 120— namely, that there is no difference between Brahman and its other forms due to the negation of distinctions between homogeneous and heterogeneous entities— there is an absence of valid cognition (*pramā*) regarding such [differences].

Since it is impossible for [the effect] to have the status of primary material cause (*mukhyopādānatva*) in the sense of being its objective domain, even though there may arise an error regarding the non-difference of another form acquired through a failure to understand the intent of the scripture, nevertheless, everyone accepts that [the effect] has the status of primary material cause in the sense of being its objective domain; and in this very same way, it also possesses the status of being the object of the cognition of non-difference from the effect.
Therefore, since primary material causality (*upādānatva*) in Brahman is untenable, non-primary material causality results in a state of non-causality; thus, nothing is inconsistent.
The proofs for [Brahman's] material causality will be established in the *Rāmānujamataikyaprakāśa*. As for what was stated:

The claim that Brahman’s status as an agent contradicts your own position is incorrect; for the term "agent" is not conventionally applied to substrates such as mother-of-pearl, and since the omniscient Lord possesses true knowledge regarding all objects, He cannot be subject to error, which would also contradict the great respect [accorded to Him].
Both positions are untenable. As for its delusive nature:
"Thus I quickly create this delusion which shall bewilder people through birth; this person, deluded by the Lord's māyā..."
"The vision of misfortune does not resort to you because of yours [your nature]"—
through such statements, there is no contradiction based on the distinction of qualified recipients (adhikāribheda);

however, even though there is the conventional usage of "seeing" elephants and so forth in one who possesses illusory power (māyāvin), there is an absence of the conventional usage of "agency" (kartṛtva).

Such agency is indeed primary, consisting in the possession of immediate knowledge, desire to act, and volition directed toward the material cause, just as in the case of a potter and others; since this fourfold view of agency is accepted by all, there is nothing inconsistent. This also applies to the *Tadananyatva* (Non-difference from That) section.

121) "By that [reasoning], the difference from independent causes is here negated"—this should be understood as explained in the *Anuvyākhyānasudhā* in a manner consistent with this [view]. Therefore, [the cause] is distinct from both the sentient and the insentient.

It is thus established that Brahman, known as Nārāyaṇa, who is denoted by all Vedic terms, is the one and only cause— both the efficient and the material cause— of the birth and so forth of the entire world without exception. This concludes the exposition on the unity of Brahman as both the non-different efficient and material cause.

Is this not indeed improper? For Brahman is understood from the Vedānta texts to possess two forms—as gross and subtle, and so forth—and as Brahman with attributes (saguṇa), such as "whose desires are true" and "whose resolves are true.
This is because it has been determined exactly thus in the section [of the Brahma-sūtras] beginning with *na sthānato 'pi parasyobhayaliṅgaṃ sarvatra hi*.

And thus, Brahman with attributes (*saguṇa-brahma*) is denoted by all such Vedic terms as "truth" (*satya*) and "knowledge" (*jñāna*), because of the actual existence of the qualities that serve as the grounds for their application; whereas Brahman without attributes (*nirguṇa-brahma*) is indicated by all those same Vedic terms through secondary signification (*lakṣya*), from which words turn back.

"Soundless, touchless, formless, and imperishable"—thus it was spoken by means of non-utterance, according to the Śruti. Brahman with attributes (saguṇa-brahma) itself, when devoid of all qualities such as omniscience which consist of Māyā, is Brahman without attributes (nirguṇa-brahma) alone, designated as "the distinct" (vivikta). Thus, given this great divergence of opinion here, how [can] that which is called Nārāyaṇa be the Supreme?

If it is argued that Brahman is denoted by all words, it is replied to this: first of all, it is not logically tenable for the Supreme Brahman to possess two primary forms, because that would contradict such scriptural passages as "One only, without a second. Nor can it be said that the two forms are themselves one and the same; for if one were to postulate two forms...
122) Because there would be no purpose [for creation] and because it is impossible for that which is devoid of attributes (nirguṇa) to be the cause of the world,
Brahman— known as Īśvara— is accepted as being characterized by attributes such as omniscience and as having *māyā* as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for that purpose.

It must be stated [that this is not so], because of the scriptural hearing that the one, qualityless Brahman alone is the cause of the world, in such passages as: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second; it thought; it manifested name and form," and so forth. Nor can it be argued that at the time of dissolution, Brahman alone remains in a state of sleep, with its activities such as the creation of the world unmanifested.

The play of *mudrā* is that which is known through such Vedic scriptures as "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent," and so forth; it is denoted by terms such as "void" (*śūnya*) and "devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇa*). Furthermore, upon re-creation, that very same [reality], having become manifest, undergoes activities such as the creation of the world;
it is agitated by the desire to create (*sisṛkṣā*) and is accompanied by the causal material and other factors known as *prakṛti*, *māyā*, and so on.
Brahman itself is designated as "with attributes" (saguṇa).

It must be stated that the descriptions of it as "with attributes" or "without attributes" (nirguṇa) are justified respectively by its possession of non-material (aprākṛta) qualities and its being devoid of material (prākṛta) qualities.

For it has already been stated that although the descriptions of Brahman as both with attributes (*saguṇa*) and without attributes (*nirguṇa*) are possible due to differences in time or differences in intention regarding the single Brahman itself, two primary forms are nonetheless impossible;
this remains true even when all incarnations (*avatāras*), such as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, are understood to possess both attributed and unattributed natures according to the speaker's intention.

Furthermore, there is no dispute among all [schools] regarding the non-difference of the fundamental form (*mūlarūpa*), as this has been determined exactly so in the section beginning with "Not even on account of place" (*na sthānataḥ*).

If it is objected that, such being the case, it is contradictory for Brahman—which is of a single form—to be both the primary denotation (*vācyatva*) and the indicated meaning (*lakṣyatva*), we say no; for there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) to accepting that one and the same [form] is both primary and [indicated]. Nor is it the case that it is only the indicated meaning...

It must be stated that [the Brahman] is the primary meaning according to such scriptural passages as "from which speech turns back" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4.1). For it cannot withstand the following dilemma:
is the primacy of an object of knowledge its being cognizable by a word through its primary power (*śakti*), or is it its being cognizable by a word through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*)?

The first [alternative] is not tenable because it is impossible; for the word *lakṣya* (the indicated) lacks denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to Brahman. Nor should it be argued that it is appropriate for Brahman to possess the meaning of the word *lakṣya* through its etymological derivation as a passive (*karma-vyutpatti*)—meaning "that which is indicated" or "known"—based on the ground for application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*) consisting in being an object of knowledge (*jñeyatva*). This is because [Brahman] is precisely what is understood by a word functioning as an indicator (*lakṣaka*).

This is because it is not accepted that the basis for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) constitutes the denotation of the word *lakṣya*; or alternatively, because even through the etymological derivation from the instrument (*karaṇa*), the primary meaning of the word is simply the instrument of knowledge. Nor is conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) of the word *lakṣya* possible with respect to Brahman, because there is an absolute absence of any general usage [of the term] in that sense. Indeed, [such usage] is not found in the Vedas or other scriptures regarding Brahman.
The use of a word in its secondary (lakṣya) sense is something observed previously. It has been stated that "the abundance of usage alone is called conventional meaning (rūḍhi).
Nor should it be argued that the Vedic usage in such passages as "from which words turn back" (*yato vāco nivartante*) itself indicates a conventional meaning;
for even there, a word in its secondary sense is heard. Furthermore, "words" (*vācaḥ*) refers to expressive words [and not to Brahman].

Since [the words] turn back and are not capable of conveying [the meaning], it is logical that the word which is the indicated (lakṣya) sense— conceived through the impossibility otherwise of the direct Vedic statement (śrauta-śruti)— is itself "Vedic" by virtue of its attainment. Otherwise, [if this were not the case],
[one would have to rely on] the impossibility otherwise of the relationship between the end and the means (sādhya-sādhana-bhāva) between the sacrifice and gold.

Because it would follow that a postulated *apūrva* (unseen potency) would not be Vedic, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that dharma and adharma are cognizable solely through the Veda would be undermined.
Thus, [the *apūrva*] is postulated because otherwise a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) would be inexplicable.

Because the Soma and other items prescribed by the injunctions of qualifiers, as well as the mantras to be applied by means of direct Vedic statements inferred from their indicative power (*liṅga*) and so forth, are not themselves subject to the injunctions of those explicit injunctions.

Nor should it be argued that [the Upanishads] do not fall under the category of injunctions for Vedic application (*vaidika-viniyoga-vidhi*), because there is no evidence to support the claim that words functioning as indicators (*lakṣaka*) alone are what convey Brahman. Furthermore, such words as "from which speech turns back" (*yato vāco nivartante*) and "he beholds the Person dwelling in the city, higher than the high" (*parātparaṃ puriśayaṃ puruṣam īkṣate*) are indeed expressive words (*vācaka*).
It must be said that the impossibility of the knowability [of the Veda] otherwise than by being an object of cognition (*bodhya*) is precisely what leads to its postulation.

However, in this case, because one hears words that express it, there is again the certainty of the absence of such a postulator. This is because the word *vāk*—in the phrases *gīrvāṇī* and *sarasvatī*—refers to speech in general, and thus refers to sound in general.
Given that something is cognizable, its being entirely uncognizable is only conceivable through the impossibility of its otherwise being knowable;

however, being cognizable by a word that functions as a *lakṣaka* (indicative) does not establish its being uncognizable by words in general— just as being fat establishes eating at night— but on the contrary, it proves the opposite.

It should not be said that even the state of not being understood by the denotative word is itself imagined through the "inexplicability" (anupapatti), since it is precisely the absence of that [understanding] which accounts for it.
Therefore, [the definition is]: being knowable while not being understood by any word denoted by the term "śrauta," and [being knowable] while being knowable in its entirety.

Since it is only that which is appropriately knowable (*jñeyatva*) that serves as the conceptualizer, there is no proof whatsoever of the word's denotability (*padabodhyatva*) as the defined object (*lakṣyaka*).
[This is because] the sacrifice, being subject to extremely rapid destruction, [cannot produce a result] occurring at a later time.
(125) It is logical that the *apūrva* (unseen potency), known as dharma and adharma, which is not established by other means of knowledge, must indeed be based on scripture (*śrauta*).
This is because, in injunctions such as "One should sacrifice with Soma," the establishment of a qualified injunction necessitates the injunction of the qualifiers already established.

The Vedic nature of *soma* and the like, as well as of those mantras whose application is determined by indicative marks (*liṅga*) and the like, is appropriately established as Vedic because their application is enjoined by a scriptural injunction (*vidhi*) that is itself inferred. In this regard, the Vedic nature of *soma* and the mantras, as well as their status as being established by the application-injunctions of specific injunctions (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), [is thus justified].

Because that [other case] is established by valid cognition (*pramita*), there is a disparity in the application of that logic; therefore, since there is an absence of any means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend a primary denotative power (*śakti*) for the word "Brahman" with respect to its designated object (*lakṣya*), it is logical that its being a designated object is not primary.
Rather, because of its wondrous nature, it is inexpressible, inconceivable, and yet to be known.

"Even the world says on earth that [Brahman] is 'inexpressible,' which is most wonderful"— by such statements, just as the quality of being inexpressible is figurative (gauṇa) in Brahman due to its association with qualities such as wonderfulness, so too it is logical that its being an object of indication (lakṣyatva) is likewise merely figurative, owing to its association with the quality of inexpressibility.

For this very reason, the second [position] is not tenable. This is because, if the word "lakṣya" (the indicated) were itself to indicate Brahman, then the status of being an "indicated" (lakṣyatva) and the resulting non-literal status (amukhyatva) of that which is understood by it would be established by the logic previously cited; furthermore, this non-literal status of a secondary (lākṣaṇika) meaning has been determined in the sections concerning "the commonality among those moving forward" (*prasarpiṣu sāmānyāt*) and so forth. More on this [will follow].
This should be seen in the *Svāgataniṣedhaikya-prakāśa*, the *Nyāyāmṛta*, and other such works; this is the summary.
Therefore, Brahman is one, being both with attributes (*saguṇa*) and without attributes (*nirguṇa*), according to the Śruti.
"By means of understanding the primary and secondary [meanings], thus in the definitive conclusion of the Vedānta,
there is no contradiction whatsoever among the three types of views.
This is the illumination of the unity indicated by all the words.

But even so, since we accept that knowledge of Brahman devoid of modes (*niṣprakāraka*) is the means to liberation, the contradiction remains exactly as it was. For [the scriptures state]: "Knowing Him thus, one goes beyond death"; "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme"; "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow"; and "It should be seen as one alone."
"The cessation of conceptual proliferation, auspicious, peaceful, non-dual—this they consider the fourth. That is the Self;
that is to be known. Since such scriptural passages state that knowledge devoid of modes alone is a constituent of liberation, [the opponent] says: "No, because—"
For although there may appear to be a contradiction at first glance, in the final analysis there is no contradiction;
indeed, it is established that knowledge possessing that specific mode is the means for liberation.
Thus, while knowledge possesses that mode, it likewise possesses the state of being devoid of modes.

When it is stated that [the teachings] are primary and secondary, the contradiction is easily resolved. Even when a contradiction is perceived due to a lack of understanding regarding the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the scripture, no contradiction exists once the meaning of the scripture has been investigated through *mīmāṃsā*. He explains this very point with the words "with its modes" (*saprakārakam*): the direct (*aparokṣa*) knowledge of Brahman, together with its modes, alone is the means to liberation.

It is established as follows: when it is stated that having a mode (*saprakārakatva*) is primary while being devoid of a mode (*niṣprakārakatva*) is secondary with respect to knowledge, the contradiction is resolved without effort; this is the meaning.
Now, one might object: how can the state of being devoid of a mode, which is established by the cited scripture (*śruti*), be primary? For that very [state]...

Because it is understood that this is the primary meaning; for instance, in the first sentence, "Having known that very [Self], one goes beyond death" (p. 127), the nature of Brahman is denoted by the word "that" (*tat*).

When it is stated, "Having known [Him], one transcends death," it is understood that knowledge whose object is the essential nature alone (*svarūpamātra*) is the means to liberation. This is not like [the injunction] "One who has been initiated should study," because of the reference by the two words *tam* and *evam* to the previously mentioned subject characterized by attributes such as having a thousand heads.

It must be stated that this is the establishment of non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpakajñāna*). Since that attribute serves as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) and is thus a means for the realization of the true nature (*svarūpa*), it is the true nature itself—by virtue of being perfect bliss—that ought to be seen as the supreme human goal;
otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural statement, "It is to be perceived in one way alone" (*ekadhāivānudraṣṭavya*). In one way...

The meaning is that it possesses a single object (*ekaviṣayatākam*). Nor should it be argued that because the suffix *thāl* denotes a "manner" (*prakāra*), its meaning is "having a single manner," and thus the intention of [the text] being non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) is not established;
for in the verbal cognition produced by the word-potency (*śakti*) regarding the Brahman you accept, there must necessarily be multiple manners (*nānāprakārakatva*).

For it is difficult to establish that [the cognition] is of a single nature by its very being; whereas for me, there is no contradiction in the fact that even in a non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpakabodha*) based on secondary indication (*lākṣaṇika*), there is a single objective referent (*ekaviṣayatā*). Thus, in all such statements as "The knower of the Self transcends sorrow," it is understood that knowledge of the essential nature of Brahman is a constituent part of liberation, and that this consists in the knowledge of the essential nature alone.
It is the state of having the essential nature alone as its object, while not having as its objects any properties (dharma) or other attributes distinct from that essential nature;
and such knowledge is indeed devoid of a mode (niṣprakāraka), whereas knowledge qualified by properties and the like is precisely that which has a mode (saprakāraka).

For "being a mode" (prakāratva) is simply the state of being the counter-correlate (pratiyogitva) of the relation of qualification (vaiśiṣṭya) as it appears [in cognition]. Therefore, [this is] that which serves as the means to liberation.

If it is argued that for the knowledge of Brahman, the absence of qualifiers (*niṣprakārakatva*) is the primary [nature] as established by scripture (*śrauta*), we say no; for the absence of qualifiers in verbal cognition (*śābdajñāna*) contradicts all empirical experience (*sarvānubhava*). To explain:
For instance, it is undisputed among all [scholars] that every cognition produced by a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is determinate (*savikalpaka*);

indeed, it is only by the logicians (*tārkika*) themselves that indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) is admitted. And although, even if a cognition having the delimitor of the word-meaning as its qualifier (*padārthatāvacchedaka-prakāraka*) arises from a word through primary denotation (*śakti*), and through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*)...
A cognition whose mode is the delimiting property of the object of reference (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) is not entirely absent;

indeed, a cognition consisting of the mere essence (*svarūpa*) without any mode is established by experience as arising from words. Nevertheless, although worldly verbal cognition is experienced as being determinate (*savikalpaka*), it is [nonetheless] a factor for liberation (*mokṣāṅga*).

The knowledge born of Brahman is not experienced as being conceptual. They consider that which is the cessation of the phenomenal world, auspicious, non-dual, and the Fourth—that is this very [Brahman]. "Verily, he who knows thus becomes the fearless Brahman. He who perceives here as if there were multiplicity goes from death to death. Thus indeed should it be perceived.

Because of contradictions with such scriptural passages, it is understood through the two terms "cessation of the phenomenal world" (*prapañcopaśama*) and "non-duality" (*advaita*) that [Brahman] is indeed devoid of all modes (*niṣprakāraka*).
This is because by the term "cessation of the phenomenal world," the destruction of the phenomenal world is perceived, and by the term "non-duality," the absence of duality is perceived;
furthermore, since even "manifestation" is included within the meaning of the words "phenomenal world" and "duality," for one who is here...

Even in the passage "He sees as it were manifold," since the attainment of what is undesirable is mentioned in reference to qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*); and because in the passage "It should be seen as one alone," there is an injunction that the object must consist solely of the single nature of self-luminous consciousness (*svarūpacaitanya*);

therefore, in accordance with these [scriptural texts], the cognitions of Brahman intended as the means to liberation in the Upanishads are cognitions devoid of any qualifying modes (*niṣprakāraka-jñāna*).

Because the state of being "other" (paratva) necessarily exists. Furthermore, even by the commentaries— which assert that explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) such as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity" convey excellence (*prāśastya*) through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—
it is accepted that the cognition of excellence arising through secondary indication is indeed non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*).

Since excellence (*prāśastya*)— consisting of the state of not being followed by a powerful undesirable result (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*) and so forth— is itself the object indicated (*lakṣya*), and since only a non-qualificative cognition (*niṣprakāraka-jñāna*) having that [excellence] alone as its object arises, [the cognition of] excellence and so forth...

Since no cognition possessing such qualifiers is admitted, it must be stated that, by the force of many proofs, the knowledge of Brahman derived from the Vedas must indeed be accepted as being non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*).

This is so because, according to the method of explaining the unity resulting from the negation of heterogeneous differences, the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-mithyātva*) would otherwise be rendered secondary.

Once it is established that the reality of phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca*) is indeed primary, the term "cessation of phenomenal manifestation" (*prapañcopaśama*) signifies the cause of the dissolution of the phenomenal world; furthermore, this [term] also implies the cause of its origination and so forth, otherwise there would be the fault of redundancy with the word "non-duality" (*advaita*). And thus, by virtue of being the cause of the world's origination and so forth...
By being devoid of internal differentiation (*svagatabheda*), it is precisely non-dual knowledge (*ajñāna*) that is expressed;

this is also the meaning of the phrase "this is non-dual" (*tadetad advayam*). Furthermore, the statement "he who sees here as if there were multiplicity" (*ya iha nāneva paśyati*) also has this very meaning, because it signifies that the cognition of difference regarding the introduction of qualities, actions, and parts within this Brahman produces what is harmful.

In the statement "it should be viewed as one alone" (*ekathaivānudraṣṭavyam*), with respect to the act of viewing, a quality called "being of a single mode" (*ekaprakārakatva*)—which serves as the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*)—is enjoined.

Nor should it be argued that a multiplicity of modes for the knowledge of Brahman has been stated; [this applies] to the original form (*mūlarūpa*) as well as in the incarnations (*avatāra*) and so forth.

Furthermore, because it is precisely the state of having a single mode of cognition (*ekaprakārakatva*) regarding the forms of the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) that is enjoined by knowledge; thus, in all these forms of the Blessed Lord, the state called oneness (*ekatva*) is the mode of cognition to be enjoined in the act of vision, residing within oneself.
Because it has been stated that the cognition of difference causes harm—

since passages such as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" and "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow" must necessarily be understood as intending that only the knowledge of the qualified [Brahman] produces liberation, in order to avoid contradiction with these texts— as for what was said:

The claim that the knowledge of excellence (*prāśastya*) produced by the knowledge of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is devoid of any qualifying mode (*niṣprakāraka*) is incorrect; for even in that case, the cognition of excellence is accepted as being determinate (*savikalpaka*). This is because, in passages such as "Vāyu is the swiftest [in carrying oblations]," the words function through secondary indication to denote excellence as qualified by the primary meanings of the word-meanings and the sentence-meaning.

Because such knowledge of commendation cannot be non-conceptual (*savikalpaka*), otherwise the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)— "Those who have gone here find firm standing, for they behold the night"— would not have as its purport the fruit consisting of firm standing. For this very reason, in the fourth [book], third pāda, in the section concerning the black antelope skin (*kārṣṇājina*), it is established that the explanatory passage regarding the fruit of the sacrifice is like a subsidiary (*aṅga*).

It is considered as follows: In the section on *satras*, with reference to the *satra* known as the *Rātrisatra*, it is heard in scripture: "Those who perform these nights (*rātrayaḥ*) indeed find firm footing here. Having established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the *Rātrisatra* is for the sake of heaven, [the siddhānta states]:
"Those who desire to find firm footing should perform these nights."

It has been established as a settled conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the ritual known as the *rātrisatra* is performed for the sake of the fruit consisting of fame, renown, and establishment through transformation.
For this very reason, in the first chapter, fourth quarter, under the section titled "And its designation" (*tadvyapadeśaśca*),

regarding the injunction "One seeking to practice sorcery should sacrifice with the Śyena," the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the word "Śyena" is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) named Śyena.
"Just as a hawk, having swooped down, seizes its prey by means of its action,
so does this [rite], having swooped down, seize the hating rival"— this is the *śyena* mentioned in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).

Because it is impossible for the term *śyena* to be an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*) based on the expression of its similarity to the bird *padārtha*, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the word *śyena* occurring in the injunctive sentence is the name of the ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*).

For this very reason, in the first section of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra* (1.4.29), "In the case of a doubtful [term], [the meaning is determined] from the remainder of the sentence," [it is stated]: "He places pebbles that are eaters... (*attāḥ śarkarā upadadhāti*).

In this context, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is reached that the substance serving as the means for anointing, implied by the word *attā*, is a general liquid substance such as oil, ghee, water, and so forth; however, upon hearing the word "ghee" in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) of the supplementary sentence, "Ghee indeed [is the essence]," the substance serving as the means for anointing is [determined to be ghee].
It was established that [the substance] is indeed ghee (*ghṛta*). For this very reason, in the section concerning the opening of the Veda (*vedopakramādhikaraṇa*),

by determining that the words "Ṛgveda" and so forth found in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) of the opening statement— "The Ṛgveda from Agni, the Yajurveda from Vāyu, the Sāmaveda from Āditya"— refer to their primary literal meanings, [it is concluded that] the Ṛgveda is recited loudly (*uccaiḥ*) and the Yajurveda in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).

In the passage beginning with *uccair ṛcā*, it was determined that for the sake of consistency, the words *ṛk* and so forth occurring within the injunctive sentences of the concluding section must refer specifically to the *Ṛgveda* and the other Vedas. In the cited topical discussions (*adhikaraṇas*), it was established that while the explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) primarily intend their own literal meanings through direct denotation (*śakti*), they secondarily intend the excellence (*prāśastya*) characterized by those meanings through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Just as in the expression "the cowherd settlement on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), the bank qualified by the Gaṅgā is the indicated object (*lakṣya*), so too here, excellence qualified by the primary meaning must necessarily be the indicated object. For this very reason, it is logical that even the cognition of that [excellence] possesses a qualifier (*saprakāraka*). Furthermore, in our view, [this applies] regarding Brahman...
By accepting that [the self] possesses distinct attributes (p.
132), it is the very knowledge of Brahman devoid of modes (*niṣprakāraka*) that is the means to liberation; however, in my view...
Because it has as its object only the essential nature whose sole flavor is the bliss of knowledge, according to your own view,
it must be stated that being entirely devoid of qualifiers (*niṣprakāraka*) is the primary [meaning],
since the term "having qualifiers" (*saprakāraka*) primarily denotes the state of having qualifiers in general as its object.

If having a qualifier (*saprakārakatva*) consists precisely in having a distinct mode of being (*bhinnadharmaprakārakatva*), then it would follow that the cognition of categories such as "knowable" (*prameya*) and "denotable" (*abhidheya*),
as well as the cognition of categories such as "genus" (*jāti*), would not be conceptual (*savikalpaka*). For even in those cases,
there exist properties (*dharma*) such as knowability, denotability, genus-ness, and category-ness.

Because the modes (*prakāra*) are non-different [from the substrate], it cannot be said that those properties (*dharma*) are different from the property-possessor (*dharmin*). This is because, since they cannot possibly be universals (*jāti*), it is universally accepted that qualities such as *upādhi* are non-different from their substrates. Nor is it untenable for them to be modes, given that they can serve as the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) to the distinction (*vaiśiṣṭya*) that appears [in cognition].

It should not be argued that "qualificative relation (*vaiśiṣṭya*) consists in difference," because everyone experiences that cognitions such as "the jar is an object of knowledge" (*prameyo ghaṭaḥ*) are indeed qualificative cognitions, and philosophical theory must follow empirical cognition.
Nor should it be argued that if difference were absent, how could even the cognition of *vaiśiṣṭya* be accounted for; for [the nature of] *vaiśiṣṭya*...

Because [the cognition] is produced by conceptual construction (*pratīti*), it lacks the status of being produced by the actual object (*vastu*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that in cases such as "this is silver," there could be no cognition having "silver-ness" as its qualifier (*prakāra*) and "mother-of-pearl" (*śukti*) as its qualificand (*viśeṣya*).

Alternatively, due to the force of a specific substitute for difference, there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) regarding a qualified cognition in a case where properties are non-different, provided that a specific [qualifier] exists.
All proofs [establishing] the identity with the Rāmānuja school will be properly demonstrated in the *Prakāśa*; this is the summary. Therefore, in the world...

Since it is observed that knowledge whose qualifiers are properties non-different from [the property] "knowable" (prameya) and so forth possesses a qualifier, one must in every respect accept that even in Vedic sentences such as "Truth, Knowledge... (*satyajñānam...*), there is only knowledge having Brahman as its qualificandum and properties non-different from "truth-knowledge-ness" (*satyajñānatva*) and so forth as its qualifiers.

However, being "without modes" (*niṣprakārakatva*) consists essentially in the absence of having distinct attributes as its modes; thus, it is established that only immediate mental knowledge possessing modes is the means to liberation. Thus ends the *Niṣprakārakajñānaikya-prakāśa*.
Is this not indeed improper? For you accept that direct mental knowledge (*mānasāparokṣajñāna*) is the means to liberation, whereas we maintain it is verbal direct knowledge (*śābdāparokṣajñāna*).

To illustrate: "Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the wisdom of Vedānta, who are self-controlled through the yoga of renunciation, and whose nature is pure sattva—they [attain] in the world of Brahman..."
At the time of the final end, all are completely liberated from the supreme death. Neither the senses nor inference [attain this];
rather, it is the Vedas alone that make him known—the Puruṣa who is the subject of the Upaniṣads.
And he is not [known] by mere logic, nor by perception, nor by anything else.
He is to be known solely through sacred scripture by devotees alone, and not otherwise.

By such scriptural and traditional (smṛti) statements, it is made known that the direct realization of Brahman has verbal testimony as its instrument. "Ascetics" refers to those in the fourth stage of life (turīyāśramin).

This is because of the means called renunciation (saṃnyāsa), characterized by the abandonment of all ritual actions; for this very reason, their internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa) are purified. Therefore...

"Thus, those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the realization born of Vedānta"—that is, the direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) of Brahman which arises from Vedānta; by that, the meaning characterized as the Supreme Reality has been firmly established.

From the statement, "Those by whom the meaning has been well-ascertained through the realization of Vedānta," it is understood that the vision of Brahman has the Vedānta as its instrument. In the second sentence, having negated the status of the senses as instruments for the knowledge of the Lord, the status of the Vedas alone as its instrument is understood. For this very reason, that [Vedānta] alone is also their basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*).

This has been established. In the third statement, it is understood from the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* that Brahman is the object of immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) produced by the means of *upaniṣad*, and furthermore, that it is the object of immediate knowledge produced solely by the means of scripture (*āgama*).
On the contrary, [it is said]: "That which the mind does not think, that by which they say the mind is thought—that alone is Brahman, you..."
If it is argued that the passage, "Know that this which they worship here is not that," negates the fact that the knowledge of Brahman has the mind as its instrument—
and therefore, since direct (aparokṣa) knowledge taught in the Śruti and Smṛti is purely verbal (śābda), the identity of their views is difficult to establish— then it is replied as follows:
The direct knowledge of Brahman is not primarily verbal;
rather, it is determined by me that its primary nature is mental.

The primary instrument for the direct realization (*aparokṣajñāna*) of Brahman is indeed the mind, because there exists evidence that it is the direct producer of that realization; its verbal nature (*śābdatva*) is not primary, as there is no evidence that words are the direct producers of it,
since the cited scriptural passages have as their purpose the means of bringing about the vision of Brahman rather than being the direct instruments of realization.

The meaning is that because there is an absence of otherness (*paratva*), there is no contradiction between us; this is the sense of the remainder [of the argument]. For instance, although many statements have been cited—such as "those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the knowledge of Vedānta"—which show that the vision of Brahman is directly caused by the Word (*śabda*).

On the contrary, by such passages as "that which the mind does not think, nor the senses, nor inference," it is understood that [Brahman] is indeed not an object of knowledge produced by the mind or the other sense organs. Nevertheless, the vision of Brahman is [attained through] the mind.
It is indeed appropriate that it is called "the instrument," for thus it is said:
"One should always behold [it] with the mind alone, with a purified mind;
and when one sees the Self by means of the self, one finds satisfaction in the self."
This is because such passages from the Śruti and Smṛti reveal that the direct knowledge of Brahman is mental (*mānasa*).
