In the first sentence, the mind is enjoined as the instrument for the purpose of seeing, just as in the injunction "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*). Therein, by the use of the particle *eva* (only), the instrumentality of the others is excluded; [the instrument] is the mind.

Alternatively, a qualified vision is enjoined. Just as in the injunction "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*), in this second sentence, a quality in the form of purity is enjoined by way of restating the mind as the instrument;
and this purity consists in being reinforced by hearing, reflection, meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), and so forth, or it is the mind itself as qualified by purity.

It is enjoined as an instrument. Regarding the phrase "and where indeed": in the Gītā statement, "when, in that very state of meditative absorption (samādhi-yoga), seeing the Self—the Blessed Lord—by means of the self—the mind—within the self—the body—one rejoices," this refers to the mind accompanied by the intermediate operation characterized by *nididhyāsana*, which consists of one-pointedness of consciousness (*cittaikāgrya*).
Thus, it is understood that [liberation] has as its instrument the knowledge of direct realization.
Hearing, reflection, meditation, and likewise devotion, as well as the perfection of knowledge, are the means; nothing else is intended as primary.
Thus, in this context, by intending to emphasize the intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*), meditation is established as the means for knowledge;

for it is stated in the *Sudhā* as well that only meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) in the form of one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgrya*) is the means for immediate realization (*aparokṣajñāna*).

In the scriptural passages cited on page 136 and elsewhere, there is no fault, because it is intended to emphasize the primary status of the subject (*dharmin*) that the mind alone is stated to be the instrument of knowledge; furthermore—
"Having heard, reflected upon, and meditated in that manner, one attains the vision of Brahman by destroying ignorance, error, and doubt"—
thus it is stated in the Smṛti. Furthermore, having pressed [the Soma] and offered it in the Āhavanīya fire, they turn back toward the west and drink the Soma in the Sadas.

Just as the injunction "they eat" (*bhakṣayanti*)—based on the direct hearing of the word *tvā* (you)—prescribes an act of eating by the same agent as the oblation and the pressing, thereby establishing that the oblation and the pressing are the causes for the eating; so too, it is logical that through the direct hearing of the word *tvā*, meditative reflection (*nididhyāsana*) alone is the means for the vision of Brahman. Nor is there knowledge [of Brahman] from hearing and so forth in that manner.
It must be stated that [the object] would possess the status of being a means (sādhanatva).
This is because its status as a means [to liberation] is established through a succession of stages by virtue of being a constituent part of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).

Nor is there any contradiction with the previously cited scriptural passages and the like, for they do not conflict with our position that the mind is the instrument. To explain: the meaning of the passage "those who have well-ascertained the object through the knowledge of Vedānta" is as follows: "strivers" (*yatayaḥ*) refers to those characterized by diligent effort.

Through the yoga of renunciation— that is, through the yoga of action (*karmayoga*) consisting of the performance of works with the understanding that they are offered to the Lord, preceded by the abandonment of attachment to their fruits— therefore they possess pure *sattva*,
meaning their internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) are stainless; and for this very reason, they have well-ascertained the meaning through the realization born of the Vedānta.

Those for whom the object characterized as the Supreme Brahman has been well-ascertained and directly realized through that knowledge of Vedānta— which consists of hearing, reflection, and meditation (nididhyāsana)— and which is a form of indirect knowledge (parokṣajñāna) consisting of the concentration of the mind (cittaikāgrya), are called "those whose goal is well-ascertained through the knowledge of Vedānta."

Thus, it is understood that immediate knowledge has meditation (*dhyāna*) as its instrument. Nor should it be argued that the mind lacks the status of an instrument; for [the term "meditation"] intends to emphasize the predominance of the quality (*dharma*).
Since there is no sublation to the mind being an instrument (*karaṇa*), the word "cognition" (*vijñāna*) is understood as qualified by being brought forth; for,

by accepting the primacy of the mind through the instrumental derivation "that by which one knows," and because this is supported by scriptural passages such as "hearing" and so on, it follows that only immediate cognition (*aparokṣajñāna*) having the mind as its instrument is attained, and not the sense organs.
In the phrase "not by inference," the negation pertains to [inference] having the generality (*sāmānya*) as its object;

whereas the restrictive statement "only through the Vedas" pertains to indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) such as hearing (*śravaṇa*), or to indirect knowledge in a mediated sense. Thus, even the statement from the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* [refers to] direct [knowledge] or...
This is because it is possible for [the term "unmanifest"] to have a different scope, either as being beyond perception or as being the object of supersensuous knowledge;

and because the statement "that which the mind does not think" can also be understood as referring to the mind as empowered by the experience of hearing, reflecting, and meditating (*śravaṇa-manana-nididhyāsana*) produced by the Vedānta. Otherwise—
When the disciplined mind abides in the Self alone,
free from longing for all desires, then that one is called a yogi.
"Just as a lamp standing in a windless place does not flicker— this is the simile remembered for the yogi of restrained mind who practices the yoga of the Self."
Otherwise, such statements from the Gītā as "where the mind, restrained by the practice of yoga, comes to rest" would be untenable;
for in that context, "when the mind— that is, the internal organ (manas)— is thoroughly restrained," meaning specifically withdrawn from sense objects.

One abides in the Self alone, and there arises one-pointedness of mind toward the Blessed Lord. Then, being thus engaged, he is said to be perfected in the yoga of samādhi. For the yogi who performs the yoga of the Self—the samādhi whose object is the Blessed Lord—there is one-pointedness of mind, as expressed by the words "of one with a restrained mind" (*yatacitta*) and "one whose mind has been withdrawn" (*pratyāhṛtamanaska*).

Because it is perceived that the mind itself— accompanied by the intermediate operation consisting of the form of meditative concentration (*lakṣaṇadhyāna*)— is the instrument for immediate (*aparokṣa*) knowledge; [this being so] for knowledge produced by the sense organs.

Furthermore, there is a fixed rule that the knowledge produced by a *liṅga* (inferential mark) and the knowledge produced by a word (*śabda*) are respectively mediate (*parokṣa*) and immediate (*aparokṣa*).
Therefore, it is established that regarding the immediate knowledge of Brahman, its being mental is primary, while its being verbal is secondary.
By this [it is explained] the status of hearing (*śravaṇa*) in the scriptural injunction: "It is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon."

The means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) constitutes a factor of direct perception (*darśanāṅga*) because of its proximity to perception and because it is not separated from the comprehension of the object of knowledge (*prameya*).
However, reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) [are factors] of the mind (*citta*).

According to the method explained in the *Vivaraṇa*— namely, that [verbal knowledge] becomes the cause for the experience of Brahman by way of its effect, which is the one-pointed mental modification (*ekāgra-vṛtti*) brought about by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) directed toward the inner self— it is an "auxiliary factor contributing to the result" (*phalopakāry-aṅga*). Thus,

as in the case of the cognition of the logical mark (*liṅga-jñāna*) in inference, it is the knowledge of the word qualified by the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*) that constitutes the instrument (*karaṇa*) of verbal knowledge.

And thus, according to the method of Vidyāsāgara’s statement— that hearing, which consists in the knowledge of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), functions as the instrument by virtue of being a cognition of a qualifier— since hearing is the cause of the excellence residing in the word that serves as the instrument,

it possesses the status of the primary member (*aṅgin*) as the instrument; whereas reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) possess the status of auxiliaries (*sahakārin*) by virtue of producing an excellence residing in the mind.

According to the reasoning of Citsukha— that even though hearing (*śravaṇa*) is a cause, it undergoes the effect of being a subordinate element (*lopakārya*)— and because the properties of the word acting as the instrument (*karaṇa*),
namely *śakti* (denotative power) and *tātparya* (intention), are the objects of hearing, hearing possesses the status of a primary member (*aṅgin*) by virtue of being included within the instrument.
Thus, according to that correct method, hearing is the primary member, while reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) are its subordinate members (*aṅga*).

As for the objection that "in your view, *nididhyāsana* alone is the primary member (*aṅgin*), while *śravaṇa* and *manana* are its members; thus there is a clear contradiction between us," this is refuted. For there is no contradiction, since the status of *śravaṇa* as the primary member is not absolute, just as *mīmāṃsā* serves as the procedural requirement (*itikartavyatā*) when Dharma is being cognized through the Veda, so too [the other two serve as requirements] when Brahman is being cognized.
With respect to the instrument called the Veda (p.
139), even reflection in the form of hearing lacks the status of being the primary act (*aṅgin*), since it is merely a subsidiary procedure (*itikartavyatā*). As for what was said:

It is not correct to claim that hearing (*śravaṇa*) consists in the knowledge of the intended meaning (*tātparya-jñāna*). For it is possible for the cognition of a word endowed with expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors to serve as the instrument (*karaṇa*); moreover, since the aforementioned hearing—which consists in the knowledge of the intended meaning—is already exhausted by its function of removing obstacles such as the error regarding the intended meaning (as stated in the *Vivaraṇa*), it cannot also be included within the category of the instrument. If it were so, then reflection (*manana*) and the other stages would likewise [have to be instruments].

Because it would result in [the two] being identical in reality (*tathātva*). For there is no difference between those two in their status as the "procedure" (*itikartavyatā*). Furthermore, regarding the cognition of a specific feature in the form of *tātparya*—namely, that "this word or sentence has this meaning as its *tātparya*"—there is the cognition of the word qualified by *tātparya*;
in that cognition, the word is the object of the *tātparya*.
According to the method stated in the *Vivaraṇa*, that "knowledge of the true meaning" [is not the means] because of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*),

it is untenable for hearing (*śravaṇa*), which consists in the knowledge of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), to be the instrument for the vision of Brahman (*brahmadarśana*). Nor is hearing, consisting in the knowledge of the intended meaning, an auxiliary act (*aṅga*) of the word, in the same way that threshing and so forth are auxiliaries of the sacrifice.

It must be stated that only that which is an auxiliary by direct application (*sannipatyopakāraka*) is included within the category of the instrument (*karaṇa*). This is because hearing cannot be included in the category of the instrument, as it lacks the status of being an auxiliary by direct application—unlike threshing and other such acts, which are auxiliaries by virtue of being subordinate to the sacrificial substance—and because hearing lacks the status of being subordinate to a substance related to sound. Furthermore:

Since auxiliaries that provide direct assistance (*sannipatyopakāraka*), such as threshing, lack the status of being subordinate (*śeṣitva*) with respect to auxiliaries that provide indirect assistance (*ārādupakāraka*), such as the *prayāja* offerings which assist toward the fruit;

likewise, it is untenable for hearing (*śravaṇa*), which provides direct assistance, to possess the status of being subordinate with respect to its auxiliary, which consists of reflection (*manana*) and meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*) that assist toward the fruit. As for that which was also stated...

As for the claim that hearing (*śravaṇa*) possesses the status of a primary factor (*aṅgin*) as an instrument because it is the cause of the excellence residing in the word which serves as the instrument (p.
that too is not [correct] when verbal cognition is to be produced by the word.

Because they are the causes of an excellence residing in the mind which serves as a cooperative factor for the word [of scripture], *manana* (reflection) and *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation) are auxiliary to *śravaṇa* (hearing), just as *prayāja* (preliminary offerings) and *prokṣaṇa* (sprinkling) and so forth— which are causes of an excellence residing in the *dīkṣaṇīyā* (initiatory rite) that serves as a cooperative factor— are directly contributing (*sannipatyāṅga*) auxiliaries to the *Soma* sacrifice.

Because [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the direct extraction of the juice (*abhiṣava*), the taking of it (*grahaṇa*), and so forth, would be subordinate parts (*aṅgatva*) with respect to that [listening].

Nor should it be said that a figurative subordination (*gauṇāṅgatva*) to listening exists for those two; for since that [listening] results in being non-subordinate (*anaṅgatva*), our desired conclusion is established. And it has been stated in the *Nyāyāmṛta*: "Figurative subordination..."

Since it culminates in the state of being bodiless (*anaṅgatva*), it follows that reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*)— which are causes of excellence residing in the mind as auxiliaries to the word— are not auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) with respect to hearing (*śravaṇa*), which is the cause of excellence residing in the word itself as the instrument. As for what was said regarding the power (*śakti*) which is a property of the word functioning as the instrument...

The claim that hearing (*śravaṇa*) is the primary element (*aṅgin*) because it is the intended object of the purport (*tātparya*) by virtue of being included within the instrument [of knowledge] is incorrect.

This is because it has already been stated that this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that preparatory rites such as the *prayāja* offerings and sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), which are subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* initiation, would themselves become primary elements with respect to the pressing of the Soma, its drawing, and so forth, which are included within the instrument known as the Soma sacrifice itself. Furthermore:

When direct knowledge arises through the word [of scripture], since the three— reflection (*manana*), meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), and hearing (*śravaṇa*)— are auxiliary factors that contribute to the result with respect to that word, they cannot stand in a mutual relationship of principal and subordinate to one another;
otherwise, it would follow that "he who desires rain, he who desires food, or he who desires heaven should praise with the *saubhara* chant."
One should perform the *nidhana* as "hiṣī" for one desiring rain; as "ūrj" for one desiring food;
and as "iti" for one desiring heaven. Thus, the procedure for the *saubhara* chant is prescribed for the attainment of the fruits mentioned in the scripture, such as rain and the rest.
Because there would be the consequence of a mutual relationship of principal and subordinate between the sacrificial materials such as the rice-grains that have reached destruction,

and because the threshing and other rites intended for the sacrifice would be subordinate to the production of the *apūrva*, and the *prayāja* and other rites would be subordinate to the production of the ultimate *apūrva*.

Furthermore, just as in the case of "one threshes rice" (*vrīhīn vahanati*), there is the direct Vedic hearing (*śruti*) of the accusative case-ending which indicates that the rice and so forth are the primary objects (*śeṣin*), whereas here there is no such direct hearing of the accusative case-ending to indicate that hearing is the primary object; and just as in the case of "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*),

there is the direct Vedic hearing of the instrumental case-ending which indicates that the animal is subordinate (*śeṣa*), so too there is the direct Vedic hearing of the instrumental case-ending indicating that reflection (*manana*) and meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*) are subordinate.

Furthermore, because of the existence of scripture (*śruti*), and because the logical mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the capacity of the object serves as the authority for *nididhyāsana* alone being the primary member (*aṅgin*), since *nididhyāsana*— in the form of one-pointed concentration of the mind upon the Blessed Lord— is capable of generating immediate, direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) in a very short time; as it has been stated in the *Anuvyākhyāna*:

"And for one who possesses direct vision [of the Self], following upon hearing and reflection, there shall arise [realization] through meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) once the reality has been correctly ascertained. And it is stated in the *Sudhā*:
"Meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) is the means for the vision of Brahman; for its accomplishment, both hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*) must also be performed."

Therefore, from the statement "Then, seeing Him as partless, one meditates upon Him," which consists of the co-occurrence of words (*padasamabhivyāhāra*), it is established that *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation) alone is the means of valid knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) for being an auxiliary to direct vision (*darśana*).
It is thus determined that hearing (*śravaṇa*) and the other stages are auxiliaries to that [contemplation]. However, such is not the case regarding hearing being an auxiliary to direct vision.

There is indeed such a statement; and for this very reason, since the fruit of nididhyāsana alone is its connection with the result in the form of direct vision (darśana), the context (prakaraṇa) also [establishes] that meditation is a subordinate member (aṅga) of direct vision, being for the purpose of meditation.

And there is evidence for hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*) acting as auxiliary factors through immediate proximity (*sannipatyopakāraka*). For it is more logical that hearing and reflection serve as auxiliary factors to the very nature of meditation (*nididhyāsana*) through immediate proximity, rather than postulating that they assist the fruit [of liberation] through remote mediation (*viprakṛṣṭa*).

For this very reason, in the second quarter of the ninth book, regarding the passage "he offers the two pārvaṇa oblations with the sruva ladle," there arises a doubt as to whether or not there is an extension (atideśa) of the two pārvaṇa homas mentioned in the scripture to the modified sacrifices (vikṛtis). In this doubt, since the word *parvan* denotes time, those two rites possess time and a deity as their [defining] factors; and because time is not something to be consecrated (*asaṃskārya*), [the rites do not transfer].

Since it is impossible for those two [offerings] to be *sannipatyopakāraka* (directly contributing) and they must therefore be *ārādupakāraka* (indirectly contributing), it follows that they are extended (*atideśa*) to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) performed on the preceding day (*pārvakālikā*).
This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the siddhāntin argues]: because the word *parvan* is derived in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāvavyutpatti*), it denotes the ritual act;
thus, since the two offerings to the deities Agni and others constitute a collective ritual, they serve the purpose of consecrating the proximate deity.

It has been established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that because they are auxiliary factors acting through conjunction (*sannipatyopakāraka*), there is no modification (*ūha*) of those two [mantras] in the case of the *saurya* and other sacrifices— which are modifications of the archetype (*samudāyavikāra*)— since the deity of the aggregate is absent therein. Furthermore, regarding the statement "He is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon" (*draṣṭavyaḥ śrotavyo mantavyo nididhyāsitavyaḥ*), [the sequence of reflection follows hearing] by virtue of the authority of position (*sthāna-pramāṇa*), specifically the proximity (*sādeśya*) consisting in the immediate succession of the recitation of reflection following that of hearing.

It should be stated that [the cooking] is an auxiliary to the *darśana* (sacrifice), because it is weaker than the indicators (*liṅga*) and so forth; furthermore, according to the rule stated in the fifth [chapter], "One should offer the *agnihotra*; one cooks the *yavāgū*," the sequence of meaning (*arthakrama*) is indeed stronger than the sequence of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*).

Just as the cooking of gruel follows immediately after the *agnihotra* oblation because it is for the purpose of that oblation, so too meditation follows immediately after [the study of the text] because it is for the purpose of direct realization.

Since hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*) serve the purpose of meditation (*dhyāna*), and since insight (*darśana*) follows immediately after meditation while meditation follows immediately after hearing and reflection, it is more easily stated that meditation alone is a constituent part (*aṅga*) of insight. This is because the authority of position (*sthāna-pramāṇa*), in the form of commonality of performance (*anuṣṭhāna-sādeśya*), establishes that meditation alone is a constituent part of insight.

And because of [the requirement for] vigilance. For this very reason, in the third chapter, sixth section, under the heading "The animal is common to all," it was determined in the section on the means of proof known as *sthāna* (position)—namely, the proximity of performance—that in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the characteristics of the animal belong specifically to the Agniṣomīya animal. Furthermore, in your own view—
The immediate cognition born from the cultivation of knowledge of the Vedāntic statements attains validity through the strength of its foundational means of knowledge.

For it has been stated by the teacher Sūreśvara Vārtikācārya that immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) is produced precisely by meditation (*dhyāna*) known as contemplation (*bhāvanā*). Nor should it be argued that nididhyāsana is unestablished as an instrument of valid cognition (*pramākaraṇa*).

Because that [direct perception] is not established even for hearing (*śravaṇa*). Furthermore, since it is the very word (*śabda*) remembered immediately after *nididhyāsana* that serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*) for immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*), something expressive [of that] has been stated; and it is said in the *Nyāyāmṛta*:
"The instrument is indeed the word itself, which is recollected again immediately after *nididhyāsana*, while *nididhyāsana*..."
Furthermore, it is possible because hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth are its auxiliaries, culminating in meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*). Alternatively,
according to the previously mentioned method and with the intention of emphasizing *dharma*,
it is meditative contemplation in the form of one-pointedness of mind alone that is the means for attaining immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*).

With the intention of emphasizing the subject (*dharmin*), it is stated that on page 144: "It is reflection (*manana*) itself— accompanied by the practice of meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) which has hearing (*śravaṇa*) and other factors as its constituent parts—
that is the means for attaining immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*)."
Both views are highly reasonable. Thus, just as the *prayāja* offerings and the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*)—

which are subsidiary parts of the *dīkṣaṇīyā*— possess a secondary subsidiarity (*gauṇāṅgatva*) toward the extraction of soma (*abhiṣava*) and its subsequent measurement (*grahaṇa*) through the *dīkṣaṇīyā* (as a part of the whole), so too does the hearing (*śravaṇa*) that removes ignorance, being a subsidiary part of meditation (*dhyāna*), [possess such a relationship].

Since the conventional usage of hearing (*śravaṇa*) as a constituent part of vision (*darśana*) is also figurative, there is no contradiction for us; thus, nothing is untenable. This concludes the illumination of the unity of hearing as a constituent part of vision.
Now, even so, in our view, liberation is the cessation of ignorance (*avidyānivṛtti*). [This occurs] "through meditation upon That, through union, and through the realization of its true nature."
Furthermore, at the end, there is the cessation of the universal illusion when the knowledge that produces differentiation has gone to absolute destruction;
for who can create a non-existent difference between the Self and Brahman?
"Until liberation there shall be difference," and so forth; this is according to the natural force (*svārasya*) of the authority of Śruti and Smṛti.

In that regard, the meaning of the Śruti passage is as follows: "Again and again and ever more"—through the intense meditation (*abhidhyāna*) upon that aforementioned Deity, through the contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) directed toward Him, through the application (*yojana*) by means of His form, and through the manifestation of reality (*tatvāvirbhāva*) resulting from the realization of reality (*tatvabhāva*).
That is to say, from the direct realization of Brahman produced by *nididhyāsana* (contemplative meditation), there is the cessation of universal *māyā*;

that is, the cessation of the root-ignorance denoted by the term *māyā*, which is of the nature of the universe because it is the material cause of the universe. Alternatively, *abhidhyāna* is *nididhyāsana*, while *yojana* refers to *śravaṇa* (hearing) and *manana* (reflection); this is the true state of being.

There is the direct realization of Brahman. From that follows the cessation of universal illusion (*viśvamāyā*), which is the cessation of the root ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) together with all its parts. Nor should it be argued that because ignorance is partless, there can be no parts; for—
Since it must be stated that [the cause] possesses multiple parts due to its following after numerous effects such as space (*viyat*) and so forth (p.
145), [it is said]:
"The unborn, unchanging, eightfold-formed *māyā* which produces transformations; the one unborn [Prakṛti]."
Red, white, and black— earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind,
intellect, and ego— thus is my nature divided eightfold.

This is because the fact that ignorance (*avidyā*) possesses parts is established by such scriptural and traditional texts (*śruti-smṛti*). Alternatively, the "meditation" (*abhidhyāna*) upon that God is His volition (*saṅkalpa*); through the application of that [volition] as a means, and because of the resulting absence of the state of being a limited entity, the world-illusion (*māyā*) ceases upon the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman—[this occurs] when the ignorance that generates differentiation has been removed.

When the substrate of the manifold of difference is utterly destroyed along with its own effects through the direct realization of Brahman, and once destruction has been attained by way of the relation of being the locus of that destruction,
who will maintain the false distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman?

The sense is that [liberation occurs] through the destruction of ignorance, which is the material cause of the manifold of difference (*bhedaprapañca*). By the statement, "No one remains in difference until liberation," it is shown that *avidyā*—which is the material cause of the manifold of difference—is *saṃsāra*, and its cessation is *mokṣa*.
This is because it has been stated: "The setting of *avidyā* is *mokṣa*; that [same *avidyā*] is declared to be *saṃsāra*. Thus, [the reality is] without attributes (*nirviśeṣa*).

The experience of the identity of Brahman and the Self is also liberation (*mokṣa*). This is precisely the meaning of the term "becoming Brahman" (*brahmībhāva*): "In that state, one who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself; he who knows it thus remains unenveloped here.
He who has happiness within, whose delight is within, and likewise whose light is solely within.
That yogi, having become Brahman, attains the extinction that is Brahman.
This is because of the authority of such scriptural and traditional texts as, "It is fit for becoming Brahman," and so forth.

In your view, however, liberation is the cessation of the individual soul's bondage to the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*). For it is said: "Bondage to the elements is transmigratory existence; liberation is release from them. Furthermore, liberation is also the manifestation of the bliss of one's own essential nature (*svarūpānanda*).

"Having attained the supreme light, he emerges in his own true form; for having obtained this essence, he becomes blissful"—according to the authority of such scriptural and traditional texts (śruti and smṛti). Thus, the contradiction between our two views regarding liberation is difficult to resolve.
If it is argued that the manifestation of their identity is therefore untenable, it is replied:

there will be no contradiction even regarding the nature of liberation for both; for it is established that the statement concerning liberation [in the case of the other] is merely secondary (*amukhya*) because it is dissolved therein.

The word "hi" (for/indeed) signifies a reason. The meaning is that by establishing the primary sense of the statements regarding the cessation of ignorance (*avidyānivṛtti*) as being the state of becoming Brahman (*brahmībhāva*), there will be no contradiction between us two even concerning the nature of liberation (*mokṣa*). To explain: the liberation consisting of the cessation of ignorance, which is favored by you, is not...
To that extent, it is primary. Because the term *avidyā* (ignorance) shares the common quality of being an obscuring factor, it refers to *prakṛti* through secondary usage (*gauṇī vṛtti*);

furthermore, because the scripture "Know *māyā* as *prakṛti*, and the wielder of *māyā* as the Great Lord" (*Māyāṃ tu prakṛtiṃ vidyān māyinaṃ tu maheśvaram*) prescribes that the word *māyā* also refers to *prakṛti*. [This is seen in the phrase] "the cessation of the *māyā* of the universe."

This is because it is appropriate for the word *māyā* occurring in the Śruti to signify its own manifestation; furthermore, since even the subtle body (*liṅga-deha*) that veils the individual soul (*jīva*) consists of the sixteen constituents (*kalās*) which are essentially *prakṛti*, liberation (*mokṣa*), which consists in the cessation of that [body], can logically be the referent of the phrase "cessation of all *māyā*" (*viśvamāyānivṛtti*). This is because liberation possesses a dual nature.

Furthermore, because even the cessation of the undesirable state consisting of the *liṅga-śarīra* (subtle body) is accepted as liberation (*mokṣa*), in your own view as well, such liberation alone is the figurative meaning of the term "cessation of ignorance" (*avidyā-nivṛtti*). Consequently, the statements regarding its being accomplished through knowledge and other means are logically consistent with being both primary in meaning and authoritative. [This applies to] that which is of a different class...

Furthermore, according to the method explained in the *Niṣedhaikya-prakāśa*, the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-mithyātva*) is secondary; and since liberation cannot consist in the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā-nivṛtti*) in its primary sense, [that definition is untenable].
Moreover: "It is called Mahāmāyā, Avidyā, Niyati, and Mohinī."

"Or rather, *prakṛti* is simply *vāsanā*, according to Your will, O Infinite One. Thus, because the word *māyā* denotes the will of the Blessed Lord, and because there is no lack of the nature of the universe within the will of the Blessed Lord...

It should not be said that "universal illusion" (viśvamāyā) is untenable, for there is no contradiction in the sense that it is the illusion which binds the universe. The primordial will of the Lord is the cause of the body's production for the bodiless individual soul (jīva); indeed, nothing whatsoever exists without it.

This is because authoritative means of knowledge establish that the will of the Lord (*īśvarecchā*) is the cause of the bondage called *saṃsāra* for the individual soul (*jīva*). Nor should it be argued that there can be no cessation of that will because it is eternal; for the term "cessation" is used figuratively to mean simply the state of the binding power of the Lord's will becoming unmanifest.

Furthermore, while there is authoritative evidence (pramāṇa) that establishes the term "māyā" as denoting *prakṛti*, there is no such authoritative evidence establishing the term "māyā" as denoting *ajñāna* (ignorance).
This is because, in the verse: "The source of transformations, ignorance (*ajñā*), eightfold, unborn, and eternal," the word used is *ajñā*.

One who knows is "jña"; one who does not know is "ajña. Thus, the term *ajñā* is appropriately understood as referring to the insentient primordial nature (*jaḍaprakṛti*), because even in the verse "the one unborn [female], red, white, and black," the word *ajā* refers to the primordial nature consisting of the three qualities.

In the passage, "Earth, water, fire, and air," the word *prakṛti* (primordial nature) is clearly heard; and likewise, we know that divine power of the Self, hidden by its own qualities, which has fifty divisions and five sections. That which is called the perishable *pradhāna* is neither day nor night.
In all such passages, since the dull primordial matter (*jaḍa-prakṛti*) alone— which serves as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the real world— is what is being propounded,

the authority of the Veda is secured and its primary purport (*mahātātparya*) is thereby attained; whereas, if [the text] were intended to refer to the ignorance (*ajñāna*) accepted by you, the world originating from that [ignorance] would be illusory (*mithyā*), and thus the authority of the Veda would be untenable.
Furthermore, this contradicts the primary purport [of the scriptures]. This will be demonstrated later. By this, [the following verse is explained]:
"When the knowledge that produces differentiation has gone to absolute destruction..."

This statement means that "non-difference" (abheda) is the absence of difference (vibheda). By figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the word "difference" (*vibheda*) is understood here as the ignorance (*ajñāna*) that causes it. Thus, when the defect called ignorance—which is the cause of difference—is utterly destroyed, who could effect a false difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, once their primary non-difference has been established?
As long as there is liberation, there would be differentiation; there would be the cognition of differentiation;

that is to say, there would be the cognition of non-differentiation which is opposed to the knowledge of reality. The sense is that after liberation, because of the absence of all defects such as [right] cognition, false cognition, and so forth—thus it has been explained.

Therefore, even you who maintain the authority of the Vedas must admit that the term "ignorance" (avidyā) refers to the category of the insentient primordial nature (jaḍaprakṛti); and you must accept, by way of figurative usage, that liberation consists in the cessation of ignorance, which is actually the cessation of the subtle body (liṅgadehin) composed of that [nature]. Thus ends the section on ignorance.

Even regarding liberation in the form of cessation (*nivṛtti*), there is no contradiction between us. As for what was said— that liberation is the experience of the identity of the self with the undifferentiated Brahman, and that this alone is the meaning of the term "attaining the state of Brahman" (*brahmībhāva*),
because such Vedic texts as "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself" serve as the authority for that— this too is not [correct].
This is because even the term *brahmībhāva*—which is a synonym for the identity of Brahman and the Self—is accepted as having a secondary (non-literal) meaning;
for instance: "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme; he enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahman";
and "For one who has attained this [Self], there is indeed delight; having reached this Self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*)."

Moving through these worlds at will and assuming forms at will, they, free from passion, depart by way of the sun’s door to where that immortal Person, whose nature is imperishable, dwells; there he attains the divine Person who is higher than the high. The seer—

He sees death; he does not see illness, nor does he see suffering. Seeing everything, he sees all; he attains everything. He becomes onefold, he becomes threefold, he becomes fivefold. Having attained the supreme light, he emerges in his own true form. There he moves about, laughing and playing.

"Whether sporting with women, or by means of vehicles, or with kinsmen, or with non-kinsmen— shaking off evil as a horse shakes its hair, and freeing myself as the moon frees itself from the mouth of Rāhu— I, having perfected my self, shall cast off this body and attain the world of Brahman. Thus [it is stated] in such scriptural passages.
Whom they call the eternal source of the source of all worlds,
the god without beginning or end, the supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa.
From that abode of Brahmā, a supreme place shines forth;
even the gods do not behold Śiva, who consists of divine splendor.
O King, that abode of the high-souled Viṣṇu blazes more intensely than the sun or fire;
by its own radiance, it is difficult for even gods and dānavas to behold.
The *yatis* go there to the god Nārāyaṇa Hari,
being joined with supreme darkness yet purified by auspicious deeds.

The great-souled ones who have attained perfection in yoga, being free from darkness and delusion, go there and do not return to this world again, O Bhārata. This place, O Great King, is eternal, imperishable, and undecaying.
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, this entire world is merely the vital breath of the Lord," according to the words of Akṣiṣeṇa in the Ākhyāna section of the Araṇyaparvan of the Mahābhārata:
"When the time for universal dissolution arrives, all [beings], together with Brahmā..."
"At the end of the Supreme, those who have perfected themselves enter the state of the Supreme;
having attained that supreme station, they rejoice in the imperishable and the mutable. (p. 150)
Having worshipped the supreme deity Hari, the imperishable, as the very Self,
some are liberated right here and never depart at any time.
Their abode is right here, and some are in the intermediate space;
others are in heaven, in Maharloka, Janaloka, and Tapoloka.
Some beings of great wisdom go to the Ocean of Milk;
there too, by means of gradual application, they draw near due to their superior knowledge.
Sālokya, proximity, Sārūpya, and Yoga—
beginning from this point and extending everywhere as far as the Ocean of Milk.
The glorious Puruṣa, known by the name Nārāyaṇa, whose bed is infinite,
is the supreme Viṣṇu whom the liberated attain; they experience his enjoyments slightly in some respects,
and somehow partake of external enjoyments such as bliss and the like.

This is established by such *smṛti* passages as well as by such *sūtra*s as "Because of the word [indicating] manifestation upon attaining [Brahman]" (*sampadyāvirbhāvaḥ svena śabdāt*). According to the maxim of "favoring the majority," the primary meaning of the term "becoming Brahman" (*brahmībhāva*) must be stated as consisting of the attainment of Brahman and similarity to Brahman; therefore, the identity of the self with Brahman (*brahmātmaikya*) is not the primary sense.

Furthermore, because this has been correctly determined in the illumination of the unity that excludes internal differentiation; and because there are few scriptural passages— such as "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman"—

that establish liberation as the state of becoming Brahman itself, neither the attainment of Brahman nor the attainment of the world of Brahman (brahmaloka) constitutes an intermediate form of liberation, for such states would be non-eternal.

It must be stated that [liberation] is to be accomplished through the worship of Brahman with attributes (*saguṇopāsana*) and so forth; for it has been thoroughly demonstrated in the *Svagataniṣedhaikya-prakāśa* that there is no Brahman with attributes distinct from the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) Brahman. [This is so] because liberation consists in the attainment of Brahman and the like.

Because the Śruti passages beginning with "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme; the knower of the Self crosses over sorrow" reveal that [liberation] is to be accomplished through the direct realization (*aparokṣajñāna*) of Brahman, it is logical that this is indeed the supreme liberation. Furthermore, other scriptural statements must be interpreted in a manner that does not contradict the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*), "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme. This is stated in the narrative known as the *Upabrahmaṇa*.
Having gone there, O Bhārata, they do not return to this world again;
for this place, O great king, is eternal, imperishable, and undecaying.

Thus, by establishing that liberation in the form of reaching the world of Brahman (brahmaloka) is characterized by non-return and permanence, the intermediate nature and impermanence [of other states] are logically justified; for in the passage "they go through the gate of the sun, free from passion," it is understood that travel via the path beginning with light (arcirādimārga) is accomplished through knowledge.

Only two paths have been established by the wise: the one beginning with light for those who possess knowledge, and the one beginning with smoke for those who perform ritual acts; such is the definitive conclusion of all the Vedas.
Thus says the Smṛti:
"Having departed from his own body, he goes indeed to the flame;
from there, to the wind, and to that son who is by name the *ativāhika*."
Then he [reached] the eastern quarter and likewise the northern year,
as well as the lightning, Varuṇa, Prajāpati, and the Sun itself.
Having reached Soma, Vaiśvānara, Indra, Dhruva, and likewise the goddess Diva,
and then reaching Vāyu as the supreme, one goes by means of him to Puruṣottama.

And because of this traditional teaching (*smṛti*): since departure by way of the sun's gate is accomplished through the direct realization (*aparokṣajñāna*) of Brahman, it is determined that liberation in the form of attaining Brahman by that route is indeed supreme liberation (*paramamukti*). Furthermore, in the cited *śruti* and *smṛti* passages, [this is established] by means of direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth.

Because it is established that the supreme Brahman alone is the object to be attained; and because even in the statement "I shall arise in the world of Brahman," the qualification "uncreated" (akṛta) is applied to the world of Brahman, it is logical that this very world of Brahman is indeed the world of the supreme Brahman. Whoever... [text fragment ends]

"He first awakened among the gods; he alone became that [Brahman]" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.18); "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself"; "Having become Brahman, he attains [the Supreme]"—according to the principle of favoring the majority of such Śruti and Smṛti passages, it is Viṣṇu alone who, having become [that], conquers these worlds. Thus, as in these cases, there is a similarity between the liberated souls and Brahman.

Furthermore, it is more logical that [the goal] has the attainment of Brahman as its ultimate purpose, according to such scriptural and traditional texts (*śruti-smṛti*) as: "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," "The stainless one attains supreme equality and even identity (*sārūpya*) through yoga," and so forth; for these clearly declare both the attainment of Brahman and identity with it. This is because the statements regarding attainment and similarity [of form]...

Furthermore, for those [passages] that leave no room for another interpretation, it is impossible for them to primarily intend the state of becoming Brahman (*brahmībhāva*); this is because of the support provided by the *smṛti*: "You pervade everything, therefore You are everything," which explains the statement regarding attainment as having non-difference as its primary purport. Moreover, the principle of favoring the majority applies to the definition of *prasaṅga*.

In the second quarter (pāda), it was considered in the section [beginning with] "Of those things possessing contradictory properties, there should be conformity with the majority," that there is a specific sacrifice called the Pañcadaśarātra. In that context, on the first day, named Agniṣṭut, the properties of the one-day Agniṣṭut are obtained by the name itself; therefore, by that very [principle], they apply there.

The *subrahmaṇyā* formula belonging to Agni is obtained [from the model sacrifice]; therefore, they say that light (*jyotis*), the cow (*go*), and the over-nighter (*atirātra*) exist here. In that case as well, because the one-day sacrifices (*ekāha*) named "Light" and so forth obtain the characteristics of those [model sacrifices] through their names, the *aindrī subrahmaṇyā* is obtained for them by means of the name alone. Therein, at the time of the *upasad*—

153) Regarding the Subrahmaṇyā formula, which is of the nature of a *tantra*, there arises a doubt: is there no fixed rule, or should it be addressed to Agni (*āgneyī*), or rather to Indra (*aindrī*)? Since there is no restrictive factor, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that there is no fixed rule; however, [the established conclusion] is that the one addressed to Agni should be adopted because of its primacy (*mukhyatva*). This being the position reached...

It has been established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the *aindrī* [verse] should be employed for the sake of greater similarity (*sādharmya*). Such is the view of the author of the Bhāṣya.
However, the author of the Vārttika maintains that the example of the *subrahmaṇyā* is not appropriate here;
for *prasaṅga* occurs only where the benefit of one thing is accomplished by means of another purpose. This is the case regarding the recollection of the deity.

For the *subrahmaṇyā-nigada* has the purpose of consecrating the form (*rūpa*). Now, that which belongs to Agni is not consecrated by [the mantra] belonging to Indra, nor is that which belongs to Indra-Agni [consecrated by it]. Therefore, since both have the purpose of consecrating both, both must be invoked separately. Having thus refuted [the opponent's view], one should consider the *ājyabhāga* mantras as examples. It is heard in the optional sacrifices (*kāmyā iṣṭayaḥ*): "To Agni..."

One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Dātṛ; [and] to Indrapradātṛ, a cake on eleven potsherds, curds, honey, ghee, water, parched grains, and rice—this mixture is dedicated to Prajāpati. Thus, there is one for Agni, one for Indra, and five for Prajāpati.

There are seven oblations therein: the *puroḍāśa* for Agni, the parched grains (*dhānā*) for Prajāpati, and so on. Because the [grains] are a modification (*vikāra*) of the [oblation] for Agni, and because the [oblation] for Agni exists in both the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), its properties are obtained. Even when there is no contradiction in the obtaining of the properties of either one, the *puroḍāśa* for Indra and the curd for Prajāpati follow their respective order, as they are modifications of the *aindrāgna-puroḍāśa* and the *sānnāyya* (curd-mixture) respectively.

And because those two [the *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa*] function only at the new moon and full moon respectively, they require the ritual details (*dharma*) of those [two]. Since honey, water, and ghee are modifications (*vikāra*) of the *upāṃśuyāja*, and since the *upāṃśuyāja* functions only at the full moon, they likewise require the ritual details of the full moon sacrifice. Thus, when these seven sacrifices have commenced together, [the procedure of] the full moon day...

The two *vājyabhāga* mantras, beginning with "vārtaghna," are obtained for the three modifications (*vikāra*), whereas for the two modifications of the *darśa* sacrifice, the *aindra-puroḍāśa* [mantras] apply.

The two *vṛdhanvat* verses for the *ājyabhāga* offerings are obtained from the *prājāpatya* and *dadhi* sacrifices; therefore, here there arises a doubt: should the two *ājyabhāgas* be performed with the mantras of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) sacrifice, or with the mantras of the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) sacrifice? When, as before, a lack of restriction would otherwise result, [the rule is established] regarding the *aindra-puroḍāśa*.
When it was argued that the two *ājyabhāga* offerings should be performed with the mantras of the *darśa* sacrifice because of the primacy of the curd (*dadhi*),

the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) was reached that the two *ājyabhāga* offerings should instead be performed with the mantras of the *paurṇamāsa* sacrifice, in order to maintain the commonality among the majority of the honey, water, and ghee.

Thus, according to the principle of favoring the majority (*bhūyonugraha-nyāya*), both examples provided by the authors of the *Bhāṣya* and the *Vārttika* indicate that since there are numerous scriptural statements concerning liberation in the form of attaining Brahman or attaining the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*), the term "becoming Brahman" (*brahmībhāva*) must also— without contradicting those texts— be understood in its secondary sense as meaning simply "attaining Brahman."

Furthermore, by the force of the rule prescribing the suffix *chvi* in the sense of "becoming that which one was not" (*abhūtatadbhāve*), it must be stated that the state of becoming something previously non-existent is intended; however, since there is no such "becoming that which one was not" regarding the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman during the state of saṃsāra, the application of the suffix *chvi* is untenable.

Because the primary meaning of the term *brahmībhāva*— which consists of the attainment of Brahman— must indeed be expressed; for statements such as "in the evening the cows become one in the cow-pen," and likewise "all become one in the supreme imperishable," must either,
through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), refer to unity of location, or, through secondary indication (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*), refer to absolute identity.
It must be said that in no way can the primary state of being Brahman be established as liberation.
[Objection: But when, for this person, everything has become the Self alone, by what and what [could there be any distinction]?
If it is argued that the Śruti statement "one should see" clearly demonstrates the soul’s transformation into Brahman (*brahmībhāva*) in liberation, we say no.

For even in that context, when for this knower all instruments and so forth have become the Self alone—that is, non-different from himself—then by what means could one see what object of knowledge? One would not see any category of object whatsoever by any means at all.

Therefore, since there is no non-difference of everything for one who is liberated, the intent is precisely to negate the non-difference of the individual soul (*jīva*) from Brahman at the time of liberation by means of pointing out an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭaprasañjana*). Otherwise, there would result the uselessness (*vaiyyarthya*) of the word *yat*, the word *asya*, the word *sarvam*, and the word *kim u*. Consequently, the term "becoming Brahman" (*brahmībhāva*) is used in a non-literal sense (*amukhyā vṛttyā*).

It must be stated that [the Upanishads] have as their ultimate purport liberation (mukti) as conceived by us, which consists in the attainment of Brahman and so forth; thus, there is no contradiction between our two views regarding liberation, and everything is consistent.
By this, my position is established: that all Vedāntas have as their intended meaning the undivided Brahman. As for your position, however:
The objection that "how can there be oneness [between Brahman and its qualities] given the contradiction that Brahman is distinguished by infinite attributes" is refuted.

This is because, according to the method explained in the section on the negation of internal difference and the manifestation of oneness, the attributes and so forth of Brahman are non-different from Brahman;
since distinct properties do not exist within Brahman, the nature of Brahman remains undivided.
Since the non-contradiction between our two views has already been established in many ways previously,

other categories of objects of knowledge (*prameya*)— whether primary or secondary— should likewise be inferred as being consistent with our own system according to their respective fitness. Therefore, [this applies] to that which is non-different from the referents of words such as "the Fourth" (*turya*) and "Śiva," and which is the supreme of all.

[The object of worship is] the cause of the birth and so forth of the entire world, in whom all existence remains; who is distinct from all sentient and insentient beings; who is devoid of internal differentiation;

who is characterized by infinite qualities such as knowledge and the rest; who is of a single nature; who is denoted by the infinite non-synonymous Vedic terms in their primary and most literal sense; and who is realized through hearing and reflection.

[It is] that which, through the cessation of the bondage of the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*) and so forth, bestows the fourfold liberation beginning with *sālokya*, by means of the object of immediate, correct knowledge produced by the mind assisted by profound reflection (*nididhyāsana*).

It is established that the great purport of all the authentic scriptures—the Vedas, Vedāntas, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth—is the supreme Brahman known as Śrī Nārāyaṇa; thus, everything is most auspicious.

Thus [ends] the exposition of the established doctrine of the venerable Ācārya Mahānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda, which is common to all [traditions], by the disciple of the feet of the illustrious Vasudhendratīrtha— the preeminent teacher among the wandering mendicants of the supreme order (paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka), who is independent in all systems (sarvatantrasvatantra)— and who is a treasury of compassion.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Advaita Doctrine," in the *Śrīmatatrayaikyaprakāśikā* composed by Aiyyaṇa, the son of Gopālācārya— the abode of mercy— and grandson of Caṇavāgu Turaiyūr Ācārya.
May there be prosperity.

[Objection: Even so, although the non-dualist (Advaita) doctrine may be established as being somehow identical to one's own view according to the method described above, it is difficult to establish the identity of one's own view with the Rāmānuja doctrine, which was stated only in brief. [Reply: This is not so; for even in that case—
The identity of the two is established by way of their being primary and secondary;
it is precisely through the means of valid cognition that the object of knowledge is proven to be primary.

In this regard, there is an absolute contradiction between the categories of "the object of valid cognition" (*pramāyā viṣaya*) and so forth; for instance, substance (*dravya*) is sixfold: time (*kāla*), primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the individual soul (*jīva*), the Lord (*īśvara*), knowledge as an attribute (*dharmabhūtajñāna*), and the eternal manifestation (*nityavibhūti*). Among these, time...
p.

157) Time (*kāla*) is indivisible, yet it is characterized by states such as moments (*kṣaṇa*), instants (*lava*), hours (*muhūrta*), days and nights (*ahorātra*), and so forth. A "state" (*avasthā*) is a particular adventitious property (*dharmaviśeṣa*). Regarding the claim that time consisting of moments, instants, and so on, is an entity distinct [from those states], that is what is accepted by them; in that regard:

It must simply be stated that the term "indivisible time" (akhaṇḍakāla) is used in a non-primary sense when applied to time in the form of a continuum delimited by moments (kṣaṇa), instants (lava), and so forth; for there is no evidence that indivisible time exists apart from moments, instants, and the like. In this regard, perception is certainly not a means of valid cognition, because, being devoid of manifest color-form and other such qualities, it cannot be perceived by the eye or other senses.

Because it is not an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); for even direct perceptions such as "the jar is here" have as their objects moments, instants, and so forth. Nor is it inference (*anumāna*), because there is no indicative mark (*liṅga*) that makes it known. Nor is it destiny (*niyati*), which is the inherent nature of time; nor is it some power like a river, which flows on inexhaustibly.
"They flow together with the rivers, and the thigh returns; they call the Pradhāna the unmanifest Prakṛti, though it possesses distinctions"— by this statement from the Bhāgavata Purāṇa,
[it is known that] from the massed darkness, O son of Vinatā...
The dust that has become accumulated should be known as double; indeed, it is not otherwise.
O son of Vinatā, from the mass of *rajas* that had been gathered,
a mass of *sattva* twice its size was likewise produced.
These two arise from the root-prakṛti, yet the root is not considered to be prakṛti;
for there is no discernible limit to the forms of prakṛti.
Thus, according to the statement in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*:
"The qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas, born of primordial nature (prakṛti),
bind the imperishable embodied soul within the body, O mighty-armed one."

And by this statement from the Gītā, since it is understood that the fundamental qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are of the nature of *prakṛti*, it is impossible for [the Self] to be possessed of them; thus, [the text speaks of] the unborn one as "red, white, and black."

This is because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and because it is understood from [the scriptures] that the qualities of *rajas*, *sattva*, and *tamas* constitute the nature of *prakṛti*. Nor should it be argued that there is a connection of difference through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), as in the case of "a blue pot" and the like; for it will be stated later that *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* lack the status of being [mere] qualities (*guṇatva*). For this very reason, this [is the case].

The statement of the Bhāgavata in the form of Brahmā, beginning with "that which consists of the three guṇas," is heard as referring to the fact that the Pradhāna is composed of the three guṇas; otherwise, the primary usage would be untenable.
Furthermore, due to the natural force of the word "mūla" (root) in the statement of the Garuḍa Purāṇa, it refers to that which is of the nature of Prakṛti and is the fundamental root.
It is perceived as simply "the three qualities" (*guṇatraya*). It is clearly understood that this [world] is produced from those three qualities.

Although *prakṛti* is singular, the use of the plural form "of the forms of *prakṛti*" (*prakṛtirūpāṇām*) indicates that it refers to the three qualities which constitute the nature of *prakṛti*. This is done so that the primary meaning of the cited *śruti* and *smṛti* may be preserved.

It must be stated that the conventional usage of *prakṛti* as being endowed with the qualities (*guṇas*) of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* is either secondary or is sustained by a specific force; thus, there is no contradiction between us on this point.
Nor is it the case that for *prakṛti* to be primarily endowed with the three qualities existing as a mass produced from the root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) is its primary definition.
This must be stated: since the three *guṇas* in their aggregated state are produced by *mūlaprakṛti*, it is impossible for them to be inherently possessed by that [state].

Otherwise, being possessed of effects such as *mahat* and *ahaṃkāra* would also have to be considered primary. Nor can it be argued that because an effect resides in its cause, being "endowed with effects" is primary in the case of the cause.

For you, who maintain the non-difference of cause and effect, such conventional usage would be untenable in the absence of a specific distinction (*viśeṣa*). Nor should it be argued that the three qualities (*guṇatraya*), when produced by primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and aggregated into a mass, do not exist at all.
p.

159) For these [evolutes] are born from the root-nature (mūlaprakṛti), but the root-nature is not considered to be born [from anything else]. Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these qualities (guṇas) are produced from the root-nature (prakṛti). Thus [it is said].

This is because it is understood that the accumulated *rajas* and *tamas* are produced from the *mūlaprakṛti*. Furthermore, according to your own view, *prakṛti* consists of twenty-four principles, being associated with the state of *prakṛti* itself as well as the states of *mahat*, *ahaṃkāra*, and so forth; for *mahat*, *ahaṃkāra*, and the rest have *prakṛti* as their material cause (*upādāna*).

Furthermore, because an effect-substance is admitted to be non-different from its cause by virtue of being an effect of that cause, and because the causal substance *prakṛti* is a single unity, the twenty-four *dhātus* would be untenable. Nor can it be argued that even if cause and effect are one,
the *prakṛti* remains distinct due to the diversity of adventitious attributes consisting of the states of *mahat*, *ahaṃkāra*, and so forth.

It should not be argued that the twenty-four-fold nature [of the principles] is established through the distinction of the qualified [whole] based on the distinction between its parts; for if the qualified were distinct from the substantive (viśeṣya), it would contradict our own tenet (avasiddhānta) and result in the impossibility of the supreme object of knowledge, which consists of non-duality of the qualified (viśiṣṭādvaita). This is because the qualifiers in the form of subtlety and grossness...

And if one accepts the non-difference of the substantive (viśeṣya) from that which is conditioned by the difference among its qualifiers— namely, the various forms of consciousness and unconsciousness qualified by their respective distinctions— then, since everything qualified by numerous qualifiers such as primordial matter (prakṛti), mahat, and egoism (ahaṃkāra) would essentially consist of the substantive which is primordial matter, and since that [substantive] is one, [the distinction between them would vanish].
The impossibility of a twenty-four-fold nature results in a "rope with nooses on both ends";

therefore, in order to maintain the established twenty-four-fold nature, one must accept either difference that performs the functions of non-difference, or else both difference and non-difference, since there is no other alternative. Thus, one must simply accept the identity of our own position.
Siddham. Thus ends the *Svarūpaikya-prakāśa*.
"Being an atom while possessing consciousness is the state of being a *jīva*; being something other than a *jīva* and insentient is the state of being the Lord (*īśvara*).
Thus, there is an absolute difference between us two based on these two substances. Any slight distinction, however, will be resolved later."

[Objection: Even so, we accept that there is a distinct substance called *dharmabhūtajñāna* (knowledge as an attribute), which is eternal and consists of the manifestation of both the knower and the known; whereas you do not accept this, and thus there is a contradiction. [Reply: This is not so, because—
The nature of being a dharma consists in its being grounded in knowledge, but it is not primarily eternal;
for there is a lack of evidence [for such eternality], since its establishment as distinct from that [knowledge] is proven by its own essential nature.
The two qualities—being an attribute (*dharmabhūtatva*) and permanence (*nityatva*)—do not both reside primarily in one [place].
The word "but" (*tu*) is for the purpose of distinction. Being an attribute resides in *vṛtti*-knowledge; permanence resides in essential knowledge (*svarūpa-jñāna*).
This is to be understood from the distinction made by the term "primary. Of that attribute-knowledge, by those two...

Because there is no evidence for their being distinct from the knowledge of the essential nature (*svarūpa-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the modification (*vṛtti-jñāna*). Regarding that aforementioned pair, the word "of the essential nature" is followed by the ellipsis "of the knowledge of the modification. Thus, the status of being an attribute (*dharma-bhūtatva*) is established for the knowledge of the modification, and eternality (*nityatva*) for the essential nature-knowledge. For these two reasons:

The meaning is that there is no contradiction. To explain: is the knowledge that exists as an attribute (*dharmabhūtajñāna*) accepted by you as eternal or non-eternal? First, it cannot be the latter, because that would contradict your own established tenets (*apasiddhānta*). Even regarding the former case, is such knowledge distinct from or non-distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*)? It cannot be the first, because in the case of such knowledge...

Because there is a lack of evidence; on the contrary, there is the experience that "the cognition of the jar has arisen" and "the cognition of the jar has perished," which reveals the impermanence of knowledge as a quality (*dharmabhūtajñāna*).
Nor is it the case that, "For there is no loss of the seer's vision, because of its indestructibility."

Likewise, through the destruction of qualities to be abandoned, qualities such as perfect knowledge (*avabodha*) and others are manifested; they are not produced, for they are eternally inherent in the self. What are experienced as arising and perishing are merely [the states of the mind].
It must be stated that this is established by taking into account the final state of knowledge consisting of the reality of *dharma*.

There is no loss—that is, no sublation—of the vision, which is the direct realization, of the Seer who is the Lord, because of His indestructibility and eternity; for the scripture has as its purport the unsublated nature of the Lord. Otherwise, [the following would apply]:
If the word *viparilopa* were to mean "destruction," it would result in the fallacy of non-distinction between the reason and the thesis; likewise,

statements such as "due to the destruction of qualities to be abandoned" (*heyaguṇadhvaṃsāt*) are intended to establish the manifestation and beginningless eternity of qualities such as knowledge and bliss that constitute the very nature of the individual soul (*jīva*).

On account of the natural force of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), it must be said that those qualities are distinct and constitute attributes (*dharmabhūta*); for even in the absence of difference, the use of the genitive is justified— just as in the cases of "the nature of a jar" (*ghaṭasya svarūpam*), "the head of Rāhu" (*rāhoḥ śiraḥ*), or "the non-apprehensibility and other attributes of a jar" (*ghaṭasya dharmā aprameyatvādayaḥ*)— as is the case with the states of primordial matter (*prakṛti*) such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*).
Because, in the absence of a state [of consciousness] that has become the dharma (the object), it is untenable for the experience of arising and destruction to have that as its object. Furthermore,

since the manifestation of all objects is possible through the knowledge of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and the functioning knowledge (*vṛttijñāna*) alone, [there is no need for] anything beyond this.

Because knowledge as an attribute (*dharmabhūtajñāna*) would be purposeless [in liberation]. Nor should it be argued that eternal *dharmabhūtajñāna* must be accepted because the knowerhood of the soul in liberation cannot otherwise be accounted for;
for even in liberation—as in deep sleep—knowerhood is established by the self-luminous nature of the soul's own essential consciousness (*svarūpajñāna*).
In your view, this is because you accept that during deep sleep, objective knowledge (*dharmabhūtajñāna*) lacks an object and is not self-luminous;

and because intrinsic knowledge (*svarūpajñāna*), while having itself as its own subject, has nothing else as its object. Furthermore, for the sake of establishing the omniscience of the liberated one, [knowledge] must be eternal and have everything as its object.

It should be stated that knowledge which has become the dharma (the objectified content) must be accepted [as the means of omniscience]. For, just as self-nature knowledge has itself as its own object, there is no sublation to its having all other things as its objects; thus, omniscience is established. Otherwise, [omniscience would be impossible].

Furthermore, it would follow that even the knowledge which has become the nature of reality (*dharmabhūtajñāna*) would not have anything other than itself as its object, since it too would be its own object.
If its establishment were to occur solely through its being the illuminator of another, then it would follow that the knowledge of one's own essential nature (*svarūpajñāna*) would also be so.
Therefore, in the state of saṃsāra there is *vṛttijñāna*, while in liberation there is *svarūpajñāna*.
Since the manifestation of all things is established by the two types of knowledge alone, you too should not accept the existence of "dharma-bhūta-jñāna" (knowledge as an attribute).
But is this not improper? For even the so-called "vṛtti-jñāna" (functional knowledge) is untenable. To explain: vṛtti-jñāna...

Is it based on the self (*ātman*) as its substrate, or based on the mind (*manas*), or based on the body? Not the first, because that would contradict your own tenets. Not the second, because it would entail the consequence that cognition is insentient (*jaḍa*), and because it would entail the consequence that [cognition] lacks the status of being a property of the self. Not the last, because it would result in falling into the position of the non-Buddhist schools. To this, it is replied: it is the mind itself.

The material cause (*upādāna*) of the functional cognition (*vṛttijñāna*) and so forth is not subject to the consequence of being insentient (*jaḍa*). Just as wind and other elements do not produce fire, it is logically consistent that the functional cognition, even though its material cause is the insentient mind, is itself non-insentient; this is likewise the case for that which has the sentient spider (*ūrṇanābhi*) as its material cause.

Furthermore, because the insentience of the thread is observed, there is no contradiction even if the material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect (*upādeya*) possess distinct natures. In reality, however, the knowledge consisting of a mental modification (*vṛttijñāna*) is indeed insentient. Nor is there any impossibility of its illuminating objects, just as the light of a lamp and the like, though itself insentient, [illuminates].

Just as a jar or other objects are illuminators [of their own forms], there is no contradiction in a mental modification (*vṛtti*), though insentient in nature, being an illuminator of its own appropriate object. Furthermore, just as an insentient object such as a staff is a property of a sentient being, so too would insentient states such as knowledge be properties of a sentient being.

Because there is no sublation [of this]. Moreover, "desire, resolve, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, fear—all these are indeed the mind alone. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.3)

For in the Śruti, it is established that [the faculties] beginning with desire (kāma) and ending with cognition (buddhi) have the mind as their material cause; furthermore, because grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya)—as in the case of "clay-pot" and the like—must necessarily be based on the relationship between material cause and its effect. Moreover—
The great elements, ego-consciousness, intellect, and the unmanifest;
the ten senses and the one [mind], and the five objects of the senses.
Desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the composite whole, consciousness, and fortitude—
this is declared to be the field (kṣetra) in brief, along with its modifications.

Thus, in the Gītā, having designated everything from the great elements (*mahābhūta*) down to the objects of the senses as "the field" (*kṣetra*), that which is characterized by knowledge (*jñāna*) and so forth, ending with fortitude (*dhṛti*), is designated as the "modifications of the field" (*kṣetravikāra*). This is because it must be stated that knowledge, desire, pleasure, pain, and the rest are modifications of the mind, which is already denoted by the single term "field."

It should not be argued that because other types [of modifications] are impossible, and because of the statement beginning with "desire and aversion are pleasure and pain," only desire and the rest—being distinct from knowledge—are modifications of the field (*kṣetra*), whereas knowledge is not a modification of anything since it is beginningless and eternal; therefore, its inclusion among those modifications is not logical. For [the text] says, "he knows."

"He desires" and "he exerts effort"— since knowledge, desire, and volition possess the same object and are characterized by a fixed sequence of prior and posterior occurrence, it is logical that they must have a single common material cause; therefore, for those factors beginning with the aforementioned knowledge and ending with fortitude (dhṛti), it necessarily follows that the mind alone must be their material cause.
Nor can desire and the like be considered modifications of the dharma-bhūta-jñāna (knowledge as an attribute), because they are specific states of it;
therefore, in this context, by the word "buddhi," it is precisely the dharma-bhūta-jñāna denoted by the term "kṣetra" that is understood.
It should not be argued that, because it is mentioned alongside the unmanifest (avyakta) principle, its permanence is likewise logical just like the unmanifest principle;

for in the Śruti passage, "Desire, volition... and so forth, since desire and the rest are known to have the mind as their material cause, one must—so as not to contradict that—state that desire and the rest are merely modifications of the mind, which is denoted by the single term "field" (kṣetra). Mind...

Furthermore, by the restrictive particle *eva*, there is a negation of any other material cause [of the vital breaths], as seen in the Śruti passage: "From the Self [come] the vital breaths and from the mind, consciousness. Moreover, this reveals that knowledge in the form of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) is produced by the mind. And: "From the Unmanifest the Great was born, and likewise from the Unmanifest the Mahat."
O Four-faced One, the principle of consciousness (vijñānatattva) has arisen from the Great Principle (mahat);
from the principle of consciousness arises the mind (manas), and from the principle of the mind arise space and the other elements.

Thus, even by the statement of the *Skanda Purāṇa*, because the reality of consciousness (*vijñāna-tattva*) is known to be produced from the principle of the Great One (*mahat-tattva*), so too, by this very designation, the word "intellect" (*buddhi*) in the *Gītā* refers exclusively to the principle of intellect (*buddhi-tattva*) produced from the *mahat-tattva* through the function of non-exclusive indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, [the qualities of] cognition, desire, and so forth, which are of the nature of mental modifications, are produced solely from the mind (*manas*), as denoted by a single term.

It must be said that there is no room for the eternally existent attribute-knowledge (*dharmabhūtajñāna*) as accepted by you in every respect. Furthermore, since attribute-knowledge exists even during the state of deep sleep (*svāpa*), it is possible for that very knowledge to have the self as its object;
therefore, it is the intrinsic nature-knowledge (*svarūpajñāna*), which is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), that possesses the self and other objects as its domain.
Because such a conceptualization is untenable. Furthermore, what is this "being an attribute" (*dharmabhūtatva*) of cognition?

Is it being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*), or being something contained (*ādheyatva*)? Not the first, because in the expression "this is also cognition," it is impossible for it to be a qualifier. Moreover, is this being a qualifier and so forth identical to its own nature (*svarūpa*) or distinct from it? Not the first, because [if it were identical,] one could not say "cognition is the qualifier."

Because simultaneous application is impossible; and because it is illogical for knowledge that is itself devoid of a counter-correlate to possess a qualifier that has a counter-correlate. Not the latter [alternative].

In cognitions such as "I am the possessor of the cognition of a jar," the self (*ātman*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). It is not the case that cognition is the qualificand; for if it were, the manifestation of a distinct qualifier and so forth would be untenable. [This is because] there must be the capacity to apprehend the qualifierhood residing in cognition, which is itself defined by the qualificandhood residing in the self.
Since, according to your own view, there is no other cognition [to perceive it],

the nature of the self, its status as the substantive (viśeṣyatva) residing therein, and the status of the attribute-cognition (dharmabhūtajñāna) as the qualifier (viśeṣaṇatva) residing therein, are established by the self-luminous substantive cognition itself and the attribute-cognition itself.
