If it were an object of cognition, it would possess a distinct subjecthood (*viśeṣyatva*) and so forth, just like the cognition itself. Furthermore, since even the attribute of knowledge (*dharmabhūtajñāna*), which is distinct [from the self], can be manifested by the self-luminous knowledge of the Self (*svaprakāśātmajñāna*) alone, it is illogical to postulate that this [attribute] is also self-luminous. Nor is the latter [alternative] tenable; for the individual soul (*jīva*) is also something to be supported by you [the opponent], and knowledge likewise serves as the substratum (*ādhāra*) for properties such as "being knowledge."

Because it is impossible for knowledge to be subject to the rule of being something that is supported (ādheya), it cannot logically be a quality (dharma). Furthermore, since qualities such as pleasure and pain already exist as qualities, there is no reason to assert that knowledge alone is necessarily a quality or a distinct substance. Nor is it the case that pleasure and so forth...
It must be stated that [pleasure, pain, and so forth] are merely particular states of knowledge which has become the nature of *dharma*;

for it has already been said that there is no evidence for pleasure, pain, and the like being modifications of knowledge. Furthermore, in the scriptural passage "Desire, volition... (*kāmaḥ saṃkalpaḥ*) and in the traditional text "The great elements, ego... (*mahābhūtānyahaṃkāraḥ*), desire and the rest are specifically restricted [to the category of *ahaṃkāra*].

Furthermore, because it has been stated that [the mind] is merely a modification (*vikāra*), and because it is illogical to include desire (*kāma*) and the like in the same category as knowledge (*jñāna*);

therefore, since there is no knowledge other than the knowledge of the self's own nature (*ātmasvarūpa-jñāna*) and the mental modification that is knowledge (*mano-vṛtti-jñāna*), when these two are combined and treated as a single entity, permanence resides only in that dual knowledge which is grounded in the knowledge of the self's own nature.

The state of being an attribute (*dharmabhūtatva*) residing in *vṛttijñāna* (cognitive modification) is, according to the analogy of the umbrella-bearer, secondary with respect to the attribute-knowledge known as *vṛttijñāna*.

In the case of the knowledge of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) which constitutes the substratum (*dharmin*), you must accept by that same logic that it is secondary (*amukhya*). However, we maintain that in the case of knowledge as a modification (*vṛtti-jñāna*), its being an attribute (*dharmabhūtatva*) is primary, whereas in the case of essential nature-knowledge, its eternality (*nityatva*) is primary; thus, you have effectively accepted both types of "primacy" that we have asserted.
Thus it is established that there is not even a scent of contradiction between us. This concludes the "Illumination of the Unity of Knowledge as a Quality."

[Objection: Even so, is it not the case that another distinct substance—different from the substance consisting of the three *guṇas* and endowed solely with the quality of *sattva*, having the nature of eternal glory (*nityavibhūti*)—is established exclusively in our own system? In that case, the identity between us two is untenable. [Reply: No, because: "That *sattva* which is proclaimed as being alone among the three *guṇas*..."
That very [reality], known as eternal prosperity, is established by means of valid cognitions.

For instance, is the eternal substance of the *vibhūti* (manifest glory) composed solely of *sattva* produced by *prakṛti*, or is it distinct from that? Not the first, because that would entail an undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*). Nor the second, because there is no evidence for the existence of an eternal *vibhūti*-substance distinct from pure *sattva*. Furthermore, [there is no evidence] for [the existence of such a substance] belonging to the Lord or the liberated souls (*mukta*).
For the sake of enjoyment, since the necessity of both the divine, auspicious form and the collection of sense objects exists, it must be asserted that for that purpose,
a non-inert substance consisting of eternal glory (*nityavibhūti*) is to be accepted.
This is for the sake of the enjoyment of the Blessed Lord and the liberated souls.
This is because the assumption of an embodiment consisting of divine, auspicious, conscious bliss, and pure being is logically tenable;

furthermore, since it is a rule that whatever is distinct from consciousness must necessarily be insentient, there is no evidence for its being insentient. Indeed, one does not employ an unestablished probandum while abandoning an established probans. Otherwise, [the logic would fail].
That which is established by such injunctions as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" does not prompt the sacrifice and so forth, which are its own effects;
rather, it prompts only that which is validated by authority, such as the grace of the deity or the *apūrva*.

Because that would result in a contradiction with that very principle. For this very reason, regarding the purchase of Soma in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, after the statement "One purchases Soma with a one-year-old cow" has been heard, it is taught: "She steps forward six steps; the Adhvaryu catches the seventh step with his joined palms. When they move the two Havirdhāna carts eastward... [and so forth].
Regarding the passage, "He should anoint the axle with what has been trimmed":
is the leading of the one-year-old cow for the purpose of both the anointing of the axle and the purchase [of Soma], and thus employed by both;
or is it for the purpose of the purchase alone, and thus employed only by the act of purchase? In this doubt, since the anointing of the axle and the purchase are two distinct things...

Since the act of leading the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) is accomplished by means of her, and because of its proximity, there is no distinction between the anointing of the dice and the ritual action regarding the steps (*padakarma*), just as with the purchase; thus, having established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the leading of the one-year-old cow serves both purposes and is employed for both, [the author refutes it] by the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*): "He purchases [the Soma] with the one-year-old cow."

In the first section of the fourth chapter, it is established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that, since the purpose of the cow is understood to be the ritual action, and since the leading [of the cow]—which consists of its consecration—is likewise for that purpose, the act of stepping on the footprints (*padakarma*), which depends upon the leading of the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) for the sake of another (namely, the ritual action), must be abandoned; rather, it is the very act of cognition (*pramitikriyā*) itself that motivates the leading of the one-year-old cow. This is established in the first section of the fourth chapter.

In the section [PMS 4.1.28] stating "The foot-rubbing is the motivator for the leading [of the animal], because it is a constituent act," and for that very reason in that same section [PMS 4.1.33] stating "And a substance consisting of a single part [is used],
because of its connection with what is already present at the time of production," regarding the scriptural injunction in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, "He cuts off the remnants for the Sviṣṭakṛt."

Regarding the doubt as to whether the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice is the motivator for both the northern half and the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), or whether it depends upon the sacrificial cake already motivated by the *āgneya* and other offerings: since the northern half cannot logically be connected with the sacrificial cake of the primary *āgneya* offering, [the cake] must be one prepared for the sake of another deity.

Since dedicating [the offering] to another deity would result in a contradiction with the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭācāra), and since it is impossible for both [the original and the new deity] to be mutually connected, the Sviṣṭakṛt sacrifice [is performed] with the previously offered sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa).

Having established the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position that [the word "uttarārdha"] is the motivator (*prayojaka*) [of the action], [the siddhāntin replies]: because the words *uttara* ("latter") and *artha* ("part") are pronouns, they denote a portion and thus depend upon some previously mentioned portion;
and since it is known from scripture that the portion belonging to the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) under discussion is intended for deities such as Agni, one must rely on that very [portion].

It has been established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice proceeds [as a subsidiary], and thus it does not serve as the motivator for the northern half of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), which is neither previously mentioned nor independently cognized.

Likewise, [the same applies] to the Lord’s form and other attributes, which consist of pure *sattva* and are of the nature of divine, auspicious consciousness and bliss, as will be established by the proofs to be stated hereafter.
Furthermore, it is logical that even for those who are liberated, there is the purpose of enjoyment; thus, there is no inconsistency.

Nor should it be argued that there is a lack of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) regarding the Lord’s embodiment consisting of consciousness and bliss, nor regarding His enjoyment of objects of that same nature, nor regarding His enjoyment of objects composed of pure *sattva*. For [the scripture says]: "Being unborn, He manifests in many ways..."

It is born; that which shines as the immortal form of bliss. This is according to such scriptural passages (*śruti*) as: "The eternal among the eternals, the consciousness among the conscious," and the statement from the *Brahmakaivarta Purāṇa*: "This body of mine is eternally blissful; it is not created by *prakṛti*. It is complete everywhere; therefore, I am Nārāyaṇa."
All forms are complete in their common and universal nature;
nevertheless, even the seers must indeed depend upon you for the vision of those who are dull-witted.
"They speak of this as the further and the near shore, which indeed deludes those who lack devotion"—
thus says the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*.
The forms such as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa are eternally complete.
Not even by the slightest atom are they distinct, and yet you delude others.
Thus, from the words of Nārada:
"The ear, the eye, the sense of touch, the tongue, and the nose as well...
And being sustained by this, he experiences sense objects.
Hari alone exists as two-fold, as the Self and the Inner Self;
eternally seated within the heart, He drinks the juice born of karma.
"That Lord Hari always drinks what is auspicious and never drinks what is inauspicious;
the activity of this one who consists of perfect bliss is never known [by others].
Such are the words of authoritative scripture (*pramāṇa*).
"Sitting nearby, the mighty-armed and glorious Bali, son of Virocana,
seized the jewel-encrusted crown of the God of gods"—
thus says the *Bhāgavata*.
Even while living, having completely abandoned all that is non-conscious (*acit*), one remains as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) alone.
This they call liberation. Indeed, being liberated from this mortal state, he becomes pure consciousness; then, in that very form, he sees, hears, thinks, and knows. This [state]—
They declare this to be liberation: "Having attained the supreme light, he manifests in his own true form;
there he moves about, eating, playing, and rejoicing—whether with three [women], or with vehicles, or with kinsmen, or with non-kinsmen," and so forth, according to the Śruti texts.
Having abandoned their mortal bodies, those whose self-bodies consist of pure consciousness,
as well as those whose senses consist of pure consciousness, entered the imperishable Viṣṇu.
Supported by his very limbs, they act through their own limbs;
they enjoy pleasures either within or outside him, and,
favored by his grace, they move about as they please.
Just as enjoyment occurs for those in the state of dream without a body,
so too in liberation there may be enjoyment even without a body.
Or by his own will, he may assume certain bodies composed of radiant energy.

"Having accepted [the food] as if waking from sleep, one may at some time renounce it"—thus say the statements of the *Brahmakaivarta Purāṇa*. "Because [the world] consists of that [Brahman] by virtue of being mere consciousness," and so forth—thus say the sūtras.
"Therein, there would be existence alone," and so forth.

This is because the words establishing that the pure *sattva* is to be enjoyed exclusively by the liberated constitute valid authority (*pramāṇa*). Regarding the phrase "unborn" (*ajāyamāna*), the absence of birth in the form of modification within His essential nature—which consists of knowledge and bliss—is directly perceived; thus, the birth of Hari is not a modification in any way whatsoever.

By the natural implication of the word "form" (*rūpa*) in the phrase "the generation of a single form manifested through the characteristic of being an object of direct perception for devotees, which is of the nature of bliss," there is established the fact that the Lord possesses a body consisting of bliss; and by the demonstration of the eternity of those who are eternal in the verse "Of the eternal among the eternal...
(*nityo nityānām...*), it is established that the Blessed One possesses a body whose essence is eternal knowledge and bliss.

In the two statements, "This body of mine is like pure crystal" and "I am eternal bliss," there is the nature of Hari’s body as consisting of knowledge and bliss; and in the two statements regarding His perfect forms, such as the forms of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, the word "form" (rūpa) refers to that body which consists of knowledge and bliss.
Only when the intent is that all incarnations are directed toward a single distinguished incarnation do their fullness, equality, and absolute non-difference become logically established;
for it is said: "The ear, the eye, and the sense of touch are the Self, the Inner Self, and Hari."

In both statements: [the Lord] drinks the auspicious—namely, the enjoyment of objects by the Lord residing in the heart of the individual soul (jīva), which consists of pure *sattva* existing within the life-faculties (*jīvendriya*) that are the objects of the soul's experience; and the enjoyment of the essence consisting of pure *sattva*, which is the result of the karma experienced by the soul and exists within the essence. He drinks this auspiciousness.
In the phrase "eternally" (*nityam*), by the natural force of the word "auspicious" (*śubha-pada*),
there is the enjoyment of the auspicious consisting of pure *sattva*; [this is] for one who is devoted [to Him], as stated in the phrase "the mighty-armed one" (*mahābāhuḥ*).

By the phrase "the crown of the God of gods," there is the crown consisting of pure *sattva*; by the scriptural statement, "having abandoned all this [unconscious matter]," it is clear that even in the case of the individual soul (*jīva*), there is a body consisting of consciousness and bliss;
and by the passage, "he emerges in his own form from the supreme light" (*paraṃ jyotiḥ*), there is a form consisting of the essence of consciousness which constitutes his true nature.

Having abandoned the mortal body, because it consists of that [pure consciousness] through mere consciousness alone— thus clearly stated in both Smṛti and Sūtra— the existence of that body consisting of consciousness there would be purely as *sattva* (pure being).
In this regard, for the sake of the utility of pure *sattva* which is otherwise useless in the context of creation, the liberated one possesses a single body composed of that very substance.

Furthermore, it must be stated that [space] is an object of experience (*bhogya*). Moreover, since space in its entirety is pervaded by the primal material cause (*mūlaprakṛti*), if the phrase "beyond darkness" were intended to establish that Brahman is not subject to *prakṛti*, it would be impossible for it to refer to the substance of the eternal divine realm (*nityavibhūti*) as you accept. Therefore, it is an effect of *prakṛti*.

It is established that pure *sattva* alone, due to its similarity in enduring for a vast period of time, is conventionally designated as "eternal manifestation" (*nityavibhūti*) in a figurative sense; thus, there is no discrepancy between our two positions even in this regard.
Thus concludes the elucidation of the unity of the substance of eternal glory.

Now, even if this were so, one might object: "Since, according to your own tenet, among the ten kinds of substances (*dravya*), the three beginning with *sattva* are of the nature of *prakṛti* and thus possess the status of substance (*dravyatva*), while the seven beginning with sound (*śabda*) and ending with power (*śakti*) possess the essential nature of substance (*dravyasvarūpatva*), the identity between us two in this regard is untenable. To this we say: no.
Since qualities such as existence (sattva) and the like are not primary substances because they possess the nature of substance [only figuratively],
their status as primary substances is now established.
For indeed, when *sattva* is stirred up, it attains a state of imbalance;
when *rajas* is stirred up, it attains a state of imbalance; and when *tamas* is stirred up, it attains a state of imbalance.

In the Śruti, since it is established that for the purpose of creation, [the soul] is subject to being impelled by the Lord like primordial matter (prakṛti) and is connected with different states, its conjunction [with the body] must be accepted as a necessary consequence; thus, its primary status as a substance (dravyatva) alone must be asserted. Furthermore:
Whatever rajas exists in the root-rajās, and whatever rajas exists in the root-tamas,
and the tamas in the root-tamas— that is the nature of the mahat-tattva.
O son of Vinatā, from the mass of darkness (tamas), the mass of passion (rajas) should be known as double its size; it is not otherwise.

By these two statements, because it is impossible for the qualities of *tamas*, *rajas*, and *sattva* to be qualities of something formless— given their status as material causes, their existence as aggregates, and their progressive doubling— and because they are subsequently described as being limited in extent,
their substantiality (*dravyatva*) is unavoidable. Furthermore, [this follows] from the absence of a substratum substance for *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

Because the status of being a quality (*guṇatva*) is untenable. Is the substance that serves as the substratum the *prakṛti* itself or something else? Not the first [option], because if a single *prakṛti* were the substratum for multiple contradictory qualities, it would result in the absurdity of a single entity having a dual nature. As it is said: "The qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—arise from *prakṛti*. Thus, regarding the qualities such as sattva...

Furthermore, because it was previously established that Prakṛti is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), the consequence would follow that [the qualities] are not produced by Prakṛti. Nor is the latter alternative tenable, as it is difficult to define [what they are]. And it should not be argued that if these were substances, the conventional usage of "qualities" (guṇatva) in the Śrutis and Smṛtis would be untenable; for [it says]: "The one unborn [Prakṛti], red, white, and black..."

In the Śruti, since the word *ajā* (the unborn) is established as being in grammatical apposition with the words *lohita* (red), etc., it follows that they are non-different from one another; however, because the three qualities (*guṇas*) such as *sattva* are mutually contradictory, their connection with the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), which is of an indivisible and unitary form, is impossible.
Therefore, according to the logic of the *pāśādhikaraṇa*, [the qualities must be understood as] belonging to the constituent parts of the primordial nature—namely, *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

Because they possess the three colors, such as white and so forth, and by the intention to express them [as such], it is possible to employ conventional expressions like "a blue pot" through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) even for those [entities]. As for that which is the unmanifest (*avyakta*) consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇa*)...

For it is more appropriate that the term "general quality" (sāmānyaguṇa) refers specifically to the existence (satva) and other qualities characterized by attributes such as whiteness; [as stated in the Bhagavad Gītā]: "Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the qualities born of Prakṛti;
they bind the imperishable embodied self within the body, O mighty-armed one."

For here too, since it is stated that they (the *guṇas*) bind the individual soul (*jīva*) in the form of the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*) and so forth, the word *guṇa* must necessarily refer to substances qualified by qualities; this is just as in the *Pūrva-tantra*,
where substances, deities, and so on, are conventionally treated as "qualities" (*guṇas*) due to their lack of primacy.

Furthermore, since there is no obstacle to treating even the root-primal nature (*mūlaprakṛti*), which consists of the three qualities (*guṇa-traya*), as being "of the nature of qualities" (*guṇatva*)— just as *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* (which are produced by the root-primal nature) are conventionally designated as "qualities" because they are not predominant—

and moreover, because in the scriptural passage "the unborn, one... (*ajāmekām...*), the words "red" and so forth [denote the individual] according to the principle of the section on generic forms (*ākṛtyadhikaraṇanyāya*).

Even though it is established that [the word "sṛṣṭi"] refers solely to the quality (*guṇamātra*), by the logic of the *aruṇādhikaraṇa*, its status as an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is also possible through the door of creation (*sṛṣṭi*) and so forth. For this very reason, that same logic was considered in the first pāda of the *śeṣalakṣaṇa* section, under the rule: "When there is a single purpose, there should be a restriction because of the unity of action between the substance and the quality," in the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.

Regarding the statement, "He purchases [the Soma] with a one-year-old tawny-eyed cow that is ruddy," there arises a doubt: does the quality of ruddiness, by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), belong to the sacrifice as a whole and thus apply to all substances mentioned in that context;
or, by accepting it as subordinate to the act of purchasing (*krīṇāti*), does it apply only to the one-year-old cow? In this doubt, [the argument begins with] "with the word 'ruddy'..."

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), having separated the word *padam* from the sentence, the instrumental case-ending is taken as restating substances (*dravya*) while the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), namely redness (*aruṇimā*), is enjoined as its qualifier; thus, it would apply to all substances mentioned in the context. However, by the force of the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) of the instrumental case, [redness] is understood as an instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the purchase (*kraya*).
Although the entity of the quality of redness, being incorporeal,
lacks the capacity to be a means for purchase (p. 174), it nonetheless [serves that purpose] by way of delimiting the substance, namely the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*), which belongs to it.

Because the purchase can be accomplished [by means of it], the scriptural statement itself—“one should effect the purchase with a substance delimited by the quality of redness”—establishes that the quality has syntactic unity with the act of purchase. Thus, the final conclusion (siddhānta) is that these qualities find their place in the very substance, the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*). And so, by that same principle, [the application of] words such as "red" and so forth...

Even if the word *ajā* refers solely to the qualities (*guṇa*), it is still possible for the qualities— sattva, rajas, and tamas— which constitute the parts of the referent of the word *ajā*, to perform the functions of creation and so forth by means of their substantial nature (*dravyatva*). Furthermore, according to the etymology "those by which people (*jana*) are counted," people [are defined] by sattva, rajas, and tamas.

Since they are classified as superior, middling, and inferior, the application of the term "quality" (guṇa) to them is justified. Therefore, even in your own view, the status of being a quality for sattva, rajas, and tamas is merely secondary; it is logical that their status as substance (dravyatva) alone is primary.
Thus, there is no contradiction between us on this point either. This concludes the illumination of the non-substantiality and unity of sattva, rajas, and tamas.

As for what was stated— that sound and the rest, up to power (*śakti*), lack substantiality (*adravyatva*)— we reply that even in that case, their substantiality is indeed primary. For instance, qualities such as sound are not the locus of a mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is a substance distinct from their own substratum, because they are of the same nature as the substance that is their own substratum.

Like "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and so forth. Nor is the reason (*hetu*) unestablished (*asiddha*), because it is cognized by means of valid cognition such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), as in:

"the cloth is white," "molasses is sweet," "the flower is fragrant," "water is cold," "fire is hot," "there is one jar," "the jar and the cloth are conjoined," "the drum resounds," and "this person is capable," and so on.

This is a perception through direct cognition (*pratyakṣa-pratīti*). First of all, it does not have as its object a quality and a substance that are absolutely distinct from one another, like a jar and a cloth;
for there is no such cognition as "the color and the jar are distinct," in the same way that one might say "the jar and the cloth are distinct.
Nor [is it a case of] qualities, substances, and so forth...

Even though there is a difference [between the two], it must be said that the cognition of a jar, a cloth, and so forth possesses distinctness because of the relationship between the substratum and the superstratum; for even the cognition of a clod of earth and the like is experienced as possessing distinctness.

Nor should it be argued that because qualities, the qualified, and so forth are inseparably established (*apṛthaksiddha*), their cognition differs from the cognition of a heap of stones and the like; for such an argument cannot withstand scrutiny. To see why: regarding the inseparable establishment of qualities and the rest, does it mean they exist as long as the substratum exists (*yāvadāśrayakālīnatva*), or that they do not exist beyond the time of the supported (*ayāvadāśritakālīnatva*)? It cannot be the first.
For it would follow that there is no state of non-separate existence (*apṛthaksiddhi*) between a jar and its dark color and so forth, because they do not persist for as long as their substrate does.
Nor can it be argued that the dark color itself has transformed into the nature of a red color; this is because [the transformation] applies to the quality...

This is because you do not accept that qualities are the material cause [of the substance], and thus you must accept that the destruction of the dark color is followed by the production of a red color whose material cause is the substance itself; furthermore, there is no dispute regarding the fact that qualities such as sound and conjunction do not persist as long as the substance exists. Nor is the latter [position] tenable, for even in the case of jujube fruits and the like...
Because it would follow that there is an absence of distinction in the cognition of those [qualities] due to the contingency of the equality of qualities and so forth; furthermore,
because certain qualities such as odor, which exist as long as their substratum, lack the state of being inseparably established,
and not all qualities possess the property of existing as long as their substratum.

For some, it is accepted that there is a twofold nature: being co-existent with the substratum for as long as it lasts (*ayāvadaśrayabhāvitva*). In both cases, however, it must be stated that there is non-separability (*apṛthaksiddhatva*) during the time of their own existence. This being so, since there is no other alternative, the identity of our own view must be respected; for we too [hold that] qualities and so forth—

Dharmas are of two kinds: those that exist as long as the substance exists (*yāvaddravyabhāvin*) and those that do not exist as long as the substance exists (*ayāvaddravyabhāvin*). Among these, those that exist as long as the substance exists are non-different [from it], whereas those that do not exist as long as the substance exists are different; for this has been accepted because it was stated in such works as the *Anuvyākhyāna-sudhā*.

Furthermore, even if one accepts that qualities, actions, and other attributes possess both the property of persisting as long as the substance exists (*yāvaddravyabhāvitva*) and the property of not persisting as long as the substance exists (*ayāvaddravyabhāvitva*), [the following remains].
It should not be asked how there can be identity of doctrine (*mataikya*) if identity of attributes (*dharmaikya*) is not accepted;

for the identity of attributes is established precisely because both [the attribute and the substratum] are inseparably established (*apṛthaksiddha*). "Inseparable establishment" means the absence of separate establishment. And "separateness" (*pṛthaktva*) is difference (*bheda*). Separateness, otherness, and difference—these are [synonyms].

For it is stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "They are designated by worldly people only figuratively (*paryāyeṇa*). Thus, that which is established as distinct—that is, cognized as separate—is *pṛthaksiddha*; that which does not possess such [separateness] is *apṛthaksiddha*. Its state is *apṛthaksiddhatva*. This means it is cognized as being non-distinct. And so, this...

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Qualities and other attributes (*guṇādayo dharmāḥ*) are distinct from their substratum (*dharmibhinnāḥ*), because they are objects of cognition as being non-different from that substratum. Whatever is an object of cognition as being non-different from something is non-different from it; for example, the nature of a jar is non-different from the jar, or as in the following case.

The reasons—such as being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*), being denotable by words (*abhidheyatva*), being a category (*padārthatva*), and being a genus (*jātitva*)—are not unestablished (*asiddha*). This is because the reason, namely "being an object of cognition as non-different from the substratum," is established through the necessity that the conventional usage of "inseparable existence" (*pṛthaksiddhatva*) accepted by you would otherwise be inexplicable. This applies to the case of real conventional usage.

This is because linguistic usage must necessarily be established by valid cognition (*pramā*). Thus, perceptual cognitions such as "the pot is white" do not have merely the quality and the possessor of the quality as their object, since they are experienced as distinct from cognitions such as "the jujube fruit in the bowl. Furthermore, there is no other cause for this [distinction] there, as no such thing is perceived.

It must be stated that the exclusion [of difference] has as its object non-difference from another entity that is perceived as absolutely distinct. Therefore, it is said that the very perception of the non-difference between attributes such as qualities (*guṇa*) and their substratum (*dharmin*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, since the operation of sense-object contact (*sannikarṣa*) is required for knowledge produced by the senses, [this applies even to] the non-difference of quality, qualificand, and so forth, with respect to the sense organ...
Since there is an absence of sensory contact (sannikarṣābhāva),
it must be explained how perception has non-difference as its object, in the case of a jar.

Otherwise, it would follow that even the non-difference of essential nature (*svarūpa*) would not be perceived. Since there is no obstacle to contact (*sannikarṣa*) when there is non-difference, there is likewise no obstacle to contact when there is non-difference between a quality and its possessor (*guṇa* and *guṇin*).

Nor is it unestablished that qualities and the like have their own substratum (*svāśrayatva*) when they are non-different from the possessor of the quality; for the relationship of substrate and superstrate (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*) [is established].

Because [the reason] is pervaded by difference; and thus it must be said that the reason is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*). For, if qualities and so forth were non-different from the substratum of qualities and so forth, one would have to postulate some other causal factor for the conventional usage of the relation between locus and located (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*), which is established through means of valid cognition such as direct perception.

Because there is no establishment of their own nature [as distinct]. Furthermore, since the non-difference of qualities and so forth from the substance is established by perception, yet effects of difference are observed—such as the linguistic usage of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in expressions like "the white cloth" and "the moving cloth"—because such usage constitutes an effect of difference; for the linguistic expression "pot" and "jar" does not constitute such an effect. Thus...
The cognition of the whiteness of a cloth lacks the state of having neither less nor more as its object [than the cognition of the cloth itself].

There is a lack of synonymy between those two words [“cloth” and “whiteness”], and there is an absence of causal efficiency (arthakriyā) such as the fetching of water. When it is said, "Bring the jar," there is the bringing of some white thing or other; but when it is said, "Bring the white thing," the jar is necessarily brought.

Just as there is no contradiction between "this is not a jar" and "this is a cloth," so too there is no contradiction between "this is not white" and "this is a cloth. Just as even a blind person has the cognition "this is a jar," so too there is the cognition "this is white. Due to contact with lamp-soot (*mahāñjana*), the whiteness of the cloth is not unperceived; such is the case regarding the perception of a white cloth in direct sensory experience (*pratyakṣa*).

You must also admit that some excellence (*atiśaya*), distinct from those non-differences, appears as the object that performs the function of differentiation. Furthermore, that excellence is called a "particularity" (*viśe�sha*) because it produces a specific effect among things that are otherwise non-different; this is established by both direct perception and the fact that the cognition of a differentiating effect would otherwise be inexplicable in the absence of such a particularity.
It has been stated that this is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
178) A "particular" (*viśeṣa*) is that which serves as the cause for the non-metaphorical linguistic usage of difference even in that which is devoid of difference; such is the particular.
The definition has been stated. Such a definition of *viśeṣa* (ultimate particularity) alone is established by the means of cognition that apprehends its substratum (*dharmigrāhakamāna*).

If it is argued: "Since the difficulties [of explaining coexistence] are resolved in all the aforementioned instances even by accepting both difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda*), what is the use of *viśeṣa*?"—we say no. For it is improper to abandon a well-established cause in favor of postulating another cause that lacks any basis in valid cognition. Moreover:

Because a "particular" (*viśeṣa*) must be admitted to effect the function of differentiation in order to account for the coexistence of difference and non-difference— which are mutually contradictory— in a single locus; and because there is no contradiction between them simply because they are both cognized in one place, since the presence or absence of contradiction is determined by what is observed through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
It should be stated that this is because of the statement in the *Anubhāṣya*: "For contradiction and non-contradiction are both perceived.
This refers to the question: what is the cause for perceiving both difference and non-difference in a single locus, given that these two are generally perceived as being incapable of coexistence?

This is because one must necessarily rely on a cause that consists of a specific excellence (*atiśaya*), which is a particularity (*viśeṣa*) inherent in the very nature of the entity consisting of the quality, the possessor of the quality, and so forth. Furthermore, even in the case of difference and non-difference, if they were entirely distinct from the substrate (*dharmin*), [a further distinction would be required] for the sake of the conventional usage of their differentiating effects.

Because a particularity (*viśeṣa*) is unavoidable; for even there, if one were to admit both difference and non-difference, it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Nor should it be argued that there is no infinite regress because difference and non-difference possess a self-sustaining power (*svanirvāhaka-śakti*);
[for we maintain that] it is precisely our accepted *viśeṣa*, which performs the function of differentiating within what is non-different, [that accounts for this].
Since difference and non-difference would, by virtue of being self-sustaining powers (*śakti*), necessarily lead to the adoption of our own [Advaita] position;

furthermore, if there were a difference between the entity and those two [difference and non-difference], the conventional usage that "difference and non-difference reside in the entity" would be untenable, because there would be no relationship between the entity and them. This is especially so in the case of an entity that is absolutely non-different.

If [it were argued that] difference and non-difference [are identical], then the relationship of locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*) and the use of the dual number would be untenable, because the reality would be merely that [non-difference]. Therefore, for the sake of consistency, one must resort to a particular (*viśeṣa*) itself; otherwise, [the aforementioned difficulties would remain].

The particularity (*viśeṣa*) existing in all things must be either non-different from the thing itself or [itself] non-different [from other particulars]. Regarding the first case, is it one or many? It cannot be the first, because it would follow that all things become one, according to the logical principle that "whatever is non-different from what is non-different is itself non-different. Nor can it be the latter, for even in that case, does there exist one particularity in each individual thing, or... [in each individual thing]...?

Or [it might be argued that] there are many distinct particulars (*viśeṣa*). Not the first [alternative], because it would entail the non-occurrence of various manifold conventional usages such as "the cloth is large," "white," "moving," and so forth;
for if manifold and multiple effects were to arise from a single entity that lacks manifold intrinsic nature, it would follow that those effects are accidental (*ākasmika*).

The latter [position] is not tenable, because it would lead to the absurdity of the specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) being rendered useless. For if one were to accept multiple specific qualities—equal in number to the distinct effects of differentiation and linguistic usage—for each individual substance, then, since those specific qualities are delimited by multiplicity which is pervaded by difference, they themselves would necessarily attain mutual difference; thus, there would be a plurality of distinct [specific qualities].

Because it would entail the consequence of differentiation even for a single entity that is non-different from its particulars (*viśeṣa*). Nor is the latter [alternative] tenable, because in your view there is no difference between the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) and the entity itself. For it has been stated in the *Anuvyākhyāna*: "The substance itself, by virtue of having infinite particulars as its nature, is the cause of manifold conventional usage. Therefore, even if particulars are admitted, there is an inconsistency.
If it is argued that this leads to an infinite regress, we say no;

for although the numerous particulars are non-different from the single object and thus non-distinct from one another, the conventional usage of distinctions—such as their multiplicity—is established precisely by the fact that they possess specific excellences known as mutual particularities (*viśeṣa*). It is not [otherwise].

Furthermore, it must be stated that for the sake of the conventional usage of differentiation regarding qualities (*guṇa*), qualified entities (*guṇin*), and so forth, one would have to accept yet another distinct entity called "excellence" (*atiśaya*) within those "particularities" (*viśeṣa*) already accepted for the purpose of such differentiating usage; and in that case as well, another particularity would be required, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Because it is accepted that those very *viśeṣas* (particularities) are self-sustaining by virtue of performing the function of differentiating other particularities within themselves, all of this is established by the means of cognition that apprehends the locus (*dharmigrāhakamāna*) of the *viśeṣa*.
This has already been stated.

Now, although in other cases the non-difference between qualities and the possessor of qualities and so forth is established by the means of knowledge consisting in the otherwise inexplicability of perception, in the case of the Lord, for people like us,

the non-difference of qualities and so forth is established solely by the otherwise inexplicability of what is heard in scripture (*śruti*); whereas for those such as Brahmā and others, it is established by their own direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Because it is authoritative. If it is asked how the impossibility of otherwise [explaining] the Vedic texts [is established], it is as follows: "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite"; "Brahman is consciousness and bliss"; "He understood that Brahman is bliss. In this way, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of words denoting qualities and the possessor of qualities is heard in scripture.

Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is the application of words with distinct grounds for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*) to a single object. This is observed in such cases as "The pot is blue" (*nīlo ghaṭaḥ*) and "The man is staff-bearing" (*daṇḍī puruṣaḥ*). One might object: "But how can there be co-referentiality between Brahman and knowledge, given that there is no difference in the grounds for the application of these two terms?"

This must be stated: since the distinction residing in the ground for the application of a term (*pravṛttinimitta*) is also capable of being the cause of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the present case, just like the difference [between the grounds themselves], so too, when non-difference is established through the scriptural perception of coreferentiality between Brahman and its attributes— as in "The knower of the bliss of Brahman" (*ānandaṃ brahmaṇo vidvān*) and so forth— [the identity follows].

In the Śruti, since the worldly convention of relation is invariably concomitant with difference, the contingency of difference might arise; however, according to the evidence already stated and to be stated, because difference among the Lord's qualities is impossible, one must necessarily accept a *viśeṣa* (particularity) alone, as otherwise the scriptural cognition of relation would be inexplicable.

Furthermore, even the testimony of authoritative tradition in the form of the lineage of Brahmā and others who have directly realized Brahman cannot serve as a means of valid knowledge in this regard. Qualities, actions, and so forth are not held to be anything other than the very nature of Viṣṇu;
therefore, there is never any mutual distinction between them at any time.
Even regarding its own nature (*svarūpa*), there is a statement of distinction; yet, just like its being the nature itself,
linguistic usage proceeds by that very [nature] even in the absence of difference.

Thus, in the *Paropaniṣad*, it is stated that non-difference and unity are devoid of distinction, just as worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is distinct [from reality]. Why then is everything attributed as a quality of Hari? Whether there is a distinction between the non-different and the non-distinct, or between the distinct and the distinct—[all these are merely conventional].
The cognition of non-distinction would indeed be unstable;
therefore, without knowing the fundamental connection, one [should understand] the one in that other way.

Due to the power of fallacious reasoning, Hari’s specific attributes are treated as if they were distinct from His nature; yet even these attributes are His very essence, and their self-sustaining capacity is likewise inherent in Him.
Thus it is said in the *Brahmatarka*:

"One alone, without a second; there is not even the slightest diversity here. He who perceives diversity here goes from death to death. Just as water rained down runs away over the mountains, so [does he]."

"Perceiving the dharmas as distinct, he follows after them alone"—from such scriptural passages as these; and from statements such as, "The person is everywhere independent, being eternal in time," and so forth, [it follows that] his own connection is with that which has such qualities and forms. His nature as a quality and his state as the enjoyer of qualities [are thus established].

"And that [power] belongs to Viṣṇu himself," so it is stated in the *Brahmatarka*. Therefore, you too must accept this authoritative distinction: that for the seven attributes beginning with sound and ending with power (*śakti*), which persist as long as the substance exists, there is absolute non-difference from the substance; whereas for those that do not persist as long as the substance exists, there is both difference and non-difference. For this very reason it has been said:
In the *Tattvaviveka*:
"All properties of an object, such as qualities, actions, and universals, are of this very nature; and that form [of the object] is destroyed as long as the object itself is destroyed."
When a division is cut away, unity remains as long as there is a thing possessing divisions;
here, the very form that is cut away is but a modification of the modifier.
And likewise between cause and effect, as well as between a quality and its possessor;
similarly between action and the agent of action, and likewise between a genus and its particular instance.

"Likewise between the qualified and the pure, and similarly between the part and the whole. Thus, the primary [relationship] between a quality (*guṇa*) and its possessor (*guṇin*) is non-difference (*abheda*). In that context, the so-called "particularity" (*viśeṣa*), which effects the function of difference, is a primary difference;
yet in some cases it is also difference-cum-non-difference (*bhedābheda*). Therefore, even in that regard, there is no contradiction between us, and everything is faultless.
Thus concludes the exposition on the unity of the seven kinds of non-substantial sounds.
But even so—

since it is stated in your own commentary, "The eternal difference [is] due to the efficient cause (nimitta), while the pair [of difference and non-difference] is due to the material cause (upādāna)," the relation of both difference and non-difference between cause and effect has been established by you; whereas by us, however—
If it is argued that since there is an absolute non-difference between cause and effect, how can there be unity [of the two] therein? We reply: No;
for while the difference and non-difference of the transformer from its transformation are primary, their non-difference is also primary; thus, no contradiction is evident.

Regarding the identity-in-difference between the material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect (*upādeya*), it is "identity accompanied by difference" that is primary; this is the remainder of the sense, meaning that this is what we accept. The word "but" (*tu*) serves to distinguish it [from other views]. Furthermore, this occurs at one and the same time, and not through a succession of times, because there would be no occasion for considering difference once [the entity] has perished. Thus, the difference accepted by you regarding those two is the primary one.
The word "sādhana" (means of proof) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Thus, there is no contradiction between these two views; their identity is clear.
The meaning is that this would be so.

What is being stated here is that since the difference and non-difference between the material cause and its effect—such as threads and cloth—is established by valid cognition (*pramita*), [the non-difference] possesses primacy (*mukhyatva*).

(183) Because absolute non-difference (*atyantābheda*) contradicts valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and lacks authoritative basis, it is secondary; for while difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda*) is possible as a metaphorical application of the term "absolute non-difference," such is not the case for us two. Thus, there is not even the slightest [similarity] between our two positions.
Regarding the phrase "the scent of contradiction":
is this not indeed improper? For it is rooted in a forgetting of our own established tenets;
for instance, the state of being an effect consists simply in the cause itself entering into a different state, and the substance that is the effect is not distinct from the cause.
Furthermore, "state" (*avasthā*) is a particular adventitious property (*dharmaviśe�sa*), because it has been stated that "states belong to the cause.

Since every distinction in conventional usage is necessitated by a distinction in properties, the non-difference between cause and effect is indeed primary; moreover, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for their difference or non-difference, as both [properties] reside in one and the same [substratum].

If it is argued that this is not so because of contradiction and the resulting fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), we say no; for although there may appear to be a contradiction regarding the aforementioned object of knowledge (*prameya*) at first glance, in the final analysis there is no contradiction. To explain: the meaning of the term "state" (*avasthā*) is an adventitious property (*dharma*). Is it unique (*asādhāraṇa*) or common (*sādhāraṇa*)? It cannot be the former.
The first [alternative] is not tenable,

because there must necessarily be a difference between the clay lump and the jar, etc., as delimited by their respective specific properties (asādhāraṇadharma)— such as being a clay lump or having a neck and so forth— which are intended to be the causes or effects of those very properties like "having a beautiful neck" and so on. Nor is the latter [alternative] tenable.

Because these [properties] lack commonality, they cannot establish the non-difference of the two by being pervasively present in both, as in the case of "death" and so forth. Otherwise, since even the "particularity" (*viśeṣa*) that produces the effects of difference would be absent, the conventional usage of difference—such as "effect" and "cause"—would not exist. Furthermore, if there were no difference between cause and effect, they would be like a jar and a cloth.

It should not be argued that, just as there is the cognition "they are distinct," there would likewise result the cognition of such a distinction between those two [aspects] as well; for, by accepting both difference and non-difference, the defects mentioned regarding the two positions do not arise. This is because, through perception, there is the direct realization of a single, gross, blue pot, according to the cognition: "I am directly perceiving a single pot. Regarding the effect...

The establishment of difference [between objects] arises from their causes. Nor should it be said that this cognition has as its object the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) which serve as its material cause (*upādāna*);
for there are many such subtle elements whose forms are unmanifest and which are beyond the reach of the senses.

This is because it is impossible for such a cognition to have that as its object. Nor can it have the primordial matter (*prakṛti*) as its object, since that too is formless and beyond the senses. It should not be argued that there is no impossibility of direct perception because the potsherds and so forth are gross, possess color-and-form, are perceptible, and are indeed the material causes (*upādāna*) of the pot.

Since even potsherds and the like, being effects, would have to be admitted as having the nature of the primordial cause (prakṛti), the aforementioned fault cannot be avoided; furthermore, in the theory of transformation (pariṇāmavāda), it is impossible for potsherds and the like to be the material causes (upādāna) of jars and the like, and because [otherwise] the cognition of oneness would be impossible.

Nor should it be argued that only subtle entities such as snow and the like are observed to possess sensory perceptibility when they exist in a state of aggregation; for in that case, according to the logic of the previously mentioned section (adhikaraṇa), the aggregate must be declared to be a distinct substance. Otherwise, the same faults already stated would apply there as well. Furthermore:
Since it is illogical for the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma) such as water, air, fire, and earth, as well as elemental objects (bhautika) such as jars and bowls,

to possess mutual conjunctions, disjunctions, cutting, and piercing if they were of the nature of a single, partless, formless primordial matter (prakṛti), it is more reasonable that they constitute distinct substances; for there can be no such [qualities] in a single primordial matter.

If it is accepted that [the cause] possesses formlessness and so forth in its state as primordial nature (*prakṛti*), while fire, water, earth, and the elements and their derivatives possess form and so forth in their manifested states, then it would follow that there is no proof for the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman either, since they would both be substrata of contradictory attributes. This is because even in that case, [the attributes belong] to the one and the same Brahman.
Because it is possible to speak of omniscience and so forth in the state of being Brahman, and likewise of limited knowledge and so forth in the state of being a living soul (jīva). Furthermore, (p.

The entire world, which consists of contradictory attributes such as darkness and light, would become one and the same, because everything in the world has a single primordial nature (*ekaprakṛti*) as its essence. This follows from the logical principle accepted in your own view—that whatever is non-different from that which is non-different from something else is itself non-different from it—just as, in my view, [attributes] such as knowledge and bliss are non-different from the essential nature (*svarūpa*). Furthermore...

Furthermore, if there were no difference between the material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect (*upādeya*), it would follow that the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is identical with Brahman, because everything has Brahman as its material cause. You, however, O venerable and great ones, are Advaitins who maintain the non-difference of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman; you are proponents of the non-difference of the entire universe, consisting of both the insentient (*jaḍa*) and the sentient (*ajaḍa*).

Nor can it be said that *pradhāna* alone, being an insentient material cause (*jaḍopādāna*), is non-different from the world, whereas Brahman, being a sentient material cause (*cetanopādāna*), is not non-different from the world which is its effect. For if there were no non-difference between the world and its material cause, Brahman would fail to be the material cause; and this is not an acceptable consequence, as it would contradict the *tadanyatvādhikaraṇa*. Furthermore, if the effect were different from its cause...

Otherwise, there would have to be weight, color, taste, and so forth residing in the product (upādeya) that are distinct from those residing in the material cause (upādāna). Furthermore, there would be no such grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) as in "the clay itself is the jar" or "the threads themselves are the cloth.
Moreover, for the sake of accounting for the cognition "the jar is on the ground," [the jar] would have to be conjoined with each individual part, such as the potsherd.

Likewise, if it were to be asserted that even a jar and the like exist on the surface of the earth by way of their state (*avasthā*), then— contradicting the admission that solid substances occupy the same location— the jar and its shards would not occupy the same location; furthermore, it must be stated that this would lead to the undesirable consequence of perceiving them as distinct entities, like a cow and a horse.

[The cloth] is [distinguished] by non-synonymous linguistic differences such as "threads" and "cloth," by numerical differences such as unity and duality, by differences in causes, and by differences in substrata such as other words and so forth.

When the difference between the material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect (*upādeya*) is established through the various distinctions of purposeful action, the differences in forms such as squareness and so forth, the distinctions of prior and subsequent time, and the distinctions of causes— according to the logic of the section on "different words" (*śabdāntarādhikaraṇa*)—

and when their non-difference is subsequently established by means of valid cognition indicating non-difference, such as grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), [the nature of reality is understood].

Since both difference and non-difference must indeed be accepted, the principles such as *śabdāntara* (differentiation by verbal root) and others have been explained in this manner in the second quarter (*pāda*) of the second book [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*]. In the section on *śabdāntara*, regarding passages such as "One should sacrifice with Soma," "He gives in a golden vessel," and "He offers the sacrificial fees," it is held that a single efficient force (*bhāvanā*) qualified by the meanings of multiple verbal roots is enjoined.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it was argued that since the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is already occupied by the meaning of one verbal root, it cannot be delimited by the meaning of another root. Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that distinct, separate efficient forces, each qualified by the meaning of a different root, are enjoined. The same applies to the section on number (*saṃkhyādhikaraṇa*), where [the word] "three" [is treated].

In passages such as "he offers oblations," it has been established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that because the verbal form is in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the numeral-denoting word "three," distinct sacrifices to that same number are enjoined. For this very reason, in the section on Qualifications (*guṇādhikaraṇa*) concerning the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice within the Cāturmāsya rites—

In the first case, regarding the statement "When the milk has been heated on the first lunar day, that [curd] is for meditation," this refers to the *āmikṣā* (coagulated milk) dedicated to the Viśvedevas; because the sacrifice to the Viśvedevas is already occupied by a quality prescribed at its origin (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*), there is no possibility of including the quality of *vājina* (whey) which is prescribed later (*utpanna-śiṣṭa*) in the formula "for the Vājins, the whey. [Therefore, it must be a separate rite] characterized by the Vājins as the deity and *vājina* as the sacrificial substance.
It has been established as the final conclusion (*siddhāntita*) that another sacrifice is enjoined.

This is because the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and the *ārambhaṇīyā* occur prior in time to the Jyotiṣṭoma and the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices respectively, and because they function as constituent parts (*aṅga*) and as causal factors; whereas those two [the Jyotiṣṭoma and Darśapūrṇamāsa] occur subsequent in time.
Furthermore, because it is to be accomplished by other causes, it has been determined that there is a distinction. (p. 187)

But surely, since difference and non-difference—which stand in a relationship such as cause and effect—are contradictory in a single locus, how can their coexistence be established? For instance, when there is no contradiction between existence and non-existence, spatial separation is indeed the cause; as, for example, in the case of Devadatta’s presence in Mathurā and his absence in Sughna, there is no contradiction.
In some cases there is a difference of time, such that the presence and absence of Devadatta in Madhurā alone are not contradictory;

in other cases there is a difference of counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*). For this very reason, there is no contradiction between the similarity and dissimilarity residing in a buffalo with respect to the counter-correlates "cow" and "pot," respectively.

And if it is argued that in the case at hand, since there is no difference in time, place, or the status of being a counter-correlative between the two other factors—cause and effect—which persist as long as the substance exists, contradiction is difficult to avoid, we say: no; for just as with difference itself, there is also a "substitute for difference" (bhedapratinidhi)—namely, a specific distinction (*viśeṣa*) between cause and effect.
Since a state of dark-blue color that is contradictory [to its opposite] must necessarily be admitted,

and because— despite the identity of the two counter-correlates (pratiyogin) in the form of cause and effect at one and the same time and place— it is established by universal experience that there is no contradiction between difference and non-difference having the same place and time as their counter-correlates, precisely due to the power of the specificities (viśeṣa) residing therein.

Nor should it be argued that this being the case, there would be no contradiction between the existence and non-existence of a jar and so forth in one and the same particular spot on the ground, which would lead to the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of contradiction;
for this has already been answered by the fact that in cases such as cause and effect, [existence and non-existence] occur in the very same place at the very same time.

Since it is precisely because the non-contradiction of difference and non-difference having the same counter-correlate is known through valid cognition that the *viśeṣa* (particularity) is accepted there as the means of reconciling them; whereas, since the contradiction between the two positive entities, such as the pot and so forth, cited as examples is itself known through valid cognition, it is impossible for the *viśeṣa* to reconcile them there. Consequently, it is impossible for contradiction in general to be abolished in the world.

The perception of existence through mutual exclusion constitutes their contradiction; however, the perception of them together in certain instances serves as the proof of their non-contradiction. This is likewise the case in situations such as that of cause and effect.
Because difference and non-difference are perceived simultaneously, there is no contradiction characterized by the impossibility of coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*) between them;
for it is self-contradictory to claim that two things perceived together are the locus of a contradiction defined by the impossibility of coexistence,
since both contradiction and non-contradiction have perception alone as their sole means of proof.

Even though atomicity (*aṇutva*) and omnipresence (*aṅgatva*) are known to be contradictory, their contradiction has been accepted by the Lord through the Śruti text: "He is subtler than the subtle and greater than the great. Thus, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: difference and non-difference having a single locus in space and time are not contradictory, because they are established as such while possessing specific qualities (*viśeṣavat*).

"By way of exclusion, like a jar and its absence. Nor should it be said that the reason is unestablished (*asiddhi*), because the valid cognition "the threads themselves, consisting of length and breadth, are the cloth" is an object of subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) as being distinct from the cognition of a [mere] relation; thus, the non-difference between cause and effect is the object [of such cognition]. Regarding the cause...
Even though the effect is non-existent, there arises a valid cognition in the form of an inference produced by such reasons as "because [the cause] exists";

this inference has difference (*bheda*) between those two as its object. Thus, it is established that both difference and non-difference, having a single locus in space and time, are cognized through valid means of knowledge. Furthermore, it has already been stated that the particular (*viśeṣa*) is also established through perception and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). Nor is this...
It must be stated that the two cognitions stand in a relationship of the sublated and the sublator;

otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of one of them being non-existent. Therefore, the establishment of both difference and non-difference follows from the persistence of the cognitions regarding both objects. For this very reason, in the third quarter of the sixth chapter of the *Pūrvatantra* (Jaimini’s *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*), it is said:
In the section concerning whether there would be a distinction [of acts] due to the dependence of actions upon other substances, it was considered:

when, in the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices, rice and other materials are not available, the question arises as to whether another substance such as *nīvāra* being employed results in those acts becoming distinct rituals, or not. This is the doubt.
Because the sacrifice has the substance and the deity as its essential nature (p.

189), when there is a difference in the substance, a difference in the action—which consists of that [substance and deity]—is necessarily entailed; therefore, they [the substances] must be distinct substances.

Since it follows that [the opponent] would be forced to admit that [action] is a distinct entity, and because even though action has substance as its nature, their absolute identity is sublated by the fact that there exists at least a slight difference in action which resides in a substance;
therefore, we accept both difference and non-difference between them. Thus, even though there is a difference between individuals such as Caitra and Maitra, the genus "Brahmin-ness" [persists].

It is established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that just as a single [entity] is accepted by the force of a recurring cognition (*anugata-pratyaya*), so too, despite the difference in substances, the oneness of action must be admitted by the force of a recurring cognition.

Nor is it the case that when there is a difference between the material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect (*upādeya*), which are designated by those terms as delimited by specific states (*avasthā-viśeṣa*), [the action of] one alone...

It should not be argued that there is the consequence of a difference [in identity] between Devadatta with contracted hands and feet and Devadatta with extended hands and feet; for since a difference in modification necessarily entails a difference in substance, it would follow that the single substantive Devadatta himself—
due to his prior connection with the attribute of having contracted hands and feet— is [different from his later state].

Furthermore, transformation into a specific state occurs because that very same entity undergoes transformation into another specific state through internal connection with the particularity of extended hands and feet; for even in that case, a difference in substance (*dravyabheda*) is intended. Otherwise, it would follow that a self distinct from the body and so forth could not be established.

This is because the self, which is the substantive (viśeṣya), is itself qualified by the body and so forth. Nor does this contradict recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), for that recognition has as its sole object the genus (*jāti*). Furthermore, it should not be argued that if a distinct substance were produced at every moment as qualified by such qualifiers as "moment" and so on, it would follow that all things are momentary (*kṣaṇika*).
Since momentariness is intended by the opponent as being characterized by the state of being the counter-positive of a destruction occurring at the very moment of its own origination,

[this objection applies] if one were to instead accept a definition of momentariness characterized by being the counter-positive of a destruction occurring in the third moment, which subsists in sound, cognition, and action.
Because there is no contradiction in the case of difference-and-non-difference, and because there is no contradiction in accepting permanence by adopting non-difference;
for eternal difference exists through the efficient cause (nimitta), while both [difference and non-difference] exist through the material cause (upādāna).

By this explanation, the objection that "because the whole (*avayavin*) does not exist, the operation of the causal factors (*kāraka-vyāpāra*) would be without an object" is refuted; for in the view that [the whole] is both distinct and non-distinct [from its parts], there is no absence of an existing object for the operation of the causal factors.

On the contrary, according to your own position, since the effect is already established as being of the very nature of the cause alone, the operation of the causal factors [would likewise be purposeless].

It would be entirely useless; nor should it be argued that its purposefulness arises from being the object of a state, because since that [state] does not exist, it is impossible for it to be the object of the operation of causal factors (kāraka), and because if one thing were produced by an operation directed toward another object, it would lead to the fallacy of over-extension (atiprasaṅga). Furthermore:

Does the denotability of the term "effect" belong to the cause—such as a lump of clay or a thread—or to a specific attribute consisting of a particular state? It cannot be the first, because terms such as "jar" or "cloth" are not applied to the causes, such as the lump of clay or the threads; for even though the term for the effect is occasionally seen to be applied to the cause, [this does not establish identity].

The first [alternative] is untenable because it is possible for that [effect] to be characterized by its specific marks (*lākṣaṇika*). Nor is the second, because in your view, since a property (*dharma*) in the form of a state (*avasthā*) is distinct from the substratum (*dharmī*), the doctrine of the non-difference of the effect from the cause would be untenable; furthermore, if there were non-difference from the cause, it would follow that the cause itself is adventitious (*āgantuka*), as it would consist of an adventitious property. Nor is the last [alternative].

Is the qualified (viśiṣṭa) specifically the nature of the qualificand and its relation, or is it something distinct? Not the first; for even in that case, would each [constituent] individually have the nature of the third, or would the combined whole have the nature of the third? Not the first, because the previously mentioned defect remains as it was; nor the last, because the word "qualified" denotes only the combined entity, and thus...

Nor is it the latter [position], because it is seized by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); for this would entail that the conventional usage "the effect is non-different from the cause" is merely figurative (*aupacārika*), since the specific linguistic expression "effect" would be [merely metaphorical].

Because we accept a distinction in the cause that serves as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), it cannot be said that the conventional usage "the boy is fire" with respect to a boy who is not actually fire is non-primary (*amukhya*). Nor should it be argued that, since you also accept non-difference (*abheda*) in your own system, how can non-difference be considered figurative; for in my view...

This is because the intention is that the conventional usage of absolute non-difference is merely figurative. Nor should it be argued that there is no contradiction on the grounds that, for me as well, since there is no other alternative for cause and effect, difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda*) alone is primary, while non-difference is secondary according to the "umbrella-bearer" analogy (*chatrinyāya*). For that very intention has already been exposed.

Because there is no effort [required]. Furthermore, the section concerning non-difference (*ananyatvādhikaraṇa*) has also been explained in the *Candrikā* as not being in contradiction with this; therefore, enough with further elaboration. Consequently, it is established that we both are in agreement on the point that there is both difference and non-difference between cause and effect. Thus.
The illumination of the identity and difference between cause and effect.

If it is objected: "Even so, there remains a contradiction; for it is our view that Brahman is the non-different instrumental and material cause (*abhinna-nimittopādāna*), whereas it is your view that He is merely the agent (*kartṛ*)," it is replied:
"The status of Brahman as the material cause is primary, while His agency is said to be primary [in its own right]."
Thus, we seek only to manifest the identity between us two.

The status of being a material cause (*upādānatva*) consists in being a cause that undergoes modification; this is not primary in the case of Brahman, which is changeless. For the omniscient [Brahman], agency alone—consisting in possessing immediate knowledge, desire to act, and volition directed toward the material cause—is primary, because it is not contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and because it is not known through such means. Thus, its status as a material cause is secondary.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is with the word *śrutāvīrita* (stated in scripture). The word *iti* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*). Since the word *eva* has the meaning of *iti*, the connection is as follows:

because of the very reason for being primary or secondary, there is no contradiction regarding our [respective] positions on the subject of being the material cause (*upādānatva*); thus, we shall endeavor to reveal the identity of their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇaikya*). This is the intended meaning (*bhāva*): the Pradhāna alone is the material cause of the world.
It is primary, because it is the direct cause of that very [effect] as if it were a modification; and Brahman is not [the cause], because of its being changeless (*nirvikāratva*).

Because there is no modification directly [in the Self]. Nor should it be argued that being modified indirectly is possible by virtue of the Self being the substratum of the *pradhāna* (primordial matter), which is subject to modification; for since the term "material cause" (*upādāna*) is used in its primary sense with respect to the *pradhāna*, which is the direct substratum of modification, it cannot be applied in its primary sense to that which is the indirect substratum.

Is it not the case that Brahman’s status as the material cause of the world is indeed primary, based on Vedic usage? For instance: "From which indeed these beings are born"; "From the Self, space was produced"; "Verily, from Bliss alone these beings are born";
likewise, "From the Imperishable, the universe arises here"; and "From this, the vital breath is born."

Therefore, this Brahman, name-and-form, and food are born; they arise from Nārāyaṇa alone. This is because the ablative case is heard in such Vedic texts, and because that [ablative] is prescribed for the material cause by the sūtra: "The source of the agent of birth" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.30). [As it says: "The wise behold Him as the source of beings, the agent, the Lord."
If it is argued that this is not so because of the use of the word *yoni*—which denotes a material cause—in the phrase "the Person who is the womb (*yoni*) of Brahman," we reply:

no. For in scripture we find, "From food arise the vital breaths; from the vital breaths, the self of beings and the mind; from the mind, consciousness; from consciousness, bliss—the womb (*yoni*) of Brahman. And in common worldly usage, we say, "Joy arises from a son. Thus, the term *yoni* is used here in the sense of a source or origin, not exclusively as a material cause.
Furthermore, since the use of the ablative case is observed even in the absence of actual material causality (*upādāna*),
it is incapable of proving that [the source] possesses primary material causality; and since there is no injunction enjoining material causality with respect to Brahman,
and since Brahman lacks direct modification, the ablative case is employed.
Furthermore, because the indicators such as the Vedic scriptures must be interpreted precisely by way of non-appropriation (*anupādānatā*).

Also, when explaining the meaning of the sūtra *janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ* according to the method stated in the *Sudhā*: "The *prakṛti* (source) of the agent of birth—that substance which, being connected with the material cause (*upādāna*), becomes the limit (*avadhi*) upon departure—is designated as the *apādāna* kāraka."

And because there is no sublation [of this view]: "The wise fully understand its source; the father is possessed of a son through the son" (ŚvetU 6.1); "The source of the young is my source, the Great Brahman" (MuṇḍU 3.1.7); and "Because it has the Veda as its source" (Brahmasūtra 1.1.3)—thus in the Śrutis, Smṛtis, and Sūtras.
Furthermore, in common worldly usage, it is said that "the source of all strife is woman," and thus the word *yoni* cannot serve as a proof for Brahman being the material cause (*upādāna*).
