Now, one might object: even so, [scripture says] "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1), and "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone" (*Aitareya Upaniṣad* 1.1.1), and "May I become many."
"May I be many, may I procreate. It became the real (*sat*) and the apparent (*tyat*). "By which, what is unheard becomes heard.

Just as, my dear, by a single lump of clay all that is made of clay would be known—the modification being a mere verbal handle, a name, while the reality is simply "clay"—and so forth; such is the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) regarding the one becoming many.

If it is argued that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is indeed the primary material cause of Brahman—since the illustrations of the lump of clay and so forth for all objects of cognition would otherwise be inexplicable—we say no; for the arguments cited are established otherwise.
To explain: first, the scriptural teaching of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), such as "I am stout" or "That thou art," [is explained] in your own system as referring to the body...

In my view, because this [statement] is based on the state of being embodied, it refers to a non-primary (amukhya) identity; thus, "idam" is a single word. It cannot be an unmanifested indeclinable (*avyakta*) functioning as a substitute for a case-ending (*vibhakti-pratirūpaka*), with the sense of "atyāgre" (in front of that), nor can it have the sense of "asya" (of that), because such an interpretation would logically fail to establish its status as a non-primary material cause (*upādānatva*).

Even regarding the volition "May I be many," it is logically consistent that this refers to the manifestation of various specific subordinate forms which act as the regulators for each respective object being created— on the strength of the scriptural statement, "Being one, he became manifold through deliberation. Nor does the Creator, having willed a multiplicity of regulatory forms, [create] fire...
It should not be said that the act of bestowing [the initiation] is contradictory; for it is logically consistent, just as one gathers disciples after having resolved, "May I become a guru.

This is because it is logically consistent either by taking the meaning to be that through the knowledge of the primary [cause], the knowledge of the non-primary [effects] results as its fruit— since otherwise the cognition of everything by means of a single cognition would be impossible—
or else by taking it to mean that the knowledge of Brahman is the cause of a cognition whose object is everything, as in the case of the cognition of smoke and so forth.

Even in the case of the cognition of fire and so forth, there is an absence of the relationship between material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect (*upādeya*) between smoke and fire; likewise, the absence of that relationship is established for Brahman and the world as well. Thus, even the three examples—the lump of clay, the iron ball, and the blacksmith—can be explained simply by the intention to show causality, predominance, and similarity; they cannot be explained by an intention to show the relationship of material cause and effect.

Because the three examples do not function as direct agents of transformation; otherwise, like a lump of clay and so forth, Brahman would be the material cause (*upādāna*) by being the direct substratum of modification. This is not an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), because it would contradict the established doctrine (*apasiddhānta*) that Brahman is the material cause only through an intermediary. [This is illustrated by] the words *ekapiṇḍa* and *maṇi*.

Furthermore, this would lead to the consequence of [the scriptures] being purposeless. Therefore, the status of Brahman as the material cause (*upādānatva*) is not primary on the basis of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānyādhikaraṇya*) and so forth.

Nor is it the case that, while Brahman is known to be changeless (*nirvikāra*), it nevertheless possesses the status of material cause by being the locus of modification through its body consisting of consciousness and non-consciousness (*cid-acit*), even though it is changeless in its own essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*).

It must be stated that [the Self] is primary, because even all the Tantrikas accept that only that which is the direct substratum of transformation is primary. Furthermore, even the individual souls (jīvas) would not be the material cause (upādāna) by way of a traditional succession, since they too are the substrata of transformations such as the body and senses; moreover, space and time also [would be so], as they are the substrata of all transformations.

There would follow the consequence that everything would be the material cause [of everything], because even the ground and so forth would entail being the material cause of jars and the like by virtue of being the substratum for transformations such as lumps of clay;
and [this would occur] through a relation other than the relation that serves as the determinant of being the locus of all things.

If one intends to express that [Brahman] is the substratum of modifications, then even Brahman would possess the status of being the locus of the world only through an instrumental relationship; thus, by virtue of being the substratum of all modifications, it would follow that Brahman is not the material cause (anupādānatva).

If Brahman were subject to modification through the very same process of modification that affects primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and other substrates, then everything derived from Brahman as its material cause would necessarily be identical with Brahman and possess the nature of all things; for in your view, there is no distinction between the material cause and its product. Furthermore, in the *Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa*, regarding that which is in the earth...

Having described the stability of the earth and other elements with the words beginning "Standing," [the text continues]: "The earth is whose body; the waters are whose body; the Vedas are whose body; the self (ātman) is whose body; the unmanifest (avyakta) is whose body"—and so forth. According to such scriptural passages, the rivers and oceans are the body of Hari; the entire universe is your body.

By such Smṛti passages as these, Viṣṇu’s being the body of all is established. The so-called "bodiness" of the Blessed Lord consists in His being the controller (niyāmaka), while the bodiness of the world, beginning with primordial nature (prakṛti), consists in its being the controlled (niyāmya); it does not mean that the Lord possesses a primary body endowed with limbs such as hands and feet. Furthermore, the Lord's governance of all objects is likewise [understood].

Furthermore, it is absolutely necessary for the sake of establishing the nature of their respective functions; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the scriptural texts denying the Lord’s body would lack a subject matter, as they would not refer to a material body. Moreover, [this applies] to the individual soul (jīva), the unmanifest (avyakta), time (kāla), and so forth.

There would be the state of being Brahman, whose nature is that of the immutable Self which is non-dual, consisting of knowledge and bliss, and which constitutes the actual referent of the word "Brahman.
If the Lord’s body were primary, then Brahman would be defined solely as qualified by that body;

and since the individual soul (*jīva*), the unmanifest (*avyakta*), time (*kāla*), and so forth would be included within the referent of the word "Brahman," Brahman itself would [be no different from] the individual soul and the rest.
There would be identity with the world, because, according to the principle of the section on names (*saṃjñādhikaraṇa*),

a difference in words indicates a difference in meaning. That section is described as follows in the second quarter of the second book of the *Pūrvatantṛ* (the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*) concerning the characteristics of difference (*bhedalakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the statement, "Because of the connection with the arising of the name," it is heard in the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma: "Now this is Jyotis, now this is Viśvajyotis, now this is Sarvajyotis; one should sacrifice with this [rite] which has a thousand-fold sacrificial fee. In that case, does [the name refer to] the Jyotiṣṭoma under discussion?

196) The summary is this: [the question is] whether, having referred back [to the archetype] by means of words such as "Jyotis" and so forth, a quality called "a thousand-fold sacrificial fee" (sahasradakṣiṇā) is enjoined therein;
or rather, whether entirely new rites bearing those very names are enjoined along with their own sacrificial fees. This is the concise statement.

By the word "it" (iti), the Jyotiṣṭoma under discussion is referred to by means of the words "jyotis" and so forth, and in that [sacrifice], the accessory consisting of a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is enjoined. Otherwise, there would result the fallacy of abandoning the subject at hand (*prakṛtahāna*) and assuming something not under discussion (*aprakṛtakalpanā*). Thus, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), because the Jyotiṣṭoma under discussion is interrupted by the word "atha," [the connection with the previous context is severed]. In the present case...

If the [passage] were intended as an injunction regarding qualities (*guṇavidhi*) with respect to an existing ritual action, then since the requirement would be fulfilled by the sentence "by this" (*eteneti*) and so forth alone, the sentence "Now this" (*athaiṣa*) and so on would be rendered redundant;

furthermore, one cannot abandon a meaning already understood through a distinct name (*saṃjñābheda*) without a subverting reason (*bādhaka*), and because the word "this" (*etacchabda*) can also refer to what is yet to be described. Thus, these are other distinct ritual actions (*karmāntara*) bearing such names.
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that [these] are enjoined. It is not the second [alternative], because the meaning of the word *brahman* is constant unity;

for, since its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is devoid of even the slightest modification, it would follow that the doctrine of *brahman* as the material cause (*upādānatā*) is merely figurative or technical (*pāribhāṣika*). This is because [the doctrine] ultimately results in [the admission that *brahman*] is not a material cause at all.
Let the elaboration cease, as it does not contradict our own position. Furthermore, Brahman cannot be the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world because He is its agent (*kartṛ*);

for the universal concomitance (*vyāpti*)—that whatever is the agent of something is not its material cause, just as a potter and the like—is accepted by all. Indeed, the Lord’s creation proceeds from His mere will; it is not the case that the agent of everything is also its material cause.

Because [the Lord] is the efficient cause is impossible— due to the existence of evidence establishing mere agency (*kartṛtva*) in the statement "He brought forth the creation," due to the existence of evidence establishing His status as the material cause (*upādānatva*), and due to the absence of any unimpeded evidence establishing Him as the material cause— the [following] was cited:
Since the possibility of [the existence of] means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been stated according to their respective scope,
and since the doctrine that Brahman is the material cause (*upādāna*), which has come down through the lineage of instruction from former teachers, is not fit to be abandoned (p.

It must be said that only the non-primary [sense] is accepted; for since the non-primary status of being the material cause (*upādānatva*) is not a true material causality, it does not contradict our own position, as has been clearly explained. Enough with this elaboration.
Therefore, it is established that the non-primary status of Brahman as the material cause is not in contradiction with our doctrine.
Thus ends the *Brahmopāsanāikyaprakāśa*.

But even so, we accept the doctrine of qualified non-duality (*viśiṣṭādvaita*) as the object of knowledge; for such scriptural statements of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) are heard, such as: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1); "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone" (*Aitareya Upaniṣad* 1.1.1); "That thou art" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.8.7); and "I am Brahman" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 1.4.10). In that regard, this...

Since it is impossible for the world and Brahman—the referents of the words "Being" (sat) and "Self" (ātman)—to be non-different, the sentences are interpreted as having a qualified meaning (*viśiṣṭārtha*). This is because, otherwise, if difference were established through the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) of the words elsewhere, it would follow that the Veda possesses a non-primary sense; therefore, it is more appropriate to maintain its primary sense. In this context, by the word "That" (*tat*), [Brahman] qualified by the subtle sentient and insentient [principles] is denoted.
Brahman is spoken of [as follows]: by the word "this" (idam), Brahman as qualified by the gross sentient and insentient is expressed.
Likewise, in the case of the words "self" (ātman) and so forth, the sentient and the insentient are grasped by the terms "sentient" (cit) and "insentient" (acit);

the subtlety of the individual soul (jīva) is due either to its atomic nature in terms of its essential form (svarūpa) or to the contraction of its attribute-knowledge (dharmabhūtajñāna) during dissolution, while that of the insentient is [due to its grossness].

Subtlety (*sūkṣmatva*) consists in having entered into the state of being a cause. Thus, during the period of dissolution (*pralaya*), the individual soul (*jīva*) and the insentient (*jaḍa*) are the referents of the terms "subtle consciousness" (*sūkṣmacit*) and "subtle insentience" (*sūkṣmacit*). Likewise, the grossness (*sthūlatva*) of the soul is the expansion of its attribute-knowledge (*dharmabhūtajñāna*), while the grossness of the insentient is its having entered into the state of being an effect; and thus, during the period of creation (*sṛṣṭi*), [they exist as such].

The sentient and the insentient constitute the referents of the terms "gross spirit" (sthūlacit) and "gross non-spirit" (sthūlācit). Being qualified by both of these means precisely having both as one's body. As it is said: "He whose self is the body, whose body is the entire universe, and whose body is the rivers and oceans—[that is] Hari."
p.

198) Since it is established by Śruti and Smṛti that "whatever exists, other than this [world], one should bow to it," etc., the fact that the world—consisting of both sentient and insentient beings—is the body of the Blessed One is simply the state of being governed by the Blessed One; it is not, however, [that the world is identical with Him].
Its status as a primary body endowed with limbs such as hands and feet arises from its non-material (aprākṛta) nature.

Furthermore, the Lord’s having that as His body consists precisely in His being its controller; for a word denoting a body ultimately refers to the embodied one. And thus, [there is a relationship] between that which is qualified by subtle cit and acit, and that which is qualified by gross cit and acit.

Because Brahman is one, this statement is said to be intended for qualified non-duality (*viśiṣṭādvaita*). In the same manner, statements such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) are also to be explained. In that context, by the word "That" (*tat*), Brahman qualified by the subtle sentient and insentient is expressed; by the word "thou" (*tvam*), Brahman qualified by the gross sentient and insentient is expressed. Here, by the term "gross sentient and insentient," [the individual soul] is meant—*tvam*.

The consciousness of the living being (*jīvacaitanya*) is said to be qualified by the body, which is its substrate. Since Brahman is the direct or indirect regulator of both the body and the consciousness of the living being, Brahman as qualified by that [body] is expressed by the term *tvaṃ* (thou). Because there is non-difference between the referents of these two terms, it is called "Qualified Non-dualism" (*viśiṣṭādvaita*). Thus...

There is no inconsistency whatsoever in maintaining that sentences concerning difference have the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman as their purport, while sentences concerning non-difference have the non-difference of the qualified [entity] as their purport. In your view, however, every cited sentence would— according to the aforementioned method— require either the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of one of the words or the figurative indication of the case-ending (*vibhakti*).

"It is concerned solely with difference, and not primarily with the non-difference of the qualified [entities]. If it is asked, "In that case, since there is a contradiction between these two views, how can there be unity?", we reply here:
"The sentences have qualified non-duality as their purport, but not in a primary sense."
"However, we do not oppose the notion of a non-primary identity based on distinction.
Thus, by means of such arguments and well-established principles accepted by others, [the opponent's position is refuted].
This conclusion is established by means of valid authorities such as scripture (*śruti*) and so forth.

Through inference, *pūrva-mīmāṃsā*, logic (*nyāya*), and authorities such as *śruti* and *smṛti*, it is demonstrated that sentences beginning with "Being alone, my dear... (*sad eva somyedam...*) convey qualified non-duality (*viśiṣṭādvaita*) by means of secondary functions (*lakṣaṇā*) and the like, but not as their primary sense (*śakti*).

The meaning is that this is established so that there may be a correct understanding and a definitive conclusion: that our position as proponents of the difference between all internal rulers (*sarvāntaryāmibhedavādin*) is not contradictory to the view that non-primary qualified non-duality (*amukhyaviśiṣṭādvaita*) culminates in the unity of the consciousness that serves as the substantive (*viśeṣya*) for both [Brahman and the individual soul] as their respective internal rulers. To explain: [the Lord is] distinguished by subtle sentient and insentient matter (*sūkṣmacidacidviśiṣṭa*).

What is the meaning of "the gross [universe] qualified by both consciousness and non-consciousness is non-different"? Does it mean that the two qualificands are non-different, or that the two qualifiers are non-different, or that the two qualified entities are non-different? Not the first, because in the doctrine of pure monism (śuddhādvaita), the conventional usage of "qualified monism" (viśiṣṭādvaita) is merely figurative, and thus our own position is established.

Furthermore, since the employment of words is under one's own control, there is no reason for resorting to a non-primary (gauṇa) usage. Nor is the second alternative [the figurative interpretation] tenable;

for it has already been established that there is both difference and non-difference between the gross and subtle consciousnesses, which stand in the relation of effect and cause. Thus, by interpreting [the term "consciousness"] as merely non-different, you would be conceding what is already accepted [by us]. This applies equally to the gross and subtle consciousnesses.

Furthermore, since it is universally accepted that even between the gross body characterized by [the self] and the pure consciousness which serves as its substrate— standing in the relation of material cause and effect— there exists only identity-in-difference (*bhedābheda*),
it necessarily follows that the non-difference of those two, which serve as qualifiers, must be merely figurative. Nor is the third alternative tenable.

In that case as well, the qualified (viśiṣṭa) must be either different from, non-different from, or both different and non-different from its qualifiers (viśeṣaṇa), the qualified (viśeṣya), and their relation (tatsambandha). It cannot be the first [option]. Furthermore, it must be either eternal or non-eternal. It cannot be the first [of these two], because the non-difference of two distinct eternal things is untenable; otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman.

Furthermore, if the two qualified entities were independent consciousnesses distinct from the Brahman-consciousness which is the substratum, it would result in a threefold division of Brahman. If, on the other hand, they were dependent consciousnesses, the aforementioned defects could not be avoided; therefore, that [position] is untenable.

Furthermore, [if it were the former], knowledge would result in not being a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*), and there would be a contradiction with established tenets (*apasiddhānta*). Moreover, during creation and dissolution, since that which is qualified by subtle consciousness and matter (*cid-acit*) would not exist, it could not be established as eternal—[this applies] to the first position. Nor is the latter [position] correct; because it is non-eternal, it cannot logically be the cause of the world. Nor can it be the case that only the substantive (*viśeṣya*) [is the cause].

It must be stated that Brahman is the cause of the world; for according to your own view, it would be a departure from established doctrine (*apasiddhānta*) to claim that Brahman—possessing a subtle body composed of consciousness (*cit*) and unconscious matter (*acit*)—is the cause of the world. Furthermore, since knowledge and other qualities cannot logically belong to Brahman as the substantive (*viśeṣya*) when it is devoid of a body and the like, its status as an agent (*kartṛtva*) would be untenable. Nor can it be argued that...

It should be stated that [attributes] such as knowledge are appropriate because [Brahman] is endowed with a divine and auspicious form; for it is accepted that Brahman, being devoid of modification in itself, is the non-different efficient and material cause only as qualified by the subtle world-body consisting of consciousness and the unconscious. Furthermore, [this is not like] the case of "the pot and the cloth are different," and so forth.

Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the difference of the qualified (*viśiṣṭa*) from the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and so forth; on the contrary, perception and other means of valid cognition apprehend that the qualified is of the very nature of the qualificand. Moreover, for one who asserts that the effect (*upādeya*) is not distinct from its material cause (*upādāna*), the qualified—which is impermanent and has the qualificand as its material cause—[would likewise not be distinct from it].

Because it is precisely that non-difference which must be stated. Therefore, the second [position]—that the qualified is neither different from the qualifier and so forth, nor is it non-different—is also not tenable. This is because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends mere non-difference, and because the perception that "the bare person is not the person qualified by a staff" is established by the experience of everyone through perception and other means.

Otherwise, if it were said, "Bring the man with the staff," there would be the bringing of the person alone; and if it were said, "Bring the person," there would be the bringing of the staff. This is because there is no distinction between the two when they are devoid of qualifiers, [just as there is none] between the words for the qualified object and its qualifier.
Furthermore, they would be synonymous.
Moreover, it would follow that there is no difference between the gross and the subtle, as both are characterized by consciousness and non-consciousness;
for the gross form of consciousness and non-consciousness would be non-different from Brahman, which is non-different from the subtle form of consciousness and non-consciousness.

In your view, as well as in my own view and in the Advaita view, there is the non-difference of bliss—which is non-different from Brahman—from knowledge, which is the very nature of Brahman. Furthermore, is the "qualified" (viśiṣṭa) the nature of the three combined, or the nature of each one individually?
It cannot be the first, because since that would be something distinct from the qualified [parts], the defects stated regarding that position would ensue. Nor...
It must be stated that the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) itself undergoes transformation into a qualified state (*viśiṣṭātmanā*) through its connection with the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*);

for otherwise, it would follow that Brahman itself directly undergoes modification. Nor can it be said that the very nature of the qualified object is merely manifested as qualified through its connection with the qualifiers; for if the connection with the qualifiers were non-eternal, [the manifestation would likewise be non-eternal].

This is because [the definition] ultimately results in its being produced (*janya*); for if it were eternal (*nitya*), then since the qualified entity would exist at all times, its being manifested (*vyaṅgyatva*) would be untenable. Furthermore, because of the absence of the gross relationship between consciousness and matter during dissolution (*pralaya*), or the subtle relationship between consciousness and matter at the time of creation (*sṛṣṭi*), its eternality is untenable. Nor [is it tenable] during dissolution...
The very world, existing in its subtle form as consciousness and non-consciousness (*cid-acit*), becomes gross in its form as consciousness and non-consciousness at the time of creation.
It should not be argued that the identity of the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) is untenable due to the difference between the two qualifiers;
for since the subtlety and grossness of the qualifier and the qualified are absolutely contradictory, their identity is impossible.

Because there is a difference between the two qualifiers— the conscious and the unconscious— which are themselves distinguished by their non-difference from Him, the difference between those qualified by them is also precluded by that [primary] non-difference.
If one does not admit the difference between the qualifiers— subtlety and grossness— and the qualified [substratum],

it would follow that there is no means of establishing the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), since there would be an absence of difference among attributes such as atomicity and magnitude, omniscience and limited knowledge, and independence and dependence.

For if there were no difference between two contradictory properties, then by the logic of "how much more so" (*kaimutika-nyāya*), there would also be no difference between their respective substrates— which are themselves differentiated based on the establishment of that [property]—

since they would be non-different. Furthermore, this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of all things being non-different, and it would result in the absence of distinction between the states of creation and dissolution.

Furthermore, because the absolute non-difference between the material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect (*upādeya*) has already been refuted, the second position—that the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) is non-different from the substratum (*viśeṣya*) and so forth—is untenable. Nor is the third position—that it is both different and non-different—possible; for this would involve a departure from established tenets (*apasiddhānta*) and would leave the defects mentioned regarding the two previous positions intact.

But even so, the qualified (viśiṣṭa) is of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal. Where both the qualifier and its relation are eternal, there the qualified is indeed eternal, even though it is non-different from the qualificand—as in "God is omniscient," and so forth; for in that case, both the qualifier, which is the nature of omniscience, and its relation [to God] are eternal.

Even that which is qualified by eternality is itself eternal and non-different from Brahman, which serves as the substantive; likewise, in the case of being "qualified by the subtle sentient and insentient," since the qualifier— the individual soul denoted by the word *cit*— is eternal, so too is the inner controller, Brahman, the substantive.

Because those two are eternal, the relationship between them— consisting of the nature of the governed and the governor— is also eternal. Therefore, the qualified substrate (the *viśeṣya*), which is absolutely non-different from Brahman, remains so even with respect to those eternal insentient (*jaḍa*) qualifiers denoted by the term "non-conscious" (*acit*),
such as primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and the like.

Because the qualifiers such as *prakṛti* (primordial nature) and so forth, the qualified— the Blessed Lord who is their inner controller— and the relationship between them, which consists in the state of the controlled and the controller, are all eternal, that which is qualified by them is also eternal.
Although the qualified object (viśeṣya) is non-different from Brahman, that which is impermanent therein— namely, the earth and so forth,

which are material and consist of the qualifiers such as "earth" and their relationship— may be impermanent; nevertheless, because the qualified object, Brahman, is eternal, its very nature remains [eternal].

It must be admitted that the qualified [Brahman] is manifested through its connection with adventitious qualifiers such as the impermanent earth and so forth; otherwise, there would be a transformation of the qualified substrate, Brahman,
into a qualified nature by virtue of its connection with adventitious qualifiers like the earth and so forth.

Because it would follow as an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that Brahman’s state of being changeless would be lost; and because if it were asserted that the entire collection of effects, such as primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and so forth, is eternal—since they are non-different from their material cause (*upādāna-prakṛti*) through a continuous series—it would follow as an undesirable consequence that all scriptural texts concerning impermanence are merely figurative in every respect. [Therefore, the texts] refer to attributes (*dharma*) in the form of specific states (*avasthā-viśeṣa*).

Furthermore, when it is stated that "sound and so forth are impermanent," since *dharmas*—which consist of specific conjunctions of parts—are non-different from the substance of the staircase, they too would be eternal; thus, it would be unavoidable that the scriptural declarations of impermanence would be merely figurative. [This applies] to those very *dharmas*, such as conjunctions, which are effects.

There is a distinction from the substance possessing *upādāna* (material cause). Since there would be the consequence of [the effect] being half-similar to its cause—namely, that effects such as earth and so forth are non-different from their material causes (*prakṛti*) which possess *upādāna*—we speak of "qualified non-duality" (*viśiṣṭādvaita*) precisely according to the principle you yourself have stated. Alternatively, by the term "effects such as earth," [we mean] through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*)...
There is no inconsistency whatsoever in including the material cause (*prakṛti*) and so forth as being accompanied by *upādāna* (appropriation).
This is for the purpose of establishing the conventional distinction between consciousness (*cit*) and its states of creation and dissolution.

A pair of qualifiers consisting of "grossness" and "subtlety" is accepted as technical (pāribhāṣika), but there is no scriptural (śrauta) qualified non-duality (viśiṣṭādvaita). With this intention, our conventional method is that the statement, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," is intended to convey qualified non-duality. The same applies to the passage, "That thou art."

By the word *tat*, Brahman is denoted as qualified by attributes such as being the controller of the world, which were previously mentioned. By the word *tvam*, Brahman is denoted in the form of the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) of the individual soul (*jīva*).

This is according to the Smṛti: "The terms 'I' and 'you' [denote the Lord] with reference to the Inner Ruler who is the Lord of lords. Thus, [Brahman is understood] through its nature as the inner ruler of the individual soul.
Being the controller of the individual soul (*jīva*) is precisely what constitutes being qualified by the soul;

furthermore, that qualified entity is nothing other than the nature of the substrate (*viśeṣya*), which is Brahman. With this intention, our tradition maintains that the statement "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) has as its ultimate purport the non-duality of the qualified (*viśiṣṭādvaita*). However, where...

The qualifier and its relation are impermanent; therein, the qualified entity itself undergoes transformation into a qualified nature due to its connection with the qualifier. Thus, in that case, the qualified is impermanent and both different and non-different from the qualified entity. Absolute non-difference is not accepted, because it would entail the cognition of the qualified even prior [to the occurrence of the relation]. For example:

In cases such as "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*), it is argued that the very nature of Devadatta, who is the substantive (*viśeṣya*), undergoes a transformation into a qualified state (*viśiṣṭātman*) due to its connection with qualifiers such as the staff; thus, it is indeed non-eternal. Furthermore, because it is both different and non-different from the substantive, there is not even a scent of contradiction for anyone regarding this qualified non-duality (*viśiṣṭādvaita*). To this, we reply: none of this... [is so].

Since the object of knowledge (*prameya*)— which was previously inferred as being an object of knowledge according to our own doctrine— is now revealed and stated, there is no dispute regarding its identity with our doctrine.

[This concerns] Brahman’s state of being the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) of both the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*), and [the nature of] the conscious and unconscious entities that function during creation and dissolution.

The non-difference from the nature of the Lord, which consists in the occurrence of creation and dissolution within the primary states of grossness and subtlety— terms which are synonymous with their technical definitions—

This is because we accept everything— including the identity between the fundamental form denoted by the word *tat* (That) and the inner-controller form denoted by the word *tvam* (Thou). This entire object of knowledge (*prameya*), consisting of the non-difference between the aforementioned forms of consciousness and unconsciousness as well as their inner-controllers, is agreed upon by all schools of thought and is accepted by you as well.

The term *viśiṣṭādvaita* (qualified non-duality) is used as a technical designation (*lākṣaṇika*), and thus it is not the primary meaning of the word. In that regard, first of all, the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the word "Being" (*sat*) in the passage "Being alone, my dear... is not the state of being qualified by subtle consciousness and matter, because the word "Being" is not commonly employed to denote Brahman as qualified by subtle consciousness and matter.
Because it is impossible for being qualified by that [property] to be the delimitor of the objecthood (śakyatāvacchedaka) when that [qualification] itself is not possible.
The designation of Brahman is traditionally held to be threefold: *oṃ*, *tat*, and *sat*.
The term *sat* is employed in the sense of existence and in the sense of goodness.

Since the word *sat* is observed to be used for Brahman according to such authorities as "Being (*sat*) shall have the nature of the Good (*sādhu*)," and since it is a synonym for the word *brahman*, the property of being Brahman (*brahmatva*) alone is the delimitor of the denotatum (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the term *sat*. Nor is it the case that [the delimitor] is merely the property of being Brahman and so forth.
The delimitor of the capacity [of the word] for the sixfold locus (satpada) is either the state of being qualified by subtle cit and acit;

however, since even the meaning of the sentence— characterized by the impossibility of its being otherwise— cannot reside in Brahman as qualified by gross cit and acit, a cognition having that as its qualifier is also achieved only through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), and is thus non-primary.

Likewise, in statements such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), since the specific states of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman at the times of dissolution and creation cannot serve as the delimiters of the primary denotative power (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the words *tat* and *tvam*, the cognition of those qualified states is also merely secondary (*amukhya*) due to its being figurative (*lākṣaṇika*). Therefore, [the meaning] pertains to the periods of creation and dissolution.

The object of knowledge accepted by us—which consists of the non-difference between the nature of the conscious, the unconscious, and the inner controller—is precisely what you call "qualified non-duality" (viśiṣṭādvaita) in a secondary sense; thus ends the auspicious invocation.
Thus ends the *Viśiṣṭādvaitatattvaprakāśa*.
p.

206) Now, as for the claim that there is no disagreement between us on the point that the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman are absolutely distinct, and thus that [the question of their identity] need not be investigated—it is said:
"The scriptural texts concerning non-difference are based on the relationship between the body and the embodied; this [apparent] unity is likewise [based on that]."
It becomes illuminated by the manifestation of the non-dual unity of the distinguished [reality].

Now, even so, we maintain that there is equality between the liberated souls of the Lord and those who have attained liberation, based on the scriptural statement: "The stainless one attains supreme equality. You, however, assert only gradation (tāratamya) in liberation by means of the proofs to be cited hereafter; therefore, regarding liberation—

If it is argued that our two positions cannot be identical because of the presence of gradation in one case and its absence in the other, it is replied here: "The scriptural statement regarding equality between the liberated souls and Brahman is non-literal, whereas the statements regarding gradation are literal; this is how I determine it."

The scriptural statement regarding the equality between those liberated from one another and those liberated from Brahman refers to a non-primary (figurative) equality; whereas scriptural and traditional texts such as "There are a hundred human joys" and so forth, which describe gradations, refer to primary (actual) gradation. This is the conclusion I am establishing.

Is there a primary or secondary equality between the Blessed Ones and the Liberated Ones, and among the Liberated Ones themselves? Not the first [alternative], because in your own view, the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman possess such opposing attributes as omnipresence and atomicity, being the subordinate and the sovereign, being the Lord of Śrī and possessing the Śrīvatsa mark, and being the cause of the world and its absence [respectively].

Because it is impossible for the scriptural declarations of equality to be taken in their primary sense if one accepts inequality based on independence, dependence, and so forth; [that which] neither the wise nor the ignorant, neither the Lord (Īśa) nor the non-Lord, nor even by gods such as Brahmā and Īśāna can ever attain—
that very nature is Kaivalya, O Hari, and you alone are that absolute one.

This is because of such scriptural, traditional, and sūtraic declarations as "except for the activity of governing the world," which state His inequality [with the individual soul]. Furthermore, the knowledge, bliss, and so forth of the individual soul (jīva) are inferior to the knowledge, bliss, and so forth of the Lord (īśvara), because they are the knowledge, bliss, and so forth of a soul.

The transmigrating soul (saṃsārī) [is distinct] like the knowledge and bliss of the individual soul (jīva). The bliss of the Lord (īśvara) is superior to the bliss of the individual soul, because it is the bliss that governs the latter; for whatever is such, is so. This is because it would contradict such inferences as: "the bliss of the servant is inferior to the bliss of the one served," and so forth. Furthermore, regarding liberated souls...

If all were identical to the Supreme Brahman— given that Brahman is defined by such scriptural passages as "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite," "from which words turn back," "soundless, touchless, formless, undecaying," and "whose desires are true,
whose resolves are true"— then, by virtue of possessing those unique attributes of Brahman, they too would necessarily become the Supreme Brahman.
For that would result in the contingency of there being multiple causes of the world. Nor can this be accepted as a desired conclusion;
for it would entail the contingency of there being many gods, which contradicts such scriptural passages as "One alone, without a second.
Nor should it be argued that those [entities] lack the very desire to create the world at its inception.

Because it is illogical for the powers of knowledge, will, action, and so forth— necessary for the creation and other functions of the world— to exist [in another] while their absence [in Viṣṇu] is asserted; and because His majesty is divided into ten million parts,
yet again consists of the essence of bliss, and is further infinite, there is no one whose majesty is equal even to a single fraction of His.

Furthermore, according to the statements in the *Nāradīya Purāṇa*: "Śrī, Śeṣa, Brahmā, and Śaṅkara," there is a prohibition against the equality of all living beings, beginning with Brahmā, with the Blessed Lord. Moreover, there is no evidence that the gradations inherent in the essential nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) are destroyed upon liberation. Even through thousands of instances of unsurpassed service to the Blessed Lord and so forth, by the Blessed Lord himself—

Furthermore, because the granting of equality with one's own master contradicts the Vedas (*śruti*), the Smṛtis, worldly custom (*loka*), and logic; for [the scriptures prescribe] unsurpassed service and so forth toward a king and the like, and [their] proximity.
Furthermore, since nowhere is there seen an expectation of absolute equality between a servant and his master,

the equality of the liberated souls with Brahman must be accepted as merely secondary (amukhya), being occasional (naimittika) and arising from a specific connection with its modifications within primordial nature (prakṛti), according to the principle established in the third and fifth sections of the *Pāda*.
That topic is described as follows: In the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it is heard in scripture:

"Seventeen [sāmidhenī verses] for a Vaiśya. Regarding this, does the seventeen-fold nature (*sāptadaśya*) being enjoined as a contingent rule (*naimittika*) enter into the rite by way of an option (*vikalpa*), without subverting the fifteen-fold nature (*pāñcadaśya*) studied within that same context?

When the doubt arises as to whether [the seventeen-fold recitation] is to be applied specifically as a sublater of the fifteen-fold recitation, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is reached that there must be an option between the two— since both the seventeen-fold and the fifteen-fold recitations are equally derived from the context (prakaraṇa), they cannot sublate one another. However, [this is refuted by the fact that] through the context, [the seventeen-fold recitation] is understood to be an auxiliary to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices by way of the *sāmidhenī* verses.
Since the *pañcadaśya* (fifteen-fold chant), which is heard as common to all officiants (*sarvādhikārin*) in the general performance,
is obtained in its general form even in the performance by a Vaiśvaka, it finds its scope specifically in the performance by Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas;
therefore, compared to this non-primary [rule], the *sāptadaśya* (seventeen-fold chant) is occasional (*naimittika*).

Since the specific rule (viśeṣa) applicable only to the performance performed by a Vaiśya is stronger—both because it has a restricted scope and because it lacks any other occasion—it is impossible to enjoin [the general rule] without subverting the established permanent rule (nitya). Therefore, it is concluded that the injunction of the occasional rule (nimittika) serves precisely as a sublater of that [permanent rule]. In that context, within the performance of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices as determined by the ritual context (prakaraṇa)—

Just as in the statement "one should recite fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses," which establishes that the constant (*nitya*) number fifteen is an auxiliary to every performance by all eligible persons, when it is contradicted by the occasional (*naimittika*) number seventeen,
one postulates that it is an auxiliary only to specific performances performed by Brahmins and Kṣatriyas; so too [is the case with] the supreme...
Because it attains equality— since even the equality with the Blessed One attained by liberated souls, which is established by scripture, culminates in the Blessed One alone.

For it must be stated that the secondary similarity [of the individual soul] refers only to a few attributes, distinct from the many unique attributes such as the sovereignty and supremacy obtained through scripture, the Śrīvatsa mark, and being the cause of the world.

In this context, with respect to similarity (*sādṛśya*)— defined as possessing many of the attributes residing in that [the primary object], while being distinct from it and not possessing the specific delimitors of capability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) such as the nature of being performed by a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya priest in the performance of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices—
the primary [object] here is the absence of suffering and supreme bliss, which are distinct from the infinite attributes such as omnipresence residing solely in the Blessed Lord.

Since it must be stated that [the term] is secondary precisely because it is figurative (*lākṣaṇika*), as it generates a cognition whose mode is other than the delimitors of applicability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) consisting of the nature of possessing a few attributes; for this very reason, it is said in the *Nyāyāmṛta*:
"But the scripture concerning supreme equality [is explained] by way of the absence of suffering, true desires, and so forth."

Furthermore, according to your own school's interpretation of the sūtra "And because of the mark of equality in mere enjoyment" (*bhogamātrasāmyaliṅgāt*), there is a partial similarity between the liberated soul and the Lord due to the fulfillment of their respective appropriate bliss—just as there is between a river and the ocean—and because of the traditional teaching:
"The difference in form is supreme bliss; the equality is the absence of suffering.
Thus, in your view, there is equality only in respect to enjoyment.

Furthermore, because it has been explained that the word "only" (*mātra*) serves a restrictive purpose— namely, that [the liberated soul] is equal to the Brahma-liṅgas with the sole exception of the activity of governing the world— and because the word "supreme" (*parama*) is not redundant, given that during the state of transmigratory existence the individual soul possesses qualities such as bliss.

Because the term "supreme" (*parama*) is justified as being meaningful for the purpose of establishing a similarity even greater than that [with Brahman]— since in liberation, by virtue of its equality with Brahman, it possesses bliss and other qualities manifested there— it has been stated in the *Manu-vyākhyāna* that "the soul's being of such a nature is merely wonderful, and nothing else."
Alternatively, even a slight similarity to pleasure and so forth [is not sufficient], as stated in the *Śeṣāsurānṛta* (p.

Or else, the word "paramam" (supreme) is in the accusative case used in the sense of the instrumental, according to the grammatical rule *ṣaṭsurdvitīyā*. This is by way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇayā*).

Or rather, it means "by the Supreme Lord," because there is no sublation of this sense; otherwise, one would have to resort to the forced insertion (*adhyāhāra*) of a word ending in the instrumental case to denote the Blessed One. By this [it is meant]:
"Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have attained my own nature."
They are not born even at the time of creation, nor do they suffer at the time of dissolution.

Thus, these statements have been explained; therefore, the primary equality of the liberated souls with the Blessed Lord is untenable. Our accepted view—that it is only secondary—must be accepted, and thus the second position alone should be adopted. This is because secondary equality is necessarily pervaded by primary gradation (tāratamya), as you yourselves have also admitted.

Since there is no intermediate state, the primary gradation alone is revealed; thus, the mutual equality of those [beings] already mentioned is also merely secondary. This is because, in your own view, you accept that Garuḍa, Ananta, Viṣvaksena, and others are superior to other liberated souls (*muktajīva*). Furthermore, this is the inquiry into bliss (*ānanda-mīmāṃsā*).

"Whatever constitutes a hundred human joys, that is one joy of the human *gandharvas*, and of the *śrotriya* who is not overcome by desire," and so forth, according to the *Taittirīya Śruti*. Then, "whatever constitutes a hundred joys of the gods born of birth (*ājānajān*),
that is one joy of the gods who are deities by action (*karmadevān*), and of the *śrotriya*..."
"Vrajin is struck by desire," according to the Vājasaneyaka Śruti; "The friends, though possessing mouths and ears, became unequal in the swiftness of their minds.
By such Śrutis as these, you should worship Him alone with the activities of your own selves.
With their minds, speech, and actions,
free from deceit, they worship the lotus feet of the Wish-Fulfilling Cow for the sake of accomplishing their goals according to their respective capacities.
(211) From the king up to Śatadhṛti, those who have attained liberation rejoice with all their qualities increasing a hundredfold at each successive stage; for such indeed is the Vedic revelation.

By such Smṛti passages; and by Sūtras such as "Because of being included within the states of increase and decrease, both [sets of arguments] are consistent, therefore [it is so]," it is established that the enjoyment, knowledge, and other attributes of those liberated like ourselves are inferior to the enjoyment, knowledge, and other attributes of the liberated Caturmukha and others, because they are the enjoyment, knowledge, and so forth of those like us.
The bliss of the nature of a liberated soul is dependent on another, like the enjoyment, knowledge, and so forth of transmigrating beings such as ourselves;

it possesses a gradation relative to a similar bliss by virtue of the property directly pervaded by being bliss-knowledge, because it is the bliss of a soul, just like the sensory bliss belonging to that same soul. [And] there is the cessation of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), as in the case of the dissolution of bondage.

When the gradation among liberated souls is established through such inferences as: "Because [liberation] resides in a substratum characterized by a gradation relative to its counter-correlate, which is the cessation of bondage to kinsmen of its own class, like the cessation of bondage from shackles," and so forth.

Because it is more appropriate that the scriptural mention of "equality" refers only to a figurative equality; nor should it be argued that the scriptural mentions of equality and so forth pertain to the liberated state, for qualities such as being learned in the Vedas (*śrotriyatva*), being unassailed by desire (*akāmahatatva*), and being free from blemish (*avṛjinatva*) are impossible in one who is still transmigrating. Rather, these qualities belong to those who have attained the fruits of their Vedic study but have not yet attained liberation. These very [qualities]...

"Because their desires are fulfilled, they are thus called 'those whose desires are destroyed' (kāmahata). By this statement from the *Bhārata*, [it is said]: "He enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahman. And by such Vedic texts as: "Make me immortal in that place where desires have been fulfilled. For he is indeed liberated when his desires are destroyed.

And by the statement of the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, since being learned in the Vedas (*śrotriyatva*) and being untouched by desire (*akāmahatatva*) are primarily attributes of those who are already liberated; as it says in the *Ānandavallī*: "Of one who is learned in the Vedas and untouched by desire" (p.

Furthermore, because it is stated that for liberated humans, their bliss is one hundred times less than the bliss of human *gandharvas*, and because you yourselves accept that a *śrotriya* who is free from desire (*akāmahata*) is liberated; "being free from desire" (*akāmahatatva*) does not mean the absence of desire (*akāmatva*).
For if that were the case, the word "struck" (*hata*) would become redundant; rather, [it means being unaffected by desire].
The state of being free from afflictions caused by desire is appropriate for those who have attained their desired objects; it cannot be otherwise.
And that [attainment] is possible only for liberated ones whose desires are true. Likewise, the state of being without blemish (*avrajinatva*) means being without sin and without suffering;
for this very reason, it is stated in the *Anuvyākhyāna*:
Freedom from evil (*apāpatva*) and freedom from suffering (*aduḥkhatva*) are here declared to be "freedom from crookedness" (*avṛjinatva*).

That which is unpleasant is called "crooked" (*vṛjina*), "suffering" (*duḥkha*), and "unpleasant" (*akānta*); because it is the cause of that [suffering], it is also termed "evil" (*pāpa*) or "crookedness" (*vrajina*).
Thus has the meaning of the name been stated by the Lord himself in the *Śabdanirṇaya*.

This is because, even among those possessing direct realization (*aparokṣajñānin*), there exists the presence of *prārabdha* karma, and thus only those who are truly liberated (*mukta*) possess the primary status. Furthermore, in the passages "of the *śrotriya*" and "he who is a *śrotriya*," the singular number is used.

Furthermore, the word "ca" (and) would be inappropriate if it were intended to signify conjunction (*samuccaya*), because such usage is not observed when multiple attributes refer to a single subject— as in the case of "Vasiṣṭha, Brahmaṣṭha, and Aruddhatīpati. Moreover, if it were intended to refer to another transmigrating being distinct from the subject under discussion,
that would be impossible, as the bliss of the Four-faced One (Brahmā) and others cannot possibly exist in any other transmigrating being.

Therefore, having described the gradation of those not yet liberated by the preceding statement, one must accept that the gradation of those very same liberated ones is stated by the passage beginning with "of the Śrotriya. And it has been said in the *Anuvyākhyāna*:
"Having first stated the state of transmigratory existence with the words 'He is one,' [it then speaks of] happiness again..."
By saying "of the learned one" (*śrotriyasya*), he states that [the merit] is a hundredfold more than that of one who is liberated;

and by speaking of one who has entered the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) as being superior to one who has already passed through the cycle of existence, he indicates it is even more than a hundredfold.

It would be appropriate for one who is already liberated to observe the statements of the Śruti; for it is said that there is a gradation among the four types of liberation—namely, *sālokya*, *sāmīpya*, *sārūpya*, and *sāyujya*. Furthermore, even in your own system, you maintain that the knowledge of Brahman in the form of devotion (*bhakti*) and surrender (*prapatti*) is the means to liberation, [and this applies] to Brahmā and the others as well.

Since there is a gradation among transmigrating beings ranging from humans to those at the lowest limit, and since the hearing [of scripture] and other means are practiced in varying degrees— ranging from much, to little, to very little— the means possess a gradation corresponding to the gradation in the object to be achieved, namely the knowledge of Brahman, which itself possesses a gradation consisting in its having as its object the qualities of Brahman in greater, lesser, or even smaller measure.

Since it is invariably concomitant with degrees of excellence in that which is to be accomplished, there must necessarily be degrees of excellence in liberation, which is the object to be accomplished;
for by the excellence of the means, one shall attain an excellent end.
Brahmā and the others are mentioned in sequence, just as they are heard in the Ānanda-śruti.
Thus, by the word of Brahmā: "Liberation indeed occurs through knowledge even for one who has performed all ritual actions;
however, bliss diminishes from performing ritual action, whereas it increases by performing auspicious deeds."
Thus, by the statement of the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*:
"The cessation of all suffering is indeed certain for the knower;
through worship, ritual acts, and devotion, there is a manifoldness of bliss. And so too by another *smṛti*.
"Your knowledge is greater and your state is higher"—
from such statements in the *Mokṣadharma* and other texts, it is stated that the gradation of the means necessitates a gradation of the results.
And this has been said in the *Smṛti* cited in the *Anuvyākhyāna*:
And it is logical that there is a superiority of the goal (sādhya) among the gods and others due to the superiority of their means (sādhana);
if there were no superiority in the goal, why would there be effort in the means?
For ten kalpas, Rudra performed austerities in the salt ocean,
abandoning all pleasures and enduring the affliction of the salty waters;
and for millions of years, Śakra drank smoke out of great misery.
For ten thousand years, Marīci, his father, performed austerities with the sun as his heat, his speech as his head,
and his body lying in the open air; having renounced pleasure with great difficulty,
he practiced dharma with exceeding devotion for a thousand years.
"Even those who know Brahman indeed exert effort with great difficulty"—

all this has been stated because there is no distinction regarding liberation. Furthermore, in your own view, according to the sūtra "vikalpo viśiṣṭaphalatvāt," [liberation is attained] through option.

Furthermore, because it is accepted that there is a gradation among the various meditations on the *dahara* (the small space) and the *akṣara* (the Imperishable), which are taught as means to liberation, depending on whether they concern greater or fewer qualities; and also because of the nature of devotion (*bhakti*) and surrender (*prapatti*), which are each a cause of liberation and consist of uninterrupted contemplation and renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*).
This is because a gradation [of results] is accepted based on the dependence or independence from karma, and on being veiled or unveiled.
And it is said in the *Bhaṭṭavārttika*: "Because of the equality of their location within a portion of space, they are enjoined without distinction.
Here, "without distinction" refers to the fact that sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and Agnihotra, which are heard in scripture as means to heaven, [are enjoined] without distinction.

Because there is a gradation based on the fact that [liberation] is to be accomplished by means of many or few merits, a gradation is said to exist even in the fruit of heaven which is to be accomplished thereby.
Nor should it be argued that if there were gradation in liberation, it would entail the occurrence of hatred, envy, and so forth,
and that because of the resulting suffering and the like, the state of being liberated would be lost.

215) Since all defects such as desire and the like have been destroyed by the direct realization of Brahman, it is logically established that even in the state of liberation, hatred, envy, and so forth—which are caused by those defects—are absolutely non-existent. And it has been stated in the *Anuvyākhyāna*:
For those whose defects have been entirely eliminated over many births, there shall indeed be direct realization of Hari; how then could hatred, envy, or the like arise from that?

If envy were indeed to arise even toward equals, why does it not arise for you? Even those who are tormented by seeing others as their equals are seen in the world to be possessed of hatred, envy, and the like; therefore, the fault alone is the cause in this matter.
If there is faultlessness therein, why is it further criticized?

For this very reason, the second [position] is not tenable, because it has already been stated that this would result in an accepted conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*). Therefore, even regarding the mutual equality of the liberated ones, the absence of suffering pertains only to certain attributes such as their own fitness, full bliss, and the distinction of the *liṅga*.

Since it is impossible for there to be a primary similarity consisting in the possession of many properties belonging to that [object] as something to be predicated, and since non-primary similarity is not incompatible with primary gradation, there is no dispute regarding the identity of our position; thus, everything is faultless.
Thus concludes the illumination on the gradations and unity in liberation.

Even so, we maintain that the knowledge of Brahman—known as *prapatti* (surrender) and *bhakti* (devotion)—is a means to liberation independently of one another. Furthermore, among these, the knowledge of Brahman known as *prapatti*, when performed even once without dependence on ritual action (*karman*), is a means to liberation; as it is said: "I, desiring liberation, indeed take refuge [in Him]."

One should unite oneself [with the Self] with the thought, "I am Brahman, indeed. There are scriptural statements such as: "Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the knowledge of Vedānta, who are self-controlled through the yoga of renunciation, and whose being is purified—they all, at the time of their final end in the world of Brahman, are liberated through the supreme Immortality," and so forth.
Abandoning all dharmas, take refuge in me alone.
I shall liberate you from all sins; do not grieve.
"To one who has surrendered even once and entreats, 'I am yours,' I grant fearlessness from all beings; this is my vow.
As long as there is affliction, as long as there is desire, as long as there is delusion, and likewise pleasure,"
Until one goes for refuge to You, the destroyer of all sins—
therein consist: the resolve for favorability, the avoidance of what is unfavorable,
the conviction that "He will protect me," and likewise the formal acceptance of His protection.
In the wretchedness of self-surrender, there is a sixfold way of seeking refuge. Through this surrender, preceded solely by a state of total destitution,
a person should seek refuge in me, knowing me as "Mādhava."
"By thus taking refuge in me, one shall have fulfilled all duties"—

such are the authoritative statements from the Gītā, Rāmāyaṇa, Viṣṇu Purāṇa, Pañcarātra, and other sources. Thus, this [work] is composed of three sections consisting of one, two, and five syllables, [and] by its meanings, it [leads to] reality and welfare.

Thus, in the verse cited by our own former teachers— which establishes that surrender (*prapatti*) is the means for attaining the desired goal— and in the scriptural authorities quoted therein, it is made known that surrender is the direct cause of liberation, consisting of the three "essences of the inner self" (*adhyātmasāra*) which are composed of purpose (*prayojana*).
But you [the Vedāntins] maintain that direct knowledge of Brahman (*brahmāparokṣajñāna*) is the means to liberation, while surrender (*prapatti*) and the like are merely its ancillaries;
thus, if it is asked how there can be identity between us when such a contradiction exists here, it is replied:
the means called surrender is not the primary one, just like ritual action (*karman*) and so forth.
The lack of contradiction here is established by means of knowledge (*jñāna*);
that is, ritual action (*karman*) and so forth lead [to liberation] through the sequence of mental purification (*citta-śuddhi*) and then through knowledge (p.

Just as [knowledge] is a means to liberation, the means called *prapatti* (surrender) is also a means to liberation only through a succession of stages—such as wisdom, devotion, and so forth—and not primarily or directly; this is the meaning of the word "ca" (and), which functions as a reason (*hetu*).
The word "ca" is used for conjunction, and the phrase "that which denotes *prapatti*" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. Therefore, that which is called *prapatti*...
The meaning is that it is established here that there is no contradiction between us, even though there is a distinction regarding *prapatti* as a means to liberation through knowledge;

for instance, is the knowledge in the form of *prapatti* intended by you to be a direct means to liberation, or is it an indirect means— either as an alternative to *bhakti*, or as an auxiliary to *bhakti* like ritual action (*karman*) and so forth?

Nor is the first [alternative] tenable; for there is no direct means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) establishing that [the Lord] is the actual achiever of liberation. Nor should it be argued that the collection of statements such as "I, desiring liberation, take refuge" constitutes such a means of valid knowledge;
for in that regard, the statement "I, desiring liberation, take refuge" is merely a restatement of the idea expressed in "We have drunk Soma, we have become immortal."
We have not [attained it through knowledge alone]. For Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone.
Just as it is said that one desiring liberation performs "cessation-activity" (*nivartaka-karma*), so too *prapatti* leads to the goal through a traditional sequence.

This is because it is logical that [the text] is intent upon the means for attaining liberation. Furthermore, regarding the knowledge of Brahman heard in such passages as: "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow," "Knowing Him thus, one becomes immortal here," and "Having seen Him, one is released, and not by any other means."
For there is no obstacle to your accepting that devotion (bhakti) culminates in knowledge (jñāna); otherwise,
even in such passages as "The knower of Brahman attains [Brahman]," immediate knowledge of Brahman— just like devotion and surrender (prapatti)— would have to be a third direct means to liberation.

Furthermore, because the term "prapadya" denotes a specific kind of knowledge, [the attainment] described in passages such as "The knower of Brahman attains [Brahman]" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.8) is not the fruit of a different means consisting of *prapatti*.
It should not be argued that, because the word *jñāna* generally denotes knowledge, it is more appropriate for it to refer specifically to *bhakti* (devotion).

For instance, in such passages as "The wise man, having known [it], does not grieve" (*matvā dhīro na śocati*) and "Having seen [it] alone, one is liberated, and not by any other means" (*dṛṣṭvaiva tam mucyate nāpareṇa*), words like *matvā* (having known) and *dṛṣṭvā* (having seen)—which denote specific forms of knowledge such as reflection and vision—ultimately culminate in *bhakti*. This is likewise the case with *prapadya* (having taken refuge).

Since there is no sublation (bādhaka) against this [interpretation] that even this [surrender] culminates in devotion (*bhakti*), otherwise, like devotion and like surrender (*prapatti*), reflection (*manana*) and vision (*darśana*) would also be direct means to liberation. Furthermore, according to your own view, just as in the case of *karmayoga* and *jñānayoga*, it is logical that surrender (*prapatti*) is also an ancillary (*aṅga*) to devotion; for an ancillary is subordinate to the principal (*aṅgin*).

Since there is no sublation (bādhaka) regarding the restatement of the fruit, the scriptural passage, "Therefore, seeking liberation, I take refuge in Him," does not intend to establish that surrender (*prapatti*) is a direct means to liberation; nor does the scriptural passage, "One should unite oneself with Brahmā, the Friend," do so, for that [passage] also [speaks of] truth, austerity, self-restraint, tranquility, charity, and dharma.

Since the *prajanana-agni*, the *hotr* sacrifices, and so forth— which have been previously introduced as purified by being subordinate members (*aṅga*) of devotion— are the subject at hand, [the passage] is intended as an injunction for the practice of devotion known as meditation (*dhyāna*), which consists of the application of the mind (*manoyoga*) as a subordinate factor of the aforementioned ritual acts; this is in accordance with other scriptural passages such as, "By means of this syllable 'Om', one should meditate upon the Supreme Person."
Because it is impossible for there to be a practice that is independent of karma; for even though the preceding statement— "Having known Him thus with the mind and the heart,

the wise man does not meet death again"— declares that knowledge in the form of devotion is the means to the fruit, one must accept that it is this very same [knowledge] which is here enjoined along with its mantra.
Because there is no sublation [of this]. Furthermore: "Thus constantly engaging the self in yoga, the yogi, freed from taint, easily attains the touch of Brahman, which is infinite bliss.

Thus, regarding the word *yuñjan* in the *Gītā*: "The yogī who thus constantly yokes his self (*ātmānam*), meditating (*dhyāyan*), with a restrained mind, attains the peace that culminates in *nirvāṇa* and abides in Me" (*Gītā* 6.15). Here too, as in the verse: "Performing [action]... the yogī of restrained mind yokes the self (*ātmanā*) through yoga," the term *ātman* refers to the Blessed Lord.
In the phrase "one who yokes yoga," meaning one who performs the practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi-yoga*), and so forth— just as in the case of "one should yoke oneself"—

since it is possible for this to be directed toward the injunction for meditation (*dhyāna-vidhi*), such as "one should meditate upon the Blessed One," it cannot possibly be directed toward *prapatti* (self-surrender) in the form of self-offering; [therefore, the text continues] "having taken up the bow of the Upaniṣads..."
Having taken up the great weapon, the sharpened arrow, one should fix it, drawing the bow with a mind absorbed in that state;
know, O gentle one, that very syllable is the target.
The *praṇava* is the bow, the self is the arrow, and Brahman is said to be the target; it must be pierced by one who is undistracted.

Since, as in the aforementioned Vedic passages, it is more appropriate here too for "yuñjīta" (one should join) to have the purpose of enjoining meditation (*dhyāna*), even such Vedic statements as "One should join the self with the Brahman, the Friend" (*brahmaṇā tvām ahaṃ sakham*) and "One should join the self with *oṃ*" (*om ity ātmānaṃ yuñjīta*) do not directly enjoin *prapatti* (surrender) as a means to liberation, nor do they.

The scriptural statement, "Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the wisdom of Vedānta," should also be understood as being directed toward *prapatti* (surrender). Furthermore: "He who neither hates nor desires is known as a perpetual renunciant (*sannyāsī*). "The wise know the renunciation (*sannyāsa*) of desire-driven actions to be true renunciation.
"He who performs desire-driven action without depending on its fruit is both a renunciant and a yogi; he is not [merely] one who has abandoned all actions."

"One who is without fire and without ritual action," and so forth—in these and other statements from the *Gītā*, the term "renunciation" (*saṃnyāsa*) refers to the offering [of actions] to the Lord by means of abandoning the desire for fruits. (p. 220)

Since it has been stated that devotion is directed toward that very portion of the two-fold path of action (*karmayoga*)— consisting of the performance of duties prescribed for one’s caste and stage of life— that takes the form of abandoning desire and the like,
it is possible that even here in this scripture, the word "renunciation" (*saṃnyāsa*) refers to that same state in accordance with its corroboration by those [other texts].

Because it is impossible for [the text] to have surrender (*prapatti*) as its primary purport; furthermore, because of the designation [of the work] as the *Gītā* in the verse: "But renunciation, O mighty-armed one, is difficult to attain through lack of yoga; the sage disciplined in yoga, O Brahmin, attains [the goal] without delay. (Gītā 18.49).

This is because the word *yoga* in the phrase *śruti-siddha-nyāsa-yoga* must necessarily refer to *karma-yoga*; otherwise, the word *yoga* would be rendered meaningless. For it is said: "In this world, he is a sage and a Brahmin who is free from desire and anger."
Thus, because it is stated that the word *sannyāsa* has the same meaning as the word *muni* found in the Śruti;

and likewise, the term *sannyāsayoga* refers specifically to the yoga of action (*karmayoga*)— which consists of the performance of prescribed duties with the intention of dedicating them to the Lord, preceded by the renunciation of desire for fruits— and not at all to the surrender (*prapatti*).

Nor should it be argued that because the yoga of action lacks the status of being a direct means to liberation, the statement that "all those who possess the yoga of renunciation are liberated" is untenable as a description of its being a cause of liberation;
for the same fault applies to *prapatti* (surrender) as well, since there is likewise an absence of authoritative evidence establishing it as a direct cause of liberation.
"But renunciation, O mighty-armed one, is difficult to attain without yoga;

the sage disciplined in yoga, O Brahmin, attains the beginningless [Brahman] before long. In this passage, just as the yoga of action is shown to be a means to liberation through a gradual succession, so too in the present context...

For that [renunciation] is established as a limb of liberation in exactly that way. Alternatively, through the yoga of renunciation—that is, through the yoga of action—those whose *sattva* is purified become pure in their inner organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Therefore, such ascetics [are fit] for hearing [the scriptures] and so forth.

They become diligent in practice; and thus, by that knowledge born of the Vedānta—which consists of hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*)—they have well-ascertained and directly realized the object characterized as the lower Brahman. They are those for whom the meaning of the Vedāntic knowledge is well-ascertained (*vedāntavijñānasuniścitārthāḥ*).

Therefore, they are liberated from that [bondage], because it is logically established that immediate (aparokṣa) knowledge alone is the direct cause of liberation. This is because, as established by the logic of the fifth section (*pañcamādhikaraṇa*), the sequence based on the meaning (*ārtha-krama*) is more powerful than the scriptural sequence (*śrauta-krama*), just as in the cases of "He performs the *agnihotra* sacrifice" and "He cooks the gruel. Thus, [the sequence] "It is to be seen, it is to be heard, it is to be reflected upon... [is to be understood accordingly].

Furthermore, because there is another scriptural passage enjoining hearing and so forth with the aim of realization, stating "it is to be meditated upon" (*nididhyāsitavya*), and because the meaning we have stated is indeed the more logical one; for if the word *sannyāsa* were taken to refer to the fourth stage of life (*turīyāśrama*), then [the text] would contradict the statement: "These other [stages], among them, renunciation (*nyāsa*) alone surpassed them."

"One should renounce on that very day; on the very day one becomes dispassionate," so says the Śruti. Furthermore: "The fourth stage is renunciation (saṃnyāsa), which is characterized by the state called 'actionlessness' (niṣkriya).
There is no dharma whatsoever found in the world higher than that."
For even if one who is devoted to that [other path] should go there, his hand is not righteous.
Devotion to Me and dispassion are declared to be the qualification for this;
according to one's qualification, even a student may renounce.
Thus it is stated in the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
"My supreme delight indeed lies in the fourth stage, renunciation (saṃnyāsa).
It is certain that for those who have no eligibility for this [renunciation], there is no [eligibility] for ritual action (karman)."

Thus, in the *Brāhma Purāṇa*, because it establishes that devotion to the Blessed One is the qualification for dispassion (*virakti*), is the supreme among all means of attainment, and is the object of the Blessed One’s highest affection, it is in every respect untenable that such a person could be intent solely upon *prapatti*.

The statement from the *Gītā*, "all dharmas," also refers to the cessation of sin in the words, "I shall liberate you from all sins. The statement from the *Rāmāyaṇa*, "to him who has surrendered even once," refers to the granting of fearlessness in the words, "I grant fearlessness from all beings. And likewise, the statement from the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*, "so great is the distress [of the devotee]," also [refers to this].

The resolve for favorability [arises] from the cessation of fatigue, affliction, and so forth; thus, even according to the statement of the *Pāñcarātra*, because of the designation of the cited *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, it is established that *prapatti* is a cause of liberation only through a traditional succession (*paramparā*). Therefore, the phrase "thus constituted" also refers to the matter of this succession, in accordance with the cited authorities.
This must be explained. Therefore, it must be stated that the cited scriptural passages from the *Smṛti* have as their sole purport the surrender (*prapatti*) consisting of devotion (*bhakti*).

For this very reason, in the introduction to the verse beginning with "Having abandoned all duties" (*sarvadharmān parityajya*), Rāmānujācārya [explains it] as having the independent surrender (*svatantra-prapatti*) as its purport.
Having stated that there is a lack of natural consistency in the previous explanation, this verse is explained as being devoted to *aṅga-prapatti* (auxiliary surrender).
