For such indeed is the statement of the Bhāṣya: "Alternatively, because the yoga of devotion (*bhakti-yoga*) results in the attainment of a person who is exceedingly dear to the Lord and is completely liberated from all sins, its commencement [is now described]."

Observing that because opposing sins are infinite, they cannot be overcome by those dharmas of atonement performed within limited time— which would render one unfit for the yoga of mental devotion— the Blessed Lord spoke the words beginning with "Having abandoned all dharmas" in order to dispel the grief of the grieving Arjuna. In that regard:
It has been stated that devotion is indeed an ancillary limb (*aṅga*) of surrender (*prapatti*). Likewise:
"For this divine illusion (*māyā*) of Mine, consisting of the qualities (*guṇa*), is difficult to overcome.
"Those who take refuge in Me alone cross over this illusion.

In explaining this verse, [it is said]: "Having taken refuge in Me, the shelter of all the worlds, they cross over this illusion consisting of the qualities (guṇamayi). Having cast off illusion, they worship Me alone."
It has been stated that surrender (*prapatti*) is indeed a limb of devotion; yet, why is it that not all proponents of the worship of the Lord perform such surrender? To this, He says:
"The wicked, the deluded, the lowest of men, do not take refuge in Me."

In the introductory commentary to the verse beginning with "māyayāpahṛtajñānāḥ," it is stated that surrender (*prapatti*) is indeed a limb of devotion (*bhakti*); there is no disparity such as that surrender is the direct means to liberation for women, Śūdras, and others,
whereas for the three higher castes it is a means to liberation through the medium of devotion.
Because there is a lack of authoritative means of knowledge [for any other way],
the conviction that "He protects" and the remembrance that "He is my lamp"—
this constitutes taking refuge; through this alone is liberation attained, and not otherwise.

Thus, since we have stated even in the *Smṛti* that surrender (*prapatti*), which takes the form of seeking refuge, is a means to liberation only through the mediation of knowledge, devotion, and so forth— and because there is no dispute regarding the identity of our views on this matter—
it follows that it is appropriate to use the first person [in the grammatical construction] to express that surrender is not a direct means to liberation, just like knowledge.

Since there is no evidence that surrender (*prapatti*) is a direct means to liberation in the same way as devotion (*bhakti*), and since it has already been stated that there is evidence for its being an indirect means to liberation, it is illogical to treat the two as alternatives. Furthermore, regarding devotion— which, when accompanied by ritual action (*karma*), is to be practiced throughout one's life— and knowledge (*jñāna*):

Because there can be no option regarding *prapatti*, which is independent of ritual action (*karman*) and is to be performed all at once; for an option between what is weighty and what is light is never observed anywhere. Otherwise, [p.

Since it is only in *prapatti*, which is the easy means (*laghūpāya*), that the engagement of all people is logically possible, whereas engagement in *bhakti*, which is the difficult means (*gurūpāya*), is impossible for anyone; and because there exists a gradation among the fruits of the *agnihotra*,
*jyotiṣṭoma*, *darśapūrṇamāsa*, and other rites, [one engages] with a view toward those respective fruits.

This is because there is the possibility of engaging in various respective actions, and because of the disparity between them. Furthermore, the alternative arrangement (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*) regarding devotion (*bhakti*) and surrender (*prapatti*) does not concern those who are capable and those who are incapable. As it has been said:
"In the case of devotion and so forth, there is an absence of capability, a lack of certainty [regarding results], and an exclusion based on scripture."

The meaning of this passage is as follows: "But [the Lord] is incapable of wasting time; thus, by the power of destiny, the virtuous—encountering the four [means] through various combinations of one, two, three, and so forth—are heard to perform their respective duties and, free from doubt, attain liberation through the method of surrendering to the Lord of Śrī. In this context, *śakti* refers to the capacity for devotion (*bhakti*).

Knowledge, lack of patience for the delay of time, and [the other two]—when these four are combined, they constitute the range of eligibility [for *sannyāsa*]. In *prapatti*, however, the absence of these four constitutes eligibility.
This [absence] is fourfold through the removal of each one individually; it is sixteenfold through the removal of each pair; and it is fourfold through the removal of each triad.

Thus, there are five types [of eligibility] based on the complete cessation [of the other means]. Since the negation of the combination of *śakti* (devotion) and the others is uniform everywhere, one becomes eligible for *prapatti* upon the presence of each individual [means], the presence of every pair, the presence of every triad, or even the presence of all four. This is the form of *bhakti*.

For a seeker of liberation who is not qualified for other difficult means, there exists the qualification for the easy means consisting of *prapatti* (surrender). Nor should it be said that the statements teaching *prapatti* are not intended to convey its true nature;
rather, in accordance with the authoritative scriptural citations cited previously, *prapatti* is indeed a constituent part (*aṅga*) of *bhakti*, and not [the primary means].

Since it has been repeatedly stated that [the means] possesses the status of an independent proof, one should proceed in any way possible without contradicting that [status], even regarding the restriction— that there is an absence of power (*śakti*) in devotion (*bhakti*) and so forth— which is established solely within one's own tradition (p. 225).
Because it is not determinable [as such], the second position—that surrender (*prapatti*) is the direct means to liberation—is untenable.

For this very reason, the third position is also not valid; for we ourselves accept that, like ritual action (*karman*) and so forth, it leads to liberation through a mediated sequence as an auxiliary to immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*), and since you have stated that other positions are untenable according to the aforementioned reasoning, [the third remains unestablished].

Since it must be stated that surrender (*prapatti*) is the cause of liberation precisely through the medium of devotion (*bhakti*), there is no inconsistency whatsoever regarding our agreement that surrender is a means to liberation.
(In the manuscript, there is a break in the text here.)
[The soul] enters the Lord Nārāyaṇa, according to the Śruti, Smṛti, Sūtra, and traditional designations beginning with "by seeing [Him]" (darśanāt).
Furthermore, because of the co-occurrence of the word denoting the fruit— namely, "the knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (brahmavid āpnoti param)—
and because it is more logical that verbal roots such as *vid*, which denote knowledge, refer specifically to immediate, direct realization (*aparokṣajñāna*).

In the passage, "It is to be seen, it is to be known, it is to be reflected upon, it is to be meditated upon," since there is an absence of any authoritative means of knowledge that could establish these words denoting "knowledge" as being direct means for attaining liberation,
they must be understood as referring to devotion known as meditation (*dhyāna*), with the vision of Brahman as its objective.

Since hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) are enjoined as constituent parts (*aṅga*), meditative absorption is connected to the fruit by means of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of its capacity, as seen in the scriptural statement, "He sees the partless one while meditating";

furthermore, by means of the context (*prakaraṇa*), meditative absorption possesses the status of the primary member (*aṅgin*), while hearing and reflection possess the status of its subordinate members (*aṅga*).
Because of the established rule: even though "it is to be seen" follows immediately after "it is to be heard," hearing is weaker than [the means of knowledge such as] inference and so forth.
Is this not indeed improper? For once the injunction for study— namely,

"One should study one's own Veda"— is established as meaning "one should effect the study with the aim of the knowledge of the meaning," it follows that a person would, of their own accord, seek out a teacher who perceives reality for the purpose of determining that meaning.

The statement "one should hear" (*śrotavya*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*), because one engages in hearing, which consists in grasping the meaning of the sentence as established by logic. Likewise, the statement "one should reflect" (*mantavya*) is also a restatement, because reflection— which consists in establishing that the subject matter taught by scripture and the teacher is logical within one's own self— is already required for the purpose of stabilizing what has been heard.
Since the duty of *nididhyāsana*— which consists in the nature of an uninterrupted stream of memory— is not obtained from any other source,

the injunction is simply "one should meditate" (*nididhyāsita*). Therefore, the claim that the phrase "it is to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*) enjoins for meditation a state of similarity to perception in the form of a more distinct manifestation is untenable.

If it is argued that, even in your own view, the injunction of another auxiliary is accepted in the Sūtra "Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa, having become learned... (*tasmād brāhmaṇaḥ pāṇḍityaṃ nirvidya...*) and in such passages, because an injunction for the repeated contemplation of Brahman following the comprehension of the meaning taught [in scripture] is admitted;

There is no obstacle to enjoining those very two—[hearing and reflection]—which are denoted by the terms *śravaṇa* and *manana*, by means of the terms *śrotavya* (should be heard) and *mantavya* (should be reflected upon). Furthermore, for a person who has already performed hearing and reflection, because the Lord is exceedingly favorable toward him, he engages in the contemplation of that favorable object out of natural inclination (*rāga*) alone; therefore, [the term] *nididhyāsitavya* [is used].

This too cannot be established as an injunction; for in that case, since there is no evidence for enjoining qualities such as "uninterruptedness" when reflecting on what is already prompted by worldly desire (*rāga*), there is likewise no evidence for enjoining qualities such as "proceeding from the mouth of a guru" here [in the case of *nididhyāsana*]. Is the "clarity of manifestation" (*viśadatarāvabhāsatva*) of *nididhyāsana* the fact that its object possesses some additional particularity? Not the first [alternative], because [this would apply to] memory (*smṛti*).

Because it is impossible for [the cognition] to have an object greater than that experienced by one's own father (p. 227). Furthermore, is the experience that generates memory perceptual (*parokṣa*) or non-perceptual (*aparokṣa*)? Not the first.

If memory, which consists of meditation produced by indirect experience, were to possess as many objects as the indirect experience itself while also possessing additional objects, then its status as memory would be untenable; for this would violate the rule that memory is necessarily produced by a prior experience, since it would lack clarity in that specific respect.

This is because there is no prior experience of that object with a greater range than that [of the current cognition]. Nor is the latter [alternative] tenable, because experience [of Brahman] is not admitted;

otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that scriptural passages such as "it is to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*) would have to be taken in their primary sense. For this very reason, the latter is not possible: since a direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) whose object is Brahman cannot logically be a memory (*smṛti*), and furthermore, [the object] is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*).

Since meditation (*dhyāna*), which consists of memory (*smṛti*) whose nature is knowledge, lacks intrinsic clarity by itself, it cannot possess the quality of being "more clear" (*viśadatara*); otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence of prescribing that donkeys, *śūdras*, and others are non-white *brāhmaṇas*.
Therefore, devotion (*bhakti*), which consists of an uninterrupted stream of memory, is not a direct means to liberation. Not so.
Devotion (bhakti) is defined as a very firm affection toward the True One, preceded by knowledge of the greatness of that very devotion.

Regarding this, the Smṛti states: "Through that [devotion] comes liberation; Viṣṇu is pleased by devotion alone and not by anything else," and so forth. Devotion is superior to all other means of attainment; there is nothing like it anywhere.

Thus, from the statement cited in the *Anuvyākhyāna* on the section concerning meditation (*upāsanāpāda*): "Therefore, through knowledge and devotion, one should become intent upon the supreme human goal;
from devotion comes knowledge, from that comes devotion, from that comes vision, and from that, [the goal] itself."
From that comes liberation, and from that comes devotion; that very devotion is the embodiment of bliss.
The Lord, pleased by devotion, bestows untroubled knowledge.
In the same way, one who has attained this vision shall grant liberation by means of it;
"Neither by the Vedas, nor by austerity, nor by charity, nor by sacrifice [is this state attained]. (p. 228)
It is indeed possible to see Me in such a form as you have seen Me;
O Arjuna, it is possible to see Me in this way through unswerving devotion.
And because, in the statement cited in the *Anuvyākhyāna* on the *Jñānapāda*— “O scorcher of foes, [one must know] the Knower and the Seer in their true nature and enter [into them]”—
it is made known that [knowledge] is the direct means to liberation by way of producing extreme serenity; likewise, we also [regard] devotion in the form of direct experience [as such].

It is accepted that liberation is achieved through the gateway of the Lord’s grace. Furthermore, the previously mentioned devotion, being a means to the knowledge that is itself a means to supreme devotion, can be designated as having liberation as its fruit by virtue of being an indirect means. This is stated while setting aside all other [means].

It might be argued that the statement establishing [knowledge] as the direct means to liberation refers to supreme devotion (*paramabhakti*), and thus there is no contradiction; however, this cannot be maintained, because we ourselves accept this very point, and therefore our desired conclusion remains unrefuted. Furthermore, in your own system, it is stated: "Only one who knows Him thus, having seen Him, is liberated, and not by any other means."

By these and other such collections of cited statements, it is made known that the direct, immediate knowledge of Brahman alone is the means for liberation. Therefore, it must be explained how devotion can be established as a direct means for liberation.
Since it is accepted that among the means established for the qualified practitioner, supreme devotion alone is the direct means to liberation;
since the direct realization of the Archetype (bimba) is the cause of supreme devotion;
and since supreme devotion is the cause of supreme grace, which is designated as "supreme favor" (paramānugraha), there is primacy of the intermediate operation (avāntaravyāpāra).

By virtue of the intention [to speak], it is possible to designate *prasāda* (divine grace) as the direct means to liberation (*mokṣa*). And it has been stated in the *Sudhā*: "O Lord of Modaka, *prasāda* is to be attained solely through devotion to Him;
Viṣṇu attains satisfaction through devotion alone, and not by any other means whatsoever."
Because of this statement [p. 229]: "Devotion to the Supreme Lord (parameśvarabhakti) consists in the prior knowledge that He possesses infinite, limitless, and irreproachable auspicious qualities."

One who possesses many qualities superior to one's own self and possessions, whose continuous stream of love remains unobstructed even by thousands of obstacles, cannot attain that direct realization (sākṣātkāra) through mantras alone; and such direct realization is achievable only through the grace of the Lord. Furthermore, the Lord, whose nature is unmanifest, cannot be reached even by a thousand means.
For it is stated in the *Sudhā*: "It [Brahman] can be directly realized only through its grace.

Furthermore, the means for such realization is contemplation (*nididhyāsana*), which is accomplished by reflection (*manana*); reflection is accomplished by hearing (*śravaṇa*); and ritual action (*karman*) and so forth are the means for hearing and the other stages—such is the established method (*paddhati*). And thus, in this...

In the *Paddhati*, there is no inconsistency whatsoever regarding [the Lord] being a direct means to liberation. Now, one might object: "But then, 'knowing Him thus, upon seeing Him alone, one is released, and not by any other'—having obtained knowledge, one attains supreme peace;
it is through His grace born of that knowledge that one is thus released. For, without the grace of Nārāyaṇa, there is no liberation, nor indeed...

In this regard, devotion alone is the means to liberation by way of [attaining] grace; yet there is no contradiction with the scriptural statements that knowledge is its means, because in those contexts the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) indicates devotion (*bhakti*). As it is stated in the *Sudhā*: "It is called 'knowledge'..."

Thus, at the occasion of commenting on the *Anubhāṣya*, [it is stated] that in this scripture, wherever the knowledge of the five-fold awakening (*jñānapañcāvabodha*) alone is taught as the means to liberation (*mokṣasādhana*), [that passage] is intended to establish that very point. (p.

In each instance, by the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*), devotion (*bhakti*) is intended. Why is it indicated? Because it has been stated that devotion is a composite of knowledge of greatness and affection; therefore, knowledge is a part or a constituent portion of devotion. Thus, there exists the relationship of being a part and possessing a part. Alternatively, [it refers] to knowledge...

The attribute characterized by the accompaniment of affection (*sneha*) is called devotion (*bhakti*). And having cited the statement from the *Anubhāṣya*: "That which is a specific variety of knowledge itself is designated as devotion," he states another perspective in the *Sudhā*: "Of knowledge itself... [meaning] if there is a specific variety of knowledge itself that constitutes an attribute characterized by the accompaniment of affection, then that is the whole (*piṇḍa*).

This is what is meant by the term "devotion" (*bhakti*). Knowledge (*jñāna*) and affection (*sneha*) are two aspects of devotion; therein, one aspect serves as an indicator for the other. Thus, by means of *ajahallakṣaṇā* (non-exclusive indication), it is established that devotion itself is [the referent]. Therefore, that which is indicated by the word "knowledge" is precisely that which is denoted by the word "devotion."

Devotion alone is the direct means to liberation among the practices established for those possessing the requisite qualification; it is not merely that which resides in the scriptures. Through supreme devotion, one becomes intent on the goal of human life by means of both realized knowledge (*vijñāna*) and devotion. From devotion comes knowledge, from that comes devotion, from that comes vision, and from that, she [liberation]. From that...

"Liberation arises from that [devotion]; that very devotion is itself [the means], and grace is to be accomplished solely through that devotion. Moreover, this [grace] is not possible without the mantra of direct realization (sākṣātkāra)," and so forth—there is no contradiction with such statements from the *Bhāṣya-ṭīkā*, because even in the cited passages from the *Bhāṣya* and other texts, the term "knowledge" (*jñāna*) can be interpreted in a compatible manner. In that regard:

In the phrase "by means of knowledge and devotion," the word "knowledge" (*vijñāna*) refers only to a single aspect of that which consists of a continuous, unsurpassed flow of love directed toward the form of the Lord— who is endowed with manifold auspicious qualities and is worthy of one's own devotion.

And thus, when it is stated that liberation occurs through the grace of the two [means], namely the direct perception of the Blessed One characterized by manifold majesty, it follows that the previously mentioned devotion alone is the direct cause of liberation.

It is said that this constitutes the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). From that [means] comes vision, and from that, the direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) of the form of the Blessed One, who is distinguished by auspicious qualities and appropriate for oneself. The suffix *-tasi* is used in the sense of the locative case. The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "only.
Thus, it is only when vision exists that [the result] is possible, even if [the other factors] are present.

According to the principle that "duality does not exist," devotion (*bhakti*) is not established through mere affection alone; rather, it is established that liberation arises only from devotion in its form as the union of both [affection and knowledge], and that such devotion exists as knowledge. Furthermore, this [devotion] does not arise without the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of that [reality].

Even this statement regarding nectar (*sudhāvākya*) [states]: "Devotion is of the nature of a synthesis of knowledge and affection. This is because it has both knowledge and love as its material causes (*upādāna*), and not merely love alone;
thus, the phrase [concludes] that it is preceded by the knowledge of the Lord's infinite and faultless auspicious qualities.

The meaning is that [the knowledge] is preceded by the cognition of its being distinguished by qualities; this is the general direction. Therefore, those who know the tradition hold that there exists something distinguished by great majesty which is the cause of [liberation]. Or else, as in such passages as:
"Knowing Him thus, upon seeing Him alone, one is liberated, and not by any other means."
The various statements in the Śruti, Smṛti, Sūtras, Bhāṣyas, Ṭīkās, and so forth, according to the fitness of their respective qualified aspirants,

have as their sole purport that the direct realization of Brahman— characterized by many faultless and auspicious qualities suitable to oneself— is the means to liberation through supreme devotion and supreme grace; and thus, in this view:

By this, the primary sense of the previously cited statements from the Śruti, Smṛti, Sūtra, Bhāṣya, and Ṭīkā—such as "Upon seeing Him alone, one is liberated; He is not to be seen by another"—is upheld. And yet...

(232) It should not be argued that there is a contradiction because, while devotion alone has been declared by many authorities to be the immediate means to liberation— preceded by the negation of other means— it is likewise declared that direct realization (sākṣātkāra) is the means to liberation, preceded by the negation of others.

In this context, it is logical that the prohibitive statement intends to exclude any other means besides supreme devotion (*paramabhakti*) and supreme grace (*paramānugraha*). Alternatively, just as grace functions as the intermediate operation (*vyāpāra*) when devotion serves as the means, so too does direct realization function as the intermediate operation when devotion serves as the means.

In passages such as "he attains satisfaction through devotion" (*bhaktyā tuṣṭim abhyeti*), the capacity of devotion to produce grace is stated with the intention of emphasizing its status as the primary operation (*vyāpāra*), which consists in the negation of other means distinct from the intermediate function of the sentence negating others. In such cases, however, when the instrument (*karaṇa*) is intended to be emphasized— as in [the statement regarding] direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) itself— [it is understood differently].

Thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever in stating that [the sense organ] produces clarity (*prasāda*). Or, for example, in such cases as "the non-defective sense organ," the sense organ is conventionally designated as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because of the intention to emphasize its status as the instrument (*karaṇa*). In such cases as "perception is the contact of the sense organ with a faultless object," the contact (*sannikarṣa*) is emphasized because of the intention to emphasize its status as the intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*).

In the view that direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*)—characterized by being the produced and the producer—is the instrument (*karaṇa*), it is possible for devotion (*bhakti*) to be the intermediate operation (*vyāpāra*), and for the word [denoting] devotion to be the operation; thus, there is no inconsistency. In this position, immediately after the direct knowledge...
It must be accepted that there exists another entity in the form of devotion (*bhakti*), whose nature consists of both knowledge and affection.
Furthermore, an extraordinary intensity of love arises preceded by the perception of the Supreme’s manifold wonders. Likewise, [there is] infinite auspiciousness...

When a specific form of the Lord suitable for one's capacity is perceived by the mind, there arises an intense flow of love accompanied by the knowledge of His supreme beauty and the excellence of His majesty.
In this view, the statement in the *Sudhā*— "preceded by knowledge characterized by auspiciousness"— is [to be understood].
The meaning is simply that [the practice] is preceded by knowledge of the majesty known as "quality-qualified quality" (guṇatvaviśiṣṭaguṇa). But this is not the case;

for in the *Anuvyākhyānasudhā*, it is stated: "Because knowledge is a constituent part of devotion (*bhakti*), in this scripture, wherever the status of knowledge as a means to liberation is mentioned, there the word 'knowledge' signifies devotion."

It should not be argued that [this view] contradicts [the scripture] because, by stating through the passage beginning with "it is perceived" (*lakṣyate*) that the immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) regarding Brahman—which serves as the means to liberation—is not distinct from devotion (*bhakti*), [such a claim would conflict with the following]. In the first position, the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers to a cognition whose object is solely the excellence of the majesty consisting of auspicious qualities; therefore, [of that...]

Even though devotion (*bhakti*) is included [within knowledge], in the second alternative (*pakṣa*), since the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) signifies the immediate realization (*aparokṣajñāna*) of Brahman as qualified by auspicious qualities suitable for oneself, there is no contradiction in its being the cause of devotion, because that [realization] is not itself included within devotion. For this very reason, it is said: "Liberation [comes] from the gods when they are pleased by devotion"; such are its qualities.

Thus, in the *Anubhāṣyasudhā*, by the passage beginning with "devotion is indeed the knowledge of qualities," it is stated that the mere knowledge of the majesty known as the "qualities" (*guṇa*) is the very meaning of the word "devotion" (*bhakti*). For this very reason, in certain scriptures, the knowledge of the majesty of the qualities and so forth is declared to be a means to liberation (*mokṣa*). It is said:
There is nothing inconsistent in the statement that the words of the *Bhāṣya*, the *Anubhāṣya*, the *Sudhā*, and so forth, are intended to convey both [meanings].

This might indeed be the case, provided that direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) of Brahman were established; however, it is not so, because there is a lack of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that very point. To explain: regarding the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman—is it...?
[The knowledge] is produced by the Vedanta; or produced by the external senses such as the eyes; or produced by the mind; or produced by an inferential mark (liṅga);
or produced by meditation. Not the first, because the directness (aparokṣa) of verbal knowledge is not admitted. Not the second, because [it is said]: "Not by the eye..."

This is because it would contradict such scriptural passages as, "It is not grasped by speech," and so forth. Nor should it be argued that the scope of the eye and other senses is extended when conjoined with the practice of yoga and the [scriptural] prohibitions; for we observe that even when the external senses have ceased their activity, one established in yoga attains the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman. Thus, the prohibition [of sensory perception]...

The first [alternative] is untenable because it is impossible for the eyes and other senses to have as their objects things such as *dharma* when they are not assisted by yoga, meditative resolve (*praṇidhāna*), and so forth. Nor is the third [alternative] tenable; for since the mind lacks independence regarding external objects, and since its own validity is not intrinsic due to its dependence on other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it would follow that *dharma* and the like are objects of mental direct perception (*mānasasākṣātkāra*), which would result in the impossibility of their being beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). It is not...

The fourth [alternative] is not tenable, because it contradicts scripture which states that [the Lord] is neither the senses nor inference. Nor is the last [alternative] correct, because direct realization cannot occur through meditation alone; otherwise, it would follow as an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that one could realize Him even by meditating on *dharma*. Therefore, if you argue that the identity between devotion (*bhakti*) and direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), as accepted by both ourselves and you, is untenable— [The response: This is not so. It is established that the Lord is perceived through the senses, for He is the object of the sense of sight, as stated in the *Śruti*: "He who is seen by the eye. Furthermore, there is no contradiction with scripture regarding the claim that He is not perceived by inference, for that refers to His essential nature (*svarūpa*). As for the objection that realization cannot arise from meditation, this is not a fault; for we maintain that the realization of the Lord arises from meditation upon Him, just as the realization of *dharma* arises from meditation upon it. Thus, there is no inconsistency in our position.

To this it is replied: since you accept the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) produced by yoga, there is no obstacle for us as well in accepting the direct realization produced by the yoga of meditation (*dhyāna-yoga*). For this very reason, the Vedāntācāryas state in the *Sarvārthasiddhi*: "The perception of those such as ourselves is twofold: sensory perception (*indriya-pratyakṣa*)..."
And there is the perception of yogis (*yogipratyakṣa*). Among these, the perception of yogis arises from the distinction between the superior and the non-superior.

In that state of union (*yuktāvasthā*), although it is produced by the external senses, its objects are restricted by the desire to know (*bubhutsā*) and so forth, and it is established solely through scripture (*āgama*). It is only the perception of the creator of the world (*jagatkartṛ*) arising from the power of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) that has been rejected.
In the *Śāstrayonitvādhikaraṇa*, the Bhāṣya states: "From Me come memory, knowledge, and its removal" (p.
Regarding this, [the commentary] explains: "Knowledge is the ascertainment of an object not produced by yoga, which is based on the senses or logical marks."

This is because the commentators have explicitly stated that yogic perception exists; this is also the case in the *Śatadūṣaṇī* within the section refuting verbal testimony as perception. As for the statement in the *Bhāṣya* regarding its having a form identical to direct perception (*darśana*), that refers specifically to the constant recollection (*dhruvānusmṛti*) which is the means to liberation, and not otherwise.

The yogic perception that has become the fruit of dharma-vigour is being negated; for all of that is heard in such passages as, "By means of dharma-vigour, you shall see [Brahman] as one sees a calf," and so forth. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Sudhā*:
"Because it is accepted that meditation (*nididhyāsana*), which consists of one-pointedness of mind, is the means for attaining immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*)."
"It is seen by the highest intellect, but it is to be perceived by the mind alone; having known Him thus with the mind and the heart,

and then with the purified mind, one beholds the Self by means of the self within the self and finds contentment therein"— such are the Śruti and Smṛti texts [referring to] the mind supported by the yoga of meditation (*dhyāna-yoga*), which consists of focused one-pointedness (*citraikāgrya*).
Since there is no contradiction between us— given that [the scripture] establishes that these are the means for attaining immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*)—

and because the mind, meditation, and yoga are designated as instruments either by intending to emphasize their intermediate operation in some cases or by intending to emphasize the subject (*dharmin*) itself in others, it follows that the mind, assisted by the dharma of yoga...

Since you yourself have accepted, according to the reasoning already stated, that the direct realization of Brahman through the senses—which is of the nature of experience—is of the form of devotion (*bhakti*), and since we have asserted its very nature as devotion, there is no inconsistency whatsoever here;
for there is no dispute regarding its being the direct cause of liberation. Thus, everything is beyond reproach.
Thus ends the *Bhaktiprapattyaikyaprakāśa* (The Illumination of the Unity of Devotion and Surrender).

But even so, is it not the case that liberation is indeed the attainment of the bliss of Brahman? In your view, however, liberation is the experience of one's own bliss. Thus, because of this contradiction between the two positions— (p.
If it is asked how there can be oneness [between the individual soul and Brahman], we reply as follows:
The scriptural statements regarding the experience of the bliss of Brahman do not refer to it in its primary sense;
rather, it is established that liberation is the primary experience of the individual soul (*jīva*). This is the repetition of the phrase "the experience of the bliss of Brahman."

The term "liberation" (mukti) is carried over [from the previous context]. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "they proceed with this meaning. Thus, scriptural passages such as "For having obtained this very essence (rasa), he becomes blissful," and so forth, proceed with the meaning that liberation for the individual soul (jīva) is the experience of the bliss that is the very nature of Brahman in its primary sense. However...

The meaning is that I am establishing that the experience of the bliss of the soul's own nature (*jīvasvarūpa*) constitutes the primary liberation (*mukti*) of the soul; for it is as follows: what is this "bliss of Brahman"? Is it the bliss that is the object of enjoyment for Brahman, or the bliss of which Brahman is the owner? Even in the first case, is the bliss enjoyed by Brahman non-different from Brahman?

Or is it non-different from Brahman? Not the first, because in your view, you do not admit that Brahman is the enjoyer of its own essential bliss (*svarūpānanda*); for the relationship between enjoyer and enjoyed is pervaded by difference.

Even if that [enjoyment] were possible through the admission of "particularity" (*viśeṣa*), our [position of] identity would still be established, since Brahman would in some way be enjoying that [bliss].

This is because it is untenable for that [world] to be the object of enjoyment for individual souls; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of liberated souls becoming non-different from Brahman.

Furthermore, since Indra, Arjuna, Saundari, and others accept the oneness of consciousness precisely through the mutual experience of each other's happiness, the proof for such experience is the oneness of consciousness itself, and nothing else.

Because of this statement. Furthermore, if one were to experience Brahman—which is by nature a single essence of knowledge and bliss—by isolating bliss alone, it would follow that the nature of Brahman possesses parts (*sāvayavatva*).
Nor is it the case that Brahman itself, whose nature is a single essence of knowledge and bliss, is experienced by the individual soul (*jīva*) in such a manner.
The experience of such Brahman alone is the experience of the bliss of Brahman;
it must be stated that this alone is the liberation of the individual soul (jīva).
For if liberation were merely the knowledge consisting of both indirect and direct experience regarding Brahman,

it would follow that the individual soul (jīva) would possess liberation even during the state of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra). Nor can it be argued that the individual soul lacks direct experience during the state of transmigratory existence.
Since there is an absence of indirect experience during the state of liberation, if liberation were defined solely as the direct realization of Brahman,

the statement that "liberation is the experience of the bliss of Brahman" would not be primary. Furthermore, according to such scriptural texts as "Having seen Him alone, one is liberated, and not by any other," even during the state of worldly existence—

Because it has been stated that [this state] exists through the direct realization of Brahman, and because the *Nāradīya Purāṇa* prohibits the enjoyment of the nature of Brahman by saying: "Neither these gods— Brahmā, Īśāna, Dāya, and the others— attain that state which is indeed absolute liberation (*kaivalya*)."

The very nature of Brahman—which is beyond the reach of speech and mind, endowed with greatness such as being undivided by space, time, and so forth—is experienced by the individual soul (jīva), which is limited in power, omniscient, and atomic; those who say that this alone is liberation are the venerable great ones who proclaim the supreme transcendence of Śrīmannārāyaṇa. Therefore—

The first [position]—that liberation is the experience of the bliss whose nature is Brahman—is not primary. Nor is the second position—that liberation is the experience of a bliss distinct from Brahman which is to be enjoyed by Brahman—tenable, because it cannot withstand critical analysis. For instance, is that [bliss] a property unique to Brahman, or is it a property belonging to something else? It cannot be the first, because [the bliss] would then be a property of a single entity, Brahman.

If that bliss which is the exclusive object of enjoyment for Brahman were to become an object of enjoyment for the individual soul (*jīva*), the aforementioned defect of non-difference (*abheda*) would remain as it was. For, according to such scriptural passages as, "He who knows the bliss of Brahman, from which words turn back along with the mind, having failed to reach it," [it is established] that [Brahman] is indeed the enjoyer of bliss, which is a quality beyond the range of speech and mind.

Because it possesses the unique characteristic of Brahman; for in the state of saṃsāra, since its natural difference has not ceased, a non-difference caused by adjuncts (*aupādhika*) produced through identification is impossible. Even during saṃsāra...

Otherwise, one would fall into the Advaita position that there is an innate non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman. As it is said: "Just as water rained upon a mountain flows away in various directions, so too, perceiving the attributes (*dharma*) as distinct, one follows after them alone."
Because it has been stated in such scriptural passages as these that there is no difference between the attributes of Brahman and Brahman itself:
"There is nowhere any happiness superior to or even equal to liberation,
except for the great bliss of Viṣṇu, which transcends the reach of speech and mind."
Thus it is stated in other Purāṇas. Furthermore, since liberation is defined as the experience of bliss that is non-different from the bliss of the Blessed Lord, [it is said]:
"Brahman is consciousness and bliss"; "He understood that Brahman is bliss";
"Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite"; and "That which shines forth is the immortal, whose form is bliss."
He who possesses the fragrance of the bliss of the true body, whose splendor is knowledge, whose supreme prowess is ever-present,
who is the knowledge of knowledge, the bliss of bliss— he is Viṣṇu, the supreme, the imperishable.

Because such Vedic passages as "Bliss is the very nature of Brahman" reveal that bliss is nothing other than the essential nature of Brahman; for it has been stated that the statements in scriptures such as "the bliss of Brahman" are justified by obtaining a specific distinction, just like the expressions "the head of Rāhu" or "the nature of a jar. Otherwise, [one would contradict texts such as] "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent," and "Being alone..."
"In the beginning, this was the Gentle One (saumya)—soundless, touchless, formless, and immutable; the Puruṣa known through the Upaniṣads.

From such scriptural passages, in order to maintain the primary sense of the texts, one would have to accept two Brahmans: one consisting of both being and non-being, and another that is inaccessible to mere words yet accessible through words alone.

Therefore, according to the principle that "the postulation of a property [is for the sake of] the comprehension of the object," since it is possible for all scriptural passages concerning bliss to have a single referent through the postulation of bliss as a specific property (dharma) alone,
the postulation of a bliss distinct from Brahman [is unnecessary].

(239) That this is the primary [meaning] has been established in detail in the *Dharmabhūtajñānaikyaprakāśa* and the *Guṇaguṇibhedaikya-prakāśa*. Let this suffice for the elaboration. For this very reason, the latter [alternative] is not [the case], because [it would imply] something other than that which has become a dharma.

If the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*) were the object of enjoyment for the individual soul (*jīva*), the fault of the resulting identity between the *jīva* and Brahman could not be avoided; furthermore, since it is impossible to define the bliss as having any attribute other than being the object of enjoyment for each respective [entity], its status as an attribute common to both is untenable. Therefore, liberation is not the experience of the bliss of Brahman, but rather [the attainment] of the *jīva*.
Liberation is indeed the experience of one's own bliss; however, just as a face reflected in a mirror—

being a reflection of Devadatta’s face— is metaphorically designated as "Devadatta’s face" because of its similarity to it, so too, since the individual soul (*jīva*) is a reflection of Brahman, the bliss of the individual soul is likewise a reflection of the bliss of Brahman.

Because of its similarity to that [Brahman], it is metaphorically designated as "the bliss of Brahman. Thus, the claim that the liberation of the individual soul (jīva) consists in either the experience of the bliss that is the very nature of Brahman or the experience of bliss as an attribute is not primary. As for what has been stated by someone else regarding the actual reality:

The unique fault of those who pride themselves on knowing the Rāmānuja school—which [claims] victory over the long-standing Vijayīndra and defeat at the hands of [Madhva]—is now stated regarding the Mādhva system:
"By whose knowledge the doctrine of that [school] shall become fit for rejection by the wise," and so forth; as for that which appears in the *Bhāṣya*...
And thus: "Because [the Self] exists as long as the body exists, there is no fault in that vision; for one who does not see [the Self] is necessarily [bound];

and for this very reason, the analogy is like the reflection of the sun and so forth. This and other such sūtras have been interpreted as being intended to establish the relationship between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman as that of the original object and its reflection. [This is supported by] citations from the *Bhāṣya*, *Anubhāṣya*, *Tattvaprakāśikā*, *Nyāyasudhā*, and the words of the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*.

The previous explanation is likewise incorrect. Is the individual soul (jīva) a reflection with adjuncts (sopādhika), or a reflection without adjuncts (nirupādhika)? It cannot be the first, as stated in the Sūtra: "And it is merely an appearance" (ābhāsa eva ca).
The reflection of the Lord is understood to be both with and without adjuncts (*upādhi*);
the individual soul (*jīva*) is without adjuncts, just as the sun is reflected in the waters of the senses.
This is because the *Paingī-śruti* declares that the reflection is without adjuncts; furthermore—

In the section beginning with "Because there is no rule regarding the unseen" (*adṛṣṭāniyamāt*), the *Tattvaprakāśikā* states that the scriptural denial of being a reflection refers to a reflection that is devoid of limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika-pratibimba*). This follows as a corollary; for this very reason, in the section beginning with "And therefore it is a comparison, like the sun and so forth" (*ata eva copamā sūryakādivat*), [the relationship] is established precisely through its difference, its dependence on that [source], and its similarity to it.

[The objection] "because [the soul's manifestation] depends on limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the sun and so forth," as stated in your own commentary, is not the second [position]. This is because, in the section concerning "that which is already known" (*jñāta eva*), it is established by reasoning that even for the eternal individual soul (*jīva*), birth is possible in relation to its limiting adjuncts; thus, they are born... of this [soul].

Regarding the Supreme Self, their "origination" is also proclaimed in relation to their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), as stated in the *Vyomasaṃhitā*. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of contradicting your own commentary; for even if one disregards that [text], the origination of the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth [is still taught]. Nor should it be argued that this "origination" is merely figurative, because [the soul's state] is dependent on another.

This is because it is intended here to speak of the arising of a specific attainment (*viśeṣalābha*); such is stated in the *Tattvaprakāśikā* on this point. Furthermore, as for the statement in the *Tattvaprakāśikā* under the section beginning "And because it exists as long as the self exists, there is no fault, since that is seen": the impermanence of that which has an origin is indeed certain, as it is observed in the case of jars and other such things.

The origination mentioned refers only to the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), and not to the individual soul (*jīva*). Therefore, how could it [the soul] be non-eternal? For when the limiting adjunct possesses origination, there is an invariable rule that the reflection also possesses origination; indeed, [this is] not observed [otherwise] regarding the limiting adjunct...

241) [This is] because it would contradict the demonstration of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the reflection has no beginning, and therefore the destruction of the individual soul (*jīva*) must indeed exist; [this is so] because the soul is without limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*).

Because the destruction of a reflection is impossible without the disappearance of the object (the *bimba*), its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), and their proximity; and because the proximity of the all-pervading object and its adjunct is eternal, the soul (*jīva*) is therefore without beginning or end. Consequently, there is no contradiction with the scriptural texts regarding the soul's beginningless and endless nature, since those [texts] refer to the adjunct. Nor does the impermanence of the adjunct imply the impermanence of the soul.

It should not be said that this results in the contingency of impermanence. Neither the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) nor the individual soul (*jīva*) is [the subject]; rather, we speak of the arising and destruction of that which is reflected. But if it is asked, "From where does all this [reflection] come? [we reply: It is from the external adjunct itself, conditioned by the elements (*dhātu*) and so forth. Why is this? Because it is eternal.
This has not been stated in the two Smṛti passages, nor elsewhere:
"The limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the individual soul (jīva) is said to be twofold—the essential nature and the external.
Upon liberation, the external adjunct perishes, while [the other remains]... * * *
"But when all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) have perished, how could there be a reflection?
And how could anyone ever strive for the destruction of the Self? Thus it is said: "And by means of [spiritual] methods, because of its eternity..."
Furthermore, because the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is [identical with] its own nature, there can be no postulation of a distinct limiting adjunct;
thus, it is impossible to establish that particular doctrine. This is also stated in the *Nyāyasudhā*, p.
One should also observe the contradiction in establishing this very point in the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*).

Thus, according to your own view, the soul’s status as either a reflection with attributes (*sopādhi-pratibimba*) or a reflection without attributes (*nirupādhi-pratibimba*) is beset by internal inconsistency; therefore, by the maxim that "what is contradictory cannot be established," [it is untenable].

The doctrine that the individual soul (*jīva*) is a reflection simply does not hold together. Thus, the entire system of Rāmānuja appears consistent only at first glance; for it is only through the power of your own intellect that [this is seen], as has been stated regarding the individual soul.

Whether it be a reflection with adjuncts (*sopādhi-pratibimba*) or a reflection without adjuncts (*nirupādhi-pratibimba*): it is not the first case, and so forth; we do not say that there is a reflection with adjuncts in that context. Nor should it be argued that this contradicts the Śruti which states, "The individual soul (*jīva*) is without adjuncts for the Lord (*īśa*), just as a rainbow is for the sun," because [in that case] there would be an absence of reflectivity.

The Śruti [states]: "With respect to the object of the reflection that is without limiting adjuncts... [and so on]. [The opponent's claim] that there is a contradiction with the Bhāṣya because [the reflection] is dependent on the sun and other objects of comparison through its distinctness, dependence on that [original], and similarity to it, is rooted in a failure to understand the secret of our established doctrine (*siddhānta*).
Among these, the first is the internal cause for the manifestation of the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*). As it is stated in the *Gītā-bhāṣya*:
"The individual soul, having attained the nature of consciousness, is a reflection of Keśava.
And this has been stated in the *Bhakti-pada* [of the *Bhāgavata-tātparya-nirṇaya*] and in the *Sudhā* commentary on the *Sūryakādivat* section of the *Brahma-sūtra*.

The internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth are external causes for the appearance of things contrary to their true nature (*svabhāva-viparītāvabhāsa*). Depending upon that, the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) is said to be twofold: its own essential form (*svarūpa*) and the external one.

And so forth. It is stated in the *Prathamaskandha-tātparya*: "The individual soul (*jīva*) perishes along with the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); because the adjunct is its very nature, there is no postulation of a separate adjunct.
Thus, the soul consists of nothing but the adjunct; and in this way, the adjunct takes the form of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is its own essential nature.

Now, it may be argued that, like a mirror or similar object, the adjunct (*upādhi*) serves as the locus of reflection in one part [of the Self]; and the state of being the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) for a single Jīva is established through the force of a specific relationship characterized by the nature of the prompted and the prompter. Thus, the internal organ is essentially identical with the Jīva’s own nature.

"In the commentary on the *Bhāṣya*, during the occasion of explaining [the passage], it is stated in the *Tattvaprakāśikā*: 'The meaning is that it becomes reflected (*pratiphalita*) due to the distinctions of the locus of reflection (*pratiphalanādhikaraṇa*), form, limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), time, middle, high, and so forth. In the *Tattvapradīpikā* as well, the meaning is that the state of being a reflection (*pratibimba*) and the state of being the possessor of the reflection (*pratibimbakaratva*) are attained."

Thus it has been said. In this way, there exists the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as the essential nature [of the individual]. Precisely with this intention, there is the statement that "the individual soul (*jīva*) is not a limiting adjunct of the Lord (*īśa*)," and so forth; for the limiting adjunct does not exist apart from that which is possessed of the adjunct (*upahita*). Rather, since even the adjunct itself becomes a reflection, [the individual soul] is thus a reflection reflected within that which is without a [further] adjunct.
Even the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is of the nature of one's own essence (*svarūpa*), is made to attain the state of being a reflection;

however, it is not [reflected] in a single part as in the case of a mirror and so forth. Thus, the statement concerning the absence of being a reflection conditioned by a distinct limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), or the statement concerning being a reflection without a limiting adjunct (*nirupādhi*), has that very [point] as its purport.

The Bhāṣya statement, "not because of dependence on adjuncts (*upādhi*) and so forth," is also intended for that very purpose. Therefore, there is some slight objection [to the view] that the individual soul (*jīva*) is a reflection with an adjunct. It is not the second [alternative]. For in the *Guṇasūtra-bhāṣya* on the section beginning with "only when known" (*jñāta eva*), it is stated: "Their origination is also taught in relation to the adjunct."

(244) The objection that "it would be contradictory" and so forth is incorrect, because the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), being subject to origination and destruction, is distinct from the soul; thus, it is accepted therein that there is no [real] difference [between souls] due to their limiting adjuncts. This is also the commentary on the *Bhāṣya*.

Because it is rooted in the thorough knowledge of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), for instance, in the section [of the Brahma-sūtras] beginning with "But it is known from scripture alone" (*jñota eva*), the term "limiting adjunct" (*upādhi*) does not refer to a limiting adjunct that causes the soul (*jīva*) to be a reflection;
rather, it refers to the body which possesses origination and serves as the basis for the conventional usage of "origination. For this very reason...

Since it follows that the individual soul (*jīva*) is also beginninglessly eternal, [the opponent argues: the soul arises from the Lord himself; for the *Kāṣāya* Śruti states, "These very conscious selves, having perished, enter the supreme light," and "They are never born, nor do they ever enter. Thus, the non-arising of the soul is logical; how could there be the arising of that which is beginninglessly eternal?
In the aphorism "Because [the objection] is applicable in the case of doubt," it is logical that origination occurs in relation to the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) consisting of the body;

for the *Vyomasaṃhitā* states: "The conscious selves, who are both eternal and non-eternal in relation to the Supreme Self, originate in dependence upon those adjuncts," because they possess a connection with a body subject to origination.

Since it has been established as a settled conclusion that the birth of the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed possible, the term "limiting adjunct" (*upādhi*) in that context is intended to mean specifically the limiting adjunct in the form of the body which acts as the cause. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Anuvyākhyāna*: "Individual souls are said to possess birth due to their connection with the body. In that [text],...

Because the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) in the form of a locus for reflection is not the subject under discussion, the conjunction with moist fuel (*ārdrendhana-saṃyoga*) is the limiting adjunct for the connection between fire and smoke; and "being produced by the cooking of vegetables" (*śākapākajatva*) is the limiting adjunct for [the inference of] blackness— since there is an absence of a locus for such a limiting adjunct in those cases— it is not the case that the soul (*jīva*) is merely beginningless.
It should not be said that "origination is primary and [the rest] would be mere metaphorical designation" (p.
because it is accepted in all cases that the attainment of specific qualities is entirely dependent on something else.

Since this has been established in exactly that manner in both the *Anuvyākhyāna* and the *Sudhā* in the section on *prakṛti*— namely, that "the attainment of particular states dependent on another constitutes transformation (*anyathābhāva*) through non-cessation"— therefore, with respect to the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) which is the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*).

Because it is reflected, it is logical that it possesses a reflection with an adjunct (*sopādhi-pratibimba*). Since there is an absence of reflection in something distinct from its own nature—such as in a mirror or other adjuncts—it is accepted [as having] a reflection without an adjunct (*nirupādhi-pratibimba*), because this must be postulated since the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would otherwise be inexplicable; and as for what was said:

As for the objection that there is a contradiction in establishing the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the section by stating "because it has become the very nature of the self" (*yāvadātmabhāvitvāt*), that is not so; for when the reflection is declared to have the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) as its cause, since the original object (*bimba*) is all-pervading and beginningless and endless, the connection with various beginningless karmas is not untenable, and thus there is no lack of authority in the scripture (*śruti*).
Because there is also no contradiction with the establishment of our own tenet (*siddhānta*).

[Objection: But then, since it has been stated that even a distinct limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)—in the passage beginning "the limiting adjunct of the individual soul (*jīva*) is twofold... and external"—serves as the locus for the reflection of the soul, how [is this so]?
It should not be said that [the objection] was stated with the intention that [the reflection] depends on distinct limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*);

for, since such limiting adjuncts consisting of the external and internal organs lack the status of being the substratum for the reflection of the subject (*dharmin*), the aforementioned fault does not arise.

It should not be said that there is an impossibility regarding your [proposed] usage; for even though the external and internal organs lack the status of being limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) as substrates for reflection—like a mirror and so forth—their status as limiting adjuncts and the corresponding usage are nonetheless possible by virtue of their being designated as the "individual soul" (*jīva*). External and internal...
Because the experiences of pleasure, pain, and so forth— along with their instruments and substrates— which culminate in grasping, are established by the experience of the living being (jīva).

Since the manifestation of such pleasure, pain, and so forth is seized by the destruction of its adventitious nature (*aupādhikatva*), that view is untenable. Because worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is not primary— being merely manifested and expanded by the unfolding of one's own cognition— an experience of liberation consisting of such bliss is also not primary.
Because everything belongs to Brahman, there is no dispute regarding our identity as we are His beloved; for this very reason,
we have attained union.

It should not be argued that because the experience of the bliss of one's own nature (*svarūpānanda*) is eternally established, it cannot be a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*). For even if it is eternal by its very nature, that objection remains equally applicable; [therefore, the goal is rather] the experience of the bliss of one's own nature as qualified by the cessation of bondage, which is achieved through knowledge, devotion, and so forth.

Even the experience of the bliss of Brahman, which is the goal to be accomplished through spiritual practice (*sādhana*), is— in a secondary sense— the experience of the bliss of the individual soul (*jīvānanda*); thus,
because it is an experience of the bliss of one's own essential nature (*svarūpasukha*), there is no defect whatsoever due to the identity of our respective views.
It is established that "all thought is auspicious.
May my gurus, beginning with the illustrious Ānandatīrtha, be pleased.
Thus [ends] the work of the illustrious Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya, who is independent in all philosophical systems...

In [this work] composed by one named Aiyaṇa—the son of Gopālācārya, who was the son of Śrī Vāṇāturairāmācārya; and who was a repository of the compassion of the venerable feet of Śrī Vasudhendratīrtha; and who possessed an exceptional proficiency in exposition and other sciences, being unlike any other, under the guidance of the venerable Mahānandatīrtha Bhagavatpādācārya.
The third chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Unity of Rāmānuja’s Doctrine," from the *Trimataikyaprakāśikā*. May it be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
And thus this book is completed.
May there be prosperity.
